n: Tyre was destroyed, in part, by Nabuchodonosor. Cyrus permitted all the captives of this, as well as of other countries, to return. --- Cethim; Cyrus, or rather Macedonia. Merchants come thence no longer.
Island. Tyre was originally surrounded with water. A communication with the land was made afterwards, Josue xix. 29. (Calmet) (Ezechiel xxvii.) (Worthington)

Nile. Hebrew Shichor, or "muddy water," designates that river, Josue xiii. 3. --- River. The overflowing of the Nile gave fertility to Egypt, insomuch that Tyre and other nations were supplied by it with corn.

Strength: people who sail. Septuagint, "but the strength....replied: I," &c. Sidon will not be concerned for the fall of her rival. She alleges that she has nothing to do with Tyre. That city would not allow that it was a colony of Sidon, ver. 12. (Calmet)
Seas. The rich Tyrians did so. (St. Jerome) --- Septuagint, "to Carthage." Hebrew Tharsis, in Cilicia. (Calmet) --- Hence Nabuchodonosor did not find a sufficient reward, Ezechiel xxix. 18.
Sojourn. Many fled, others were made captives.
Earth. The merchants were as rich as kings, or the latter sent their merchandise to Tyre, Ezechiel xxvii. 33.
Girdle, fortress; or rather, thou art naked, like a slave, chap. xx. 4.
Daughter; colony. (Calmet) --- Oppressed. Literally, "calumniated." (Haydock)
It. Hebrew adds, "for fishermen." It was formerly covered with water. (Eusebius, præp. ix.) --- Ruin. The fall of Babylon has been denounced, chap. xiii.

King Nabuchodonosor, whose two sons reigned but a short time. The captivity of the people of God began also the year of the world 3398, and ended the year of the world 3468, the first of Cyrus. --- Harlot. She shall be re-established, (Calmet) and shall invite people to her markets. (Sanchez) --- Before Cyrus, she had kings, but they were of small power. The city was become very rich, and well fortified, when Alexander [the Great] was stopped by it for seven months. See Ezechiel xxvi. 14. (Calmet) --- Tyre had rejoiced at the misfortunes of the Hebrews, and was punished by the like captivity. (Worthington)
Commit. Septuagint, "be the emporium for all." Great injustice prevailed formerly among merchants, so that it is represented as a dishonest calling. (Haydock)

Sanctified to the Lord. This alludes to the conversion of the Gentiles. (Challoner) --- Before, the Tyrians were great enemies to the Jews, 2 Esdras xiii. 16., and 1 Machabees v. 15. Our Saviour wrought a miracle in favour of one of this country, Matthew v. 22., and Zacharias viii. 20. (Calmet) --- Continuance. Literally, "old age." Aquila, "with changes of dress." (Haydock)

f: Commentary on Isaiah

The burden of Tyre. Howl, you ships of the sea, for the house is laid waste from which they were wont to come: from the land of Cethim it has been revealed to them. Be silent, you who dwell in the island, the merchandise of Sidon. The prophet Ezekiel sets forth more plainly and more fully both the overthrow of Tyre and the causes of the overthrow, saying: Son of man, because Tyre has said of Jerusalem: Aha, the gates of the peoples are broken, she has turned to me, I shall be filled, she is deserted. Therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against you, O Tyre, and I will cause many nations to come up against you, as the sea comes up in waves, and I will scatter the walls of Tyre, and destroy its towers, and I will scrape its dust from it (Ezek 26:2ff.). And who these many nations are, which will flood over Tyre like the surging sea, he teaches by name in what follows: Behold, I will bring upon Tyre Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon from the North, a king of kings, with horses and chariots and horsemen, and a great company and people. Your daughters that are in the field he will slay with the sword; and he will surround you with siegeworks, and will heap up a mound round about, and will raise the shield against you, and will set mantlets and battering rams against your walls, and will destroy your towers with his weapons, and the rest that follows to the end of the vision. For in another prophecy too, which is seen to be against the Egyptians, the same Scripture weaves in: Son of man, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has made his army serve a great service against Tyre: every head made bald, and every shoulder rubbed bare, and no wage has been paid to him, nor to his army, for Tyre (Ezek 29). By this he signifies that a mound was heaped up over a long time by the army of Babylon, so that he tried beforehand to do what Alexander did afterwards, joining the island to the mainland (Quintus Curtius, book 4). Just as, therefore, we have read above God's threats against Babylon and the Philistines, and Moab, and Egypt, and the Edomites and Ishmaelites, because they mocked the captivity of his people, so now too a prophecy is woven against Tyre, hostile and mocking at the overthrow of Jerusalem: that it too is to be destroyed by the same enemy. We have read the histories of the Greeks, and especially of those who describe the wars of the Assyrian nation; and there we find that after the captivity of Jerusalem the Palestinians, and the Arabs, and the Damascenes, and after them the Egyptians were overthrown. And that these nations, and Tyre above all, always attacked Israel and rejoiced at its overthrow, the prophet Amos explains at the opening of his volume (Amos 1), and the Psalmist, briefly singing praises to God, declares: O God, who will be like you? Do not keep silent, nor be restrained, O God. For behold, your enemies have made a noise: and those who hate you have lifted up the head. They have devised malicious counsel against your people, and have plotted against your holy ones. They have said: Come, and let us destroy them from being a nation, and let the name of Israel be remembered no more. For they have plotted with one mind, together they have made a covenant against you: the tents of the Edomites, and the Ishmaelites, Moab and the Hagarenes, Gebal and Ammon and Amalek, the foreigners with the inhabitants of Tyre (Ps 82 [83]:1ff.). From all these we learn that the weight of God's wrath came upon Tyre the harlot, who is described here under the figure of a prostitute, and in Ezekiel under the metaphor of a ship (Ezek 27). Howl, he says, you ships of the sea. For this we read in the Seventy of Carthage; and in the Hebrew there is THARSIS (תרשיש), about which I have argued both on the prophet Jonah and in a certain letter. And because Carthage is a colony of the Tyrians, we can in the present place take Tharsis not only as the sea in general but also as Carthage: that ships no longer come to Tyre from Africa, nor from the land of Cethim, which some interpret as Cyprus: for to this day there is among them the city of Citium, from which came Zeno too, the heresiarch of the Stoic sect; although many of our writers, and especially the beginning of Maccabees, consider Cethim to be the islands of Italy and Macedonia. For Scripture records this, that Alexander king of the Macedonians went out from the land of Cethim.
Commentary on Isaiah

The word of Tyre. What we thought about the burden, or word and taking up, of Tyre according to the Hebrews, we have said above in the book of the historical explanation of the ten Visions. Now we shall run briefly through the whole prophecy against Tyre according to the ἀναγωγὴν and the edition of the Seventy. Tyre is called SOR (צר) in the Hebrew tongue, and is rendered into our speech as distress. Every soul, then, that is taken up with vices and evil thoughts can be called sor.

Howl, you ships of Carthage, for they have perished, and shall come no more. From the land of the Kittim she has been led captive. To whom are the inhabitants of the isle become like? The merchants of Phoenicia, crossing the sea in many waters, the seed of merchants like harvests brought in, the merchants of the nations. For Carthage, in the Hebrew is written THARSIS (תרשיש), which all have translated alike. And Tharsis means contemplation or searching out of joy. Kittim too, which in Hebrew is called CHETIM (כתים), means sea congealing; and for Phoenicia, Sidon is read among them. Those, then, are rebuked whom a throng of evil thoughts surrounds, and who, wishing, as the Apostle says, to become rich, fall into temptations and snares of the devil, and many harmful desires, which drag men down into the deep (1 Tim 6). And they are told that they must howl, knowing that all the trading of this world will perish, and the contemplation of joy and gladness be turned into mourning and tears. For this sea can be sailed no longer, but all things will freeze; and the colonies of the Tyrians will be led captive to punishment.
Letter 2.3

Still, it was when humanity was in this state that the Word—the Son—came to seek and to find that which was lost. Even before he came, he tried to restrain us from such foolishness, crying out, "Don't be like the horse and the mule which have no understanding and whose mouth must be held in with bit and bridle." And because his own people were careless and acted as the wicked did, Isaiah, praying in the Spirit said, "You are to me like merchants of Phoenicia."
Commentary on Isaiah

And in naming it an island he does not lie: for afterwards it was made part of the mainland by Nebuchadnezzar or by Alexander, when many mounds were heaped up in the narrow strait for its capture. He also calls it the merchandise of Sidon, in keeping with the following line, in which he says: Be ashamed, O Sidon. For the histories relate that Tyre is a colony of Sidon.
Commentary on Isaiah

Those crossing the sea have filled you; in many waters the seed of the Nile, the harvest of the river is its produce. That Tyre delights in trade and is the emporium of the whole world, both present times prove and Ezekiel describes at length. And that merchants cross the seas in carrying their goods, there is no one who doubts; nor does the city itself have such great wealth from the land of its own region, which is very narrow and hemmed in by the borders of Galilee and of Damascus, as it has from the shipping of goods.
Commentary on Isaiah

For those who dwell in this isle are like no others than merchants, or carriers, who are carried about by every wind of doctrine and pass from one vice to another. And we dwell in an isle as long as we are beaten by the temptations of this world, and on every side our isle and little boat is struck by the waves of the sea. Now the merchants of this isle are from Sidon, which means huntress, and in which dwell very many hunters, of whom it is written: He will deliver you from the snare of the hunters (Ps 90 [91]:3). And in another place the saint rejoices that he has been delivered from their snares, saying: Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters (Ps 123 [124]:7).
Commentary on Isaiah

The whole Nile and the fertility of Egypt pour into Tyre from close at hand. For Nile, which we read among the Hebrews as SIOR (שיחר), the Seventy and Theodotion interpreted merchants; this word means turbid, and by this signifies the waters of the Nile, as Jeremiah testifies: What have you to do with Egypt, that you should drink the waters of Geon? (Jer 2:18): for which in the Hebrew there is Sior, that is, turbid.
Commentary on Isaiah

And all the merchants of the nations are compared to crops which quickly wither, or to the harvests of the river, which have their rain not from heaven but from the earth; and therefore they will perish with the nations. Where we read the seed of merchants, in the Hebrew is written the seed of sior, by which the Nile is understood, because it has turbid waters with which the crops of Egypt are watered.
The Six Days of Creation 4.4.19

If all our acts and deeds depend on the fates acquired at our birth and not on principles of morality, why are laws established and statutes promulgated by which punishment is meted out to the wicked and security bestowed on the innocent?… Why does the farmer toil and not rather wait until it is time to convey into his storehouses the produce for which he has not labored, relying on the prerogatives of his birth? If he was destined by birth to be endowed with wealth without the expenditure of labor, he should undoubtedly wait until the earth brings forth fruit spontaneously without seed. If such were the case, he should not sink his ploughshare into the earth or put his hands on the curved scythe or undergo the expense of harvesting the grapes. Rather, the wine would without effort flow plenteously into his stock of jars. Without effort, too, he would let the wild olive berry exude its oil without the labor of grafting upon the trunk of the olive tree. In the same way a merchant who travels over the wide seas would not be in dread of the perils that threaten his own life, for it is within his power, because of a certain destiny allotted to him at birth, to come without labor into a wealth of treasure.But this is far from the accepted opinion. As a matter of fact, the farmer cleaves the earth "with deep-driven plough"; "stripped he ploughs, stripped he sows"; stripped in the glowing "heat he thrashes on the floor the parched ears." The merchant, impatient when the east winds are blowing, ploughs the sea often when the course is unsafe. Insolent and rash men such as these are condemned by the prophet, who says, "Be ashamed, O Sidon, the sea speaks." That is to say, if dangers do not move you, then shame can check and modesty confound you. "Be ashamed, O Sidon," in which there is no place for virtue, no care for safety, no young men exercised in arms and ready to fight in defense of their country. They are anxiously and entirely preoccupied with gain and the benefits derived from commerce.
On Elijah and Fasting 19.71

Therefore, after being so often ploughed by returning merchants, "Be ashamed, O Sidon, has said the sea." This is the voice of the fatigued element, as it were, saying, "Be ashamed, Sidon"; that is: Merchant, you accuse my waves although you yourself are more restless than they. Blush indeed for shame since you are not disturbed by peril. More modest are the winds than your desires. They have their rests; never do your cravings for gain take holiday. Even when the weather is quiet, never are your ships quiet. The water is churned under the oar when it is at rest from the blast. "I have not been in labor," it says, "nor have I reared, nor have I nourished up young men." Why do they disquiet me whom I do not know, whom I do not acknowledge?
Commentary on Isaiah

Be ashamed, O Sidon: for the sea has spoken, the strength of the sea, saying: I have not travailed, and I have not brought forth, and I have not nourished young men, nor brought up virgins. I said above that Tyre is a colony of the Sidonians. Hear, then, O mother, all the seas crying out together against your daughter, and in a manner uttering a voice, though by nature they cannot speak: In vain have I brought riches together; to no purpose have I gathered wealth from the whole world into Tyre: she that was rich, she that was luxurious, and once rejoiced in a multitude of peoples, in which a throng of mortals was born, a troop of children, swarms of youth, whose streets rang with the games of virgins and infants, of young men and girls, has now been reduced to solitude. It is customary to make προσωποποιΐας out of mute things.
Commentary on Isaiah

Be ashamed, O Sidon, said the sea; and the strength of the sea said: I have not travailed, nor brought forth, nor nourished young men, nor brought up virgins. And when it is heard in Egypt, pain shall seize them over Tyre. The sea of this world, in which dwell small animals with great, and the dragon which God formed to be mocked, seeing that those who had formerly been taken by the demons have been taken by the hunters of Christ, who hunt from every mountain and hill, speaks to the opposing power of the hunters, which Sidon means, and says to it: Be ashamed, O Sidon; for I have not travailed nor brought forth, nor nourished the young men taken by you, nor brought up the virgins whose folly is condemned in the Gospel (Matt 25). For my travail and childbearing, and my nourishing and bringing up of virgins, have been blotted out by the travail of the Apostles of Christ, one of whom said: My little children, of whom I travail again until Christ be formed in you (Gal 4:19). And: I gave you milk to drink, not solid food (1 Cor 3:2). And again: I wish to present you all as a chaste virgin to Christ (2 Cor 11).
Pastoral Care, Part 3, Chapter 28

Sidon is brought to shame, as it were, by the voice of the sea, when the life of one who is fortified and supposedly steadfast is reprobated in comparison with the lives of those who are worldly and are being tossed about in this world. For often there are those who, returning to the Lord after their sins of the flesh, evince themselves the more zealous in doing good works, as they realize they were worthy of condemnation for their deeds. And often certain people who persevere in preserving the integrity of the flesh, on perceiving that they have less to deplore, think to themselves that the innocence of their lives is sufficient and do not arouse themselves by zealously striving to be fervent in spirit.
Morals on the Book of Job, Preface to Book 1, Section 5

Divine Providence has compassed us about and cut off all excuse. All openings to people's equivocating arts are in every way closed. A Gentile, one without the law, is brought forward to confound the iniquity of those that are under the law; which is well and summarily shown by the prophet, when he says, "Be ashamed, O Sidon, says the sea." For in Sidon we have a figure of the steadfastness of those settled upon the foundation of the law, and in the sea of the life of the Gentiles. Accordingly, "Be ashamed, O Sidon, says the sea," because the life of those under the law is convicted by the life of Gentiles, and the conduct of people in a state of religion is put to confusion by the conduct of those living in the world, so long as the first do not, even under vows, observe what they hear enjoined in precepts. The latter by their manner of life keep those ways so that they are not in any wise bound by legal enactments.
Commentary on Isaiah

When it has been heard in Egypt, they will grieve when they hear of Tyre. This is plain: that the Egyptians, after they have heard that a most mighty and neighboring nation has been destroyed by a long siege, know that destruction is drawing near to them too.
Commentary on Isaiah

When Egypt hears this, which in Hebrew is called MESRAIM (מצרים), which means ἐκθλίβουσα, that is, afflicting and constraining, it too will be terrified, understanding that it too will suffer the same things that Tyre has suffered. And while this is referred to all vices, it can also be perceived in the diversity of the heresies, when, one heresy being taken, another trembles, and in the confusion of one the other perceives that it is to be taken. And as it is said of Sodom: For if the signs had been done in them which were done in Capernaum, they would have remained until this day; and it is added: But it shall be more tolerable for Sodom in the day of judgment than for you: so we learn of Tyre and Sidon, the Savior saying: But it shall be lighter for Tyre and Sidon in the day of judgment than for that city (Matt 11:21ff.). Hence too the Canaanite woman, who understood that her daughter, that is, her soul, was grievously vexed by a demon, is said to have come out of the borders of Tyre and Sidon to pray to Christ. For she could not otherwise have gone to meet the Savior, unless she had left the borders of Tyre and Sidon.
Commentary on Isaiah

Go to Carthage; howl, you who dwell in this isle. Is not this your disgrace from the beginning, before she was delivered up? Her feet shall lead her far off to sojourn. What follows, Her feet shall lead her far off to sojourn, has been added from the Hebrew, and is marked beforehand with an asterisk, that is, with shining stars. O Tyrians, you who dwell in distress and abide in an isle, exposed on every side to the waves of temptations, depart from it, and go to Carthage, that is, Tharsis, and hasten to true joy, mourning your old sins and the ancient disgrace which you either inflicted on others or suffered from them. And I command this because you see Tyre, your city, about to move from its seats and purpose to other borders, when, having laid aside their old error, they have bowed their necks to the Gospel of the Savior; so that those who formerly dwelt in distress may depart far off and become sojourners and dwellers in the teaching of the Lord the Savior.
Commentary on Isaiah

Cross the seas, howl, you who dwell in the island. Again, for sea and Tharsis the Seventy translated Carthage. We read in the histories of the Assyrians that the besieged Tyrians, when they saw no hope of escape, embarked on ships and fled to Carthage, or to other islands of the Ionian and Aegean sea. Hence too it is said in Ezekiel: No wage has been paid to him, nor to his army, for Tyre (Ezek 29): because all the wealth of the city had been carried away, and all the nobles had left it empty.
Commentary on Isaiah

Is not this yours, which gloried from the days of old in its antiquity? He convicts Tyre of pride, because it gloried in the antiquity of its founding and did not look to God, but, recalling the names of its fathers, thought itself eternal.

Its own feet will lead it far away to sojourn abroad. He means those who had remained in the city and were led captive to Babylon.
Commentary on Isaiah

Who has devised this against Tyre, once crowned? Read Ezekiel again (Ezek 27), and you will learn from the lament over its prince how great the glory of Tyre was. He calls it crowned because, as a king among a great multitude of men raises his head adorned with a diadem, so Tyre, gleaming and lofty in riches, and shining with gold and gems and silk and purple, was esteemed a queen among all nations.

Whose merchants are princes, its traders the renowned of the earth. We marvel that the envoy of Pyrrhus once said of the city of Rome: I have seen a city of kings. Behold, long before those times the merchants and traders of Tyre are described as princes and renowned men: so that by this the greatness of its opulence is shown, since a merchant of Tyre could be a king in the other's words.
Commentary on Isaiah

Who has purposed these things against Tyre? Is she less, or does she not prevail? Her merchants are princes of Canaan, the renowned of the earth. The Lord Sabaoth has purposed to dissolve all the insolence of those who glory, and to dishonour all that is renowned upon the earth. The word Canaan has been added from the edition of Theodotion; for it Aquila translated merchants. The Holy Spirit therefore asks, or rather by the question affirms, that the Lord has purposed these things against the princes of Tyre, whose whole industry is to seek wealth by trading. And as in the Gospel we read of dealers in pearls (Matt 13), who, having sold all, long to buy one pearl, and who surely are to be called renowned merchants, not of earth but of heaven, so, on the contrary, the merchants of Tyre, that is, of tribulation and distress, are to be called the renowned of the earth, because whatever they do looks to the earth; and princes of Canaan, which means tossed about and shaken. For they do not set their feet upon the rock, nor can it be said of them, The rock is a refuge for the hedgehogs (Ps 39 [40]; 103 [104]:18), or for the hares; but rather they endure what the righteous man almost suffered: But my feet were almost moved, my steps had well nigh slipped (Ps 72 [73]:2).
Commentary on Isaiah

The Lord of hosts has devised this, to pull down the pride of all glory, and to bring into ignominy all the renowned of the earth. Because above, in the manner of one asking, he had said: Who has devised this against Tyre, once crowned?, now he himself answers: It is not that the threads of the fates have been spun thus, as fools think; it is not that the wheel of fortune has run; but it has been accomplished by the judgment of God and by his will, who resists the proud and gives grace to the humble (Jas 4); and he reminds the arrogant of their condition, so that through misery they may learn the power of him whose clemency they had refused to feel through his benefits.
Commentary on Isaiah

The Lord of hosts, then, purposed this counsel: to dissolve the most wicked bonds of the merchants, or rather to scatter the compacted injury through which all who are subject to Tyre grow proud. And as for what he added, and to dishonour all that is glorious upon the earth, the Lord is not the author of dishonour, but shows to be shameful what lies open to shame of itself. This indeed we read in Leviticus also concerning the Priests: With defilement he has defiled him (Lev 21), the priest, no doubt: not that he is the author of the defilement, but that he shows him to be defiled who formerly seemed clean to very many.
Commentary on Isaiah

Work your land; for ships no longer come from Carthage, and your hand no longer prevails, which provokes kings on the sea. The edition of the Seventy differs greatly in this place from the other translators and from the Hebrew itself; but let us pursue our purpose. Above he had said: Go to Carthage; howl, you who dwell in the isle. Now he says the opposite: since ships no longer come from Carthage, work your land. For it profited Tyre that the foreign ships perished, so that she is compelled to work her own land, of which it is said in the Proverbs: He who works his land shall be filled with bread (Prov 12:11): so that she may live not from the uncertain hazard of the waves and of shipwrecks, but from the fruits of her own work, of which it is sung in the psalms to the righteous man: You shall eat the labours of your hands (Ps 127 [128]:2). It is written in Hosea that the ways of the harlot were hedged by the Lord with thorns, so that she could not follow her lovers, in order that, driven by this necessity, she might return to her first husband. And this we often observe in the affairs of the world too: many who, through prosperity and abundance of all things, could not perceive the Lord, come to understand him through want, and are converted to the works of righteousness, after their hand no longer prevails to enjoy the felicity of this world, the hand which formerly provoked kings on the sea, or according to Symmachus, troubled them; kings whose heart is in the hand of God. And would that we too, scorning the trade of this sea, might work our land, and by no means wait for the ships of Carthage, or the ships of Tyre which used to go to Carthage, lest we be made subject to the power of the dragon who rules in the sea! But let us fix a steady step upon the land, or rather, hastening to heavenly things, let us work our land, so that, sowing here, we may reap there. Our hand too, which formerly was busied with the affairs of the world, and through power and felicity could move even kings, that is, the saints, from their standing, let it become feeble in the affairs of the sea, so that it may be strong in the work of its own land.
Commentary on Isaiah

Pass through your land like a river, daughter of the sea: there is no girdle for you any more. As, he says, a river, or, as the Hebrew has it more expressively, a stream, for it is called IOR (יאר), is easily crossed on foot, so you too, led into captivity, will pass through your land, O daughter of the sea, either because you are an island, or because it was written of you above: The sea has spoken, the strength of the sea: I have not travailed, and I have not brought forth. And what sense his next words have, there is no girdle for you any more, Symmachus teaches more openly: you will no longer be able to resist, that is, you will not have the strength, nor your loins girded for fighting, so as to be able to go out against your adversaries.
Commentary on Isaiah

The Lord Sabaoth has commanded concerning Canaan to destroy its strength, and they shall say: You shall no more do injury and iniquity to the virgin daughter of Sidon. That Tyre and Sidon are in the land of Canaan we have shown above also, setting forth the testimony of the Gospel, in which we read that the Canaanite woman, or Syrophoenician, came out of the borders of Tyre and Sidon and met the Lord the Savior. Now every soul that is set amid the waves of the world and is carried about by every wind of doctrine is to be called Canaan, which means as it were a tossing or a shaking. Hence it is said also to the adulterous old man: Seed of Canaan and not of Judah, beauty has deceived you (Dan 13). It profits Tyre and its distresses, then, that the Canaanite strength should perish, so that it may be said to its inhabitants that they can no longer do injuries and oppress by iniquity the virgin daughter of Sidon. Whoever is taken by the devil in the turmoil of various vices, and is delivered over to the outrages of shame, so as to pollute the body with pleasures and foulness, he is the son or daughter of Sidon. And this is to be known: that Sabaoth is not found in the Hebrew, and on the contrary virgin has been added from the Hebrew.
Commentary on Isaiah

He has stretched out his hand over the sea, he has troubled kingdoms. Who stretched out his hand? From the very tenor of the discourse there is no doubt that it is God, of whom he said above: The Lord of hosts has devised this, to pull down the pride of all glory. He stretched out his hand, then, over all the seas, signifying the world and the earth, and troubled all the nations, among which you too, O Tyre, were troubled; or else over the sea, in which you are properly situated.
Commentary on Isaiah

The Lord has given command against Canaan, to crush its strong ones. He shows what the sea is over which the Lord stretched out his hand, saying: He has given command against Canaan. For Tyre was founded in the land of Canaan. Read the Scriptures, and especially the Gospel (Mark 7), where the Syrophoenician woman, pleading for her daughter, comes out of the land of Canaan, and is called a Canaanite woman. And at the same time, because he had said: He has stretched out his hand, lest you should believe that the Lord works with limbs and by bodily function, he added, he has given command, so that for God to have done is to have commanded.
Commentary on Isaiah

And he said: You will no more glory, suffering calumny, O virgin daughter of Sidon; rise, cross over to Cethim: there too there will be no rest for you. God, who devised to pull down the pride of all glory, who gave command against Canaan to crush its strong ones, himself says: You will by no means glory any longer, nor trust in your own power. O virgin daughter of Sidon, that is, colony of the Sidonians, you will indeed flee in ships to the islands of the West, or to Cyprus, and the other lands of Macedonia and Greece; but there too, with God against you, you will not be able to find rest. Besides, everyone who is a wanderer and a stranger in the world, and of uncertain abode, is always in straits, continually in grief.
Commentary on Isaiah

If you go to the Kittim, not even there shall there be rest for you; and if to the land of the Chaldeans, it too has been laid waste by the Assyrians. Siim founded it; they set up its ramparts, they raised its tower: its wall has fallen. What follows has been added from the edition of Theodotion under asterisks: Siim founded it; they set up its ramparts; they raised its tower; and joined without asterisks: its wall has fallen. The Kittim are interpreted a stroke consummated or perfect; the Chaldeans in this place, as it were breasts; the Assyrians, reproving. The etymology of Siim we too have not been able to find, and the other translators rendered it by the very name with which it is written among the Hebrews. It is said, therefore, to Tyre, that although she strive to go to the Kittim and avoid the stroke of her distresses, she cannot find perfect rest even there. And again, if she desires to go to the Chaldeans and enjoy their fertility and the abundance of all things, she will find them too desolate, the Assyrians reproving their barrenness; just as the Apostle also delivered sinners to Satan (1 Tim 1), that they might learn not to blaspheme: they are delivered to the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved. And Siim laid the foundations of the Chaldeans, by whom I understand the most wicked demons, who raised both the ramparts and the proudest towers of the Chaldean city against the knowledge of the Lord. But all their building has fallen into ruins; for there follows, its wall has fallen. For unless the Lord builds the house, they have laboured in vain who build it (Ps 126 [127]:1). We often see in the world some men pass from one pursuit to another: for example, those who have fared badly in soldiering pass over to trade; and again advocates take up the arms of warriors. They change their occupation in order to change their misfortune; and nonetheless, by the dispensation of God, for those whom he deigns to save everything turns out contrary to their striving, so that through want and miseries they are compelled to have confidence not in themselves but in their Creator.
Commentary on Isaiah

Behold the land of the Chaldeans, such a people there was not: Assyria founded it for captivity; they carried away its mighty men, they undermined its houses, they made it a ruin. Howl, you ships of the sea, for your strength has been laid waste. Because he had said above: Its own feet will lead it far away to sojourn abroad; and again, Pass through your land like a river; and because the people of Tyre was twofold, those who had fled and crossed over to Cethim, and those who had remained in the city, he speaks to both. Of those who had fled he said above: Rise, cross over to Cethim, there too there will be no rest for you. Of those who had remained and were led into captivity: Behold, he says, the inhabitants of the land of the Chaldeans, whose power no peoples had before, and which was founded by the Assyrian, have carried away the mighty men of Tyre. They undermined not only the walls but all the dwellings of the city, and made it a ruin. Since, then, some have fled and others have been captured, howl, you ships, whether of the sea or of Carthage; for your mart and your colony has been destroyed. And at the same time consider how he has praised the Chaldeans. He did not say, such a people will not be hereafter: for the kingdom of the Romans is more powerful and harsher; but, there was not before. He who denied what went before conceded what follows.
On Elijah and Fasting 20.73-74

"Howl," he says—he repeats it—"O you ships of Carthage, for your strength is laid waste. And it shall come to pass in that day, Tyre shall be abandoned;" and below, "but after seventy years, Tyre shall be as the song of a harlot." Behold what words the prophet employs, and how he does not avoid the baseness of words of this kind. We ourselves sometimes avoid them, not because our tongue is more chaste than theirs, but our authority inferior. For very great is the force of words in the vivid exposition of such things, so that they who do not blush at their sins blush at least at the names of their sins. "Tyre shall be," he says, "as the song of a harlot." Beware, lest, when someone sees those dances being performed, and unseemly words being sung, he says, "Behold, Tyre has become the song of a harlot."
Commentary on Jonah, Chapter 1, Verse 3a

Furthermore, the Hebrews claim that Tarshish generally represents the sea, as in the psalms: "With a violent wind, you will destroy the ships of Tarshish," that is, the sea, and in Isaiah: "Wail, ships of Tarshish." I recall speaking about this several years ago in a letter to Marcella. The prophet, therefore, was not seeking to flee to a specific place, but he was hastening to continue toward wherever it was the sea would take him. Indeed, a terrified fugitive is rightly more interested in seizing the first opportunity to sail than he is in selecting a place of refuge. This also we are able to say: he who thought that "God is known in Judea" only and that "his name is great in Israel" only, once he felt him in the waves of the sea, confessed and said, "I am a Hebrew, and I fear the Lord of heaven who made the sea and the dry land." But if he made the sea and the dry land, how can you who abandoned the dry land think it possible to avoid the Creator of the sea in the midst of the sea? At the same time, the salvation and conversion of the sailors taught him that the great multitude at Nineveh could also be saved by confessing like he did.We are able to say of our Lord and Savior that he left his native homeland, assumed flesh and, in a manner of speaking, fled from heaven and came to Tarshish. That is, [he came] to the sea of this world, about which it is said elsewhere: "This is the sea, great and vast, where there are creatures without number and animals both small and large. Ships navigate there with the dragon whom you formed to play in it."
Commentary on Isaiah

Howl, you ships of Carthage, for your strength has perished. The ships of Carthage, that is, of Tharsis, are bidden to howl; for they have not, as above, perished or shall not come, but their strength has perished. For Tharsis, according to another interpretation, is rendered into our tongue consummation of six, or of gladness. Now we read that this world was made in six days, and according to the traditions of the Church it will afterwards be consummated. All the goods of this world, then, and the whole labour of mortals, are compared to the uncertain course of ships, because they will quickly perish, and all the strength of those who sail will be dissolved. Hence it is written in Solomon also: The wise man has gone up to strong cities, and has destroyed their fortifications (Prov 21:22). For whatever is composed by the art of the heretics, of worldly wisdom, and of opposing doctrines, the churchman destroys, and teaches that it is subject to his feet.
Commentary on Isaiah

And it shall come to pass in that day that Tyre shall be forsaken seventy years, as the time of one king, as the time of a man. And after seventy years Tyre shall be as the song of a harlot. Take a harp, go about, harlot city given over to forgetfulness. Play well on the harp, sing much, that you may be remembered. And after seventy years God will visit Tyre, and she shall be restored again to her former state; and her trade shall be with all the kingdoms of the world upon the face of the earth. And her trade and her hire shall be holy to the Lord; but it shall not be gathered for themselves, but for those who dwell before the Lord. All her trade, to eat and drink and be filled in common store, a memorial before the Lord. What is said, a memorial before the Lord, and upon the face of the earth, and as the time of a man, is not found in the Hebrew, but has been added in the Greek. Now Tyre, once straitened, is let go for seventy years, so that, the time of desolation fulfilled, she may turn her once harlot's song into the praises of God, and, taking up the harp, may have all its strings sounding in concord; so that, after she has played well in concord and sung much, there may be a remembrance before God of her who on account of fornication had been given over to forgetfulness; and that she may be restored to her former state, and have the riches of the kingdoms of the whole world, and that the wages of her labour may by no means be gathered for the Tyrians, but for those who dwell in the sight of the Lord, and that they may eat and drink and be filled with all the good things which have been brought together by the labour of all for the gladness of the banquet. The divine word exhorts Sidon and Tyre to repentance, and promises that her labours and wages are to be sanctified to the Lord. Who among sinners would not have hope of salvation, if only he sings well, and all the strings of the virtues, which once had been slackened, are tuned to the praises of the Lord? We read in Psalm 44 (45), which pertains especially to the union of the bridegroom and the bride, that is, to God the Savior and to the mysteries of the Church, that it is said among other things: The daughters of Tyre with gifts, the rich among the people shall entreat your face (Ps 44 [45]:13). And the bridegroom himself speaks again to the Tyrian bride: Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear; and forget your people and your father's house, for the king shall desire your beauty (ibid. 11, 12). Hence in the description of her beauty too it is added: The queen stood at your right hand, in a vesture of gold, surrounded with variety (ibid. 10). And again: All the glory of the king's daughter is within (ibid. 14). And if the king desired the beauty of the penitent Tyrian woman, who has the ornaments of various virtues, how much more shall her hire and her trade belong not to those who remain in Tyre but to those who dwell in the sight of the Lord! These, after they have done penance, shall hear from the Lord the Savior: Eat, my friends, and drink, and be inebriated, my dearly beloved (Song 5:1). And what it is to eat and drink and be filled with the common store of all the virtues, the faithful reader understands. That the temple was desolate for seventy years Jeremiah (Jer 29), Daniel (Dan 9) and Zechariah (Zech 7) teach. And in Ezekiel (Ezek 16) we read of Sodom that it shall be restored to its former state, and of Egypt that, after the desolation of the land of Egypt and the drying up of the seven rivers, it shall recover its old fertility. Now the number seven and seventy, which is made up either of single days or of seven decades, signifies a perfect and consummated repentance; so that Tyre rightly, the time of repentance fulfilled, returns to her former state. Of this harlot, I think, that saying too in the Proverbs of Solomon is signified in mystical speech: Do not heed a most wicked woman; for honey drips from the lips of a harlot woman, which for a short while fattens your throat, but afterwards you will find her more bitter than gall (Prov 5:2-4). For she looks out through the window of her house into the streets (Matt 7), because wide and spacious is the way that leads to death; and whatever foolish young man she sees (for the wise she does not dare to tempt) passing by the corners, those who have lost the straight line, she speaks to him in the darkness and in the gloom, and under the appearance of pleasures leads him like a victim to death. If she is converted, and sings well, and fulfils the time of years of perfect repentance, she shall eat and drink and be filled. Let Novatian hear this, and be silent.
Commentary on Isaiah

And it will come to pass in that day, you will be in oblivion, O Tyre, for seventy years, like the days of one king. From this place to the end of this prophecy prosperous things are announced to Tyre: that it ought to repent; that it is to be built again; that the overthrow of Tyre is to last only seventy years, the years during which the temple of God too was desolate: so that the city that mocked at the ruins of another should also match the time of that one's ruins. The seventy years of one king many think to be said of Nebuchadnezzar, the years during which the kingdom of the Assyrian nation continued in Jerusalem. Others think it is said in general: that he who has had a long time of reigning cannot go beyond seventy years.
Commentary on Isaiah

But after seventy years it will be for Tyre like the song of a harlot. Take a harp, go about the city, harlot given over to oblivion; sing well, repeat the song, that you may be remembered. Because you have committed fornication with very many nations, and your former lovers have despised you, desolate and naked and filthy with the squalor of captivity, take up the harp now, redouble your songs, go about the city, lament your former brothel, and wash away with tears the traces of your old error, so that you may call forth the mercy of God upon you.
Commentary on Isaiah

And it will come to pass after seventy years, the Lord will visit Tyre, and will bring it back to its wages, and again it will commit fornication with all the kingdoms of the earth upon the face of the earth. That all these things were fulfilled according to the history is shown by the concordant writings of the Greeks and Phoenicians: that after seventy years it was restored and returned to its former power, and became the mart of all the nations; and these, I think, are called fornications: so that, as he who commits fornication enters the brothel and pays the wage of debauchery, so the trader, flocking in from the whole world, has filled up the beauty of the city as of a harlot.
Commentary on Isaiah

And its merchandise and its wages will be sanctified to the Lord: they will not be hidden away nor laid up. For its merchandise will be for those who dwell before the Lord, that they may eat to the full and be clothed even to old age. We find that these things have not yet been done according to the history; unless perhaps it is to be thought that after the building of Jerusalem and the restoration of Tyre the cities were friendly to each other, and Tyre often sent gifts to the temple of God: as we read in Ezra too (Neh 13:16), that he drove off the Tyrians who were selling fish on the sabbath, and did not allow them to enter the city: and from this one item of trade one must judge of the rest as well. The Jews put off their vain hopes into the future, declaring that these things are to be fulfilled after the Antichrist, in the thousand years. Nor is it surprising if those invent such things who, having spurned the truth of Christ, are to receive the Antichrist, the instrument of the devil, since even judaizing Christians contend that these things were said of the blessedness of the thousand years. But I, just as in the vision of Babylon I understand the time of the consummation under the type of its overthrow, and in Egypt refer to the time of Christ the altar of the Lord set up when the idols were destroyed, and in the vision of Moab recognize the throne of the Savior set up in its land, and in the visions of Damascus and all the others have no doubt that they are mysteries of our own times, so also in the vision of Tyre, which is the last, I interpret it of the time of Christian felicity: that after it was built and recovered its former state, and every merchant entered its harbor according to the old custom, their merchandise and their labor too are dedicated to the Lord. Let us behold the Churches of Christ built in Tyre; let us consider the wealth of all, that it is not laid up nor treasured, but given to those who dwell before the Lord, who, serving the altar, partake of the altar (1 Cor 9). And the Tyrians minister, not for riches, nor for heaping up the wealth of the priests, but for supplying the necessities of life: so that, according to the Apostle, having food and clothing, we may be content with these (1 Tim 6). And note that he did not say that the merchandise and wages of Tyre sanctified to the Lord are to be given to those who dwell in Jerusalem, as the Jews think, but to those who are before the Lord, who serve him. For so too the Lord has ordained, that those who preach the Gospel should live by the Gospel (1 Cor 9). And to serve the Lord and to dwell before him is a matter not of place but of merit.

n: Earth. After the ten preceding threats, the prophet denounces destruction to the whole world, (Worthington) at the day of judgment; though he may also allude to the desolation of the promised land, as our Saviour joins both in the same prediction, Matthew xxiv. (Calmet)
Priest. All distinctions shall be disregarded. (Worthington) --- When Jerusalem was taken, all became captives.
Weakened: Joakim, &c., are made prisoners. The greatest monarchs must come before God's tribunal.

Sin. Towards the end of the world iniquity will abound, and men shall rage against each other, Matthew xxiv. (Worthington) --- They will also feel the effects of sin. --- Mad: abandoned to their passions, (Deuteronomy xxviii. 28.) excepting only the elect. (Menochius) --- Few. The Chaldeans permitted only a few of the poorest sort to remain, 2 Paralipomenon xxix. 10.
The drink. Hebrew shecar, "palm wine."
Vanity. Jerusalem, (Calmet) or any other city, will be all in confusion. (Haydock) --- In, as was the case in times of mourning, Jeremias ix. 21. (Calmet)
Sea. The few elect (ver. 13.) being rescued from the misery of the world, shall praise God. (Haydock) --- They are exhorted to lift up their heads, Luke xxi. 28. (Menochius)

Instruction. The Church is like an island, compared with the rest of the world; or it preaches the gospel to all nations, and to the islands, like Great Britain. (Worthington) --- Apostolic men are required to preach incessantly to all sorts of people. Hebrew, "in light;" or Pagnin, "in vales." (Menochius)
I said. The prophet, or any other, may speak thus in the latter days. (Calmet) --- Myself. I cannot recount what horrid pains I beheld. (St. Jerome) (Menochius) (2 Corinthians xii. 4.)
Snare. He alludes to the methods of taking wild beasts, Job xviii. 11. --- Opened, as they were in the days of Noe[Noah]. (Calmet) --- All sorts of misery hang over us.
Night, unexpectedly, (Haydock) and with the utmost speed. (Calmet)

High. The stars, which in many places of the Scripture are so called. Some commentators explain that these words here signify the demons of the air. (Challoner) --- The apostate angels will be judged, 1 Corinthians vi. 3., and Matthew xxiv. 29.

Visited. Hence Origen (Prin. iii. 6., &c.) took occasion to assert, that the damned would one day be released, though the Scripture so often declares the contrary. The prophet speaks of the future liberation of the Jews; (Calmet) or he intimates that after many days, yea throughout eternity, the reprobate will still be punished. (Menochius)
Blush: be turned into blood, Joel ii. 10. Dreadful calamities shall ensue, to usher in the great day of judgment. (Calmet)

f: Commentary on Isaiah

Behold, the Lord will scatter the earth, and will lay it bare, and will afflict its face, and will disperse its inhabitants; and as the people is, so will the priest be; and as the servant, so his master; as the handmaid, so her mistress; as the buyer, so he who sells; as the lender, so he who receives the loan; as he who demands repayment, so he who owes. With scattering the earth will be scattered, and with plundering it will be despoiled: for the Lord has spoken this word. After the particular rebuke of the individual nations, Judea, Babylon, the Philistines, Moab, Damascus, Israel, Egypt, the desert of the sea, Edom and Arabia, the valley of vision, and at the last Tyre, in the explanation of which we have said what we could, the prophetic discourse now describes what the whole world is going to suffer at the consummation, and the prophecy is by no means about the individual nations, but about all of them alike. And first, what torments the impious are going to suffer; and how, according to the Gospel and the Apostle, heaven and earth and the fashion of this world pass away (Matt 24; 1 Cor 7), and sinners are led down into hell (Ps 30 [31]), of whom it is written: They shall go into the lowest parts of the earth, they shall be delivered into the hands of the sword, they shall be the portions of foxes (Ps 62 [63]:10). Then, because according to the quality of their merits there are many mansions with the Father, it is told how the saints are caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and are to be with him always (John 14; 1 Thess 4). For the earth scattered, the Seventy translated the world corrupted; and for its face afflicted, that is, the earth's, the same translated, and he will uncover its face, so that the dead may come forth from their tombs; or he will lay it bare, so that all its works may be brought out into public view, and its inhabitants be dispersed into different places, destined for rewards or for punishments.
Commentary on Isaiah

Then there will be no difference between noble and base, priest and layman, servant and master, handmaid and mistress, rich and poor, the lender and him who is pressed by debt, buyer and seller. For all will stand on equal terms before the judgment seat of Christ, and there will be no respect of persons with God (Rom 14; Col 3). Of this Job too speaks in almost the same words: The small and the great are there, and the servant who does not fear his master (Job 3:19). And the Savior in the Gospel, to whom all judgment has been committed, bears witness in full discourse.
Forty Gospel Homilies, Homily 17

We are put as guards in the vineyards, but we do not cultivate our own. When we are involved with external affairs, we neglect to watch over our own activities. I think that God suffers greater outrage from no one, dearly beloved, than from priests. Those he has placed to reprove others he sees giving an example of wickedness in their own lives. We who ought to have restrained sin, ourselves commit it. More seriously, priests who ought to give of their own possessions frequently plunder the goods of others. If they see others living humbly and chastely, they often make fun of them. Consider what will become of the flocks when wolves become shepherds! They undertake to guard the flock and are not afraid to waylay the Lord's flock.We do not seek to gain souls; we devote ourselves daily to our own pursuits, we attend to earthly matters, we strive for human praise with all our will. From being set over others we have greater freedom to do anything we like, and so we turn the ministry we have received into an occasion for display. We abandon God's cause, and we devote ourselves to earthly business; we accept a place of holiness and involve ourselves in earthly deeds. What is written in Hosea is truly fulfilled in us: "And so it will be, like people, like priest."
Pastoral Care, Part 2, Chapter 7

And this indeed is what the Lord, in the wrath of just retribution, menaced through the prophet, saying, "And there shall be like people, like priest." For the priest is as the people, when one who bears a spiritual office acts as do others who are still under judgment with regard to their carnal pursuits.
Forty Gospel Homilies, Homily 17

What is written has surely been fulfilled in us: And it shall be, as with the people, so with the priest. For the priest does not differ from the people when by no merit of his own does he transcend the common conduct.
Commentary on Isaiah

The earth, therefore, will be scattered, and all earthly works will be reduced to nothing, so that, the image of the χοϊκοῦ having been abolished, the image of the heavenly may remain. For the first man was from the earth, earthly, and the second from heaven, heavenly: as is the earthly, such also are the earthly; and as is the heavenly, such also are the heavenly; so that, as we have borne the image of the earthly, we may bear also the image of the heavenly (1 Cor 15:47-49). Hence the same Apostle says: Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God (ibid., 50). Not that, as the heretics say, the nature of bodies perishes, but that this corruptible puts on incorruption, and this mortal puts on immortality. And all these things will come to pass, because what is to come the Lord has spoken through the prophets.
Commentary on Isaiah

The earth has mourned and has wasted away, and has been weakened; the world has wasted away, the height of the people of the earth has been weakened, and the earth has been slain by its inhabitants. LXX: The earth has mourned, the world has been corrupted, the lofty of the earth have mourned, but the earth has acted impiously because of its inhabitants. God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble (Jas 4:6). Hence the first sentence is against those who are lofty on the earth, that all things which are now strong may be weakened because of those who have mingled blood with blood, and, in the manner of the blood of Abel, have made the gore of the slain cry out to God (Gen 4).
Commentary on Isaiah

Because they have transgressed the law, they have changed the ordinance, they have broken the everlasting covenant. Because of this a curse will devour the earth, and its inhabitants will sin; therefore its tillers will go mad, and few men will be left. LXX: Because they have transgressed the law, they have changed the precepts, the eternal testament. Because of this a curse will devour the earth, because its inhabitants have sinned; therefore the inhabitants of the earth will be poor, and few men will be left. Let the Jews hear, who boast that they alone have received the law of the Lord, that first all the nations and the whole world received the natural law, and that the law was given afterwards through Moses for this reason, because the first law had been broken. Of it the Apostle speaks: For when the Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature the things that are of the law, these, not having the law, are a law to themselves: who show the work of the law written in their hearts (Rom 2:14). Those, then, who have kept these laws will obtain rewards; but those who have neglected them will endure what the prophetic discourse now threatens.
Commentary on Isaiah

And as in the beginning God blessed every creature that he had made (Gen 1), so at the consummation of the world he will curse those who are earthly, and who were not sojourners but inhabitants of the earth, and sinned in it; who, forgetting their condition, have raged against one another in mutual fury. And few will remain who have the heavenly image; or, according to the Seventy, the inhabitants of the earth will be poor, because they have lost their spiritual riches.
Commentary on Isaiah

The vintage has mourned, the vine has been weakened, all who were glad of heart have groaned. The joy of the timbrels has ceased, the sound of those who rejoice has been stilled, the sweetness of the harp has fallen silent; they shall not drink wine with song, the drink will be bitter to those who drink it. The city of vanity has been crushed, every house has been shut, with no one entering. There will be an outcry over wine in the streets; all gladness has been forsaken, the joy of the earth has been carried away. And desolation has been left in the city, and calamity will overwhelm the gates: for these things will be in the midst of the earth, in the midst of the peoples. At the consummation of the world, the remembrance of past delights will be the matter of torments. Hence also that rich man clothed in purple at his banquet, who had received his good things in his life, lifting up his eyes from hell, sees Lazarus at rest (Luke 16). And the Lord, rebuking the rich, the luxurious and those who laugh, says in the Gospel: Woe to you rich, for you have received your consolation. Woe to you who are now filled, for you shall hunger. Woe to you who now laugh, for you shall mourn and weep (ibid., 24, 25). When, therefore, the resurrection of the dead has come, and the day of judgment has arrived, then will mourn the wine and the vintage of which Moses speaks: Their vine is of the vine of Sodom, and their shoot of Gomorrah. Their grape is a grape of gall, their cluster is one of bitterness. Their wine is the fury of dragons, and the incurable fury of asps (Deut 32:33). Then every drink, or, as it is said in Hebrew, sicera, that is, drunkenness, which overturns the state of the mind and does not allow men to keep watch, will be changed into bitterness: it counterfeits honey for a time to those who use it, and in the end is found more bitter than gall. Then all the sweetness of those who rejoice, and the sound of timbrels and harp, will be turned into lamentation and groaning. Let us press this testimony upon those who at banquets are wanton not only with gluttony and drunkenness but also with their ears, so that through all the senses the strength of the soul grows soft.
Commentary on Isaiah

The city of vanity will be crushed, or every city, or the spiritual Babylon, which sits clothed in purple upon seven hills, whose punishments we read in the Apocalypse of John (Rev 18). And he did well to say the city of vanity. For if it is said of heaven and earth and of all things that are earthly: Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity (Eccl 1:2), how much more must this be said of one city, which is a small part of the whole world! Then the houses whose ceilings are now gilded, and whose walls, while the poor die of cold without roof or hut, are clothed with veneers of marble and shine with the gleam of sawn ivory, will remain empty.
Commentary on Isaiah

There will be an outcry in the streets over wine, not in the strait and narrow way that leads to life, but in the broad and spacious one that leads to death (Matt 7): over the wine and drunkenness of the error of those who have slept their sleep, and all the men of riches have found nothing in their hands (Ps 75 [76]). For the joy of the earth has been carried away into heaven, and desolation has been left in the once most crowded city, and the calamity of its inhabitants will overwhelm the gates of the busy streets, through which the throngs of the peoples used to stream in.
Commentary on Isaiah

According to the Seventy, all that we have understood of the saints can be referred to the impious: that when the vintage is finished, then they cry out, set in punishments. But those who have escaped the number of the impious rejoice in the glory of the Lord, and the waters of the peoples of this world are troubled.
Commentary on Isaiah
And that we might know plainly that the destruction of the whole world is being announced, he added: These things will be in the midst of the earth, in the midst of the nations, or of the peoples.
Commentary on Isaiah

As if a few olives that are left were shaken from the olive tree, and the grape clusters when the vintage is finished. These will lift up their voice and give praise; when the Lord has been glorified, they will neigh from the sea: therefore glorify the Lord in teachings, in the islands of the sea the name of the Lord God of Israel. How far the translation of the Seventy differs in this place from the Hebrew truth, the following words will show. LXX: As if someone were to shake an olive tree, so they will shake them; and if the vintage ceases, these will cry out with clamor. But those who have been left upon the earth will rejoice together with the glory of the Lord; the water of the sea will be troubled; therefore the glory of the Lord will be in the islands of the sea, the name of the Lord will be glorious, of the Lord God of Israel. When few men have been left, when the curse has devoured the earth, and there is desolation in the city, and all these things have happened in the midst of the earth, in the midst of the peoples and nations, so great will be the fewness of the saints, of whom the Lord speaks in the Gospel: Many are called, but few chosen (Matt 20:16); and so violent the oppression of the righteous, that even the elect of God, if it were possible, would be tempted; and their fewness is compared to the very rare berries of olives, of which, when they have been shaken down and gathered, scarcely a few remain at the tops of the branches; and to the way that, when the vintage is finished, the poor, driven by need, are accustomed to go round the empty vines and gather a few grapes.
Commentary on Isaiah

These, then, who remain, and after the vintage and the pressing of the world have been able to escape the hands of the persecuting Antichrist, or the burning of the impending punishment, will lift up their voices on high and will praise God. When the Lord comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels, and they see him reigning in majesty, then they will neigh in the likeness of horses, exulting in the greatness of their joy, and they will neigh from the sea of this world.
Commentary on Isaiah

Therefore you who are now instructed in the Holy Scriptures, and know that such great joy and such great rewards are reserved for you, glorify the Lord in teachings, hearing that which is written: He who glories, let him glory in the Lord (2 Cor 10:17). Not at all in the land of Judea, but in the islands, that is, in the Churches of this sea and world, in which is blessed and praised the name of the Lord God of him who was once Israel, or, of the man who sees God.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 2:5.24

By "sea" he means the multitude of nations, and by "coastlands," perhaps, he means cities. All their inhabitants will "raise their voices" when the divine wrath comes upon them. But the majesty of Christ will somehow be in the sea, that is, in all those nations, and they will realize that it is through divine Providence that they are destroyed and annihilated. They are destroyed because their impiety provoked the Almighty God; hence they will reject their gods who are unable to help them. That is how the majesty of the Lord is celebrated. It is clear that the purpose of the prophecy is to point to the mystery of Christ and to remind about the coming salvation in him.… Now, when the preaching of the holy apostles, which leads the nations from the idolatry to the grace of Christ, is spread to the ends of the earth, then, he says, "they shall cry aloud from the sea," that is, all the nations of the world.
Commentary on Isaiah

From the ends of the earth we have heard praises, the glory of the Righteous One; and I said: My secret is mine, my secret is mine: woe is me. LXX: From the wings of the earth we have heard portents: hope for the righteous; and they will say ※ my mystery is mine ⁚. This, which is said, my mystery is mine, is not found in the Seventy, but has been added in the Greek from the translation of Theodotion. Again, for what they put as woe, so as to join it to the following verse, in the Hebrew is said OI LI (אוי לי), which properly means woe is me. Also for ends, which we have set down for the sake of explaining the sense more openly, the Hebrew has MECCHENAPH (מכנף), which means wing, not end. These, then, of whom it was said above: They will lift up their voice and give praise, when they have neighed from the sea, and have glorified the Lord in teachings, and have seen the name of the Lord God of Israel praised in the islands of the sea, then will sing with harmonious voice and say: From the wings of the earth, that is, from the prophets and from the saints of the Lord, who, having taken the wings of a dove, hasten to the kingdoms of the heavens, we have heard his praises proclaimed; and that the glory or hope of the Righteous One is not vain, but all things are fulfilled in deed. So, while the saints say these things, and neigh from the sea, and lift up their voice and give praise, the Prophet speaks to himself: When, he says, I had heard these things, and perceived that the prophecy of the Prophets was to be fulfilled in the overthrow of the world, I said to myself with the inward feeling of my heart: I cannot tell all that I see. My tongue cleaves to my throat, my voice is shut in by grief. Woe is me, what a train of punishments passes before my eyes! I see as present the things that are to come. But those err who think this must be understood as spoken in the person of God, not following the order of the matter. And I wonder in what sense, for psalms and praises, which in the Hebrew reads ZEMROTH (זמרות), the Seventy translated portents, unless perhaps it is a sign and a portent that, the people of the Jews being shut out, the once unbelieving multitude of the nations is saved.
Commentary on Isaiah

The transgressors have transgressed, and with the transgression of transgressors they have transgressed. Terror and the pit and the snare are upon you, who are an inhabitant of the earth; and it shall be that he who flees from the voice of terror shall fall into the pit, and he who extricates himself from the pit shall be held by the snare. LXX: Woe to the transgressors who transgress the law. Fear and the pit and the snare are upon you who inhabit the earth. And it shall be that he who flees fear shall fall into the pit, and he who comes out of the pit shall be caught by the snare. This is the cause of my mourning and groaning, on account of which I said a second time, my secret is mine, my secret is mine: because all have transgressed the law of God, and the Lord's punishment is by no means put off, nor is it foretold as future, but it is imminent, and holds the inhabitants of the earth captive. And when they think they have escaped, they will fall from one thing into another, and wherever they turn they will not evade the impending wrath of the Lord.
Commentary on Isaiah

For the floodgates from on high have been opened, and the foundations of the earth will be shaken. With breaking the earth will be broken, with crushing the earth will be crushed, with shaking the earth will be shaken. With tossing the earth will be tossed like a drunken man, and it will be removed like a tent of one night, and its iniquity will weigh it down, and it will fall, and will not add to rise again. Therefore no one will escape the terror and the snare and the pit of the Lord, because the floodgates from on high, or, as the Seventy translated more plainly, the windows of heaven have been opened, so that the Lord might look down upon all the sins of men, which before, because he did not punish them, he seemed to sinners not to know. But after he has seen all the works of mortals through the opened windows, the foundations of the earth have been shaken, according to what is written in another place of the gaze of God: Who looks upon the earth, and will make it tremble (Ps 103 [104]:32).
Commentary on Isaiah

Then the earth will be broken and crushed, and shaken and tossed in the likeness of a drunken man: not that the earth itself is reduced to dust and to nothing, but that all earthly things pass away, and another manner of life succeeds. And as a drunken man does not know what he is doing, but, his sinews growing dull with drunkenness, neither foot nor mind stands to its duty: so the whole earth, that is, all men who dwell on the earth, will be drunk with the greatness of the evils and the punishments, and will be stupefied at all that they see. And as a tent or pavilion of one night is moved from place to place, and the place of the former tent is abandoned by the traveler, so that no trace remains of the past lodging: so the fashion of this world will pass away, and the earth will be deserted which has been weighed down by its iniquity, whose weight and most grievous burden is described in Zechariah: Who sat upon a talent of lead (Zech 5:7). And it will fall, he says, and will not add to rise again. Not that the resurrection of men and of all who dwelt on the earth is denied, but that there will by no means be an earthly manner of life and the state of the former life, since human bodies rise again for this purpose, that souls may be clothed with the same bodies that they had laid aside before, and may receive from God either the good or the evil that they did upon the earth.
Commentary on Isaiah

And this is the sense of the whole passage: The windows of heaven have been opened, so that, as the Lord looked out upon earthly sins, every fashion of earthly works might pass away and fall, and by no means rise again to its former state. In that day, that is, in the day of judgment, the Lord will visit upon the host, or upon the adornment, of heaven on high, so that he may judge not only earthly but also heavenly things. And what the adornment or host of heaven is, let us learn from the writing of Moses: Beware lest, looking up to heaven and seeing the sun and the moon, the stars and all the adornment of heaven, you be deceived and worship them (Deut 4:19). And the Lord will visit, according to the idiom of the Scriptures, the host and army of heaven as one sick and in need of the knife and cautery, according to this: I will visit their sins with a rod, and their iniquities with scourges (Ps 88 [89]:33). For in what follows too we read: My sword has been made drunk in heaven (below, Isa 34:5); and in Job: The stars are not clean in his sight. And: Against his angels he has found something perverse (Job 25:5). He will visit also upon the kings and princes of the earth, the rulers of this darkness, and the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places. Of these princes, who preside over the various provinces, it is written also in Daniel: The prince of the kingdom of the Persians came out to meet me, and the prince of the kingdom of the Medes, and the prince of the kingdom of the Greeks (Dan 10).
Commentary on Isaiah

These princes, then, who did not keep their rank, the Lord will gather in the day of judgment, bound together as in one bundle, and will cast them into the pit of hell, so that in them too may be fulfilled what is written of the impious: He opened a pit and dug it, and he fell into the ditch which he made (Ps 7:16). And they will be shut up in prison, according to what the Lord says: Depart into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels (Matt 25:41). But what follows, And after many days they will be visited, seems to applaud my friends who grant repentance to the devil and the demons, in that after long times they are visited by the Lord. But let them consider that the divine Scripture did not say openly, They will be visited by the Lord, or, they will be visited by the angels, but absolutely, they will be visited. From this ambiguity of the word both remedy and correction can be understood: that after the righteous have received their rewards, those are visited in perpetual punishments. Yet it must be known that human frailty cannot know the judgment of God, nor pass sentence on the greatness and measure of the punishments, which has been left to the Lord's decision.
Against the Pelagians 2.24

He [Isaiah] was pricked by the thorn of sin; you are decked with the flowers of virtue. "The moon shall be ashamed, and the sun confounded, when the Lord shall punish the host of heaven on high." This is explained by another passage. "Even the stars are unclean in his sight";21 and again, "He charges his angels with folly." The moon is ashamed, the sun is confounded, and the sky covered with sackcloth. Shall we fearlessly and joyously, as though we were free from all sin, face the majesty of the Judge? After all, the mountains shall melt away, that is, all who are lifted up by pride, and all the host of the heavens, whether they are stars or angelic powers, shall fade away like heavens when the heavens shall be rolled together as a scroll.
Commentary on Isaiah

And it will be in that day: the Lord will visit upon the host of heaven on high, and upon the kings of the earth who are upon the earth. And they will be gathered together in the gathering of one bundle into the pit, and they will be shut up there in prison, and after many days they will be visited. And the moon will blush, and the sun will be confounded, when the Lord of hosts reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and has been glorified in the sight of his elders. For what we have translated, and the moon will blush, and the sun will be confounded, the Seventy translated, the brick will melt, and the wall will fall; what the cause of the error is, the following words will show. The sun in the Hebrew language is called by three names: SEMES (שמש), and HAMMA (המה), which means heat, and HERES (חרס), which signifies ὄστρακον, that is, potsherd or dryness. MAOR (מאר), however, which in Greek is called φωστήρ and in Latin luminary, is common to the sun and the moon. Again, the moon is called JAREE (ירה), which in Greek is called μήνη, because it makes a month by a circuit of thirty days, and LABANA (לבנה), that is, white or bright. In the present place, then, for LABANA, that is, moon, the Seventy translated brick, which in Hebrew is called LEBENA, deceived by the ambiguity of the word. Again, for HAMMA, that is, heat, by which is understood the sun, they put wall, which in Hebrew is called HOMA (הומה).
Commentary on Isaiah

Then the moon will blush, and the sun will be confounded, according to what the Apostle says: For the creation itself groans and travails (Rom 8:22), seeing that men who enjoyed its light have done nothing worthy of the goodness of God, who makes his sun rise upon the righteous and the unrighteous (Matt 5): as if a steward and bailiff, when the master comes, were to see the household subjected to various torments and not having fulfilled his precepts at all. Of this same passage the Savior teaches more fully in the Gospel: The sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens will be moved, when the sign of the Son of man has appeared in heaven, and all the tribes of the earth have beaten their breasts, and have seen the Son of man coming with the clouds of heaven in power and much glory (Matt 24:29, 30). We have learned of the overthrow of the earth, the visitation of the host of heaven, the gathering of the kings and princes into one bundle, and their thrusting down into the pit, and the keeping of the prison, and the visitation of those shut up after a long time, the blushing of the moon and the confusion of the sun. After all these things the Lord of hosts will reign on Mount Zion and in the heavenly Jerusalem, of which it is written also in the Epistle to the Hebrews: And in the sight of his elders he will be glorified (Heb 12). Such an elder was Abraham, who died in a good old age and was gathered to his fathers (Gen 25). Such were the elders whom Moses too is commanded to choose, whom he knows to be elders (Num 11): for the gray hair of a man is his wisdom (Wis 4:8); who imitate the Ancient of days, whose hair is described as white, so that length of age may be shown (Dan 7:9). This can also be understood of the ecclesiastical rank, if only they do not destroy the dignity by their works.
On the Gospel of Mark 4:13.24

The stars on the day of judgment will be seen obscurely, not because of a gradual waning of their own light but due to the overwhelming brilliance of the true light, who is the supreme Judge coming in majesty, and the light of the Father and the holy angels. Nevertheless, nothing should prevent us from understanding that the sun, the moon and other stars will be deprived temporarily of their own light, as happened to the sun at the Lord's passion. But because the moon, which should have been full at that time, lay hidden behind the earth, Joel's prophesy remains unfulfilled still today, for after he had said "the sun will be turned to darkness," he added, "and the moon to blood before the great and magnificent day of the Lord comes." Isaiah also spoke about the day of judgment, saying, "The moon will be ashamed and the sun confounded when the Lord of hosts reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem and is glorified in the presence of Jerusalem's elders."

n: Amen. He approves of God's judgments (Haydock) against Jerusalem. (Worthington)
City; Jerusalem, or rather Babylon, (chap. xxi.; Calmet) or every city (Haydock) in the world. (Menochius) --- Strangers: the temples of idols.
People; the Chaldeans, or their conquerors.
Poor; Juda, whom Nabuchodonosor's fury could not exterminate.
Away. Cyrus (Calmet) shall reduce Babylon the great. (Haydock)
