Mountain of Sion, a figure of the Church, and of heaven. The Jews shall feast: yea, some of all nations shall partake of the blessed Eucharist, and obtain heaven. The expressions are too grand for a corruptible feast. (Calmet) --- Wine. Literally, "of vintage," (Haydock) on which occasion great rejoicings were made. (Hesiod, Hercul. 297.) --- Protestants, "of wines on the lees." (Haydock) --- In the East, the wines were very thick, Psalm lxxv. 9. (Calmet) --- On the rejection of the Jews, the Gentiles were converted. (Worthington)
Tied. He will open their eyes to the truth of the gospel. They shall be no longer as criminals, expecting death, or mourning.

Ever. Hebrew, "he shall swallow up death in victory," 1 Corinthians xv. 54. Christ, by dying, conquered death, and rescued us from its power, if we do not voluntarily subject ourselves to it again. This was faintly represented by the liberation of the captives.

Mountain: the Church. (Calmet) --- Moab. That is, the reprobate, whose eternal punishment, from which they can no way escape, is described under these figures. (Challoner) --- The Machabees probably executed this vengeance on Moab, 1 Machabees v. 6.
Hands. All his exertions and fury will prove useless. (Haydock) --- Moab shall lie prostrate.

f: Commentary on Isaiah

O Lord, you are my God: I will exalt you, I will confess to your name, for you have done wonders, ancient faithful designs: amen. For you have made the city a heap, the strong city a ruin, the house of strangers, so that it is no city, and will never be built for ever. Because of this a strong people will praise you, the city of mighty nations will fear you. For you have become strength to the poor, strength to the needy in his tribulation, a hope from the whirlwind, a shade from the heat: for the spirit of the mighty is like a whirlwind driving against a wall. Like heat in thirst, you will bring low the tumult of strangers; and as with scorching heat under a cloud, you will make the offshoot of the strong wither. LXX: O Lord my God, I will glorify you; I will praise your name, for you have done wonderful things, an ancient true counsel, so be it. For you have made cities a heap, strong cities, that their foundations might fall. The cities of the impious will not be built for ever. Therefore the people of the poor will bless you, and the cities of men who suffer iniquity will bless you. For you have been a helper to every lowly city, and a protection to those who are sad because of want; you will deliver them from most wicked men: a shade of the thirsty, and the spirit of men who suffer iniquity, like faint-hearted men thirsting in Zion, from the impious men to whom you have delivered us. The exposition of this place is twofold. The Jews think it is the voice of the saints and of the believing people, when God has done against the whole world the things said above, and the prophecies of all the prophets have been fulfilled; and the overthrown city they interpret as Rome, which is to be utterly destroyed; and the strong people, which praises the Lord, and to which the Lord has become strength in its tribulation and distress, they refer to Israel, which has been freed from the persecution of the nations as from most burning heat and thirst.
Commentary on Isaiah

But others, both better and more correctly, understand it as said in the person of the prophet, giving thanks to the Father for the passion of the Lord Savior, because he has done wonders and has fulfilled his ancient designs in truth, when those standing at the right hand will hear: Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world (Matt 25:34). Understanding this, Paul too said: As he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and spotless (Eph 1:4); and, desiring that what he prophesies should come to pass, he adds the Hebrew word AMEN (אמן), for which the Seventy translated so be it. And the Lord in the Gospel often uses this word: Amen, amen, that is, truly, truly I say to you (John 6:54).
Commentary on Isaiah

And why he praises and confesses to the name of the Lord, and what these wonders are, and the ancient designs which he showed true in deed, follows: For you have made the city a heap, the strong city a ruin, the house of strangers, so that it is no city, and will never be built for ever. The once strong city is understood as Jerusalem, which has become the house of strangers; of whom the Savior says in the psalm: Strange children have lied to me, strange children have grown old and have limped in their paths (Ps 17 [18]:46). This city, when it has been destroyed, will never be built for ever, so that the dreams of a thousand-year kingdom and of a golden and jeweled Jerusalem may be laid to rest.
Commentary on Isaiah

And when Jerusalem has been destroyed for its impiety, a strong people will praise the Lord. And who the strong people is, the following verse shows: The city of mighty nations will fear you. While those blaspheme, the people of the nations will fear you. For the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom (Prov 9:10). And a strong people will praise you, and the city of mighty nations will fear you, that is, the Church gathered from the nations.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 3:1.25

Israel was called to the knowledge of God through the tutoring of the law and was richly endowed with the things of God. It was delivered [from Egypt] and inherited the Promised Land. Although there were many other peoples living in other parts of the world, all were alien to spiritual matters and heavenly things. They had not tasted the gifts that come from God. They were, as it were, naked and unclothed, enjoying neither divine protection nor shelter from on high, nor the spiritual wealth that comes from virtue nor other things worthy of praise or admiration.When Christ appeared, destroying the arrogance of the devil, he led the nations to God the Father, and they basked in the splendor of the true light and shared in his glory. Enjoying the splendor of the way of life according to the gospel, they offered hymns of thanksgiving to the God and Father for these gifts. Thus the text says, you have carried out a "faithful plan formed of old," O Lord, recapitulating all things in Christ and enlightening those in darkness, destroying the mighty powers of this age. That is, like "fortified cities the impoverished people will bless you" and whole cities will "glorify you." Having become a "help to all" and "protection" to those whose ancestral traditions were impoverished, you have saved them from wicked people.
Commentary on Isaiah

For you have become strength to the poor, to your Christ, of whom we read also in the Psalms: Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and the poor (Ps 40 [41]:1). And in Zechariah, according to the Hebrew truth, the poor man, that is, EBION (אביון), is described as sitting upon the colt of an ass (Zech 9). Strength to the needy, in the tribulation of his passion, a hope from the whirlwind of the cross, and a shade from the heat, when he said: Father, into your hands I commend my spirit (Luke 23:46). For as when the wind is dashed against a wall and passes by, so the whirlwind of the blaspheming Jews could not harm him.
Commentary on Isaiah

And to use another comparison: as an offshoot is scorched by most grievous heat and droops, so you will make the tumult and clamor of the strangers, that is, of those who have become strangers to you, wither and perish. According to the Seventy translators, I could not find in this place, I do not say the sense, but the order and sequence of the words. And for that place where we have translated, like heat in thirst, for which in the Hebrew is written BASAION (בציון), which among them means pathless place or thirst: why they turned pathless place and in thirst into in Zion, the error is plain, from the likeness of the words SAION and SION (Both ציון), since it is marked with the same letters.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 3:1.25

Perhaps this is what the prophet is referring to, that is, those in Israel who were thirsting for the coming of the Savior. They desired to see the Savior and Redeemer of all. One such person was the righteous Simeon. When he took the infant Jesus in his arms, he said, "Lord, now let your servant depart in peace, according to your word; for mine eyes have seen your salvation which you have prepared in the presence of all peoples, a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to your people Israel."
Catechetical Lecture 11:5-7

Having been counted worthy of this holy chrism, you are called Christians, verifying the name also by your new birth. For before you were deemed worthy of this grace, you had properly no right to this title but were advancing on your way toward being Christians.Moreover, you shall know that in the old Scripture there lies the symbol of this chrism. For at the time Moses imparted to his brother the command of God and made him high priest, he anointed him after bathing him in water. And Aaron was called Christ or anointed, evidently from the typical anointing. So also the high priest, in advancing Solomon to the kingdom, anointed him after he had bathed in Gihon. To them, however, these things happened in a figure, but to you not in a figure but in truth; because you were truly anointed by the Holy Spirit. Christ is the beginning of your salvation. He is truly the first fruit, and you are what follow. If the first fruit is holy, obviously its holiness will pass to the remainder also.
Keep this teaching unspotted, for it shall teach you all things, if it abide in you.… For this holy thing is a spiritual safeguard of the body and salvation of the soul. Of this the blessed Isaiah prophesying of old time said, "On this mountain shall the Lord make for all nations a feast; they shall drink wine, they shall drink gladness, they shall anoint themselves with ointment."
Commentary on Isaiah

After the passion of the Lord, then, when he has freed him from thirst and heat and whirlwind, the Lord will make, not at all for the people of the Jews, but for all nations, on Mount Zion a fat feast, burnt offerings full of marrow, and the wine of a vintage refined from the lees, so that he may cast down and cause to be swallowed up the face of death and of the bond by which all peoples were bound; and he will break the net of death, and the web that had caught all nations. And according to the Apostle, death will be swallowed up for ever (1 Cor 15). And the Lord will take away the tear from every face, when, death being overcome, the kingdom of Christ has come, and the reproach of the human race, which had been made to the image of the Creator, has escaped the slavery of the devil and of death. Nor is it surprising if according to Symmachus death is called a ruler, since the blessed Apostle said: Death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those who had not sinned, in the likeness of the transgression of Adam (Rom 5:14). The Ruler of all peoples, or the face of darkness upon all peoples, and the web that was woven over all nations, some wish to be understood as the Antichrist, who is to be consumed on the Mount of Olives, as we also said on the last vision of Daniel. According to the Seventy, a feast of gladness is prepared for all nations on Mount Zion, in which they will drink the wine which the Lord promised that he would drink with his saints in the kingdom of his Father (Matt 26 and Luke 22); and they will be anointed with ointment, so that, reborn in Christ, they may be made a new people; whence it is said: Deliver all these things to the nations, which Israel once celebrated in type and image. For this is the counsel of the Lord, that all things should be transferred to the nations, because death has been swallowed up (1 Cor 15), and every tear wiped away, and the reproach of the whole earth blotted out, as the rule of Christ succeeds.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 25:6-7

Having said that the Lord will reign in Zion and Jerusalem, Isaiah leads us to the mystical meaning of the passage. Thus Zion is interpreted as a high place that is good for surveillance, and Jerusalem is the vision of the world. In fact, the church of Christ combines both: it is high and visible from everywhere, and is, so to speak, located on the mountain. The church may be understood as high also in another way: there is nothing low in it, it is far removed from all the mundane things, as it is written, "I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth!" Equally elevated are its orthodox and divine doctrines; thus the doctrine about God or about the holy and consubstantial Trinity is true, pure and without guile. "The Lord of hosts will make for all people," not just for the Israelites elected for the sake of their patriarchs but for all the people of the world. What will he make? "A feast of wines on the lees; they will drink joy, they will drink wine. They will be anointed with myrrh on the mountain." This joy, of course, means the joy of hope, of the hope rooted in Christ, because we will reign with him, and with him we will enjoy every spiritual joy and pleasure that surpasses mind and understanding. By "wine" he points to the mystical sacrament, that of the bloodless sacrifice, which we celebrate in the holy churches.
Commentary on Isaiah

And the Lord of hosts will make for all peoples on this mountain a feast of fat things, a feast of the vintage: of fat things full of marrow, of a vintage refined from the lees. And he will cast down on this mountain the face of the bond that was bound upon all peoples, and the web that he wove over all nations. And he will cast down death for ever, and the Lord God will take away the tear from every face, and the reproach of his people he will take away from all the earth: for the Lord has spoken. LXX: And the Lord Sabaoth will make for all nations upon this mountain: they will drink gladness, they will drink wine. They will be anointed with ointment on this mountain. Deliver all these things to the nations, for this counsel is upon all nations: death, prevailing, has devoured. And again: The Lord God has taken away every tear from every face, and the reproach of his people he has taken away from all the earth. For the mouth of the Lord has spoken. For what we have rendered, the face of the bond that was bound upon all peoples, Aquila translated, the face of darkness upon all peoples. And whereas Aquila said darkness twice, Theodotion named darkness once, the rest alike. For this Symmachus translated, the face of the Ruler who rules over all peoples. And what the Seventy meant to say for this place, Deliver all these things to the nations, is plain to the reader: that they set down not the words of Scripture but their own sense, because all the mysteries of the Law and of the Temple were to be transferred to the Churches of the nations.
Letter 44.9

In the Old Testament the jaw of death is bitter, since it is said, "Strong death is all devouring." In the New Testament the jaw of death is sweet, for it has swallowed death, as the apostle says: "Death is swallowed up in victory! O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?"
Letter 74.5

Stricken by the indecency of this act [the golden calf], Moses broke the tablets and shattered the head of the calf and beat it to powder in order to destroy all traces of impiety. The first tablets were broken so that the second ones might be repaired whereon, through the teaching of the gospel, faithlessness, now utterly destroyed, vanished. Thus Moses shattered that Egyptian pride and by the authority of the eternal law checked that loftiness overreaching itself. Therefore David says, "And the Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon, and shatter them like the calf of Lebanon. Thus the people swallowed all faithlessness and pride, so that impiety and haughtiness might not swallow them. For it is better that each person be master of his flesh and its vices, that it may not be said of him that all-powerful death has devoured him, but rather, "death is swallowed up in victory!"
Commentary on Hosea

For which reason the Apostle placed: "Death has been swallowed up in contention; where is your contention, death? Where is your sting, O death?" And explaining the power of the testimony, he said: "But the sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law; but thanks be to God, who has given us victory through our Lord Jesus Christ." Therefore, what he interpreted as the resurrection of the Lord, we cannot nor dare interpret differently. Death, hell, and the devil may be understood, who was killed by the death of Christ, about whom Isaiah also speaks: "Death has been swallowed up by victory" (Isaiah 25:8, LXX translation). And afterwards it follows: "The Lord hath taken away every tear from every face." Now, however, some understand that the two brothers who were separated by death, according to the history of that time, are Israel and Judah, so that what was then prefigured partly may now be felt in its entirety, and that with every human race Israel and Judah must be liberated and redeemed.
SERMON 155:2

The apostle said, "With the mind I serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin," not by giving my members over to committing iniquities but only by feeling lust, without however giving a hand to unlawful lust. So when he said, "With the mind I serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin," he went on to add, "There is therefore no condemnation now for those who are in Christ Jesus." For those who are in the flesh there is condemnation; for those who are in Christ Jesus no condemnation. In case you should assume this is going to be the case after becoming a Christian, that is why he added "now."What you must look forward to afterward is not even to have any lust in you which you have to contend with, which you have to combat, which you must not consent to, which you have to curb and tame; look forward to its simply not being there afterward. I mean to say, if what is now contending with us from its base in this mortal body is going to be there afterward, the taunt "Where, death, is your striving?" will be untrue. So let us be quite clear about what it is going to be like afterward. Then, you see, will come about the word that is written: "Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where, death, is your striving? Where, death, is your sting? For the sting of death is sin; but the power of sin, the law." Because desire was increased, not extinguished, by being forbidden. The law gave sin power by simply commanding through the letter without assisting through the spirit.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 3:1.25

It is appropriate and necessary that at the time the "mystery" is handed over, the "resurrection of the dead" is included. For at the time we make the confession of faith at holy baptism, we say that we expect the resurrection of the flesh. And so we believe. Death overcame our forefather Adam on account of his transgression and like a fierce wild animal it pounced on him and carried him off amid lamentation and loud wailing. Men wept and grieved because death ruled over all the earth. But all this came to an end with Christ. Striking down death, he rose up on the third day and became the way by which human nature would rid itself of corruption. He became the first born of the dead, and the first fruits of those who have fallen asleep.We who come afterward will certainly follow the first fruits. He turned suffering into joy, and we cast off our sackcloth. We put on the joy given by God so that we can rejoice and say, "Where is your victory O death?" Therefore every tear is taken away. For believing that Christ will surely raise the dead, we do not weep over them, nor are we overwhelmed by inconsolable grief like those who have no hope. Death itself is a "reproach of the people" for it had its beginning among us through sin. Corruption entered in on account of sin, and death's power ruled on earth.
Commentary on Isaiah

And they will say in that day: Behold, this is our God; we have waited for him, and he will save us: this is the Lord, we have waited patiently for him; we will exult and be glad in his salvation. For the hand of the Lord will rest on this mountain; and Moab will be threshed under him as straw is crushed in the wagon. And he will stretch out his hands under him, as a swimmer stretches them out to swim, and his glory will be brought low with the dashing of his hands. And the fortifications of your lofty walls will fall, and will be brought low and pulled down to the ground, even to the dust. When death has been swallowed up for ever, the people of God which has been freed from the hand of death will say to the Lord: Behold, this is our God, whom the unbelieving thought only a man; and we have waited for him, that is, we have believed his words, that he will fulfill his promises, and he will save us. Therefore, snatched by his help from the jaws of death, we will exult and be glad in him; and his hand and his power will rest on this mountain, of which we read above: When the Lord of hosts reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and has been glorified in the sight of his elders (Isa 24:23). And Moab, which means from the father, will be crushed as straw is wont to be crushed by the wagon. He speaks according to the custom of Palestine and of many provinces of the East, which, for lack of meadows and hay, prepare straw for the feeding of animals. Now there are iron-shod carts, with wheels turning in the middle in the manner of saws, which crush the stubble and break it up into straw. As, then, straw is crushed by iron-shod wagons, so Moab will be crushed under him, whether under the power of God or in himself, so that nothing whole remains in him.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 3:1.25

You recognize the one who gives you joy to drink and wine in addition, anointing those in spiritual Zion with myrrh. You recognize that he is true God and Son of God by nature, and although he appeared in the form of a servant, by becoming man he became the source of salvation and life for all, being in all things like those on earth though without sin. The prophet indicates that they are all but pointing [to Christ] with their finger when they say, "Behold our God in whom we have hoped, and we will rejoice in our salvation." I think that this text applies especially to the Israelites who were nurtured in the words of Moses and were not ignorant of the predictions of the holy prophets. They waited for the time of the coming of the Savior and Redeemer, the Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore, as I have already said, Zechariah the father of John [the Baptizer] when he prophesied in the Spirit said of Christ, "He has raised up a horn of salvation." And Simeon when he took the holy child in his arms said, "Behold, my eyes have seen the salvation which you have prepared before the face of all people." Recognize then what had been announced of old, the one who is the hope of all, the Savior and Redeemer, they said, according to Isaiah, "Behold our God."They confess that God will give rest on this mountain. And it seems to me that mountain here refers to the church, for it is there that one finds rest. For we heard the words of Christ: "Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest."
Commentary on Isaiah

So the prophetic discourse, although it weaves its prophecy generally about the consummation of the world, yet, so as not to seem to neglect present things entirely, names Moab, which was an enemy of Israel, so much so that it made them commit fornication with the Midianites and be consecrated to the idol Baal-peor, which means Priapus; against which Jeremiah speaks: Chemosh will go forth into captivity, his priests and his princes together (Jer 48:7); and again: Moab will be confounded in Chemosh, as the house of Israel was confounded in Bethel (ibid., 13), and other things like these. And from one idol and the demon who presided over this idol, he indicates that all the adverse powers are to be brought low and led down into Tartarus, and crushed like dust. But if this is how it will be, where is the repentance of the devil?
Commentary on Isaiah
And as one who swims is wont to stretch out his whole body, so he will be dashed from his power to the ground, and in falling will make a noise.
Commentary on Isaiah
And all the fortifications of his lofty men, or of his walls, as is contained in the Hebrew, will fall and be brought low, and will be pulled down to the ground, broken to the dust.

n: Day. Under the law of grace, Christians sing this and such like canticles. (Worthington) --- Sion. This word is not in Hebrew, &c., though it be understood. (Calmet) --- Other nations have their respective cities. All Christians admit this one. (Worthington) --- The captives continue to return thanks. Yet the Holy Ghost speaks chiefly of the Church, and of the general resurrection. (Calmet) --- Bulwark. Faith and good works. (Worthington)
Truth. The Jews who returned from Babylon, were more virtuous than their ancestors, as the prophets intimate; though they have Christians principally in view.
Away: condemning the virtuous, as if they were fools. (Menochius) --- Symmachus, "our work, or fiction, is taken away." Hebrew may have other meanings. (Haydock)
You, people of Juda.
High: Nabuchodonosor and his empire.
Needy. The Jews shall behold the ruin of the city by Cyrus, (Calmet) who was of a contemptible nation. (Haydock)
In. God will remove every obstacle, at their return.
Night of distress.
Justice. Clemency would therefore be ill placed. If the Israelites had not been led away captives, would they ever have been reformed?
Not see. Let them perish, or live to witness the glory of the Jews.
Works, both in punishing and rewarding. (Calmet) --- God crowns his own gifts. (Estius)
Lords of Babylon, (Calmet) and our own passions. (Haydock)
Giants; the proud emperors of Babylon, whom thou wilt destroy. Septuagint, "physicians;" as Rephaim has also this meaning.

Nation of the Jews. (Calmet) --- Septuagint, "add evils to them, O Lord; add evils to the nobles of the land." (Haydock) --- Hebrew may have the same sense. --- Ends: princes, or the Chaldeans, sending them also into captivity; or thou hast propagated thy Church over the world.
They. Septuagint, "We," &c. (Calmet) --- Affliction is a wholesome medicine. (Haydock)

Wind. Our expectation of aid from others has been disappointed. (Calmet) --- Septuagint, "the spirit of thy salvation, which thou hast wrought on the earth. We shall not fall, but the inhabitants of the earth shall fall." (Haydock) --- Their copies must have been different from ours. --- Fallen. The Chanaanites are left for our trial and punishment. (Calmet)
Dead: a civil death, shall regain their liberty; and those who have left this world in a state of virtue, shall be happy. --- Ruin. Cyrus liberated the Jews, having conquered Babylon.
Away, and Cambyses be destroyed, Ezechiel xxxviii. 11. (Calmet)
Shall cover her stain no more. This is said with relation to the martyrs, and their happy resurrection. (Challoner) --- The blood of the saints shall demand vengeance. (Calmet)

f: Commentary on Isaiah

In that day this song will be sung in the land of Judah: The city of our strength, the Savior, a wall and an outer wall will be set in it. LXX: In that day they will sing this song in the land of Judea: Behold a strong city, and our salvation will set a wall and a surrounding wall. When Moab has been brought low and pulled down to the ground, even to the dust, and all enemies laid beneath the feet of Christ, then this song will be sung in the land of Judah, or Judea, each of which means confession: so that, as we have understood Zion and Jerusalem as the heavenly city, so we may also understand the region of this city as the heavenly confession. Indeed, the saints, unwilling to sing the song of Judea in a foreign land, say: How shall we sing a song to the Lord in a foreign land? (Ps 136 [137]:4). I think that this is the song which in another place too the saints are commanded: Sing to the Lord a new song (Ps 95 [96]:1). And this song will be what follows: The city of our strength, the Savior (Matt 5). Which is this city? The one which, set on a mountain, cannot be hid. Of which it is written also in another place: The rush of the river makes glad the city of God (Ps 45 [46]:4); and again: Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God (Ps 86 [87]:2). The founder of this city is he of whom the Father speaks: he has built my city; nay rather, the city of our strength is the Savior, that is, Jesus. And a wall and an outer wall will be set in it: the wall of good works, and the outer wall of right faith, so that it may be enclosed by a double fortification. For it is not enough to have the wall of faith, unless faith itself is confirmed by good works. This wall and this outer wall, or surrounding wall, is built of living stones, which, according to the prophet, are rolled upon the earth. For what we have rendered, outer wall, Symmachus translated bulwark: so that the walls themselves are girded with fortifications, and with rampart and ditch and other walls, which in the building of camps they are accustomed to call breastworks.
Commentary on Isaiah

Open the gates, and let the righteous nation enter, keeping the truth. The old error has gone; you will keep peace: peace, because we have hoped in you. You have hoped in the Lord for everlasting ages. LXX: Open the gates, let the people enter which keeps righteousness, and keeps the truth, laying hold of the truth, and keeping peace: peace, because they have hoped in you, O Lord, for ever. This whole song, which the saints are to sing in the land of confession and praise, suddenly changes persons, and is woven as if by question and answer. The people of God had said: The city of our strength, the Savior, a wall and an outer wall will be set in it. The Lord answered, or rather commanded, not those who had said this, but the angels who presided over the gates of the Lord's city, that they should open the gates, and let the righteous nation enter through them, keeping the truth, or, as is said in the Hebrew, EMMUNIM (אמונים), which in our language is rendered faiths, in the plural number, not the singular. Which are the gates that are opened by the angels, so that there may enter, not the people of the Jews, which has been cast off, but the righteous nation, which from faith has received the name of the faithful? Surely those of which the holy man speaks: Open to me the gates of righteousness; having entered them, I will confess to the Lord (Ps 117 [118]:19). But no one will be able to enter these gates except one who has been freed from the gates of death, as the Psalmist said: You who lift me up from the gates of death, that I may declare all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion (Ps 9:15). For when we have been snatched from the gates of death, then we shall be able to sing all the praises of the Lord in the gates of the daughter of Zion. And as I consider the gates of death to be sins, of which it is said to Peter: The gates of hell shall not prevail against you (Matt 16:18), so I consider the gates of righteousness to be all the works of the virtues; and he who has entered them will find one gate, of which it is said: This is the gate of the Lord, the righteous shall enter by it (Ps 117 [118]:20). And as through many pearls one comes to the one pearl, so through many ways and gates we come to him who says that he is the way and the gate, through which we enter to the Father.
Commentary on Isaiah

After the words of the people and the answer of the Lord, and again the voice of the people, the Prophet speaks to the believers: You have hoped, or hope in the Lord, for everlasting ages, and the rest that follows. According to the Seventy, he enters the gates of the Lord who keeps righteousness in good works, and keeps or embraces the truth in the truth of faith, so that through good works and faith he may come to the peace which surpasses all understanding, and may merit to receive that peace; because he has believed in God, who is the eternal rewarder of good works (Phil 4). Hence also in another place it is written: You have desired wisdom: keep the commandments, and the Lord will grant it to you (Sir 1:33).
Commentary on Isaiah

After the word of God, the people answered in Hebrew JESER SAMUCH (יצרסמך), which Aquila and Symmachus translated alike, πλᾶσμα ἐπηρεισμένον, that is, our error has been taken away, or our thought has been made firm, which before wavered between you and the idols, so that we are by no means carried about by every wind of doctrine, but believe with our whole mind in you, the Lord Savior. For this, so that the sense might be made plainer, we translated, the old error has gone. And because our thought has been made firm, therefore you will keep for us the peace which you promised to the Apostles, saying: My peace I give you, my peace I leave you (John 14:27); and not once only but a second time, so that the recompense which is promised with a double word may be secure, according to what the Apostle too said: Rejoice, again I say rejoice (Phil 4:4). And this he obtains of whom it is said in Leviticus: Man, man, of the children of Israel (Lev 17); and in the book of Numbers: Man, man, whose wife has defiled his bed (Num 5:12): so that the double man and the double husband may obtain a double peace. And we merit peace, they say, because we trust in you with our whole mind.
Commentary on Isaiah

In the Lord God, the strong one, for ever: for he will bow down those who dwell on high; he will bring low the lofty city, he will bring it low even to the ground; he will pull it down even to the dust. The foot will trample it, the feet of the poor, the steps of the needy. LXX: O great eternal God, who have brought low and pulled down those who dwell on high, you will destroy strong cities, and will bring them down even to the pavement, and the feet of the meek and the lowly will trample them. These things too the Prophet speaks, who answered from that place where he had said above, Hope in the Lord for everlasting ages; and he joins to it what we have now set forth: In the Lord God, the strong one, for ever, and the rest. For the Lord God, the strong one, the Hebrew has three names, IA (יה) and ADONAI (יהוה) and SUR (צור), of which one signifies invisible, another ineffable, another mighty; the first of them is placed as the last syllable in ALLELUIA (הללו יה). And let the diligent reader observe this, that we sometimes divide the text in setting out a testimony, because the edition of the Seventy produces one sense, and the translation rendered word for word from the Hebrew another. The Prophet says, then: Hope in the Lord for everlasting ages: in the Lord God, the strong one, for ever, whose help is everlasting.
Commentary on Isaiah

For he will bow down those who dwell on high, because everyone who exalts himself will be humbled; those who boasted that they had Abraham as their father, and said in insult of the Lord: We were not born of fornication (John 8:41). He will bring low the lofty city: as the Jews think, Rome; as we prove to be more correct, Jerusalem, which killed the Prophets and stoned those who were sent to it, and at the last killed the son of the householder, so that, the heir being slain, the inheritance might perish (Luke 13). Nor is it called a city, which in Hebrew is said IR (עיר), but CARIA (כריה), which Aquila translated πολίχνην, which we can call either little city or hamlet or small town; and Jerusalem is frequently called by this name in the Scriptures. And he did well to set down a double humbling, He will bring low, he will bring it low: first under the Babylonians, when the temple was destroyed; the second time under Titus and Vespasian, whose ruin remains until the end.
Commentary on Isaiah

And because it is said in the words of the Savior, Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted (Luke 14:11), we can refer this not only to men but also to the adverse powers. According to the Seventy, the Prophet sings praises to God because he brings low all the proud, and razes the fortifications of all cities to the ground, and the feet of the saints, the meek and the lowly trample them.
Commentary on Isaiah

The foot will trample it, and he repeats and joins the feet of the poor, without doubt of Christ, of whom we have said above too: He has become strength to the poor, strength to the needy in his tribulation. The steps of the needy, namely of the Apostles, who, imitating the poverty of the Lord, obtained also the privilege of his power; who, not being received, shook off upon it the dust of their feet.
Commentary on Isaiah

The path of the righteous is straight, straight is the track of the righteous for walking; and in the path of your judgments, O Lord, we have waited for you; your name and your memorial are in the desire of the soul: my soul has desired you in the night. LXX: The way of the righteous is straight, the way of the righteous has been made straight, and prepared. For the way of the Lord is judgment; we have hoped in your name, and in the remembrance which our soul desires. The Prophet is still speaking of Christ, of whom he had said above: The foot will trample it, the feet of the poor. The path of this righteous one, then, is straight, or, to coin a new word, straightnesses, which the Greeks call εὐθύτητας, and which we can call more in the Latin manner equities; and in Hebrew they are called MESSARIM (משרים). In the one path of Christ, then, all righteousnesses are found; and for that reason he trod and wore it with his own foot, so that whoever wishes to walk along it may walk with an unstumbling course.
Commentary on Isaiah

In this path of the Lord's judgments the saints have waited for him, and have hoped in him, because hope does not confound. And they have had his name and memorial in the desire of their soul, saying: My soul has longed to desire your judgments at all times (Ps 118 [119]:20); and again: My soul desires, and has fainted for your salvation (ibid. 81). And he who has the name of the Lord in his desire desires nothing else. And this must be noted, that the desire for the Lord is not in the flesh but in the soul, according to what we read in another psalm: My soul has thirsted for God, the strong, the living (Ps 41 [42]:2). For the flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh (Gal 5). For these are opposed to one another, so that we do not do the things we wish.
HOMILIES ON 1 TIMOTHY 14

But, as I said, at the crowing of the cock their President comes, and gently touching the sleeper with his foot, rouses them all. For there are none sleeping naked. Then as soon as they have arisen they stand up, and sing the prophetic hymns with much harmony, and well composed tunes. And neither harp nor pipe nor other musical instrument utters such sweet melodies, as you hear from the singing of these saints in their deep and quiet solitudes. And the songs themselves too are suitable, and full of the love of God. "In the night," they say, "lift up your hands unto God. With my soul have I desired Thee in the night, yea with my spirit within me will I seek Thee early."
Commentary on Isaiah

And what follows, In the night, according to the Seventy is joined to the following passage, according to the Hebrew to the former one. And he can say, My soul has desired you in the night, who says confidently with the Psalmist: Every night I will wash my bed, I will water my couch with tears (Ps 6:7). Night and darkness can also be taken for tribulation and distress. Hence in another psalm too the Prophet sings of the security of the righteous: The sun will not burn you by day, nor the moon by night (Ps 120 [121]:6), that is, neither in prosperity nor in adversity will you ever be moved from your place.
Commentary on Isaiah

But also with my spirit within my breast, from the morning I will watch for you. LXX: From the night my spirit rises early to you, O God: for your judgments are a light upon the earth. We wish both to follow the Hebrew and not to pass over the common edition entirely, and by this necessity of things we are compelled to seek different understandings in a different order and wording. So what is said, from the night, is, according to the Seventy, as we said, the beginning of this passage; according to the Hebrew, the end of the preceding one; although even according to the Seventy it can be taken at the end of the preceding testimony, so that the sense is: My soul desires you in the night; and afterwards it begins: in the morning my spirit rises to you, O God. And it rises in the morning for this reason, because your precepts are a light upon the earth. For, keeping your commandments, and illumined by the light of those of which it is said, The precept of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes (Ps 18 [19]:9), I cannot sleep, but desiring you at all times, I rise to you with my spirit. And this must be observed, that while still placed in the night we desire the Lord with the soul; but after our spirit within our breast has moved itself toward God with the whole mind, let us watch for him in the morning: and, to speak more plainly, night and desire are joined to the soul, but morning and watching to the spirit. Further, he watches for God with the spirit within his breast who can say: Out of the depths I have cried to you, O Lord (Ps 129 [130]:1).
Commentary on Isaiah

When you have done your judgments on the earth, the inhabitants of the world will learn righteousness. Let us have mercy on the impious, and he will not learn righteousness; in the land of the saints he has done wickedly, and he will not see the glory of the Lord. LXX: Learn righteousness, you who dwell upon the earth. For the impious has ceased, and he will not learn righteousness upon the earth; he will not do truth; let the impious be taken away, that he may not see the glory of the Lord. Let us speak first according to the Hebrew, and when we have chosen to express the sense of the Prophet, then let us pass to the Seventy translators. As long as you do not exercise your judgments upon the earth, and neither repay good to the good nor evil to the evil, your righteousness, O Lord God, is unknown on the earth. But when on the day of judgment you have rendered to each what he deserves, according to the quality of his works, then your righteousness will be known in the world, which before seemed unjust among the unbelieving, so that one of the saints too said: But my feet were almost moved, my steps had well-nigh slipped: for I was zealous over the wicked, seeing the peace of sinners (Ps 72 [73]:2).
Commentary on Isaiah

According to the Seventy, the inhabitants of the earth are commanded to learn righteousness. For every man seems righteous to himself; but God knows the hearts of all, who will render to each according to his works (Prov 21). And in another place of the same book it is said: There are ways of a man which seem straight; but their ends look into the depth of hell (Prov 14:12). Hence we ought to learn righteousness, and not trust in our own judgment. For there is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness (Eccl 7); not because he is righteous, but because he seems to himself to be righteous. But if Christ has been made for us by God wisdom and righteousness, sanctification and redemption (1 Cor 1), those who are commanded to know righteousness are commanded this: to learn and know Christ. And I command you, he says, to learn righteousness for this reason, because the impious has been taken away, and his kingdom destroyed, who, as long as he reigned on the earth, could neither know righteousness nor do truth; of which it is written elsewhere that grace and truth came through Jesus Christ (John 1:17). And because the impious does not do truth on the earth, he will be taken away: for he does not deserve to see the Lord reigning.
Morals on the Book of Job, Book 23, Section 39

For "night" is this present life, and as long as we are in it, we are covered with a mist of uncertain imaginations as far as the sight of inward objects is concerned. For the prophet was sensible that he was held by a certain mist in his sight of the Lord, when he says, "My soul longed for you in the night." As if he were to say, I long to behold you in the obscurity of this present life, but I am still surrounded by the mist of infirmity.
Forty Gospel Homilies, Homily 25

Anyone who has been able to reach out for the truth has been on fire with this love. For this reason David said, "My soul has thirsted for the living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?" And he counseled us, saying, "Seek his face continually." And for this reason the prophet said, "My soul has desired you in the night, and with my spirit within my breast I will watch for you in the morning." And again the church says to the Lord in the Song of Songs, "I have been wounded with love."It is right that the soul, after bearing in its heart a wound of love brought on by its burning desire, should reach out for healing at the sight of the doctor. And so, again, it says, "My soul melted when he spoke." The heart of a person who does not seek the face of his Creator is hardened by his wickedness, because in itself it remains cold. But if it now begins to burn with the desire of following him whom it loves, it runs since the fire of love has melted it. Its desire makes it anxious. Everything that used to please it in the world seems worthless; it finds nothing agreeable outside of its Creator; things that once delighted the heart afterwards become grievously oppressive. Nothing brings it consolation in its sadness as long as the one it desires is not beheld. The heart sorrows. Light itself is loathsome. Scorching fire burns away the rust of sin in the heart. The soul is inflamed as if it were gold, for gold loses its beauty through use, but fire restores its brightness.
HOMILIES ON JOHN 12

For our Lord Jesus Christ came, not only that we might behold His glory here, but also that which shall be. For therefore He saith, "I will that these also be with Me where I am, that they may behold My glory." Now if the glory here was so bright and splendid, what can one say of that which shall be? for it shall appear not on this corruptible earth, nor while we are in perishable bodies, but in a creation which is imperishable, and waxes not old, and with such brightness as it is not possible even to represent in words. O blessed, thrice blessed, yea many times so, they who are deemed worthy to be beholders of that glory! It is concerning this that the prophet says, "Let the unrighteous be taken away, that he behold not the glory of the Lord." God grant that not one of us be taken away nor excluded ever from beholding it.
Commentary on Isaiah

To which the Lord answered: Let us have mercy on the impious; which all, except the Seventy, translated alike. And the sense is: rather let the impious obtain mercy, and learn my clemency, while he too is saved. And again, to the Lord as he speaks, the Prophet answered in the person of human impatience: And he will not learn righteousness. And the sense is: and how will he be able to know your righteousness, if he has experienced only clemency? And he gives the reasons why he wishes him to learn the righteousness of God: because he has acted wickedly in the land of the saints, and has fought continually against your saints, he ought to feel torments. And again the Lord, tempering the sentence, says: And let him not see, or he will not see the glory of the Lord. And the sense is: it is enough for him, in place of all punishment, that he will not see me reigning with my saints in my majesty. Some wish the impious one, that is, RESA (רשע), to be understood as the devil, of whom it is written in the ninth psalm: You have rebuked the nations, and the impious has perished; you have blotted out their name for ever and for ever and ever. The swords of the enemy have failed unto the end, and their cities you have destroyed (Ps 9:6). But let us take the impious generally either for the sinner or for one who does not have the worship of God.
Commentary on Isaiah

O Lord, let your hand be exalted, and let them not see: let them see, and let the zeal of the people be confounded, and let fire devour your enemies. LXX: O Lord, your arm is lofty, and they did not know; but knowing they will be confounded: zeal will seize the untaught people, and now fire will eat the adversaries. What he had said above, and he will not see the glory of the Lord, can be understood thus: You ask, O Prophet, that I should not have mercy on the impious, lest, if I have had mercy on him, he who has acted wickedly in the land of the saints should begin not to know righteousness; I answer you: will he then not see the glory of the Lord? Will he then not behold my triumphs, he who rather ought to see me reigning, so that he may know how great a good he lacks? And this is to be read more pointedly, with the voice of one asking a question.

In the resurrection itself it is not easy to see God, except for those who are clean of heart; hence, "Blessed are the clean of heart, for they shall see God." From here on he begins to speak of that world where all who rise again will not see God, but only those who rise to eternal life. The unworthy will not see him, for of them it is said, "Let the wicked be taken away lest he behold the brightness of the Lord." But the worthy will see him, and of such the Lord spoke when, though present, he was not seen, saying, "He that loves me keeps my commandments, and he that loves me shall be loved of my Father, and I will love him and will manifest myself to him."

In this human form the good will see him in whom they have believed; the wicked, him whom they have despised. But the wicked will not see him in the form of God in which he is equal to the Father, for as the prophet says, "The wicked shall be taken off that he may not see the glory of the Lord," and, on the other hand, "Blessed are the clean of heart, for they shall see God."

Then, therefore, we shall come and we shall enjoy the one thing; but the one thing will be all things to us. For what was it I said, my brothers, when I began to speak? What is that sufficiency which we shall possess when we shall have no need? What is the sufficiency which we shall possess? I had intended to say, "What will God give to us which he will not give to them?" "Let the wicked be taken away that he may not see the glory of God." Hence God will give his glory to us so that we may enjoy it; and the wicked will be taken away that he may not see the glory of God. His coming means his return from the judgment to his kingdom. The Lord comes to us after the judgment, because he lifts us up from his human appearance in the contemplation of his divinity; his coming means that he leads us to the vision of his glory. We see in his divinity after the judgment the one we beheld in his humanity at the judgment. At the judgment he comes in the form of a servant and appears to everyone, since it is written, "They will look on him whom they pierced." To which the Prophet answered: O Lord, let your hand be exalted, and be stretched out to strike, so that the impious may not see you, and may not enjoy the light of your glory, not even for repentance. And it is the fire of repentance, which tortures their hearts because they have lost such a Lord. This can also be understood of the Jews, who did not know Christ, the arm of the Lord, and when they have seen and recognized him whom they had fastened to the gibbet, will be confounded. Then the untaught people, not knowing the law of God, will be roused by the goads of zeal, when it sees that the nations have succeeded to its place, and burns with the fire of regret, or with the pain of punishment, when it hears that which is written: Depart into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels (Matt 25:41).

Note that there are two kinds of zeal, one full of love, the other full of hatred. The former is indicated in the words, "The zeal of your house has devoured me"; the latter, in the words, "Zeal has taken hold of the senseless people, and now fire shall devour your opponents."

Whenever you see a man living in wickedness, and enjoying great prosperity, and suffering no calamity, on this account lament for him the more, because, being under the power of disease and grievous corruption, he increases his own weakness, becoming worse by luxury and indolence. For punishment is not in itself an evil, but the real evil is sin. The latter separates us from God; the former leads us to God, and mitigates His wrath. How is this shown? Hear the prophet saying, "O priests, comfort ye, comfort ye my people. Speak to the heart of Jerusalem, and say that she has received of the Lord's hand double for her sins." And again: "O Lord our God, give us peace, for thou hast repaid all to us."
HOMILIES CONCERNING THE STATUES 6:14

But I say all this now, and select all the histories that contain trials and tribulations, and the wrath of kings, and their evil designs, in order that we may fear nothing, save only offending God. For then also was there a furnace burning; yet they derided it, but feared sin. For they knew that if they were consumed in the fire, they should suffer nothing that was to be dreaded; but that if they were guilty of impiety: they should undergo the extremes of misery. It is the greatest punishment to commit sin, though we may remain unpunished; as on the other hand, it is the greatest honour and repose to live virtuously, though we may be punished. For sins separate us from God; as He Himself speaks; "Have not your sins separated between you and Me?" But punishments lead us back to God. As one saith, "Give peace; for Thou hast recompensed us for all things." Suppose any one hath a wound; which is the most deserving of fear, gangrene, or the surgeon's knife? the steel, or the devouring progress of the ulcer? Sin is a gangrene, punishment is the surgeon's knife. As then, he who hath a gangrene, although he is not lanced, hath to sustain the malady, and is then in the worse condition, when he is not lanced; so also the sinner, though he be not punished, is the most wretched of men; and is then especially wretched, when he hath no punishment, and is suffering no distress.

O Lord, you will give us peace: for you have wrought all our works for us. LXX: O Lord our God, give us peace: for you have rendered all things to us. It must be noted that after he has rendered to us our works, he is going to give peace, and how they set out the reasons why they ask for peace. For they say that for all the works which they have wrought upon the earth they have endured torments, and that it is just that after punishments and tortures they should obtain mercy. Or otherwise: Because the consummation of the world has come, and all that you spoke through the Prophets has been fulfilled in deed, and you have rendered all that you promised, grant us peace, which surpasses all understanding.

The time when our external enemy the devil will be under our feet is when the internal enemy, covetousness, has been healed, and we shall be living in peace. What sort of peace? The sort that "eye has not seen nor ear heard." What sort of peace? The sort that no imagination can conceive and no quarreling intrude on. What sort of peace? The sort about which the apostle said, "And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts." About this peace the prophet Isaiah says, "O Lord our God, give us peace, for you have given us everything you promised." You promised Christ; you have given him to us. You promised his cross and the shedding of his blood for the forgiveness of sins; you have given them to us. You promised his ascension and the sending of the Holy Spirit from heaven; you have given them to us. You promised us a church spread throughout the world; you have given it. You promised there would be heretics to try us and put us through our paces, and the church would triumph over their errors; you have given this. You promised the abolition of the idols of the heathen; you have given it.

What's the meaning of "Where, death, is your sting?" It means, "Where is sin?" You ask, and it is nowhere. "For the sting of death is sin." They are the apostle's words, not mine. That is when we will be able to say, "Where, death, is your sting?" Sin will be nowhere, neither to take you captive, nor to assault you nor to tickle your consciousness. For the Son of God indeed, being himself the Word, is Lord of all. But we once were subject from the first to the slavery of corruption and the curse of the law. Then by degrees fashioning for ourselves things that were not, we served, as says the blessed apostle, "them which by nature are no gods." Ignorant of the true God, we preferred things that were not to the truth. But afterwards, as the ancient people when oppressed in Egypt groaned, so when we too had the law "engrafted" in us, according to the unutterable sighings of the Spirit made our intercession, "O Lord our God, take possession of us"; then, as "he became a house of refuge" and a "God and defense," so also he became our Lord. Nor did he then begin to be, but we began to have him for our Lord.

O Lord our God, lords have possessed us without you: only in you may we remember your name. LXX: Lord our God, possess us: O Lord, besides you we know no other, we call upon your name. For this reason we seek mercy and peace, which is to be granted after all things, because lords have possessed us without you, namely the idols, or the demons who sit by the idols; and we ask nothing else but that, after very many errors, we may be worthy to remember your name. According to the Seventy, those who said, Lord God, possess us, pray for this, that after peace has been restored to them they may become the possession of God. This indeed we read also of Wisdom, which according to the Hebrew speaks in Proverbs: God possessed me, the beginning of his ways (Prov 8:22), although some copies wrongly have creature for possession. Then it follows: But before all the hills he begot me. For how can begetting be fitted to a creature, when it rather suits possession? It is written in Deuteronomy: Is not he your father, who possessed you, and made you, and created you? (Deut 32:6). And this must be considered, that he did not say, the Lord, or God, possessed you, and made you, and created you; but father, so that the clemency of the name might soften the severity of the power. And what follows, O Lord, besides you we know no other, does not exclude the Son, but joins him to the Father; for he did not say "We know no other," but "Besides you we know no other." And since the Son says, I am in the Father and the Father in me, we do not know the Son outside the Father (John 14:10), because we know him in the Father. And indeed we name his name too, saying in the Lord's Prayer: Our Father, who art in heaven (Matt 6:9).
Commentary on Isaiah

Let the dying not live; let the giants not rise again. Therefore you have visited and crushed them, and have destroyed all memory of them. LXX: For the dead will not see life, nor will physicians raise them up. Therefore you have brought on, and destroyed, and taken away every male of theirs. Symmachus, in his manner, more plainly: The dead will not give life; the giants will not raise up. Therefore you have visited and crushed them, and have utterly destroyed all memory of them. Let us speak first according to the Seventy. The question seems difficult, how the dead do not see life. It is solved thus: they do not see life so long as they are dead. As if we were to say, a blind man does not see the light so long as he is blind; but if he has recovered his health, he will look upon the light: so too he who is dead in iniquity and sins cannot live before he is given life by righteousness and the virtues, through him who says, I am the life (John 14). Hence God is also called the God of the living, not of the dead (Matt 22). For the soul that sins, it shall die (Ezek 18:4). We read in the Epistle written to the Hebrews: Not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works (Heb 6:1). But if sins are called dead works, why should not, on the contrary, the virtues be called living works? And what follows, Nor will physicians raise them up, its sense is plain: the fables of the poets are condemned, who boast that Virbius was raised up by Aesculapius. And this is to be said not only of the dead, but of every infirmity: that without the mercy of God the art of healing avails nothing. But how? Unless the Lord builds the house, they have labored in vain who build it: unless the Lord guards the city, he has watched in vain who guards it (Ps 126 [127]:1, 2). So unless the Lord has cured the sickness, the physicians labor in vain who desire to heal the sick. Unless the Lord has guarded health, they guard it in vain who even publish precepts for guarding health in their own books; and one must always learn, not only in the health of the body but also in that of the soul: Bless the Lord, O my soul, who heals all your sicknesses (Ps 102 [103]:1, 3). Further, those who persist dead in sin, and can recover the health of the soul by no art of medicine, will be utterly destroyed and taken away by the Lord, and whatever is strong in them, which is called the male, will be wholly removed. Hence Pharaoh too does not wish to kill the female sex, which is frail in itself and can easily perish, but every male, which, if it has grown up and come to manly age, is killed with difficulty (Exod 1). According to Symmachus, the dead will not give life, because, being dead in sin, they cannot give life to others, nor is praise seemly in the mouth of a sinner. And the giants, that is, RAPHAIM (רפאים), will not raise up others, they who themselves, according to the book of Genesis, are called the falling. And the Lord visits them, so that all memory both of the dead and of the giants may be blotted out. For he alone it is who raises the dead, of whom it is said: As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so the Son also gives life to whom he will (John 5:21). We can call the dead the images of dead men, and the giants the demons who sit by their images. Nor should it trouble us why the Seventy translated male and the other translators memory, since among the Hebrews both are written with the same three letters, ZAI (ז), and CHAPH (כ), and RES (ר). But when we say memorial, it is read ZACHAR; when male, ZOCHOR. And they think that Saul was deceived by this ambiguity of the word when he fought against Amalek and killed every male of them (1 Sam 15). For when God commanded that he should blot out all memory of Amalek under heaven, he, for memory, led astray not so much by error as by the desire for plunder, interpreted males, not knowing that saying of the Apostle: Do not err, God is not mocked (Gal 6:7).
Morals on the Book of Job, Book 17, Section 30

For hence it is said by the prophet, "The dead shall not live; the giants shall not rise up again." For whom does he call "the dead" except sinners, and whom does he designate "giants" except those who over and above take pride in sin. Now the former do "not live," because by sinning they have forfeited the life of righteousness; these latter too "cannot rise up again" after death because after their transgression they are swollen with pride and do not have recourse to the remedies of penitence.

You have been indulgent to the nation, O Lord, you have been indulgent to the nation. Have you been glorified? You have removed far all the ends of the earth. LXX: Add evils to them, O Lord, add evils to the glorious of the earth: you have made far off all the ends of the earth. The evils which the Seventy put twice are not found in the Hebrew; but because he had said above, Therefore you have brought on and destroyed, and taken away every male of theirs, following the same sense they added of their own, evils: so that those who are glorious on the earth may be crushed by double evils. Further, according to the Hebrews the sense is far otherwise, and in agreement with the earlier discussion. The Lord had said: Let us have mercy on the impious. The Prophet had answered: And where is your righteousness? especially since he has wrought such great evils against your saints. To which the Lord: And he will not see, he says, the glory of the Lord. Again the Prophet: Let your hand be exalted to strike, and let them not see your glory, which they do not deserve to behold. To which the Lord: Let them see rather and be confounded. Again the Prophet: O Lord, give us peace, and possess us, who remember your name. But let the impious and the proud not live, nor rise again in glory, but crush all memory of them. And he gives the reasons why he desires them to perish: You have been indulgent to the nation, O Lord, you have been indulgent to the nation; have you been glorified? And the sense is: You have often had mercy on the nations, that is, on the human race, and have exercised toward them an incredible clemency; have they known you? Have they glorified your name? Have they not, on the contrary, withdrawn far from you? For security breeds negligence, and negligence contempt.
Commentary on Isaiah

O Lord, in distress they have sought you; in the tribulation of murmuring your teaching was to them. LXX: O Lord, in tribulation I remembered you; in small tribulation your teaching was to us. Because, being indulgent, you have often been despised and not glorified, but on the contrary all have withdrawn from the knowledge of you, therefore, O Lord, strike them, so that in distress they may seek you, and in the tribulation of murmuring your teaching may be to them: when so great a weight of evils presses upon them that they do not even dare to cry out confidently, but swallow their pain in silence. According to the Seventy, the Prophet remembers the Lord in tribulation, according to what is said in the psalm: Out of tribulation I called upon the Lord, and he heard me in a broad place (Ps 117 [118]:5). And in another place: To the Lord I cried when I was troubled, and he heard me (Ps 119 [120]:1). Hence the Apostle says: We are troubled, but not distressed; we suffer persecution, but are not forsaken (2 Cor 4:8). And in another place: The sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come, which will be revealed in us (Rom 8:18). But if a small tribulation teaches, and amends, and corrects, how much more a great one, when we are reminded of our condition and remember the power of God!

As a woman who has conceived, when she draws near to the birth, cries out in pain in her pangs: so have we become before your face, O Lord. We have conceived, and as it were travailed, and have brought forth spirit. LXX: And as a woman in travail, when she draws near to the birth, cries out in her pain: so have we become ÷ to your beloved ⁚ because of fear of you, O Lord; we have received in the womb, and have travailed, and have brought forth the spirit of your salvation, which we have made upon the earth. As a woman drawing near to the birth is compelled by pain to cry out, so we seek you in distress, and before the face of the dread of you we have conceived, and travailed, and brought forth, not children of the flesh, but of the spirit: so that we may believe in you with our whole mind, and learn through torments him whom we did not perceive through benefits. What the Seventy added, so have we become to your beloved, for which the others translated, so have we become before your face, O Lord, is to be marked beforehand with an obelus. But we can take the beloved of the Lord as Christ, for fear of whom we conceive, and travail, and bring forth, and make the spirit of salvation upon the earth. An apostolic man can say this too, when he instructs the peoples and imitates the apostle Paul: My little children, with whom I travail again until Christ be formed in you (Gal 4:19). Or is it to be doubted that the apostle Paul made the spirit of salvation upon the earth, who preached the Gospel from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum (Rom 15), and as a wise architect laid the foundation, besides which no one can lay another, which is Christ Jesus (1 Cor 3)? Whether, then, we read, because of fear of you, O Lord, we have received in the womb, or according to the Hebrew, before your face, O Lord, we have conceived, and have received in the womb, both pertain to this: that from the fear and remembrance of the Lord we conceive the word of God, and our heart is illumined as we say: The light of your countenance has been signed upon us, O Lord (Ps 4:7). And, show your face, and we shall be saved (Ps 79 [80]:4).
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 43

That there are also some souls that conceive offspring, the prophet made clear when he said: "from fear of you, Lord, we conceived in the womb and travailed and gave birth to a spirit of salvation which you made upon the earth". For just as in those who are pregnant the seed is formed and shaped, so also in the soul that receives the word, the conception of the word is gradually formed and shaped within it. And this I think is what Paul says to the Galatians: "my children, whom I again bring forth in travail until Christ be formed in you", which is as though he were to say: until the word be formed and made manifest in you. In the epistle to Timothy he says likewise that a woman shall be saved "through the bearing of children, if she abide in faith and love and holiness with chastity". But who is this woman, if not the soul that conceives the word of God and of truth, and gives birth to good works like to Christ? But it is irrational to suppose that what he says was said of a bodily bearing: "the woman, being seduced, fell into transgression; but she shall be saved through the bearing of children, if she abide in faith and love and holiness with chastity". Therefore the souls that have newly received the word and, being still established as pregnant, have not yet borne fruit in it, having it intelligibly in the womb, cannot endure the discourse that stands "in the holy place" opposing the truth, nor stand firm so as not to be seduced by its persuasions.

The soul therefore conceives from this seed of the word and forms the conceived word within itself, until it brings forth the spirit of the fear of God. Amen!".

This and no other is the meaning of the words of Isaiah: "We have conceived and brought forth the spirit of salvation."

Salvations we have not wrought on the earth; therefore the inhabitants of the world have not fallen. LXX: We shall not fall, but the inhabitants of the earth will fall. A different translation must needs have a different sense too. According to the Hebrew this is said: Because we have done nothing worthy of your mercy, therefore the impious have not fallen, but to this day prevail and possess the earth. But the Seventy assert this: that while the saints make the spirit of salvation upon the earth, those who are inhabitants of the earth fall; although between world, which in Hebrew is called THEBEL (תבל) and in Greek οἰκουμένη, and earth there is much difference.
