Even now let us rejoice somehow or other in this hope derived from the promises of one most faithful, until that richest of all possible joys arises, when "we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is," and our joy nobody shall take from us. Of this hope, you see, we have also received already the acceptable and freely given pledge that is the Holy Spirit, who produces in our hearts the unutterable groanings of holy desire. "For we have conceived," as Isaiah says, "and have brought forth the spirit of salvation." And, "when a woman is in labor," the Lord says, "she has sorrow, because her day has come; but when she has brought forth, there is great joy, because a human being has been born into the world." This will be the joy that nobody will take away from us; on the day when we are brought forth into the eternal light from this conception of faith. So meanwhile let us fast and pray, while it is still the day of bringing forth.
Homilies on the Gospels 2:13

"When a woman gives birth, she is sorrowful because her hour has come." He refers to holy church as a woman on account of her fruitfulness in good works and because she never ceases to beget spiritual children for God. He says also in another place about this, "The kingdom of heaven is like yeast which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour until the whole [mass] was leavened." A woman took some yeast when the church, by the Lord's generosity, secured the energy of love and faith from on high. She hid this "in three measures of flour until the whole [mass] was leavened" when she performed her ministry of imparting the word of life to parts of Asia [Minor], Europe and Africa, until all the bounds of the world were on fire with love for the heavenly kingdom. The one who said sadly to those who were departing from the purity of the faith, "My little children, for whom I am again in travail, until Christ be formed in you," was indicating that he was among this woman's members. They testified that they were among her members who were enkindled with heavenly desires, who cried out in praise of their Maker, "It is out of fear of you, Lord, that we have conceived and been in travail and given birth to the Spirit."
AGAINST HERESIES 5:34.1

Then, too, Isaiah himself has plainly declared that there shall be joy of this nature at the resurrection of the just, when he says: "The dead shall rise again; those, too, who are in the tombs shall arise, and those who are in the earth shall rejoice. For the dew from Thee is health to them."
ON THE RESURRECTION OF THE FLESH 31

Unquestionably, if the people were indulging in figurative murmurs that their bones were become dry and that their hope had perished—plaintive at the consequences of their dispersion—then God might fairly enough seem to have consoled their figurative despair with a figurative promise. Since, however, no injury had as yet alighted on the people from their dispersion, although the hope of the resurrection had very frequently failed among them, it is manifest that it was owing to the perishing condition of their bodies that their faith in the resurrection was shaken. God, therefore, was rebuilding the faith that the people were pulling down. But even if it were true that Israel was depressed at some shock in their existing circumstances, we must not on that account suppose that the purpose of revelation could have rested in a parable. Its aim must have been to testify a resurrection, in order to raise the nation's hope to even an eternal salvation and an indispensable restoration and thereby turn off their minds from brooding over their present affairs. This indeed is the aim of other prophets likewise. "You shall go forth," [says Malachi], "from your tombs, as young calves let loose from their bonds, and you shall tread down your enemies." And again [Isaiah says], "Your heart shall rejoice, and your bones shall spring up like the grass," because the grass also is renewed by the dissolution and corruption of the seed. In a word, if it is contended that the figure of the rising bones refers properly to the state of Israel, why is the same hope announced to all nations, instead of being limited to Israel only, of reinvesting those bony remains with bodily substance and vital breath and of raising up their dead out of the grave? For the language is universal: "The dead shall arise and come forth from their graves; for the dew which comes from you is medicine to their bones." In another passage it is written: "All flesh shall come to worship before me, says the Lord." When? When the fashion of this world shall begin to pass away. For he said before, "As the new heaven and the new earth, which I make, remain before me, says the Lord, so shall your seed remain." Then also shall be fulfilled what is written afterwards: "And they shall go forth" [namely, from their graves] "and shall see the carcasses of those who have transgressed: for their worm shall never die, nor shall their fire be quenched; and they shall be a spectacle to all flesh," even to that which, being raised again from the dead and brought out from the grave, shall adore the Lord for his great grace.
Catechetical Lecture 18:15-16

Isaiah the prophet says, "The dead men shall rise again, and those who are in the tombs shall awake." And the prophet Ezekiel, now before us, says most plainly, "Behold, I will open your graves and bring you up out of your graves." And Daniel says, "Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall arise, some to everlasting life and some to everlasting shame."67And there are many Scriptures that testify of the resurrection of the dead. For there are many other sayings on this matter. But now, by way of remembrance only, we will make a passing mention of the raising of Lazarus on the fourth day and just allude, because of the shortness of the time, to the widow's son also who was raised. And merely for the sake of reminding you, let me mention the ruler of the synagogue's daughter, and the rending of the rocks, and how "there arose many bodies of the saints which slept," their graves having been opened. But especially be it remembered that "Christ has been raised from the dead."
Catechetical Lecture 4:31

Do not listen to those who say that this body is not raised up; for raised it is, as Isaiah witnesses, saying, "The dead shall arise, and they in the tombs shall be raised." Or, as Daniel says, "Many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall arise, some to everlasting life and some to everlasting shame." But while rising again is the common lot of all people, the manner of rising again is not alike for all. For while we all receive everlasting bodies, those bodies are not alike for all. That is to say, the righteous receive such bodies as may enable them to join with the band of angels throughout eternity, while sinners received bodies in which to undergo through the ages the torture of their sins.
Commentary on Hosea

Let us love that dew about which Moses speaks: "Let my doctrine drop as the rain," and about which Isaiah says: "Thy dead men shall live, together with my dead body shall they arise. Awake and sing, ye that dwell in dust: for thy dew is as the dew of herbs, and the earth shall cast forth the dead."
Commentary on Hosea

In the same way that the Lord becomes the light, the way, the truth, the bread, the vine, the fire, the shepherd, the lamb, the door, and many other things to believers, so also does he become the dew to us who are in need of his mercy and know ourselves to be feverish with sin, about whom Isaiah said, "The dew which is from you is their health."
Commentary on Isaiah

Let your dead live, let my slain rise again: awake and give praise, you who dwell in the dust, for your dew is a dew of lights, and the land of the giants you will pull down to ruin. LXX: The dead will rise again, and they will rise again from the tombs, and those who are in the earth will rejoice. For your dew is their healing, but the land of the impious will fall. While the saints travail and bring forth the spirit, and the inhabitants of the earth fall, because they have not wrought salvations on the earth, those whom the Apostle calls the dead in Christ, and who have been slain for the name of the Lord, will rise again in glory (1 Thess 4). And because their death is sleep, they are said, not, as according to the Seventy, to rise again, but to awaken and to wake up. Hence Lazarus too, who was to be awakened, is called sleeping by the Lord (John 11). All the martyrs, then, and the holy men who shed their blood for Christ, and whose whole life was a martyrdom, will rise again and awaken, and will praise God their Creator, they who now dwell in the dust, of whom it is written in Daniel: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth will rise again, some to everlasting life, and some to reproach and everlasting confusion (Dan 12:2). And in John the Evangelist we read: The hour will come, and now is, when those who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live, and those who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment (John 5:28, 29). For the dew of the Lord, surpassing, as in the fables of the poets, all the Paeonian herbs, will give life to the bodies of the dead. And as, when seeds have been cast into the earth, the dew little by little makes the plants grow and come to the fruits of their kind, so the dew of the Lord, which is put for mercy, will be a dew of very many lights, which in Hebrew is called OROTH (אורות). But the land, that is, the bodies of the Raphaim, namely of the giants and the impious, the Lord will pull down into everlasting punishments. Indeed, for RAPHAIM (רפאים) the Seventy alone translated the impious. And because we read above, The dead will not see life, nor will physicians raise them up, for which Aquila and Symmachus translated Raphaim and giants, we ask what the cause of the error is, that for the Hebrew RAPHAIM some put giants, others physicians. If the Hebrew word RAPHAIM has VAU following its first letter RES, it is read ROPHAIM (רופאים) and signifies physicians; but if it is written without the letter VAU, it is read RAPHAIM, and is translated giants. And at the same time, because he had said above, The dead will not see life, so as to show more plainly that it was not said there of those dead by the law of nature and the separation of soul and body, but of those who are dead in sin, he now on the contrary says to God: Your dead will live, who have been slain for your sake; who are not called dead absolutely, as the Seventy translated, but, according to the Hebrew, where it is said JEJU METHECA (יהיו מתיך), your dead.
Commentary on Zechariah

But the heavens too shall give their dew, the heavens of which it is written in Psalm 18 (19): The heavens tell the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands. Of these heavens it is said in the song of Deuteronomy: Rejoice, O heavens, with him, that is, with the Lord and Savior, whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son; it is he who speaks with Moses: Let my speech be awaited like the rain, and let my words come down like the dew. For those who were dead in sins shall rise again, and those who lay in whitewashed sepulchres, which are full of dead men's bones, shall be raised up, and those who dwell in the earth shall rejoice. And what the cause of the joy is, the following words show: For the dew which is from you is their healing.
City of God 20.21

The first part [of the verse] concerns the resurrection of the just, but the last few words may be taken to mean "the bodies of the wicked will fall into the ruin of damnation." In regard to the resurrection of the just, the attentive reader will notice some distinction. "The dead shall rise" refers to the first resurrection; "those in the graves" refers to the second; and in the following words we may not improperly find a reference to the saints whom the Lord will find alive on earth. As for the word "your dew is their health," we are not wrong in taking "health" to mean "immortality," that most perfect health which needs no daily medicine of ordinary food.
1 CLEMENT 50

All the generations from Adam to this day have passed away; but those who were made perfect in charity by the grace of God live among the saints; and they shall be made manifest at the judgment of the kingdom of Christ. For it is written, "Enter into your chamber a little while, until my wrath and anger pass, and I remember the good day and will raise you up out of your graves."
ON THE RESURRECTION OF THE FLESH 27

When we read, "Go, my people, enter into your closets for a little while, until my anger passes away," we have in the closets graves, in which they will have to rest for a little while, who shall have at the end of the world departed this life in the last furious onset of the power of Antichrist. Why else did he use the expression closets in preference to some other receptacle, if it were not that the flesh is kept in these closets or cellars salted and reserved for use, to be drawn out thence on a suitable occasion? It is on a similar principle that embalmed corpses are set aside for burial in mausoleums and sepulchers, in order that they may be removed from there when the Master shall order it. Since, therefore, there is consistency in thus understanding the passage (for what refuge of little closets could possibly shelter us from the wrath of God?), it appears that by the very phrase which he uses, "until his anger passes away," which shall extinguish Antichrist, he in fact shows that after that indignation the flesh will come forth from the sepulcher, in which it had been deposited previous to the bursting out of the anger. Now out of the closets nothing else is brought than that which had been put into them, and after the extirpation of Antichrist shall be busily transacted the great process of the resurrection.
HOMILIES ON GENESIS 2.3

He builds, therefore, the ark and makes in it nests, that is, certain storerooms, in which animals of diverse kinds may be received. Of which the prophet also says: "Go, my people, enter into your storerooms, hide yourself for a little while, until the fury of my wrath passes by." This people, then, which is saved in the Church, is compared to all those, whether men or animals, which were saved in the ark.
Commentary on Isaiah

But according to the anagogy, the people of God is commanded to enter into its chambers, or storerooms, for ταμεῖα means both: to shut, according to the precept of the Gospel, the door of its chamber (Matt 6), and to say with the Prophet: Set a guard, O Lord, on my mouth, and a fortified door to my lips (Ps 140 [141]:3); and to hide itself a little, however little, until the wrath of the Lord passes, so that it does nothing for the sake of glory, but enjoys the good of conscience and awaits God alone as judge. And the storerooms which are to be shut and hidden by those who have become rich in works and words are prudence, temperance, fortitude, justice, so that the left hand may not know what the right hand does, so that we may enjoy the riches of the Law and the Prophets and the Gospel. And that all the days of our life are short and very small, Jacob, exceeding a hundred years, says: Small and very evil are my days (Gen 47:9). And the wrath of the Lord that is to pass is that which those store up for themselves who are unwilling to do penance; after it has passed, the storerooms will by no means be shut any longer, but what is written will be fulfilled: Nothing is hidden that will not be revealed, and secret that will not be made manifest (Luke 8:17).
Commentary on Isaiah

Go, my people, enter into your chambers, shut your doors upon you: hide yourself a little for a moment, until the indignation passes. For behold, the Lord will come forth from his place, to visit the iniquity of the inhabitant of the earth against him; and the earth will disclose its blood, and will no longer cover its slain. LXX: Go, my people, enter into your chambers, shut your door: hide yourself a little, however little, until the wrath of the Lord passes. For behold, the Lord from the holy place will bring wrath upon the inhabitants of the earth, and the earth will disclose its blood, and will no longer hide the slain. Above he had said of the saints, The dead will rise again, and those who are in the tombs will rise again; for the dew from you is their healing; and on the contrary of the impious, but the land of the impious will fall. Now he speaks to the saints: because resurrection has been promised to you, until the wrath of God rages against sinners and the impious, enter into your tombs and hide yourselves, for it is a short time until the indignation of God passes. For indeed the Lord comes forth from his place, because the Lord is merciful and compassionate, and the most clement father is compelled to strike his negligent children, and in a manner to be changed from his own judgment, so that he may visit and bring his wrath upon the inhabitants of the earth, of whom it is said in Hosea: Cursing and lying and adultery and theft have been poured out upon the inhabitants of the earth (Hos 4:2). And in the Apocalypse we read three times, Woe upon the inhabitants of the earth (Rev 8:13). But the righteous, although they are seen on the earth, yet their citizenship is in the heavens; they can say, I am a stranger on the earth, and a sojourner, as all my fathers were (Ps 38 [39]:13), and they enjoy the dwelling of the Most High, of whom the holy man speaks: He who dwells in the help of the Most High will abide in the protection of the God of heaven (Ps 90 [91]:1). Then the earth will disclose its blood, of which God speaks to Cain: The voice of your brother's blood cries to me from the earth, which has opened its mouth to receive your brother's blood from your hand (Gen 4:10, 11). This can also be understood of the Martyrs, who shed their blood for Christ and cry out beneath the altar of God: How long, O Lord, do you not avenge our blood on those who dwell upon the earth? (Rev 6:10). Of them Moses too says in the Song: The blood of his sons will be vindicated and avenged, and he will repay vengeance to his enemies (Deut 32:43). This blood the earth which had received it will disclose, and it will by no means cover the slain of the Lord, but will bring them out into public view for the condemnation of those who killed the Martyrs. Let this be understood of the simple resurrection.
LETTER 36

Certainly there are two things that make us hope for the bliss of the just and the end of all suffering: death and the resurrection from the dead. In death is rest, as the prophet says, "My people, enter into your chambers, hide yourself a little until the indignation of the Lord pass away." But in the resurrection there is perfect happiness in the whole person, that is, in flesh and spirit. Consequently we are not to think that both of these are to be marked by the labor of fasting but rather by the rejoicing of refreshment.
Commentary on Isaiah

And what follows, For behold, the Lord from the holy place will bring his wrath, signifies this: that the wrath of God begins from the saints, or that all his vengeance is just and holy, not coming down from disturbance of mind, as is usual among men, but from zeal to correct. And I consider the earth of the inhabitants to be that of which it is written: Let the earth hear the words of my mouth (Deut 32:1). And: Give ear, O earth (Isa 1:2). And again: Earth, earth, hear the word of the Lord (Jer 22:29). For as those who dwell on the earth, so those who are in the flesh cannot please God (Rom 8). And earth in this place signifies the soul that lives carnally. And it will disclose its blood, if it has caused anyone to stumble, and deserves to hear with Cain: The voice of your brother's blood cries to me from the earth, which has opened its mouth to receive your brother's blood (Gen 4:10, 11). All blood, then, will be required on the day of judgment, nor will the earth hide its blood; and the slain whom it has killed, whether willingly or through negligence, it will bring out into the open.

n: Hard. Septuagint, "holy." (Calmet) --- Leviathan. That is, the devil, the great enemy of the people of God. He is called the bar serpent from his strength, and the crooked serpent from his wiles, and the whale of the sea, from the tyranny he exercises in the sea of this world. He was spiritually slain by the death of Christ, when his power was destroyed. (Challoner) --- It may also literally refer to Nabuchodonosor, and the king of Egypt, or rather to Cambyses, or Holofernes, but particularly Cambyses. (Calmet)
Vineyard; the Church of Christ, (Challoner) or Judea. It may be the beginning of a noted song. (Calmet)
Drink; or, as the Hebrew may also be rendered, I will continually water it. (Challoner) --- God will protect his people. (Calmet)

In me, against the Church; nor shall I become as a thorn or brier in its regard; or march against it, or set it on fire: but it shall always take fast hold of me, and keep an everlasting peace with me. (Challoner) --- God rather speaks of the enemy. If he attempt to lay waste this vineyard, I will chastise him. (Calmet)

Rush in. Some understand this of the enemies of the true Israel, that shall invade it in vain. Others of the spiritual invasion made by the apostles of Christ. (Challoner) --- Protestants, "He shall cause them that come of Jacob to take root." Septuagint, "those who come are children of Jacob." (Haydock)

Struck. Hath God punished the carnal persecuting Jews, in proportion to their doings against Christ and his saints? (Challoner) --- God punished Israel as a father: but he will destroy the Chaldeans, &c. (Calmet)

Cast off. When the synagogue shall be cast off, thou shalt judge it in measure, and in proportion to its crimes. (Challoner) --- The Israelites have been rigorously punished. (Calmet) --- He, &c. God hath designed severe punishments in the day of his wrath. (Challoner)
Jacob; viz., of such of them as shall be converted. (Challoner) --- Altar, dedicated to idols: then he shall obtain pardon. (Calmet)
City. Jerusalem, (Challoner) or more probably Babylon, of which he is going to speak.
Women. The princes shall be weak and irresolute. (Calmet) --- Septuagint, "Hither, ye women, coming from the shew. For it is not an intelligent people."

River Euphrates, even to the Nile. (Haydock) --- Nabuchodonosor laid waste all the intermediate countries. Afterwards Cyrus gave the people liberty. On the death of Cambyses, the nations were in consternation; and it was only during the peaceable reign of Darius that Israel returned, though not in a body, as the Jews had done twenty years before, chap. xxvi. (Calmet) --- By one, into the Church of Christ, John xi. (Menochius)
Trumpet. The preaching of the Gospel for the conversion of the Jews. (Challoner)

f: Commentary on Isaiah

In that day the Lord will visit with his hard and great and strong sword upon Leviathan the bar serpent, and upon Leviathan the twisting serpent, and he will slay the whale that is in the sea. LXX: In that day God will bring the holy and great and strong sword upon the dragon, the fleeing serpent, upon the dragon, the twisting serpent, and he will slay the dragon that is in the sea. The Hebrews hand down that the devil, that is, the slanderer, which is a Greek name, is called in Hebrew SATAN (שטן), that is, adversary. Hence in Zechariah too it is said: Satan, that is, the adversary, stood at his right hand to oppose him (Zech 3:1). And he is also called BELIAL (בליעל), that is, apostate, transgressor, and without yoke. Hence the Apostle too: What fellowship, he says, has Christ with Belial? (2 Cor 6:15). And wherever the Seventy put sons of pestilence, in the Hebrew is written sons of Belial. Hence also that which is sung in the psalm about the mystery of the Savior, The son of iniquity shall not proceed to harm him (Ps 88 [89]:23), in the Hebrew is said the son of Belial. And he is called by other names too, as is written in another psalm: You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample the lion and the dragon (Ps 90 [91]:13). This dragon is properly called in the Hebrew language LEVIATHAN (לויתן). He is the great whale of whom it is told in mystical language in Job that he is to be caught by Christ: Who is going to catch the great whale (Job 40:20); for there too Leviathan is put for whale; and again: But you will draw the dragon with a hook, you will put a halter about his nostrils; and immediately: This is the beginning of the Lord's creation, which was made to be mocked by his angels. And in the psalm: This is the great and wide sea: there are creeping things without number, small animals with great. This dragon which you have formed to mock him (Ps 103 [104]:25, 26). Of him John too writes in the Apocalypse: There was a battle in heaven: Michael and his angels fought with the dragon, and the dragon fought, and his angels, and they did not prevail, nor was a place found for them in heaven (Rev 12:7ff.). And: The great dragon was cast out, the ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, who makes the whole world go astray; and he was cast down to the earth, and his angels with him; and there it is said: The accuser of our brethren has been cast out, who accused them before our God (ibid., 12:10). And it must be noted that in the psalm and in Job the dragon, that is, Leviathan, is said to have been made for this purpose, that he might be mocked by the angels. Hence also the Apostles receive power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and upon all the power of the enemy (Luke 10). Because, then, from the place where it is written, Behold, the Lord will scatter the earth and will lay it bare (above, Isa 24:1), or, according to the Seventy, Behold, the Lord will destroy the world and will make it desolate, up to the present passage, judgment has been foretold against the world at the consummation of the world, and the last enemy, death, will be destroyed (1 Cor 15): therefore the final sentence is against the devil, that the holy and great and strong sword be brought upon him, or, according to the Hebrew and the other translators, the hard sword. For it is not said CADESA (קדשה), as the Seventy thought, which, if it were so, would signify holy; but CASA (קשה), which is properly translated hard. Hence also Kish, the father of Saul, is interpreted hard. And the holy, or hard, sword, on account of the sense of him who suffers it, some of our writers understand as the Word of God, of which the Apostle says: For the word of God is living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword (Heb 4:12). Hence in another place too we read that a two-edged sword goes out of the mouth of the Savior (Rev 19). And when at the end of the world the holy, or hard, and great and strong sword has been brought against Leviathan, who at the beginning of Genesis is called the most cunning serpent above all the beasts (Gen 3:1) that were on the earth, he will flee who was never accustomed to flee, not knowing that which is written: Whither shall I go from your spirit, or whither shall I flee from your face? (Ps 138 [139]:7). A certain poet in his Gigantomachy jested finely about Enceladus: Whither do you flee, Enceladus? Whatever shores you reach, you will always be under God. And this Leviathan, the fleeing serpent, is called in the Hebrew BARI (ברי), which Aquila translated bar, Symmachus shutting in, Theodotion mighty. I think he is called bar, or the one who shuts, because he has shut many in his prison and subjected them to his own power; and he has nothing straight in him, and for that reason is called twisting, nor can he imitate the rod of the Lord, of which it is written: A rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom (Ps 44 [45]). Him the Lord will slay with the breath of his mouth (2 Thess 2), him who was once the inhabitant of the sea, of its salty and bitter waves. Let those who say that the devil will do penance and obtain pardon explain to us how they take what is written: And he will slay the dragon that is in the sea, or the whale. For in the second place in the present passage he is not called Leviathan in the Hebrew, but THANNIN (תנין), which properly means whale. Hence the Hebrews suppose that Leviathan dwells under the earth and in the ether, but Thanniim in the sea; which is a Jewish fable. And what is said at the end of this passage, in that day, Eusebius joins to the former chapter, lest the following prophecy be fitted to this time. But the Hebrews and the other expositors join it to the following, which we are now about to set forth.
Morals on the Book of Job, Book 4, Sections 15-16

For "Leviathan" is interpreted to be "their addition." Whose "addition," then, but the "addition" of people? And it is properly styled "their addition," for since by his evil suggestion he brought into the world the first sin, he never ceases to add to it day by day by prompting to worse things.Or indeed it is in reproach that he is called Leviathan, that is, styled "the addition of men." For he found them immortal in Paradise, but by promising the divine nature to immortal beings, he as it were pledged himself to add somewhat to them beyond what they were. But while with flattering lips he declared that he would give what they did not have, he robbed them cunningly even of what they had. And hence the prophet describes this same Leviathan in these words, "Leviathan, the serpent: even Leviathan that crooked serpent." For this Leviathan crept near to people with tortuous windings through the false promise of what he would give them; for while he falsely promised things impossible, he really stole away even those which were possible.
Morals on the Book of Job, Book 17, Section 51

For who is described by the designation of the "serpent" but our old enemy, at once slippery and crooked, who for the deceiving of humankind spoke with the mouth of a serpent? Of whom it is said by the prophet, "Leviathan the serpent, the crooked one"; who was for this reason allowed to speak with the mouth of a serpent, that by Leviathan's vessel humanity might learn what he was that dwelt within. For a serpent is not only crooked but slippery as well; and so because he stood not in the uprightness of truth, he entered into a crooked animal.… He spoke to man by means of a slippery animal because if one does not resist him, he secretly slips into the interior of the heart. Now "the dens" of this serpent were the hearts of wicked people.
Commentary on Isaiah

In that day the vineyard of pure wine will sing to him. I the Lord, who keep it, will suddenly give it to drink: lest perhaps it be visited, I keep it night and day. LXX: In that day the good vineyard is his desire, that he may be its prince. I am a strong city, a city which is besieged: in vain will I give it drink. For they will be taken by night, and by day the wall will fall. The Hebrew in this place differs much from the edition of the Seventy; therefore let us discuss the particulars as we have set them out. The vineyard of which Isaiah speaks above, A vineyard was made for the beloved on a horn, in a fertile place: how it ought to be understood, let us learn from his own teaching: For the vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth is the house of Israel (Isa 5:1); of which it is sung in the psalm: You brought a vine out of Egypt, and so on (Ps 79 [80]:9). To this vineyard too he gives the cup of purest wine to drink through Jeremiah (Jer 25). For when he had sent him to give drink to all the nations, and the Prophet had willingly offered himself for this office, he is commanded first to make Jerusalem drunk. Hence he says: You have deceived me, O Lord, and I was deceived (Jer 20:7). Jerusalem, then, will drink, and an unmixed draught is given it to drink, so that it may learn lamentation and weeping. And the Lord says that he has guarded it for a long time and has given it a place for repentance, and because it would not be converted, it is to be made drunk suddenly. For he says that he has done this by days and by nights, so that it might always be kept by his help. But the Seventy call the same vineyard beautiful, in which were the Law and the Prophets, the priesthood and the high priesthood, and the knowledge of God, as Scripture says: God is known in Judea, his name is great in Israel (Ps 75 [76]:1). Others think that, according to their edition, it pertains to the Church, than which nothing is more beautiful, and of which it has been said: Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God (Ps 86 [87]:3): which is the princess of her mother, and says in the Song of Songs: The sons of my mother have fought against me (Song 1:5). And she says: I am a firm city, a city which is besieged. And he did well to say is besieged, not is taken by storm. And immediately he adds concerning the Synagogue, which has been turned from head into tail: In vain do I give it the drink of my teachings, for it will be taken in the darkness of its error. And because it did not receive the open light, its wall has fallen by day, that is, all that it thought its help; and there will be none of the adversaries who does not take it, which we ought to understand of the adverse powers.
On Isaac and the Soul 5.39

It is the soul, too, that says, "I am a strong city, a city besieged." The city is besieged through Christ, the city is that heavenly Jerusalem, in which there are interpreters of God's law and men skilled in doctrine in great abundance; through them one seeks the Word of God.
On the Death of Satyrus 2.17-18

Therefore let us flee these evils and elevate our soul to the image and likeness of God. The flight from evils is the likeness of God, and the image of God is gained through the virtues. And so, like a painter, he has painted us with the colors of the virtues. "See, I have painted your walls, Jerusalem." Let us not wipe away with the brush of neglect the props of the painted walls of our soul. And so "I have painted the walls," with which we can turn away the enemy. The soul has its walls; from them it stands forth and concerning them it says, "I am a strong city, a city besieged." By these walls it is guarded, and by them it is protected under siege. And truly the soul is a wall, which stretches forth over the camp. And therefore the bride says in the Song of Solomon, "I am a wall, and my breasts are like towers." The wall that the Lord painted is good, even as he says: "On my hands I have painted your walls, and you are always in my sight."
The Six Days of Creation 6.8.49

You have in Isaiah the speech made by the soul of a just man or of the church: "I am a strong city, I am a city besieged," defended by Christ and besieged by the devil. But one whom Christ aids ought not to be fearful of a siege. [Such a person] is defended by spiritual grace and is besieged by the perils of this world. Hence also it is said in the Song of Songs, "I am a wall, and my breasts are as a tower." The wall is the church, and the towers are her priests, who have full power to teach the natural and the moral sciences.
Commentary on Isaiah

Indignation is not in me: who will make me a thorn and a brier in battle? I will march upon it; I will burn it up together. Or rather shall I hold fast my strength? It will make peace for me, peace it will make for me. LXX: There is none that has not laid hold of it. Who will set me as keeper of stubble in a field? Because of this adversary I have driven it back. Therefore the Lord has done all that he arranged: I have been burned; its inhabitants will say, we will make peace with him, we will make peace with him. According to the Hebrew, this is the sense: I, who by days and nights have always preserved my vineyard, lest the boar out of the wood should lay it waste, lest the beasts should devour it, have I no indignation, and do I not know how to strike the sinner, and to render to each what he deserves? Where Aquila put thorn and brier, in the Hebrew is written SAMIR (שמיר) and SAITH (ושית), which signify adamant and places full of brambles. Hence he says: Who will teach me to be hard, and to overcome my clemency, and to advance savage in battle and contest, so that I may march upon the vineyard which I kept before, and burn that which I had hedged with my wall? Or rather will my strength bring this about, that I defer my wrath, and save by the clemency of the Gospel those who were by no means saved by the authority of the Law? And according to the Hebrew it is to be read ἐμφατικῶς: Who will make me hard and cruel, so that I overcome my nature? For this indeed is signified by the desert and by the thorns: that I should crush, as in battle, and burn that which I have always guarded with my diligence. Or rather shall I hold fast my strength, which without doubt is Christ, and of which we read, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor 1:24), so that it may make peace for me and reconcile the world? According to the Seventy, this is the sense, if we take it in the person of the Church: I am a firm city, a city surrounded by many enemies, I who in vain gave cups to my enemy the Synagogue. For it will be taken by night, and its wall will fall, and there will be none of the adverse powers which does not lay hold of it. Again I will speak: What does it profit me to guard her, who has stubble in her, not grain, who is so uncultivated that she is full of briers and thorns, whom I wished to save? But because she deals with me as an enemy, I have withdrawn from her. And the Apostles, born in me and from me, said: It was necessary that the word of God should be spoken first to you; but since you have rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles (Acts 13:46). Therefore the Lord will do what he threatened, so that all in her burn, surrounded by Roman fire. Or certainly they burn with vices and sins, so that they cannot quench the burning darts of the devil. For all are adulterers, their hearts like an oven. And those who formerly dwelt in her, after they have cried out, The city is taken and burned, will leave her, and, reconciling the world to God, will say: Let us make peace with him, let us make peace with him, that is, with Christ, always writing in their Epistles: Grace be with you and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord (1 Cor 1:3). Of whom we read in this same Prophet: How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good tidings of peace! (Isa 52:7). Some refer this place to the Churches: that they are indeed guarded by God, but many in them bear no fruit; and for that reason they are set on fire by the burning zeal of a good teacher, so that they cry out and confess their error, and afterwards make peace with God, being truly called sons of Jacob.
Commentary on Isaiah

Those who come forth from the root of Jacob, Israel will blossom and bud, and they will fill the face of the world with seed. LXX: Those who come are the sons of Jacob: Israel will bud and blossom, and its fruit will fill the world. After the Apostles, preaching the Gospel in the whole world, have said, We will make peace with Christ, we will make peace with him, those who were of the seed of Jacob on high, and have attained to the apostolic dignity, will be called sons of Jacob. Then Israel will bud and blossom, seeing that the whole world has been filled with the teaching of its sons and has borne most abundant fruits, which while it remained in Judea it had not borne.
Commentary on Isaiah

Has he struck him according to the stroke of him who struck him? Or as he killed his slain, so was he killed? This place is understood in two ways: either against Jerusalem, so as to say that it was not struck by God as it itself struck Christ and his Apostles; or against the multitude of the nations, in that, while they persecuted and shed Christian blood, the Apostles and apostolic men nonetheless took care of their salvation and reconciled them to God.
Commentary on Isaiah

In measure against measure, when it has been cast off, you will judge it. LXX: Quarreling and reproaching, he will send them away. According to the Hebrew, this is the sense: As Jerusalem did, so will it receive, and according to the measure with which it measured, it will be measured back to it. And it will receive the measure heaped up when the time of judgment has come and God has cast it off. According to the Seventy, what is said depends on what precedes. For Israel will not be struck as it struck, nor killed as it killed: Israel, which quarreled against the Apostles, and reproached its teachers, and commanded them not to speak in the name of Christ. Therefore the Lord will cast them off and drive them out of his flock.

He has meditated in his hard spirit through the day of heat. LXX: Was it not you who meditated with a hard spirit to kill them, with a spirit of fury? According to the Hebrew this is said: with the measure with which it measured, Jerusalem will receive; therefore God in his hard and vehement spirit has meditated, or spoken, against it in the day of heat, that is, in the time of persecution, when the day of indignation and punishments is more burning. According to the Seventy, it is said to Jerusalem itself, or to Israel: Was it not you who, in your most hard and cruel spirit, and in the fury of your blasphemies, desired to kill the Apostles and teachers of the Lord?
Commentary on Isaiah

Therefore by these things iniquity will be forgiven to the house of Jacob, and this is all the fruit, that his sin may be taken away: because he has made all the stones of the altar like stones of ash dashed to pieces; the groves and the shrines will not stand. LXX: Therefore the iniquity of Jacob will be taken away, and this will be his blessing, when I have taken away his sin, when he has made all the stones of the altars crushed like ash ground small, and their trees will not endure, nor the idols. He gives the reasons why, after the Jews have laid hands on the Lord, they may obtain pardon if they are willing to do penance, so that the prayer of the Savior may be fulfilled: Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do (Luke 23:34). Therefore, he says, iniquity will be forgiven to the house of Jacob, and its sin will be taken away, so that it may merit the blessing of God, which had called down a curse upon itself, saying: His blood be upon us and upon our children (Matt 27:25); because through the Apostles of the stock of Israel the Gospel will be sown in the whole world, and idolatry will be destroyed, and the altars will be ground down to dust, the groves will be cut down, the shrines will fall, and the knowledge of the one God under the mystery of the Trinity will be preached.
Commentary on Isaiah

For the fortified city will be desolate; the beautiful one will be left, and abandoned as a desert. There the calf will feed, and there he will lie down and consume its topmost shoots. LXX: Their idols will be cut down like a grove, and the flock dwelling far off will be abandoned like a forsaken flock, and it will be for a long time for pasture, and there the flocks will rest, and after a long time there will not be in it anything green, because it has been dried up. Jerusalem, the city once firm and fortified, because it did not receive the son of the householder, but said, Come, let us kill him, for this is the heir, and the inheritance will be ours (Matt 21:38), will be desolate. And she who was once beautiful, of whom it is said in Ezekiel too, You ate fine flour and honey and oil, and you became exceedingly beautiful (Ezek 16:13), and in whom dwelt he of whom it is written, Beautiful in form above the sons of men (Ps 44 [45]:3), will be left and abandoned as a desert, as the Lord says to the Apostles: Arise, let us go hence (John 14:31). There the calf will feed, the Roman army, of which it is said in another place under the name of the boar: The boar out of the wood will lay it waste, and the solitary wild beast has fed upon it (Ps 79 [80]:14). And there he will lie down and consume its topmost shoots, under the metaphor of a vineyard and its shoots, so that nothing green, nothing of the tendrils, remains in it, but the enemy consumes all. According to the Seventy, because they did not receive the good shepherd, therefore they will be like a forsaken flock, and will lie open to the bites of the beasts; and nothing green will remain in them, because drought will possess all things.
AGAINST MARCION 4.43

The women, returning from the sepulcher and from this vision of the angels, were foreseen by Isaiah, when he says, "Come, you women, who return from the vision," that is, "come" to report the resurrection of the Lord. It was well, however, that the unbelief of the disciples was so persistent, in order that to the last we might consistently maintain that Jesus revealed himself to the disciples as none other than the Christ of the prophets.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 141

And there were many women there, watching from afar, who had followed Jesus from Galilee, ministering to him; among whom was Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James and Joseph, and the mother of the sons of Zebedee (27, 55. 56). They report that Isaiah prophesied concerning these women when he said: Women coming to the spectacle, come; for it is not a people having wisdom. For he calls women those who had been from afar and from afar were watching Jesus; he calls them to the word, that they may indeed forsake the senseless and forsaken people and come to the new covenant. And I judge those women to be blessed who are built up unto blessedness by the spectacle of the word and by the death of the body of Jesus; for everything that is in Christ, if it be truly seen, makes the beholder blessed.

Therefore they look upon the mortification of the body of Jesus and the manner in which he commended "his spirit" to the Father by his prayers. These first followed him from Galilee, and — that I may say it boldly (using the authority of the Scripture that teaches it) — they followed him from Galilee "of the Gentiles", not from a straight nor a firm one, but from one having a certain circuit (for this is what Galilee is understood to mean, that is, ROLLING or WHIRLING); and leaving this, they followed Jesus, not idly, but doing the things that were commanded by him, and they delighted him; for they followed him ministering.

And every soul that shares in some distribution of graces and in the Lord himself ministers to Jesus a ministry like the ministries of the angels, concerning whom it is written that "the angels, approaching, ministered to him".

Many therefore were watching Jesus then, but the chief ones are named, as being those who watched more attentively and ministered more fully and followed better: Mary Magdalene, more fitting to the interpretation of the name of her homeland, which is called Magdala (and that place is interpreted MAGNIFICATION).

And this Mary Magdalene was of magnification for no other reason than that she had followed Jesus and had ministered to him and had watched the mystery of his passion. And among the chief ones there was also

Mary the mother of James and Joseph, or (as Mark says) "the mother of James the less and of Joseph", according to the name of the patriarch Jacob, the SUPPLANTER of his brother, and of Joseph, over whom, when he was born, his mother said: "may the Lord add to me another son".

This one too, therefore, following the Lord and ministering and watching the dispensation of his passion, was so because she had been the mother of some faithful person — not of anyone great (such as the patriarch Jacob had been), but of a lesser one, and of another Joseph. And among the women there was also

the mother of the sons of Zebedee, perhaps some woman established in the ministry of THUNDER

on account of her faith and holy life, and because she followed the Lord and ministered to him and had been a beholder of all the things that had been done concerning him, for the sons of Zebedee were called "SONS OF THUNDER". For his sons were John and James: therefore John heard the words of the seven thunders, which, as being more eminent than all Scripture, he received a command not to write. But if it is proper also to conjecture and to state the name of the mother of the sons of Zebedee,

I say that this very woman had been called Salome, which means PEACEABLE. And I have conjectured this seeing that in Matthew and Mark three chief women are named, concerning whom the present discourse is held; and the present evangelist sets forth that two of them are "Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of James", but that the third is called the mother of the sons of Zebedee; whereas in Mark that third one is called "Salome". And according to Mark, those who had followed Jesus from Galilee "went up to Jerusalem" with Christ.

For this is the end of those who forsake the Galilee "of the Gentiles" and follow Jesus, that they not only go up to Jerusalem, but also go up into it together with Jesus.

For this is what is signified by their being reported to have gone up together with Christ.
Commentary on Isaiah

In the drought of its harvest the women coming and teaching it will be crushed. For it is not a wise people: therefore he who made it will not have mercy on it, and he who formed it will not spare it. LXX: Women coming from the spectacle, come: for it is not a people having understanding; therefore he who made them will not have mercy on them, and he who formed them will not spare. What is said, In the drought of its harvest they will be crushed, for which the Seventy translated, there will not be in it anything green, because it has dried up, according to the Hebrew is coupled with what follows, according to the Seventy with the preceding sense. Let us speak first, then, according to the Hebrew. When the time of the drought and the harvest of Jerusalem, and, to speak more openly, of its devastation, has come, the throng of the synagogues will run together from the whole world to lament Jerusalem and console her evils. Or he is speaking openly of the women who, with bared breasts, strike their arms till they bleed; and the prophecy of the Lord will be fulfilled: Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but lament over yourselves and over your children (Luke 23:28). And it is a great unhappiness for the people to learn songs of lamentation from women; just as it was a reproach to the people of Israel when, in the book of Judges (Judg 4), the Lord wrought salvation by the hand of the woman Deborah, and at the time of the approaching captivity, while the men were silent, the woman Huldah prophesied (2 Kgs 22). But for this reason the women will be crushed by the long journey, worn out by weakness, hunger and squalor, and they will teach the wretched people, because it is not a wise people, nor has it understood its Creator, who, neglected and despised by them, will not have mercy on his handiwork and will not spare his creature. According to the Seventy, it is said of Mary Magdalene, and the other Mary, and the rest of the women, who first saw the Lord rising again, and held his feet, and merited to hear from him: Do not fear: go, tell my brethren to go into Galilee, and there they will see me (Matt 28:10). Of these women, long before they were born, the prophetic discourse foretells, and calls them from the spectacle of the Lord's Passion and Resurrection, so that they may preach the Gospel, and, according to the Hebrew, teach Jerusalem, or the land of Israel, that this is the Lord and God. For since the people of Israel did not have wisdom at that time, when the Lord suffered, and the prophetic oracle was fulfilled, Save me, O Lord, for the holy one has failed (Ps 11 [12]:1), and, All have turned aside, together they have become unprofitable: there is none who does good, there is not even one (Ps 13 [14]:4), the women are called from the spectacle, so that they may announce to the Apostles what they themselves have seen. But Israel, of which it was said (above, Isa 1:3), Israel has not known me, and my people has not understood, provoked its most clement Creator and maker to bitterness, so that he by no means has mercy on it. These things are indeed said piously; but how they agree with the rest, and are fitted to the times of the consummation of the world, is a difficult interpretation.
Commentary on Isaiah

And it will be in that day: the Lord will strike from the channel of the river to the torrent of Egypt. LXX: And it will be in that day: the Lord will shut in from the trench of the river to Rhinocorura. Had he not added, in that day, by which we are taught that what he is about to say is to be coupled with what precedes, we could have expounded a sense proper to this passage; but now everything is to be referred to what precedes. Since the fortified city will be desolate, and the once beautiful one will be left as a desert, and there the calf will lie down and consume the shoots of the vineyard, and all things will be dried up, since it is not a people having understanding, and because of its folly it has obtained no mercy from its Creator: therefore the Lord will strike, or shut in, from the channel or stream of the river to the torrent of Egypt, so that in all Judea, which was once the land of promise, no word of teaching may be found, nothing of the knowledge of the Scriptures; of whom the Apostle too speaks: That we may not give heed to Jewish fables and commandments of men who turn away from the truth (Titus 1:14); and again: For there are many both insubordinate and vain talkers and deceivers, whom one must refute, especially of the circumcision (ibid., 10). And the channel, or stream, of the river, according to the history, we can call the Euphrates, as it is written also in the seventy-first psalm: He will have dominion from sea to sea, and from the river to the end of the world (Ps 71 [72]:8). Others think it is the Jordan. And this must be noted, that in the borders of Judea it is called river, in the territories of Egypt torrent, which has turbid waters and not perpetual ones. For the torrent of Egypt, the Seventy translated Rhinocorura, which is a town on the border of Egypt and Palestine, expressing not so much the words of the Scriptures as the sense of the words. And what we have said, will strike, for which the Seventy translated συμφράξει, that is, will shut in, Aquila and Theodotion translated ῥαβδήσει, which can be understood either as will strike with a rod or will count under the rod the number of his flock, so that it may be taken not in a bad but in a good sense.

And you will be gathered one by one, O children of Israel. LXX: But you, gather one by one the children of Israel. O children of Israel, for which Symmachus translated house of Israel: when your adversaries have been struck from the stream of the river to the torrent of Egypt, that is, from the Euphrates to the Nile, you yourselves will be gathered to the faith of the Lord one by one, because the throng of the Jews did not believe; by which he signifies that few of the Jews will believe in the Lord Savior. Or certainly, O Apostles and apostolic men, since the multitude of the Jews does not believe, bring back from the whole world as many as you can, like sick sheep, to the folds of the Lord, and gather them with the people of the nations, so that that may be fulfilled which the Apostle Paul and Barnabas say to the Jews: It was necessary that the word of God should be announced first to you; but since you have judged yourselves unworthy of salvation, behold, we turn to the Gentiles (Acts 13:46).
Commentary on Isaiah

And it will be in that day: a blast will be sounded on a great trumpet; and those who had been lost from the land of the Assyrians, and those who had been cast out into the land of Egypt, will come, and they will worship the Lord on the holy mountain in Jerusalem. LXX: And it will be in that day: they will sound with a great trumpet; and those who had perished in the region of the Assyrians, and those who had perished in Egypt, will come, and they will worship the Lord upon the holy mountain in Jerusalem. In this place the Jews promise themselves empty hopes: that at the consummation of the world, when the Antichrist, their ἠλειμμένος, as it is said, has come, the dispersed people will be gathered from the Assyrians and from the land of Egypt, and will come to Jerusalem, and, the temple having been built, will worship the Lord their God. This cannot stand at all according to the letter. For not from the Assyrians and from Egypt only, but from the whole world, those who are to believe in Christ will be called. This, therefore, is what it signifies: that at the last trumpet, according to the Apostle Paul (1 Cor 15), all who had perished among the Assyrians and in Egypt come to the Lord. Nor did he say all the children of Israel, but all who had perished, by which he signifies the multitude of the nations: that those bound to idolatry and to the magic arts and to philosophy come to the faith of Christ and worship him in the Church. And the great trumpet can be understood as the word of the Gospel, of which we read also in this same Prophet: Go up upon a high mountain, you who bring good tidings to Zion: lift up your voice, you who bring good tidings to Jerusalem (below, Isa 40:9). The holy mountain, then, and Jerusalem is that of which we have often spoken: You have come to Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and many thousands of angels, and the Church of the firstborn, who are enrolled in the heavens (Heb 12:22). Thus far it has been spoken of the consummation of the world, from the place at which we began to expound, Behold, the Lord will scatter the earth and will lay it bare (above, Isa 24:1), which is contained in the present volume. Now, with Christ helping, nay rather inspiring us, let us pass on to the ninth, which will hold the beginning of another prophecy.

n: Ephraim. That is, the kingdom of the ten tribes. (Challoner) --- Flower. The pride of the kingdom shall thus decay. (Menochius) --- Head. Samaria, situated on a hill, having under it a most fertile valley. (Challoner) --- See Amos ii. 6., and iv. 2. Samaria was taken in the sixth year of Ezechias.
The Lord. By his instrument, Salmanasar. (Haydock) --- Hebrew, "behold the strong one, and the mighty to the Lord, as," &c. (Calmet) --- Septuagint, "behold the Lord's fury....as." (Haydock)
Up. Theglathphalassar was captivated with the beauty of the country, and made it tributary. But Salmanasar, fearing a revolt, destroyed it, 4 Kings xvii. 4.
People, who returned to the service of God; or it refers to the kingdom of Juda.
Gate. Ezechias reunited the divided kingdoms, and inspired his troops with courage, bringing them back victorious, 2 Paralipomenon xxx. 1., and 4 Kings xviii. 7. (Calmet)
These also. The kingdom of Juda. (Challoner) --- Ezechias could not correct every abuse; though what is here specified, regards rather the reigns of his successors.
Place. All was defiled: they gloried in their shame.
Breasts? St. Paul seems to allude to this text, 1 Corinthians iii. 2. (Calmet) --- The abandoned Jews ask contemptuously, if they be to be taught like children? (Haydock)

Command, &c. This is said in the person of the Jews, resisting the repeated commands of God, and still putting him off. (Challoner) --- They deride the prophets, speaking words of no meaning, as if their predictions were no better. (St. Jerome) --- Think they that we have to learn the first elements, or to join syllables together? (Calmet) --- Hebrew Tsav latsav, &c. (Haydock) --- The Nicholaites abused these words. (St. Epiphanius 25.) --- Why do they not speak plain? Sometimes terrible things are denounced, then subjects of joy! Isaias answers, that since they pretend not to understand, God will lead them into a country where they shall indeed have to learn the language, like children, chap. xxix. 11. (Calmet) --- Protestants, "for precept must be upon precept....line upon line....here a little, and there a little. For with stammering lips," &c. (Haydock)
Hear. To leave off their wicked practices, and cruelty. The Jews would not understand: therefore Christ spoke to them in parables, chap. vi. 9., and Matthew xiii. 14., &c.
Taken. God will make his prophets speak, notwithstanding your repugnance; or he will reduce you to the necessity of learning an unknown language. (Calmet)
Men, who make a parade of your knowledge, (Haydock) to turn the most sacred things into ridicule.
Protected. Their conduct spoke this language. They would not fail to make alliances with Egypt, and to trust in idols, whatever the prophets might say to dissuade them. (Calmet)

Stone. Christ. (Challoner) --- The Jews and Grotius would apply it to Ezechias. But he was already on the throne, and never could realize these glorious promises. The people were not to believe in him, &c. (Calmet) --- Hasten. Let him expect his coming with patience. (Challoner) --- It would be delayed some time. Hebrew may also signify "stagger;" (Calmet) in which sense the Septuagint and the authors of the New Testament seem to have taken it. "Whosoever believeth in him, shall not be confounded." See Romans ix. 33. (Haydock) --- Isaias promises a Redeemer, though these people were unworthy; and then returns to his own times. (Menochius)

Measure. In the days of the Redeemer, they shall lead a virtuous life, (Calmet) or the scorners shall be treated with rigour. --- Protection. The wall, (Menochius) or lies, (ver. 15.; Calmet) on which you depend, shall turn to your confusion. (Haydock)

Hear. Under the last kings of Juda, the misery was continual. Captivity opened the eyes of the people, and they were afterwards more docile. The murder of Christ, and the subsequent evils which befell the nation, seem to have had a quite different effect. They will at last submit to his yoke. (Calmet)

Straitened. It is too narrow to hold two: God will have the bed of our heart all to himself. (Challoner) (1 Corinthians x. 20., and 2 Corinthians vi. 14.) (St. Jerome, &c.) --- The Jews explain it of the utmost distress, to which the people would be reduced, so that they would not be able to assist a friend, Amos iii. 12. (Forcr.[Forerius?]) (Calmet)

As in, &c. As the Lord fought against the Philistines in Baal Pharasim, (2 Kings v.) and against the Chanaanites, in the valley of Gabaon, Josue x. (Challoner) --- Strange. He punished unwillingly. (Calmet) --- "It is not God's work to ruin what he has created." (St. Jerome) --- He will punish in an extraordinary manner those scoffers, ver. 15., and Numbers xvi. 29. (Piscator)
Earth. Nabuchodonosor will take a complete and speedy vengeance, chap. x. 22.
Sow. The works of the husbandman vary, so will God's punishments be inflicted with measure, according to each one's deserts, ver. 27., and Wisdom vi. 7. (Calmet)

Gith. Heberw ketsach. Septuagint, melanthion. (Haydock) (Pliny, [Natural History?] xx. 17.) (Menochius) --- Septuagint have not expressed all the terms of the original, (Haydock) being perhaps ignorant of their meaning. (St. Jerome)
God. From him proceeds every useful invention. The pagans attributed the discovery of corn, &c., to their idols.
Saws, or heavy instruments. It would be thus crushed too much. (Calmet)
But. Septuagint, "it shall be eaten with bread. For I will not be angry with you for ever, nor shall the sounds of my bitter wrath trample upon you." (Haydock)
This also, &c. Such also is the proceeding of the Lord with his land, and the diverse seeds he sows therein. (Challoner)

f: Commentary on Isaiah

Woe to the crown of pride, to the drunkards of Ephraim, and to the falling flower of the glory of its exultation, who were on the summit of the most fertile valley, going astray from wine. Behold, the strong and mighty one of the Lord, like the onrush of hail, a whirlwind that shatters; like the onrush of many waters overflowing and sent forth upon a spacious land. With feet shall the crown of pride of the drunkards of Ephraim be trodden down. And the falling flower of the glory of its exultation, which is upon the summit of the valley of the fat, shall be like an early fruit before the ripeness of autumn, which, when the beholder has looked upon it, as soon as he has taken it in his hand, he will devour it. LXX: Woe to the crown of insolence, the hirelings of Ephraim: a flower falling from glory upon the summit of the fat mountain, you who are drunk without wine. Behold, the wrath of the Lord is strong and harsh, like hail that is borne headlong, having no shelter, which falls violently like a multitude of waters dragging the soil along and making room for itself: with hands and feet shall the crown of insolence, the hirelings of Ephraim, be trodden down. And the flower that falls from the hope of glory on the top of the lofty mountain shall be like an early fig, which whoever sees it will long to devour before he takes it in his hand. Let us speak first according to the history, then according to tropology, and lastly according to the prophetic prediction. The divine word speaks against the ten tribes who reigned in Samaria and who, on account of Jeroboam, who was of the tribe of Ephraim, were called Ephraim. And it calls them a crown of pride, because, compared with the two tribes that were called Judah, they were loftier both in number and in strength. And it calls them the drunkards of Ephraim, since they did not understand their Creator, but in place of the Lord worshiped the golden calves in Dan and Bethel. These were once in the flower of the Lord, and in glory, when they were ruled by David and Solomon and, among the twelve tribes, worshiped God in the temple of Jerusalem; they were on the summit of the most fertile valley, which in Hebrew is called GE SEMANIM (גיא שמנים). This signifies the place where the Lord was betrayed; above the summit of this valley the temple of the Lord is situated. These men were made drunk with the wine of error and madness, which Jeroboam mixed for them. Therefore the Lord threatens them with punishment: that, as a whirlwind of hail shatters all things, and the onrush of overflowing waters sweeps away whatever it finds in its path, so they would be destroyed by the army of the Assyrians, and whatever remained would be carried off to the mountains or cities of Media. He compares the glory of the ten tribes to a crown of varied flowers, which had such beauty that, just as someone who, before summer and autumn come, sees a πρόδρομον fig on the tree, devours it as soon as he has taken it in his hand, so too the Assyrian, when he saw the ten tribes, would lay them waste and devour them, and leave nothing at all of the former people in Samaria. Let this have been said briefly according to the history. Let us pass to allegory. According to our exposition of the prophet Hosea, in which we referred Ephraim and Joseph and Samaria and the ten tribes, which were cut off from the body of the twelve tribes and abandoned the temple of the Lord, to the heretics, these are truly, according to the Septuagint edition, a crown of insolence: they blaspheme the Lord, and do everything for the sake of payment, and have fallen from the glory of the Lord; nor do they follow the slenderness of the manna and the humility of the Church, but they dwell on the most fertile mountain, drunk without wine. Therefore the strong and harsh wrath of the Lord, which is going to punish them, is compared to headlong hail, which falls not on roofs but on the heads of mortals, and to the floods of many waters, which drag along whatever they find in their way. This crown of insolence, the hirelings, are called Ephraim, who, according to the Apostle, for the sake of base gain have fallen from the flower and the hope and the glory of their former faith, and dwell in pride, and are the sweetest food of the devil, who devours them daily (1 Pet 5). According to the prophecy we can say this: that he calls the scribes and Pharisees, who blasphemed the Lord, a crown of insolence. And they were called the hirelings of Ephraim on account of Judas, who, of the tribe of Ephraim and of Iscarioth, a village of that same tribe, sold the Lord for a price; he truly, the flower of apostolic glory, fell upon the most fertile mountain, of which we think it was said: Jacob ate and drank and was filled, and grew fat, and the beloved kicked (Deut 32:15). Or, according to the Hebrew: upon the valley of the fat, that is, Gessemanim: in which the name of the place is also signified in which Judas betrayed the Lord. And it is called the fat valley, or the valley of the fat, on account of its fertility, and on account of the scribes and Pharisees who seized the Lord there: of whom it is written in the psalm: Fat bulls have besieged me (Ps 21 [22]:13). This valley of the fat, that is, Gessemanim, is named a second time in this chapter; and I wonder how the Seventy first called it a fat mountain and afterward a lofty mountain. The betrayer was drunk not with wine but with avarice and the incurable fury of asps, and with the food of the devil, who entered into him after the morsel (John 13), and he was utterly devoured, because his prayer was turned into sin, and not even his repentance had the fruit of salvation. The Hebrew word SACCHORE (שכורי) is ambiguous, and means either drunkards or hirelings. Hence Issachar too means there is a reward; and SACHAR (שכר) is μέθυσμα, that is, drunkenness. And the rest translated drunkards: the Seventy alone translated hirelings.

In that day the Lord of hosts shall be a crown of glory and a garland of exultation to the remnant of his people, and a spirit of judgment to him who sits upon judgment, and strength to those returning from war to the gate. But these also have not known because of wine, and have gone astray because of drunkenness; the priest and the prophet have not known: they are swallowed up by wine because of drunkenness, they have gone astray in drunkenness: they have not known the seer, they have been ignorant of judgment, or wonderfully. For all the tables are filled with vomit and filth, so that there was no more room. LXX: In that day the Lord Sabaoth shall be a crown of hope, which is woven of glory, for the remnant of the people. They shall be left in a spirit of judgment upon judgment, and strength forbidding to kill. For these have been deceived by wine: they go astray because of strong drink; the priest and the prophet have lost their minds because of strong drink; they are swallowed up because of wine, they have staggered, that is, φάσμα; a curse shall eat this counsel: for this counsel is for the sake of avarice. After the whole land of Samaria, that is, of the ten tribes, has been destroyed by the Assyrian's flood, and the crown of pride of the drunkards of Ephraim has been trodden underfoot and devoured like an early fig, then the Lord himself shall be a crown of victory to the remnant of the people of Israel, that is, of the two tribes, Judah and Benjamin; and a spirit of judgment to him who sits upon judgment, doubtless to Hezekiah king of Judah; and the strength of those who, when the whole region had been ravaged, returning from battle, shut themselves up in the city. This we shall read in this same prophet (below, Isa 37), when one hundred and eighty-five thousand armed men of the army of the Assyrians were destroyed by the stroke of an angel. But these also, that is, Judah and Benjamin, were made drunk with the wine of idolatry, and, despising the worship of the temple, venerated the images of demons, and did not know the Lord, the seer, who beholds all things. For all their tables, and their whole worship, were filled with vomit and filth, so that not only in the temple but on the tops of the mountains and in wooded places they filled everything with the filth of idolatry, and the Lord had no place of habitation among them. Let this have been said according to the letter. Further, according to tropology, let us follow the former understanding, and not leave the Seventy translators untouched. For when the heretics, who have climbed the most fertile mountain of pride, have been devoured by the mouth of the devil, the Lord shall be a crown of glory to those who dwell in the Church and who, compared with the multitude of the many who go astray, are few in number. And he shall be in a spirit of judgment upon judgment, because the Lord will wash away the filth of the sons and daughters of Zion by the spirit of judgment. But if anyone has blood, he will be purged not by the spirit of judgment but by the fire of burning; and he shall be strength to the people, and shall forbid it to be killed by those who are drunk with the wine of dragons and have gone astray because of strong drink. We have often said that wine is what is made from vines; but strong drink is every drink that can intoxicate and overturn the state of the mind, which Aquila properly translated drunkenness, whether it is made from wheat or barley or millet, or from the juice of fruits, or from the fruit of palms, or from any other kind. Therefore the priests and prophets of the heretics have lost their minds because of strong drink, and are swallowed up because of wine, such as were Prisca and Maximilla and their chief Montanus: and they did not know what they were saying. They are made drunk with wine when they misunderstand and pervert the holy Scriptures; with strong drink, when they misuse worldly wisdom and the snares of the dialecticians, which are to be called not so much bonds as phantasms, that is, certain shadows and images that quickly perish and dissolve. A curse shall possess the counsel of such men, who suppose that godliness is gain, and do everything for the sake of avarice. Of this phantasm the Apostle too spoke: Giving heed to spirits of error and doctrines of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy (1 Tim 4:1-2). The third explanation is that, after the Lord has overthrown the scribes and Pharisees, and their associate Judas the betrayer, who had been a thief from the beginning, for he himself carried the purse of the money for the poor (John 12 and 13), he then becomes a hope and a crown of glory to those of the Jews who believed in the Lord; doubtless he means the apostles, whom he reserved for the preaching of the Gospel and did not allow at once to shed their blood for Christ. For all the scribes and Pharisees were made drunk with the wine and strong drink of which we spoke above, the priests as well as the false prophets. But their snares and plots came to nothing, since both Judas himself, who betrayed him, did it for money, and the priests, who corrupted the betrayer with money, did it out of fear of their own rejection. For he himself, making a scourge of cords, cast out of the temple those who sold oxen and sheep, and by his own authority overturned the seats of those who sold doves and the tables of the money-changers, saying to them: It is written: My Father's house shall be called a house of prayer, but you have made it a house of trade, or a den of robbers (Matt 21:13).
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 3:1.28

The prophet expounds on the destiny of those in Israel who believed in Christ, because Israel did not perish completely, as the remnant of Israel was saved, according to the prophecy. Quite a number of people believed in Christ, and his apostles were, so to speak, the first fruit. Therefore at that time the Lord of hosts will be as a crown of hope and a diadem of glory to the remnant of his people. The Lord of hosts will crown the believers with hope and glory, that is, with hope of future blessings and with glory because they will reign with him. They will become the recipients of the highest honor and will be worthy of adoration and glory. What glory can be compared with that received in the kingdom of Christ? In another passage Isaiah also says, "You shall also be a crown of glory in the hand of the Lord and a royal diadem in the hand of your God," since Christ will crown those who believe in him with unending glory and bless them with the most joyous hope. And the remnant of Israel will participate in all of this after the others, the Gentiles, are received in Christ. Realizing their glory in Christ, they cry to their heavenly God and Father, "O Lord, crown us with the shield of your favor." For when it pleased their God and Father, he revealed himself as an unbroken shield and became the Christ who defends us from the arrows of the evil one and keeps his people.

According to the anagogy, that Hebrew text in which we said: For all their tables are filled with vomit and filth, so that there is no more room, can be referred to the heretics, and to the scribes and Pharisees, in this way: that we say all their teaching and all their mysteries are full of vomit and filth, since they do not digest the food of the holy Scriptures nor make it life-giving to the whole body, but void it unripe and stinking, so that God finds no place in them. But I wonder what Theodotion meant, that for the Hebrew word called CISOA (קיאצאה), for which Aquila translated vomit of filth and Symmachus simply vomit, he should say ἐμετὸν δυσαλίας, that is, vomit of dysalia, a word I have not been able to find read anywhere among the Greeks, unless perhaps he coined a new name for a new thing. Indeed among the Hebrews too it is a compound, since vomit is called CI, and SOA filthy. Whatever, then, causes nausea and vomiting can be called δυσαλία.
