Whom shall he teach knowledge, and whom shall he make to understand what is heard? Those weaned from the milk, those drawn from the breasts: for command, command again; command, command again; wait, wait again; wait, wait again; a little there, a little there. For with speech of lip and with another tongue he will speak to this people, to whom he said: This is my rest; refresh the weary, and this is my refreshment, and they would not hear. And the word of the Lord shall be to them: command, command again; command, command again; wait, wait again; wait, wait again; a little there, a little there; that they may go and fall backward, and be broken, and be snared, and be taken. LXX: To whom shall we announce evils, and to whom shall we announce tidings? those who are weaned from the milk, who are drawn from the breast. Expect tribulation upon tribulation; wait for hope upon hope; yet a little, yet a little: because of the mockery of the lips, because of another tongue with which they will speak to this people, saying to them: This is the rest for the hungry, and this the crushing, and they would not hear. And the word of the Lord shall be to them: Tribulation upon tribulation: expect, expect; hope upon hope: yet a little, yet a little; that they may go and fall backward, and be broken, and be endangered, and be taken. Who, he says, is worthy of the teaching of the Lord, who, by the words of the Savior, who says: He who has ears to hear, let him hear (Matt 11:15), understands with the heart what he has taken in with the ears? Who these are the following verse shows: Weaned from the milk, drawn from the breast: those who are no longer fed with the milk of infancy but eat solid food; who are drawn from the breast with Isaac, for which joy Abraham made a great feast (Gen 21); these deserve to hear the mysteries of the Lord and to understand what the priest and the prophet do not know, drunk and swallowed up by wine, who went astray and did not know the seer, because all their tables were filled with vomit and filth. These, when the prophets announced what was to come and threatened torments unless they did what had been commanded, used to say in mockery: Command, command again; command, command again, that is, give orders, give orders, command what we ought to do. And since they abused the patience of God, who defers his wrath in order to show mercy, they used also to say this, jesting, in the person of the prophets: Wait a little while, wait a little, the things we have foretold will come. All this they said among the people, because they did not believe the words of God; and at once the prophet adds: God will no longer speak to you in these words, to command what you ought to do and that you should wait for what is to come, but he will speak to you in present fury, he who had earlier said to the people: This is my rest, refresh the weary: I have labored a long time, in nothing have I found rest. The foxes have holes, and the birds of the sky nests; but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head (Matt 8; Luke 9). And this is my refreshment, that I may at some time rest in you. They would not hear, and despised my warnings; wherefore what they used to say to the prophets in jest: Command, command again; command, command again: wait, wait again; wait, wait again: a little there, a little there, mocking my patience, since they thought I was threatening things I would never do: let them feel it fulfilled in fact, so that they go to destruction and fall backward with an incurable ὀπισθοτόνῳ; and may never advance to the things before, nor be able to say with the Apostle: Forgetting the things that are behind, we stretch forward to those that are before (Phil 3:13); but may they be broken and snared, and be taken either by the Babylonian or by the Roman army. Where we have said: Command, command again; command, command again: wait, wait again; wait, wait again; a little there, a little there, in the Hebrew it is written thus: SAU LASAU, SAU LASAU; CAU LACAU, CAU LACAU: ZER SAM, ZER SAM; and a most unclean heresy is accustomed to misuse these words among simple and deceived people, to cause terror by the novelty of the expressions: namely, that whoever has learned these words and remembers them in their intercourse will pass without any doubt into the kingdom of heaven. We read in the Apostle: In other tongues and with other lips I will speak to this people, and not even so will they hear me, says the Lord (1 Cor 14:21). This seems to me taken from the present chapter according to the Hebrew; and we have observed this in the Old Testament (apart from a few testimonies which Luke alone uses, who had a greater knowledge of the Greek language): wherever anything is cited from the old instrument, they set it down not according to the Septuagint but according to the Hebrew, following no one's translation, but rendering the Hebrew sense in their own language. Symmachus, Theodotion and the Seventy understood this place differently, and because it is long to speak of them all, let us run briefly through the Seventy translators, who are read in the churches. The people of the Jews having been rejected, the priests and prophets who were drunk with strong drink and went astray, and the curse having eaten up the counsel they formed for the sake of avarice, to whom shall we announce the tribulations to come for Christ's sake? to whom the evils in return for which the crown of virtues is prepared? Surely to those who are weaned from the milk, who are drawn from the breast: doubtless he means the apostles: Expect tribulation upon tribulation. He is speaking to the company of the apostles and of all believers, that each should prepare himself not for one tribulation but for many, so that when he has been afflicted and pressed down he may hope again, and have hope upon hope. And if what has been promised delays a little, let him not be unbelieving: for a little, a very little, and what has been promised will come. For tribulation works patience; patience, proof; proof, hope; and hope does not confound (Rom 5:3-5). And this very tribulation will be doubled by the detraction of lips, and by the blasphemies of the persecutors, with which they rage with rabid mouth against the people of God. Further, the apostles and apostolic men will speak to the people of the Jews, saying: This is the rest for the hungry for righteousness, and this the crushing and the narrowness that leads to life. When they preached this, the ungodly would not hear. Hence what was said to the people of God: Endure tribulation, endure tribulation; expect hope, expect hope: yet a little, yet a little, will be turned into punishment for those who would not hear the word of the Lord, so that they fall and go backward, and run into the peril of siege and death, and are taken with no end of miseries. That the Seventy alone translated the Hebrew word DEA, which all rendered knowledge, as evils is an evident error. For the first letter, DALETH or RES, are distinguished by a small stroke. If, then, it is read DEA (דעה), it means knowledge; if REA (רעה), malice: not from the evil that is the contrary of good, but from distress.

And your covenant with death shall be blotted out, and your pact with hell shall not stand; when the overflowing scourge passes through, you shall be trodden down by it. When it passes through, it shall take you away: for in the morning, at daybreak, it shall pass through, in the day and in the night, and vexation alone shall give understanding to the hearing: For the bed is straitened, so that one must fall out, and a short cloak cannot cover both. LXX: Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I will put into the foundations of Zion a precious stone, chosen, a corner stone, honorable, in its foundations; and he who believes shall not be confounded. And I will set judgment in hope, and my mercy in the weight; and those who trust vainly in a lie, since the tempest shall not pass through us, and shall not take from us the testament of death, also your hope in hell shall not remain. If the coming tempest passes through, you shall be trodden down by it: when it passes through, it shall take you in the morning, in the morning it shall pass through: by day and by night there shall be a most evil hope. Learn to hear, you who are in tribulation: We cannot fight, and we ourselves are too weak to be gathered together. I had said to you, he says: Hear the word of the Lord, you scornful men, or afflicted princes of my people, and do not have a covenant with death nor a pact with hell, you who, despising my precepts, have made a lie your hope, and, boasting, or rather despairing, say: by a lie we shall be protected. Therefore the Lord, who is merciful and compassionate, patient and abounding in mercy (Ps 144 [145]), says that, against your will, he will lay in the foundations of Zion a stone chosen and tried and precious and a corner stone. Of this the Apostle too speaks: As a wise architect I have laid the foundation (1 Cor 3:10); and again: For no one can lay another foundation than that which is laid, which is Christ Jesus (ibid., 11). This stone is truly, and a second time, called a stone, just as in Leviticus man, man is said twice; and a corner stone, because it joined together the peoples of the Circumcision and of the Gentiles, of which it is said in the psalm too: The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner (Ps 117 [118]:22). These are the builders and masons who are now called scornful men and princes of the people that is in Jerusalem. Of this stone we read in Daniel too, that it was cut from the mountain without hands and filled the whole world (Dan 2): because the dispensation of the divine offspring took a human body, and the fullness of the Godhead dwelt in it bodily. Upon this stone, which by another name is called the rock, Christ built the Church, and, according to the Hebrew, founded it with a firm foundation; in which whoever believes shall not be confounded, or, according to the Hebrew, let him not hasten: that is, lest the coming of Christ should seem slow to him. For when they have begun to be stricken in vengeance for the contempt and neglect of God's precepts, then they understand the thing that they heard.
Commentary on Isaiah

And what follows: For the bed is straitened, so that one must fall out, and a short cloak cannot cover both, has the sense we read in the Apostle: You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot be partakers of the table of the Lord and of the table of idols (1 Cor 10:20-21); and elsewhere: What participation has righteousness with iniquity? What fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial? What part has the believer with the unbeliever? What consent has the temple of God with idols (2 Cor 6:14-15)? He speaks under the metaphor of a most chaste husband, who says to an adulterous wife: One little bed cannot hold me and the adulterer with you, and a short cloak cannot cover both the husband and the paramour. O Jerusalem, then, to whom he speaks in Ezekiel too under the person of a fornicating wife (Ezek 16:21), and whom at the beginning of Hosea he calls a harlot and an adulteress (Hos 3), if you wish to be joined in my embraces, cast away your idols: if you serve idols, you cannot have me. This according to the Hebrew.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the glory of the God of Israel was there, not because it took delight in such a neighbor, but so that by its presence it might destroy the idol of jealousy and the temple; hence the overthrow of the city and of the temple also follows after a short time; and it is written in Isaiah that a narrow bed can by no means hold two, and a short cloak cannot cover both, Scripture signifying that saying of the Apostle: What agreement has Christ with Belial? The temple of God with an idol?
Commentary on Isaiah

For as on the mountain of divisions the Lord shall stand, as in the valley of Gibeon he shall be angry, that he may do his work, his strange work, that he may perform his work, his work is foreign to him. And now do not mock, lest perhaps your bonds be tightened. For I have heard from the Lord God of hosts a consummation and a cutting short upon the whole earth. LXX: As a mountain of the ungodly the Lord shall rise up, and he shall be in the valley of Gibeon; with fury he shall do his works, a work of bitterness, and his fury shall deal as with strangers: and his bitterness is strange. And do not you rejoice, lest your bonds be strengthened, since I have heard from the Lord God Sabaoth things completed and cut short, which he will do upon all the earth. The Lord promised that he would lay a precious stone in the foundations of Zion, so that hail might overthrow the lie and the hope of the ungodly, and a mighty tempest might blot out the covenant with death and the pact with hell. Since the scornful princes would not receive it, just as once, when David reigned, the Lord cut down his adversaries against the Philistines on the mountain of divisions, which in Hebrew was called PHARASIM (פרצים), from which the place also took its name; and as in the valley of Gibeon, under Joshua the leader, when, in the confidence of God dwelling in him, he said: Let the sun stand still at Gibeon, and the moon over against the valley of Aijalon (Josh 10:12), and the sun stood still for the space of one day, and many of the foreigners perished: so the Lord shall be angry against the ungodly and the scornful, that he may do his work. For it is not the Lord's work to destroy those whom he created, but to do a strange work, which pertains to cruelty rather than to mercy. And again he repeats the very same thing in other words: that he may perform his work. It is not his work to punish sinners, but foreign and strange to him that he who is the Savior should punish.
Commentary on Isaiah

According to the Seventy, the Lord himself is said to be about to rise like a mountain of the ungodly and to be in the valley of Gibeon, that he may do his works, which are all one work of bitterness: and this should by no means seem blasphemous. For it does not say that the Lord will be a mountain of the ungodly, but like a mountain, which seems most heavy to the ungodly and those who bear it. Just as a negligent son and a sick man may think a father and a physician cruel if they restore them to health with blows and with the cautery of discipline. For the Lord will rise up and will be in the valley of Gibeon on account of those who, though for their sins they stand in a low place, are lifted up into pride by the swelling of their mind. For Gibeon means hill: that he may do his works, which are works of bitterness, when he is compelled to change his clemency and, instead of sweet, becomes bitter.
Homilies on Ezekiel 2.4.20

Hence Isaiah, contemplating our salvation and [Christ's] passion, well said: "That he may do his work, his strange work; that he may perform his work, his work is strange to him." For the work of God is to gather the souls that he created and call them back to the joys of the eternal light. But it is not the work [of] God in his essence to be flogged, to be smeared with spittle, to be crucified, to die and to be buried, but this is the work of a sinful person who deserved all these things for his sins. But [Jesus] himself bore our sins in his own body on the tree. And he who in his own nature always remains incomprehensible deigned to be comprehended in our nature and to be flogged, because if he had not assumed the attributes of our weakness he could never have raised us to the power of his fortitude.… And he does his strange work that he might do his proper work, because insofar as he bore our sins in infirmity he led us who are his creatures to the glory of his fortitude in which he lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, through ages of ages. Amen.
Commentary on Isaiah

Since, then, the Lord is going to rise up from his patience and will by no means spare, just as he did not spare on Mount Pharasim and in the valley of Gibeon, I warn you, O scornful men, by no means to laugh at my prophets, nor to think that what they announce will not come, lest, if you persist in mocking, the bonds of your sins be tightened (For each one is bound fast by the cords of his own sins (Prov 5:22), or the time of captivity come upon you. For what the Lord was postponing in time, the bonds, the captivity and the punishments, or the last day of judgment, he is now about to fulfill in fact, and to consummate and cut short. Therefore I, the prophet, announce to you the things I have learned from the Lord God almighty are to come upon the whole earth, so that you may forestall the impending wrath by repentance.
Commentary on Isaiah

Therefore you who are one day to suffer these things, do not now rejoice with that joy with which the rich man too rejoiced, clothed in purple at his banquet and neglecting the poor man Lazarus (Luke 16), lest perhaps your bonds become stronger. For what the Lord is going to do, and to fulfill his sentence in fact, this I have both heard and announced to you in full. And as for what he added: Upon all the earth, according to the history understand the borders of Judea; according to the anagogy, of the whole world.
Commentary on Isaiah

Give ear and hear my voice: attend and hear my speech. Will the plowman plow all day that he may sow, will he break up and hoe his ground? When he has leveled its surface, will he not sow gith, and scatter cumin, and put wheat in rows, and barley, and millet, and vetch in their borders? And he will instruct him in judgment; his God will teach him. For gith shall not be threshed with saws, nor shall the wheel of the cart go round over the cumin; but gith shall be beaten out with a rod, and cumin with a staff: but bread shall be crushed. Yet the thresher shall not thresh it forever, nor shall the wheel of the cart vex it, nor shall he crush it with its hoofs. And this has gone forth from the God of hosts, that he might make his counsel wonderful and magnify righteousness. LXX: Give ear and hear my voice: attend and hear my words. Will he who plows plow all day, or will he prepare the seed before he prepares the ground? When he has leveled its surface, will he not then sow gith and cumin, and again sow wheat, and barley, and millet, and spelt in your borders, and you shall be instructed by the judgment of God, and shall rejoice? For gith is not cleaned with harshness, nor does the wheel of the cart go round over the cumin; but gith is beaten out with a rod, and cumin is eaten with bread. For I will not be angry with you forever, nor shall the voice of my bitterness trample you down; and these portents have gone forth from the Lord. Take counsel, exalt a vain consolation. He is now speaking also to the same men to whom he had said above: Hear the word of God, you scornful men, who rule over my people that is in Jerusalem; and he commands them to hear his voice and attend diligently to his speech.
Commentary on Isaiah

God dispenses the human race in various ways: now he punishes, now he has mercy; now he rebukes, now he defends; that is, now he plows, now he sows, now he reaps the ripe fruits, and when they are reaped he threshes them on the floors, and governs his world as he will. Gith and cumin, that is, all the nations that did not receive the knowledge of him nor have the precepts of the Law, he corrects with a rod and a staff; but the wheat, that is, the people of the Jews, he will torment with great punishments. For to whom more is entrusted, from him more will be required. And the servant who knows the will of his lord and does not do it shall be beaten with many stripes (Luke 12:47); and in another place it is written: The mighty shall suffer torments mightily (Wis 6:7). Yet he will not torment them forever. For it is one thing to be ungodly, another to be a sinner. What we have interpreted of the nations and the Jews, others expound of the people and the priests: that the unlearned common people in the day of judgment will be chastised like gith and cumin with a rod and a staff, but the priests, who had the key of knowledge, will be tormented with great punishments; and that this happens by the judgment of the Lord, who shows in all things his wonderful counsel and the truth of his righteousness, so that from those who have received more, more is required.
LETTER 22.20

I praise wedlock, I praise marriage, but it is because they give me virgins. I gather the rose from the thorns, the gold from the earth, the pearl from the shell. "Does the plowman plow all day to sow?" Shall he not also enjoy the fruit of his labor? Wedlock is the more honored, the more what is born of it is loved. Why, mother, do you grudge your daughter her virginity? She has been reared on your milk, she has come from your womb, she has grown up in your bosom. Your watchful affection has kept her a virgin. Are you angry with her because she chooses to be a king's wife and not a soldier's? She has conferred on you a high privilege; you are now the mother-in-law of God.
Commentary on Isaiah

Will the farmer, he says, always plow so that he may cast the seed? Will he not first break up the ground and turn over the furrows with the plowshare, and break the lumps lying there with rake and hoe, so that when he has leveled the surface of the earth and first softened the hard fields, he may then scatter gith or cumin, and sow wheat, and barley, and millet, and spelt in their borders, according to the variety of the land and of the seasons: for all things are not sown at once. For spelt, which the Greeks call ζέαν, some understand vetch.
Commentary on Isaiah
And God by his judgment instructs the farmer himself, that is, the sower, by nature, and teaches him to know what cultivation to apply to which seed.
Commentary on Isaiah

Then, when the time of reaping has come, gith and cumin, which are the weaker seeds, are not ground by the wheels of the carts, which, made of iron like saws, are driven round and dragged over the reaped crops; but they are beaten out with a rod and a staff, which are commonly called flails.
Commentary on Isaiah

Where we have translated: gith shall be beaten out with a rod, and cumin with a staff, the Seventy, meaning I know not what, translated: but cumin is eaten with bread. Indeed the old Greek translators too, in rendering the Hebrew, were silent about this expression, perhaps because they had nothing to say.
Commentary on Isaiah

And that passage in which we, according to the Hebrew, have put: Yet the thresher shall not thresh it forever, nor shall the wheel of the cart vex it, nor shall he crush it with its hoofs, the Seventy translated not word for word but according to the sense: For I will not be angry with you forever, nor shall the voice of my bitterness trample you down: showing that refreshment is to come to sinners after torments, and that these things have gone forth from the Lord as portents and wonders. Hence sinners who are afterward to be punished are commanded to take counsel and exalt their consolation, by no means a vain one, as was added by the Seventy, but consolation absolutely. For God would never command them to exalt their vain consolation, which would be of no profit to them.
Commentary on Isaiah

But bread, that is, the wheat from which bread is made, is ground by iron wheels, and all its stalk is crushed into chaff. Yet it is not always vexed and ground, nor at all times crushed by the hoofs of the wheels; for which in the Hebrew it says by their horses: so that, since he had spoken of the hoofs of the wheels, he might keep the metaphor in the rest. Some would have it that, because he named hoofs and horses, herds of mares are meant, which are usually let into the threshing floors to tread out the grain; but Scripture could not say what the province of Judea did not have.
Commentary on Isaiah

But this, that is, that gith and cumin are beaten out with a rod and a staff, while wheat and barley and spelt, and perhaps millet too, are ground by iron wheels, not forever, is the judgment of God, who in all things shows his wonderful counsel and displays the greatness of his righteousness in all. These things we have said παραφραστικῶς, so that we may more easily understand the sense for which they are said.

n: Ariel. This word signifies the lion of God, and here is taken for the strong city of Jerusalem. (Challoner) --- It was destroyed by the Chaldeans, (4 Kings xxv.) and still more by the Romans, 40 years after. (Calmet) (Worthington) --- Ezechiel (xliii. 15.) styles the altar of holocausts Ariel. --- Took. Septuagint. The Hebrew means also "inhabited." (Haydock) --- Sion was called the city of David. (Calmet) --- The invasion (Haydock) of Sennacherib is here foretold (Forcr.[Forerius?]) two years before, chap. xxxi. 10.

Trench. Sennacherib did not besiege the city, chap. xxxvii. 33. But he made preparations for it, and his sentiments are expressed, (Calmet) together with the fatal consequences which he felt, when his army was offered up (Haydock) as a victim on the altar of holocausts, ver. 1.
Circle. Thus provisions were cut off. (Calmet)
The Python. The diviner by a spirit. (Challoner) --- Jerusalem shall hardly dare to make a noise. (Calmet)
Away. The numbers, and speedy downfall of the Assyrians, are described. (Haydock)
Thunder. Psalm lxxv. 7. Tharaca was coming to assist Ezechias, chap. xxxvii. 36. (Calmet)
It, in their dreams.

Be, &c. Though God spared the city, for the sake of the good, He will not fail to punish scoffers, in due time, as He now declares. (Haydock) --- Drunkenness. You shall suffer for your crimes, (chap. xxviii. 7.) or be affrighted.

Sleep, or compunction, (Romans xi. 8.; Calmet) denoting their obstinacy. (St. Chrysostom) --- Visions. Protestants, "the seers." (Haydock) --- The Jews perceived but very imperfectly the meaning of the prophets, when they spoke of a future Redeemer, God and man. They are now more infatuated, (Calmet) having a veil on their hearts, 1 Corinthians iv. 3. Both learned and ignorant refuse to believe, excusing themselves, ver. 12. (Haydock) --- The more they read the Scriptures, the less do they understand. (Calmet)

Men. Our Saviour applies this to the Jews. The evangelists follow the Septuagint, Matthew xv. 8., and Mark vii. 6. (Calmet) --- "This people approacheth to me, (Grabe adds, with its mouth and with) their lips they honour me, but their heart is far from me. Yet in vain do they honour me, teaching the commands of men and doctrines." (Haydock) --- They still continue to corrupt God's word by their false interpretations.

Hid. At the approach of Sennacherib, the politicians were confounded. But the obstinate blindness of the Jews in the midst of such a blaze of predictions, which are evidently accomplished in Jesus Christ, excites admiration. That their ancestors should have found them obscure, is not so wonderful. The prophets foretold this event; and the reprobation of the synagogue, which had been so highly favoured, is a proof of the truth of the Christian religion, 1 Corinthians i. 18. (Calmet)
Not. So it is in vain to think that your hypocrisy or excuses will deceive God, chap. xxviii. 15. (Haydock)

Charmel. This word signifies a fruitful field. (Challoner) --- Shall Carmel be presently a forest or barren mountain? No. But I will work a greater miracle, ver. 18. Jerusalem shall rejoice, and Sennacherib shall be filled with dismay.
Rejoice. Our Saviour alludes to this text, (Luke vii. 22.) which, under the figure of the deliverance from captivity, points out the vocation of the Gentiles, chap. xxxv. 5., and xlii. 7, 19.
Prevail. Wicked princes, scoffers, &c., (ver. 10., and chap. xxviii. 7.) shall be exterminated. Ezechias promoted piety with greater zeal after his deliverance.
Gate. False prophets rose up against those who spoke the truth, and condemned them unjustly. (Calmet) --- The just, Christ. (Menochius)
Israel. They shall serve God with fidelity and gratitude, chap. xxx. 22. (Calmet)
Murmured. Magicians, (Grotius) or false sages, chap. xxviii. 9. (Calmet)

f: Commentary on Isaiah

I know that I have read that Ariel means my light of God, which is far otherwise. For here the first syllable is written with ALEPH and RES (אר): but light, which in Hebrew is called OR, has between ALEPH and RES the middle letter VAU, which is not found in the present name. And they refer all that is now said against Ariel to the heretics, who reckon their own doctrine to be the light of God, and who are to be overcome by the true David: and all their solemnities are to be taken away, and their present joy changed into future sorrow; and God commands them to do penance, lest they begin to eat with the Moabites and be like the Gentiles. For he himself will overcome Ariel, and will encompass all their strength and riches with his army. And with towers, that is, with the teachers of the Church, he will bring their words low to the earth, so that they will by no means set their mouth against heaven, but will be written in the earth and speak from the earth, and become like dust shaken off by a wheel; and all the riches of the ungodly will be compared to a point and a moment of time, when he visits them in his majesty, descending in whirlwind and tempest and the fire of punishment; and they will understand that all their riches, and the pomp of their words, and the twists of their arguments, are like the dream of one who eats and drinks in vain: they who have made war against Jerusalem, the vision of peace, or against Ariel, the mightiest lion, and lastly against Mount Zion, upon which the city of the Church is set and cannot be hidden.
LETTER 108.9

[Zion] formed the city that David formerly stormed and afterwards rebuilt. Of its storming it is written, "Woe to Ariel, to Ariel"—that is, God's lion2 (and indeed in those days it was extremely strong).
Commentary on Isaiah

Woe to Ariel, Ariel, the city which David besieged. Year has been added to year, the solemnities have rolled round. I will surround Ariel with a rampart, and it shall be sad and mourning; and it shall be to me like Ariel. And I will set as it were a ring round about you, and I will cast up a mound against you, and set up fortifications for your siege. You shall be brought low, you shall speak from the earth, and your speech shall be heard from the ground, and your voice shall be like that of a python from the earth, and from the ground your speech shall mutter. And the multitude of those who winnow you shall be like fine dust, and the multitude of those who have prevailed against you like passing ash. And it shall be suddenly, at once: it shall be visited by the Lord of hosts with thunder and the shaking of the earth, and with the great noise of whirlwind and tempest, and of the flame of devouring fire. And the multitude of all the nations that have fought against Ariel, and all who have made war and besieged and prevailed against it, shall be like the dream of a night vision. As the hungry man dreams and eats, but when he has awakened his soul is empty; and as the thirsty man dreams and drinks, but after he has awakened he is still faint and thirsty, and his soul is empty: so shall be the multitude of all the nations that have fought against Mount Zion. LXX: Woe to Ariel, Ariel, the city which David besieged. Gather the produce, eat year upon year, for you shall eat with Moab: for I will press Ariel hard, and its strength and its riches shall be mine, and I will encompass you like David: and I will throw up a rampart round about you, and set towers around you, and your words shall be brought low to the earth, and your speeches shall sink into the earth. And your voice shall be like that of those who speak from the earth, and down to the pavement your voice shall grow weak. And the riches of the ungodly shall be like dust from a wheel, and the multitude of those who have oppressed you like ash that is swept away; and it shall be in an instant, suddenly, from the Lord Sabaoth. For there shall be a visitation with thunder, and shaking, and a great noise, a mighty tempest, and a flame of devouring fire. And the riches of all the nations that have made war against Ariel, and all who have fought against Jerusalem, and all who have gathered against it and afflicted it, shall be like one who sees a dream by night. And they shall be like those who hunger in their sleep and eat, and when they rise their dream is vain; and like one who thirsts in a dream and drinks, and when he rises he will still thirst, and his soul has hoped in vain: so shall be the riches of all the nations that have made war against Mount Zion. Where we have translated Woe, in the Hebrew is written OI (הוי), which among them is sometimes used in the vocative case, so that it does not lament Ariel but calls it; although in the present place it is to be taken as a lament. Ariel too means lion of God; and for city, which Aquila translated πολίχνην, that is, little town or little village, they read in the Hebrew CARIATH (קרית), which properly signifies village, and in the Syriac language is called Cartha; whence the village of the woods too is called CARIATH JARIM (קרית יערים). Indeed above too (cf. Isa 1:21), where we read: How has the faithful city Zion become a harlot?, for city Cariath is written, that is, village: which, to express Aquila's translation word for word, we can call citylet. Therefore Ariel, that is, lion of God, is the name given to Jerusalem, once most strong; or, as others think, to the temple and altar of God that was in Jerusalem. And what follows: Which David besieged, for which Symmachus translated camp of David, and Theodotion circumvallation of David, in the Hebrew reads HANA (חנה), which the most learned of the Hebrews held to signify dwelling place. If, then, we read: which David besieged, let us refer it to that time when David took the citadel of Zion, while the blind and the lame resisted, and Joab first climbed the heights of the buildings (1 Chr 11). But if according to Symmachus and Theodotion, it is to be understood that David restored and fortified it; year has been added to year, or taken away, as Aquila translated; and the solemnities have rolled round. For when the temple was overthrown and the Jewish worship taken away, all their festivity perished.
Commentary on Isaiah

At the beginning of this chapter too, where we have said: Year has been added to year, or taken away, they translated: gather the fruits, or produce, year upon year: eat, for you shall eat with Moab. And the sense is: before the acceptable year of the Lord, of his preaching, comes, or rather the two years, of which we read in the Canticle of Habakkuk according to the Hebrew: In the midst of two times you shall be known (Hab 3), sow for yourselves in tears, that you may reap in joy (Ps 125 [126]). It is written in the Gospel according to John that the Lord came to Jerusalem at three Passovers, which make two years (John 2:13). And what follows: For you shall eat with Moab, is not in the Hebrew. Of this we can say that, unless they gather for themselves the fruits of repentance, they will begin to eat with those who do not enter the Church of the Lord forever. The other points in which they seem to differ are plain, and from what we have expounded their interpretation is easy.
Commentary on Isaiah

And the Lord says that he will surround Ariel with a rampart, with the Babylonian army, and that it will be sad and mourning when it has been destroyed by them. And again, under Jeshua son of Jozadak the high priest, and Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, and Ezra and Nehemiah, when Haggai and Zechariah prophesied, it will be like Ariel, in that it will have the likeness of the ancient temple, but not have its magnificence and adornment.
Commentary on Isaiah

A second time also the Lord threatens that he will surround Ariel with a ring, and cast up a mound against it, and set up fortifications for its siege, and that what he himself says, lamenting Jerusalem in the Gospel, will be fulfilled: If you knew the things that are for your peace, for days shall come upon you, and your enemies shall surround you with a rampart, and besiege you, and you shall be brought low to the ground (Luke 19:42ff.). And Jerusalem shall be trodden down by the nations until the time of the nations is consummated.
Commentary on Isaiah

For in other words the prophet now says the same thing: that, brought low, it speaks from the earth, and its speech is heard from the ground; and its voice is like that of a python from the earth, and from the ground it mutters like sparrows; so that by these words he signifies the νεκυομαντείαν of the magicians, by which they are said to call up souls and to hear the thin voices of shades, or rather of demons. Indeed for python Aquila translated magician, which in Hebrew is called CHEB (כאב), for which the Seventy translated those speaking from the earth. By these words it is indicated that the ruin of the temple will remain until the consummation of the world, so that, having collapsed into ashes, it will never be raised again.
Commentary on Isaiah

And so great an army of Roman power will encompass you, O Ariel, that it will be compared to countless dust, like ash flying through the air. Hence he compares to dust and ash not the weakness of those who made war against them, but their multitude, which is equal to the countless sands.
Commentary on Isaiah

And this will be suddenly, at once, so that in the midst of peace sudden wars arise under Nero, and the Lord of hosts visits Jerusalem with thunder, and with the shaking of the earth, and with the whirlwind of tempest, and with the flame of devouring fire, by which he signifies that the temple was to be burned.
Commentary on Isaiah

And the Romans, who, when the Jews had been overcome and Jerusalem overthrown under Titus and Vespasian, offered to the Capitol spoils from the vessels that once were God's, and thought that what they had done was the work of their own valor and of the power of their gods, not of the wrath of God, will possess all their riches as in a dream and in a vision of the night. And as one who is hungry thinks, while sleeping, that he is eating in his dreams, and one who is thirsty, his throat parched with thirst, drinks rivers, and when he has awakened his thirst becomes fiercer, having been mocked by an empty drink: so the multitude of all the nations which, subject to Roman power, fought against Mount Zion, will have their riches as in a shadow and a cloud and a dream of the night, riches which they will leave behind by an early death. In the place where we have put: all who have made war and besieged and prevailed against it, the Seventy translated: and all who have fought against Jerusalem, which is not in the Hebrew.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 10

And those who sleep are those who, when they ought to be taking heed and watching with the soul, are not doing this. But by reason of great want of attention they are nodding in resolution and are drowsy in their reflections, such as "in their dreaming defile the flesh, and set at nothing that which is highest in authority, and rail at dignities." And these, because they are asleep, live in an atmosphere of vain and dreamlike fancies concerning realities. [They do not admit] the things that are actually true, but [they are] deceived by what appears in their vain imaginations. In regard to [them] it is said in Isaiah, "Like as when a thirsty man dreams that he is drinking, but when he has risen up is still thirsty, and his soul has cherished a vain hope, so shall be the wealth of all the nations, as many as have warred in Jerusalem."
On Joseph the Patriarch 6.38

Let us speak of him who thought he was happy since he was chief butler and believed that this was the summit and crown of all power, that he would give the cup to the king. This was his glory, this was his grandeur in this world; when he was deprived of this he felt sorrow, and when he was restored to it he rejoiced. But this is a dream, and all worldly power is a dream, not a reality. To be sure, he saw by way of a dream that his preeminent position was restored to him. Isaiah also says that people of this kind are such as take delight in prosperity in this world. One who eats and drinks in his sleep thinks he is filled with food and drink, but when he awakens, he begins to be more hungry; then he understands how insubstantial were that dreamer's food and drink. Just so, one who is asleep in this world and does not open his eyes to the mysteries of God, as long as he is in a deep corporeal sleep, supposes that such worldly power is of some importance, seeing it, as it were, in his dreams. But when he has awakened, he discovers how insubstantial the pleasure of this world is.
Commentary on Isaiah

Be stupefied and wonder: waver and stagger, be drunk, and not with wine; reel, and not with drunkenness. For the Lord has mingled for you a spirit of deep sleep: he will close your eyes; your prophets and your princes, who see visions, he will cover. And the vision of all shall be to you like the words of a sealed book, which, when they give it to one who knows letters, they will say: Read this, and he will answer: I cannot, for it is sealed. And the book shall be given to one who does not know letters, and it shall be said to him: Read; and he will answer: I do not know letters. For spirit of deep sleep the Seventy translated compunction; Theodotion ecstasy of mind; Aquila καταφορὰν, that is, heavy sleep; which in Hebrew is called THARDEMA (תרדמה), and which Scripture records was sent by God upon Adam (Gen 2), when the woman was made from the rib of his side. And Jonah snored in this same sleep in the ship (Jonah 1). And the whole prophecy after the overthrow of Jerusalem and the temple, that is, of Ariel, is against the scribes and Pharisees, who, having the key of knowledge, neither enter themselves nor allow others who wish to enter. Scripture says to Pharaoh, "To this purpose have I raised you that I may show my power in you; and that my name may be declared throughout all the earth." Then, making a conclusion to both passages, he says, "Therefore he has mercy on whom he will and whom he will he hardens." Obviously he treats neither of these with injustice but both with mercy and truth; in spite of that there is an uprising of insolent weakness on the part of those who attempt to comprehend the unsearchable depth of the judgment of God according to the interpretations of the human heart. The apostle refutes this view when he says, "You will say therefore to me: Why does he then find fault? For who resists his will?" Let us imagine this as said to us. What other answer should we make than the one he made? If such ideas disturb us also because we, too, are human, we all have need to listen to the apostle saying, "O man, who are you that replies against God? Shall the thing formed say to him that formed it: Why have you made me thus? Or has not the potter power over the clay, of the same lump to make one vessel unto honor, another unto dishonor?" If this lump of clay were of such indifferent value that it deserved nothing good any more than it deserved anything evil, there would be reason to see injustice in making of it a vessel unto dishonor. But when, through the free will of the first man alone, condemnation extended to the whole lump of clay, undoubtedly if vessels are made of it unto honor, it is not a question of justice not forestalling grace, but of God's mercy. If, however, vessels are made of it unto dishonor, it is to be attributed to the judgment of God, not to his injustice—far be from us the thought that there could be any such with God! Whoever is wise in this matter with the Catholic church does not argue against grace in favor of merit, but he sings mercy and judgment to the Lord, that he may not ungratefully deny his mercy or unjustly upbraid his judgment.
Commentary on Isaiah

Is it not yet a little while, and a short time, and Lebanon shall be turned into Charmel, and Charmel shall be reckoned as a forest? And in that day the deaf shall hear the words of the book, and out of darkness and gloom the eyes of the blind shall see. And the meek shall increase their joy in the Lord, and the poor among men shall exult in the Holy One of Israel: for he who prevailed has failed. The scorner is consumed, and all who watched for iniquity have been cut down: who made men sin by a word, and tripped up him who reproved in the gate, and turned aside in vain from the righteous. Let the Jews answer, and the friends of the bare history alone, who seek not fruit on the tree but only the leaves and the shade of words, which quickly withers and perishes: how at the coming of the Lord the Savior (since from the times of Isaiah to the dispensation of the flesh he assumed is, compared with eternity, a short and little space of time) Lebanon, a mountain of Phoenicia, was turned and transferred into Mount Carmel, which in Hebrew is called CHERMEL (כרמל), and lies on the border of Palestine and Phoenicia, overlooking Ptolemais (though another mountain too is called Carmel in the holy Scriptures, where lived Nabal the Carmelite (1 Sam 25), a foolish and wicked man, who had as wife Abigail, who on her husband's death married David; for while he lived she could not take David as husband, lest she be called an adulteress if she were joined to another man); and how Charmel is reckoned as a forest and as unfruitful trees? Since they cannot say this, let them hear that Lebanon, which means whitening, refers to the people of the nations, which, washed in the Lord and its former filth purged away, ascending wholly clean, leans upon the Savior in the person of the Church; and of it it is said in the Song of Songs: Who is this who comes up whitened, leaning upon her kinsman (Song 8:5); and that this people is transferred into Charmel, that is, into the knowledge of circumcision, so as to recognize the mysteries of the spiritual and true circumcision, and to be in the place once held by the people of the Jews; while those who would not receive Christ are reckoned as a forest and as barren trees, which cannot praise the Lord with the fruit-bearing trees.
Commentary on Acts 9

Note that [Paul] taught Greeks in Jerusalem, and Jews in Damascus which is a Gentile city, even though this should signify that Gentiles were to be included in the city of God and Jews were to fall into the faithlessness of the Gentiles, in accordance with what Isaiah said, "Lebanon shall be changed into Carmel, and Carmel shall be regarded as a wasteland."
Commentary on Isaiah

When Lebanon has been changed into Charmel, and Charmel into a forest, then those who before were deaf and could not hear the words of the prophetic book (of which we said above that all holy Scripture is called one book, as the Preacher says (Eccl 12:11): The words of the wise are as goads, and as nails fixed deep, which are given from the councils by one shepherd) shall hear, and shall speak, those to whom the Savior will say: Ephphetha, which means be opened (Mark 7). And where we translated: out of darkness and gloom the eyes of the blind shall see, whose interpretation is easy, Aquila and Theodotion and Symmachus translated: The eyes of the blind shall see darkness and gloom: to show that the mysteries of Christ were to be laid open to the people of the nations, which before was blind, according to what is said: Dark water in the clouds of the air (Ps 17 [18]:12). And in the same psalm it is written of God: He made darkness his hiding place (ibid., 12). And in Proverbs we read: A wise man hearing these things will be wiser, and the prudent will possess government; and he will understand a parable and dark speech, the sayings of the wise and riddles (Prov 1:5-6). Indeed Moses too, that he might understand and see God (Exod 20), entered into the cloud and into the thick darkness, of which it is said in the Psalm: Thick darkness under his feet (Ps 17 [18]:10).
Commentary on Genesis 1:2.4-5

Neither was heaven created in any six-day period and the stars illuminated and the dry land separated from the water and the trees and vegetation planted. Rather, Scripture customarily uses "day" to denote an unspecified period of time, as the apostle did when he said, "Behold, this is the day of salvation." He was not referring to a particular day but to the entirety of the time of the present life in which we labor for eternal salvation. The prophet also spoke not of one specific day but of numerous moments of divine grace, saying, "In that day, the deaf will hear the words of this book." Moreover, it is difficult to understand how in one day God made heaven and earth and all the brush of the field and every plant of every region, unless we say that all creatures were created simultaneously in formless matter, according to which it is written: "He who lives forever created all things together."
Commentary on Isaiah

When those who were before blind have either beheld all the mystical things, or have lifted their eyes from blindness and darkness to see, so that the true light may rise for those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death: then the meek, of whom it is written: Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth (Matt 5:4); or the poor, whose prince says in the psalms: This poor man cried, and the Lord heard him (Ps 33 [34]:7); and: who shall judge the poor of the people, and shall save the sons of the poor (Ps 71 [72]:4), of whom it is said to the Jews: You have despised the counsel of the poor man: these shall increase their joy in the Lord, so that he who glories may glory in the Lord (2 Cor 10); and the poor among men, or those despaired of and despised by men, who before had no knowledge of the Law, shall exult in the Holy One of Israel, who says: Be holy, for I am holy (Lev 11:44).
Commentary on Isaiah

And there is every exultation, because he who prevailed has failed. The scorner is consumed, or the arrogant and proud one, who had said: By strength I will do it, and by wisdom; I will remove the bounds of the nations and lay waste their strength; who mocked all, so much so that the saint too said: My loins are filled with illusions (Ps 37 [38]:8). And all who watched for iniquity have been cut down, or destroyed, whose destruction, because of their evil watchings, does not slumber: who made the whole race of men sin by a word of blasphemy, so that they denied the Word of God and set their mouth against heaven. He means the demons, who, wicked themselves, made all men sin in speech, blaspheming with various dogmas; and as far as in them lay they tripped up him who reproved in the gate and in judgment, and made him turn aside from righteousness, who was in the gates of the daughter of Zion, lifted up from the gates of death; and who rebuked those who hated him who reproved in the gates. What we have understood of the devil and his angels, the Nazarenes think was said against the scribes and Pharisees: that the δευτερωταί have failed, who before mocked the people with most wicked traditions, and watched day and night to deceive the simple, who made men sin against the Word of God, so that they denied Christ the Son of God.
Commentary on Isaiah

Therefore thus says the Lord to the house of Jacob, he who redeemed Abraham: Jacob shall not now be confounded, nor shall his face now blush: but when he sees his sons, the works of my hands, in his midst sanctifying my name: and they shall sanctify the Holy One of Jacob, and shall proclaim the God of Israel; and those who err in spirit shall know understanding, and the mutterers shall learn the Law. LXX: Therefore thus says the Lord concerning the house of Jacob, which he separated from Abraham: Jacob shall not now be confounded, nor shall he now change his face; but when he sees his sons, my works: for my sake they shall sanctify my name, and they shall sanctify the Holy One of Jacob, and shall fear the God of Israel; and those who err in spirit shall know understanding, and the mutterers shall learn obedience; and what follows, ÷ and the stammering tongues shall learn to speak peace ⁚, is to be marked with an obelus. When, he says, the deaf have heard the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind have seen, and Lebanon has been turned into Charmel, and Charmel reckoned as a forest, so that the meek and the poor rejoice in the Lord, and the proud man and the scorner fail: then Jacob shall be confounded, who now, for the time being, is not confounded. He means the times of Isaiah. And his face shall blush, so that blushing and confusion may be an occasion of salvation, especially when he sees his sons, that is, the Apostles and apostolic men, who were of the race of the Jews, performing the mighty works of the Lord in the midst of the nations, and proclaiming the name of Christ to the Gentiles, and saying: Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name (Matt 6:9). For they will sanctify the Holy One who sprang from Jacob, and will teach the God of Israel among the nations, so that, having abandoned idols, they say: How false are the idols our fathers possessed, and there is none among them who gives rain; and then those who now err in spirit shall know the understanding of God, and those who once murmured against the Lord in the wilderness shall learn the Law, of which before they had no knowledge. For if they had received Moses, they would have received the Lord Jesus Christ too, since Moses spoke of him.
Commentary on Isaiah

What at the beginning of the chapter we translated according to the Hebrew: Thus says the Lord to the house of Jacob, he who redeemed once Abraham, and brought him out of the Chaldeans, and led him into the land of promise (Gen 11), is perfectly plain. But what the Seventy translated: Thus says the Lord concerning the house of Jacob, which he separated from Abraham, can be understood thus: that he separated the scribes and Pharisees, who blasphemed the Lord, from Abraham, who saw the day of the Lord and rejoiced (John 8). For if they had been sons of Abraham, they would have done the works of Abraham. And the Apostle argues that those are to be called sons of Abraham (Heb 11) who have the likeness of Abraham's faith, that is, the people of the nations, which was called the son of Abraham not from works but from faith.

n: Of me. Ezechias was guided by human prudence, in making an alliance with Egypt, though he might have just reasons for refusing to pay tribute to the Assyrians, 4 Kings xviii. 20. (Calmet) --- And. Septuagint, "alliances not by," &c. (Haydock)
Down, with presents, ver. 6., and 4 Kings xviii. 20.
Shame. Egypt had been defeated before Sennacherib's approach.
Hanes. Chaldean, "Taphanes," (Jeremias ii. 16.) or Daphnæ Pelusiæ. (Herodotus ii. 30.) --- In the Arabic, Nome, which formed part of (Haydock) the dominions of Tharaca. (Calmet)

Burden. This title seems unnecessary, and may be added by some Jew, (chap. xxi. 13.) though the Chaldean and others explain it, "They carry on their beasts, presents to the south," to the nations of Arabia and Egypt, infested with lions, &c. The rest of the prophecy is against the Jews, who cannot well be styled beasts of the south. (Calmet) --- Basilisk. The ibis devours many serpents on their flight from Arabia into Egypt. (Herodotus ii. 5.; Solin. xxxii.)
Cried. Hebrew, "called it Rahab, (or pride) it is rest." The people are indolent, though they will make great promises. (Calmet)

Box. This word was covered with wax. (Propertius iii. 3.) --- Write, that none may pretend that they were not admonished. Some think that this was addressed to Jeremias: but Isaias spoke to his incredulous countrymen.
See not. Such were the dispositions of their heart, chap. xxviii. 15.
Us. Mention God no more, or let him not meddle with our affairs. Seek not to reclaim us, we are pleased with our delusion. (Calmet)

Oppression. Literally, "calumny," (Haydock) or rebellion against the Assyrians. This was contrary to the respect due to God's name, used in the ratification of treaties, how wicked soever those princes might be.
For. Psalm lxi. 3. If God had not miraculously cut off the army of Sennacherib, what would have become of the kingdom of Juda?
Be. Septuagint, "groan," as Origen, &c., read. If you be seriously converted, and trust not in Egypt, you need not fear.
Ones, or chariots. (Calmet) --- Egypt was famous for horses, Deuteronomy xvii. 16. (Forcr.[Forerius?]) --- Rebsaces ridicules the Jews for the want of them, 4 Kings xviii. 23. (Haydock)
Five. A small number shall put you to flight. (Menochius) --- Mast, set up after a shipwreck, to warn others, or as a signal, chap. xxxiii. 23.
Wait for him. Having convinced Ezechias that he ought to trust in no other, the Lord rescues him from the hand of Sennacherib. (Calmet)
Weep. The citizens expected certain death, (Haydock) or slavery. (Calmet)

Water. The land will be reduced to a miserable condition by the ravages of Sennacherib. (Haydock) --- The following was a sabbatical year, ver. 23., and chap. xxxvii. 30. --- Teacher. It seems that Isaias, &c., had been silent. He spoke after Ezechias had sent for him, and God promises that the people shall not be left without guides. (Calmet) --- Christ will not abandon his Church. (Menochius)

Garment. Hebrew, "ephod," belonging to the idol, or its priests. Ezechias had prohibited idolatry at first. After his deliverance he was still more zealous, and even those who had formerly retained an affection for idols, saw their vanity, and became sincere.
Floor. They shall not have straw only, but wheat, &c., to denote abundance.
Towers, or chief officers of Sennacherib. All shall be luxuriant.

Sevenfold. Exceedingly great, equal to the light of 49 days. (Calmet) --- The fame of Ezechias spread widely. His kingdom was a figure of that of Christ, when this was more perfectly realized, the preaching of the gospel having dispelled the darkness of error. (Calmet) --- He alludes to the day of judgment. (St. Jerome) (Menochius)
Name. Majesty of God, (Calmet) in the future ages. (Haydock)
Error. The unjust government of Sennacherib, who endeavoured to engage all in idolatry.
Night. When the festivals commenced. (Calmet) --- He may particularly mean that night, when the destroying angel slew the Egyptians. (Vatable) --- Pipe. Music. (Haydock) --- This was not prescribed.
Stones. The Angel raised the storm, which destroyed many, while the rest in a panic fell upon one another, chap. ix. 5., and xxxvii. 36.
Rod. Sennacherib is terrified, who a few days before insulted the living God.
Harps. The sound of thunder will fill the people of Ezechias with joy, while the enemy shall perish irrecoverably. (Calmet)

Topheth. 'Tis the same as Gehenna, and is taken for hell. (Challoner) --- The Assyrians perish amid horrid cries (Haydock) and thunders, which resembled the noise made by drums, and by children who were burning in the arms of Moloc, 4 Kings xviii. 4., and xxiii. 10., and 2 Paralipomenon xxix. 16. Some think that the carcasses of the Assyrians were to be burnt in this common sewer of Jerusalem. But they were too far distant, chap. xxxvii. 33. (Calmet)

f: The Instructor Book 1

Reprimand is disapproval expressed in correction or strongly worded blame. The Educator resorts to this method of training when he says through Isaiah, "Woe to you, apostate children, says the Lord, that you would take counsel and not of me, and make treaties and not of my Spirit." He flavors each pronouncement in turn with the tart spice of fear to whet the appetite of his people for salvation and make them more aware of it, just as wool to be dyed is usually steeped first in an astringent to prepare it to preserve the dye.
HOMILIES CONCERNING THE STATUES 3:5

Let every man and woman among us, whether meeting together at church, or remaining at home, call upon God with much earnestness, and He will doubtless accede to these petitions. Whence does this appear evident? Because He is exceedingly desirous, that we should always take refuge in Him, and in everything make our requests unto Him; and do nothing and speak nothing without Him. For men, when we trouble them repeatedly concerning our affairs, become slothful and evasive, and conduct themselves unpleasantly towards us; but with God it is quite the reverse. Not when we apply to him continually respecting our affairs, but when we fail to do so, then is he especially displeased. Hear at least what He reproves the Jews for, when He says, "Ye have taken counsel, but not of Me, and made treaties, but not by My Spirit." For this is the custom of those who love; they desire that all the concerns of their beloved should be accomplished by means of themselves; and that they should neither do anything, nor say anything, without them. On this account did God not only on that occasion, but again elsewhere, uttering a reproof, speak the same language. "They have reigned, but not by Me; they have ruled, and they made it not known to Me." Let us not then be slow to take refuge in Him continually; and whatever be the evil, it will in any case find its appropriate solution.
Commentary on Isaiah

Some think this place was written against the ten tribes in Samaria, because, seeking help from the Egyptians, they were taken captive by the Assyrians. According to tropology: all who, despising the religion of God, return to their vomit, and, having lost the name of sons, are called most shameless dogs, take counsel not through the Lord, and strike a covenant not through the spirit of the Lord, and add sins to sins: so that, overcome by flattering vices, they also accept the perversity of false doctrines, and go down into the darkness of Egypt, seeking the help of Pharaoh, who reigns in Egypt, whose protection leads to disgrace and to everlasting reproach. For his princes are in Tanis, that is, in a humble and lowly command, most evil messengers, who labor in vain over a people that will not be able to profit them. For as the salvation of their disciples helps holy teachers, so the perdition of those seduced destroys the patriarchs of those who have fled to the help of Egypt.
Commentary on Isaiah

Woe, you deserting sons, says the Lord: that you should take counsel, and not from me; and weave a web, and not by my Spirit; that you might add sin upon sin. You who walk to go down into Egypt, and have not asked my mouth, hoping for help in the strength of Pharaoh, and having confidence in the shadow of Egypt. And the strength of Pharaoh shall be to you for confusion, and the confidence in the shadow of Egypt for disgrace. For your princes shall be in Tanis, and your messengers have come as far as Hanes. All are confounded over a people that will not be able to profit them: they were not for help nor for any use, but for confusion and for reproach. LXX: Woe, you transgressing sons, says the Lord. You have taken counsel, and not through me; and a pact, not through my spirit, that you might add sins to sins: you who go to go down into Egypt, and have not asked me, that you may receive help from Pharaoh and be protected by the Egyptians. The protection of Pharaoh shall be to you for confusion, and to those who trust in Egypt, a reproach. For there are in Tanis princes, most evil messengers. In vain shall they labor for a people that will not profit them for help, nor for use, but for confusion and reproach. After the prophecy against Ariel, and the other things that the preceding discourse set forth up to this place, there now begins another prophecy, which is shown to have been fulfilled after the hundred and fifty years that lay between Isaiah and Jeremiah. For it foretells that history which we read in the volume of Jeremiah (Jer 41), when, Jerusalem having been overthrown and all its wealth and princes carried off to Babylon, Gedaliah son of Ahikam was set over those of royal stock who had remained in Judea; and when he had been slain by treachery together with his Chaldean companions, all the captains of the warriors, and Johanan son of Kareah, and Jezaniah son of Hoshaiah, and the rest of the common people from the least to the greatest, came to Jeremiah the prophet and said to him: Let our prayer fall before you, and pray for us to the Lord your God for all this remnant. For we are left a few out of many, as your eyes behold us; and let the Lord your God show us the way by which we should go, and the thing that we should do (Jer 42:2-3). And when Jeremiah, after ten days, had answered from the word of the Lord: Thus says the Lord God of Israel: If you remain quietly in this land, I will build you up and not pull you down, I will plant you and not pluck you up, for I am appeased concerning the evil that I have done to you. Do not be afraid of the face of the king of Babylon, whom you fearfully dread (ibid., 10-11). And a little after: But if you say: We will not dwell in this land; and set your face to enter Egypt, and go in to dwell there, the sword which you dread shall overtake you there, and the famine about which you are anxious shall cleave to you in Egypt, and there you shall die (ibid., 42:13, 15, 16). The proud men answered, saying to Jeremiah: You are speaking a lie: the Lord our God has not sent you, saying: Do not enter into Egypt to dwell there; but Baruch son of Neriah is inciting you against us, to deliver us into the hands of the Chaldeans, to kill us and to have us carried away to Babylon (Jer 43:2-3). At length all the princes of the people, gathering the remnant with the women and little ones and the king's daughters, not hearing the voice of the Lord, entered Egypt, taking Jeremiah and Baruch with them, and came to Tahpanhes, so that Jeremiah, as a sign of the captivity to come, prophesied against the disobedient people the things contained in his book. What, therefore, was to happen afterward is foretold many years before; and those are called deserting and transgressing sons who, forsaking the counsel of God which they had received through Jeremiah, followed their own will, and wove a web, not by the spirit of God, which sounded to them from the mouth of Jeremiah. He put the weaving of a web μεταφορικῶς, to show an evil counsel; and they did this so as to increase their former sins with the sin of contention and pride.
Commentary on Isaiah

You who go down, he says, into Egypt, and have not asked my mouth. Not that they did not ask, but that they would not hear the counsel of the prophet, hoping for help in the strength of Pharaoh, and having confidence in the protection, or shadow, of Egypt. For the strength of Pharaoh, which is put twice in this place, the Hebrew has written MAOZ (מעוז). We have noted this so that, where we read in the last vision of Daniel (Dan 11) the God MAOZIM (מעוזים), we may understand not, as Porphyry dreams, the God of the village of Modim, but the mighty and strong God. Pharaoh among the Egyptians is the name of the royal power; and each is called by a particular name as well, as Pharaoh Neco and Pharaoh Hophra: as if we were to set Caesars and Augusti before the proper names of kings. And the strength of Pharaoh, he says, shall be to you for confusion, and the confidence in the shadow of Egypt for disgrace. The same Jeremiah writes that in Tahpanhes, a city of Egypt, he buried stones in the gate of Pharaoh's house, and said to the men of Judah: Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will send and take Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, my servant, and I will set his throne upon these stones which I have hidden, and he shall set his throne upon them. And he shall come and strike the land of Egypt: such as are for death, to death; and such as are for captivity, to captivity; and such as are for the sword, to the sword: and he shall kindle a fire in the shrines of the gods of Egypt, and burn them, and carry them away captive. And he shall wrap himself in the land of Egypt as a shepherd wraps himself in his cloak, and he shall go forth from there in peace (Jer 43:10-12). For when the Egyptians had been overcome, the Jews too who had fled to the Egyptians were taken captive.
Commentary on Isaiah

And what follows: For your princes shall be in Tanis, and your messengers have come as far as Hanes, is to be read with mockery and ἐμφατικῶς: that, despising the counsel of God, they sent their princes to Tanis, a city of Egypt, in which was the royal house of Pharaoh, and where under Moses very many signs and portents were performed, as the Psalmist says: Who did wonders in the land of Egypt, in the plain of Tanis (Ps 77 [78]:43). And the same Isaiah says against Egypt: Where now are your wise men? Let them tell you and say what the Lord Sabaoth has purposed against Egypt. The princes of Tanis have failed (Isa 19:12-13); and he records that they failed at that time when the Lord entered Egypt upon a light cloud. We do not read of Hanes, a city of Egypt, anywhere else; but from his saying: Your messengers have come as far as Hanes, we understand that it is the farthest city of Egypt, toward the Ethiopians and the Blemmyes; for which the Seventy translated: Most evil messengers shall labor in vain, who trusted in the people of Egypt, which could not profit them, and they became an everlasting reproach.
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 37

It is written in Isaiah: "the vision of the quadrupeds in tribulation and distress", and the rest, up to the place where he says: "the riches of the asps will not profit them". Let each one of us consider how great wealth of asps he has borne before this, how great riches of beasts, and how a rational man never sat upon our donkey — not the word of Moses, not of Isaiah, not of Jeremiah, nor of all the rest of the prophets — and he will see that the word of God and reason then sat upon us, when the Lord Jesus came and commanded his disciples that, going, they should untie "the colt of a donkey", which before had been tied up, so that it might walk free.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 16

But if you wish to learn yet more beasts, the prophet Isaiah will teach you, who, under "the vision" which he entitled "of the quadrupeds in the desert", speaks by the prophetic spirit certain such things concerning beasts: "in tribulation", he says, "and anguish, the lion and the lion's whelp; thence also the offspring of flying asps, who carried upon asses and camels their riches to a nation which shall not profit them". Can these things in any way be seen as said of bodily beasts, even by those who are exceedingly friends of the letter? For how can "the lion and the lion's whelp" or "the flying asps" "carry upon camels and asses their riches"? But evidently the prophet, filled with the Holy Spirit, enumerates the contrary powers of the most wicked demons, and designated that they place "the riches" of their deceptions upon souls stolid and perverse, which by a figure he compares to camels and asses. And that his soul might not be handed over to these beasts, fearing God he prayed, saying: "deliver not to the beasts the soul that confesses to you".
Commentary on Isaiah

The burden of the beasts of the South. For this the Hebrew says MASSA BEEMOTH NEGEB (משא בהמות נגב), which the Seventy translated: The vision of the four-footed beasts in the desert. The foregoing exposition, which we have woven with a very full unfolding of the history, is the interpretation of this place: that, according to prophetic custom, the burden, that is, the weight and load of torments and punishments, came not only upon Babylon and Philistia, and Moab, and Damascus, and Egypt, and the desert of the sea, and also Edom and Arabia, and the valley of Zion, and lastly Tyre, but also upon the beasts of the South, which the Seventy translated four-footed beasts in the desert. He means the tribe of Judah, which, situated in the southern part, borders on the wilderness; and those who, rejecting the prophecy of Jeremiah, when Jerusalem had been taken, would not dwell in Judea, but fled through the desert to the Egyptians. And rightly are they called beasts of the South, or four-footed beasts in the desert, because they rejected the knowledge of God, and, despising his command, fled to the images of Egypt, having hope in Pharaoh; and whoever leans on him is like one who rests upon a reed, which, when broken, wounds the hand of him who leans on it. Of such beasts the sons of Korah too spoke in the psalm: Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he has been compared to the senseless beasts, and has become like them (Ps 48 [49]:13). And what follows: This way of theirs is a stumbling block to them, can rightly be understood of the present chapter: that the way of the desert was their ruin. I know that I have read that the beasts of the South and the four-footed beasts in the desert, who, leaving the borders of Judea, fled to the darkness of Egypt, refer to the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places, and the rulers of this darkness, who through their longing for Egypt lost all their riches and former wealth. So he may have said. We, according to tropology, so as to discuss what we have not yet set out, say that all who, having deserted the Creator, have given themselves to the errors of the world are four-footed beasts in the desert of this world, from which they hope for help in vain, since they have abandoned the true help of God.
Commentary on Isaiah

In a land of tribulation and anguish, the lioness and the lion: from them the viper and the flying basilisk: carrying their riches on the shoulders of beasts of burden, and their treasures on the hump of camels, to a people that will not be able to profit them: Egypt shall help in vain and to no purpose. LXX: In tribulation and anguish, the lion and the lion's whelp: thence asps and the offspring of flying asps: who carried their riches on asses and camels to a nation that will not profit them: the Egyptians will profit you emptily and vainly. For lion the Hebrew has written LEIS (ליש); and for flying basilisk, which the Seventy translated offspring of flying asps, in the Hebrew it is called ἐμπρηστὴς and flying, which we can call the burner, and in Hebrew it is named SARAPH (שרף). Again, in the place where we translated carrying on the shoulders of beasts of burden, for beasts of burden all alike translated πώλους, that is, the foals of asses. The land of tribulation and anguish signifies the vast waste of the wilderness, through which the remnant of Jerusalem, with Johanan son of Kareah and the daughters of King Zedekiah, taking with them all they could have, fled over to Egypt. Understand the lioness and the lion's whelp μεταφορικῶς as Jerusalem and its people, as Balaam says in Numbers: Behold, the people shall rise up as a lioness, and shall be lifted up as a lion: it shall not lie down until it devours the prey and drinks the blood of the slain (Num 23:24). In Ezekiel too it is written: Take up a lamentation for the prince of Israel, and say: Why did your mother, a lioness, lie down among lions, and rear her whelps in the midst of young lions (Ezek 19:1-2)? And lest we should think that holy Scripture speaks truly of a lioness and a lion, it speaks against the nature of things, saying that from a lioness and a lion was born a viper and a flying basilisk, or the flying offspring of asps: namely, that from evil parents worse children were begotten, of whom the Gospel too spoke: Brood of vipers, who showed you to flee from the wrath to come (Matt 3:7)? And to the land of Israel it is said: You are a land on which it has not rained, nor has a shower come upon you in the day of wrath; whose princes in the midst of it are like roaring lions, seizing the prey, devouring souls by their might (Ezek 22:24-25). These offspring of vipers, or of flying asps, that is, the princes of the people and the whole crowd of the ungodly, went to a people that could not profit them, as Jeremiah says (Jer 44), that the Lord would deliver Pharaoh Hophra king of Egypt into the hand of his enemies and into the hands of those who sought his life, and that all the men of Judah who were in the land of Egypt would be consumed by sword and famine to utter destruction; so much so that the Hebrews hand down that, before Nebuchadnezzar took Egypt, Jeremiah and Baruch escaped the impending captivity by death. A certain writer expounded the lioness and the lion's whelp as the heavenly Jerusalem and the people deceived from it; and the flying basilisk, and the vipers, and the offspring of asps, as that crooked serpent of which we read above (above, Isa 14 and 27), and of which the Savior spoke in the Gospel: I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven (Luke 10:18): who, called a dragon in the Apocalypse (Rev 12), drew down with him to the earth a third part of the stars, which by the perversity of their judgment lost their former riches, abandoning them in the Egypt of this world.
Commentary on Isaiah

Therefore I have cried out concerning this: it is only pride: be still. For which the Seventy translators, meaning I know not what, translated: Announce these things, since this consolation of yours is vain. Further, Symmachus translated ταραχαί εἰσιν κατοικεῖν, that is, there are tumults, that they may dwell. The Hebrew word REEB (רהב) Aquila translated ὅρμημα, that is, onset and pride; Symmachus disturbance; the Seventy vanity; Theodotion breadth; it is written with three letters, RES and HE and BETH, and it is the very word read in the Psalms: I will be mindful of Rahab and of Babylon, who know me (Ps 86 [87]:4). And the sense is: Since in the Egyptians there is vain help, I have commanded her, that is, Jerusalem, or I have cried out, that the Egyptians had only the name of a kingdom, and pride without strength; and that Israel ought to sit or dwell in its own land, and not seek help in vain from the weak.
Commentary on Isaiah

Now go in and write for them on boxwood, and inscribe it carefully in a book: and it shall be in the last day for a testimony forever. The Hebrews say that, since in the prophets there is one spirit, and all times are joined together with the Lord, Jeremiah is commanded, and it is God's charge, that, having entered Egypt, he should write for them on boxwood, which is a wood that does not rot; or, as Symmachus translated, ἐπὶ πτυχὶ, that is, on a very broad tablet. For them, doubtless for the Jews: and that he should set it out carefully in a book, so that there may be no difficulty in reading it, so that when the prophecy has been fulfilled in fact, they may then understand that the word of the prophets is true. We run over the plain things so that we may linger on the more obscure.
Commentary on Isaiah

For it is a people provoking to anger, and lying sons, sons unwilling to hear the law of God. Who say to the seers: Do not see; and to those who look: Do not look out for us the things that are right: speak to us pleasing things; see errors for us. Take the way away from me: turn the path aside from me: let the Holy One of Israel cease from before our face. It is plain that they provoked the Lord to anger, unwilling to hear the words of Jeremiah (Jer 43). They said to him: Do not see for us what we do not want: do not forbid us the way of Egypt, nor preach the things that are right; but say what pleases us, that we may go on into Egypt, which heaps sins upon sins. Why do you press upon us what we do not willingly hear? why do you show the way by which we do not wish to go? Why do you so often repeat in our ears: Thus says the Lord, the Holy One of Israel? Let this preaching cease from us. According to tropology, all heretics are called lying sons.
