For they went out from us, but they were not of us (1 John 2); they do not hear the Law of God with the ears of the inner man, and they say to the teachers of the Churches: Do not see for us the things that are right, nor threaten the flames of Gehenna; but promise us the kingdom of heaven, so that after luxury and delights paradise may be opened to us. Why do you show me the way of the Lord, by which I do not willingly go? Why do you repeat the name of the Holy One of Israel, or the word of Israel, which does not penetrate the secret places of my breast? This indeed is said also to the people of the Church when it is negligent, if it turns away from the severity of its teachers and favors flatterers.
Catechetical Lecture 14:14

The chief priests and the Pharisees, through the agency of Pilate, sealed the tomb; but the women saw him who was risen.… The chief priests lacked understanding, but the women beheld with their own eyes. When the soldiers came into the city and told the chief priests what had happened, they said to the soldiers, "Say, his disciples came by night and stole him while we were sleeping." Well did Isaiah foretell this also, in their persons: "But tell us, and relate another error." Christ has risen and come back from the dead, and by a bribe they persuade the soldiers.
HOMILIES ON THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES 19

Say, when is a person most insulted—when he is silent, and one makes no answer, or, when he does speak (and is unheeded)? So that the insult is greater in the present case, when He does speak and thou wilt not hear: greater the contempt. "Speak not to us," we read, they said of old to the Prophets: but ye do worse, saying, Speak: we will not do. For there they turned them away that they should not even speak, as feeling that from the voice itself they got some sort of awe and obligation; whereas you, in the excess of your contempt, do not even this. Believe me, if you stopped our mouths by putting your hands over them, the insult would not be so great as it is now. For say, whether shows greater contempt, he that hears, even when hindering by this action, or, he that will not even hear? Say—if we shall look at it as a case of an insult offered—suppose one person to check the party insulting him, and to stop his mouth, as being hurt by the insults, and another person to show no concern, but pretend not even to hear them: whether will show most contempt? Would you not say the latter? For the former shows that he feels himself hit: the latter all but stops the mouth of God.
Commentary on Isaiah

Therefore thus says the Lord, the Holy One of Israel: Because you have rejected this word, and have hoped in false accusation and tumult, and have leaned upon it: therefore this iniquity shall be to you like a breach that falls, and is sought for in a high wall: since suddenly, when it is not hoped for, its crushing shall come. And it shall be broken in pieces as a potter's jar is shattered with a very mighty crushing: and there shall not be found among its fragments a sherd in which a little fire may be carried from the burning, or a little water drawn from the pit. Because, he says, you said above: Let the Holy One of Israel cease from before our face, or, as the Seventy translated, take away from us the word of Israel, therefore thus says the Lord, the Holy One of Israel, and he thrusts himself upon you against your will, so that him whom you neglected when he warned you, you may feel when he punishes. You had confidence in the false accusation and lying of the Egyptians, and leaned upon their tumult, or contradiction and pride, as Symmachus and Theodotion translated; therefore this iniquity, or sin, will turn against you, so that you will be like the suddenly falling wall of a most strongly fortified city that has been taken, whose ruin has come all at once: for so the Seventy translated. And the sense according to the Hebrew is: As the breach of a very high wall that has drawn after it a long ruin can hardly be repaired and recover its former beauty, so sudden crushing will come upon you. And to use another comparison: As a potter's vessel, if it is shattered with a very mighty crushing, is broken into pieces so that scarcely a tiny sherd remains among the fragments in which a little fire may be carried, or a little water drawn from a puddle and a pit, so you, when you have gone into Egypt, with Nebuchadnezzar pursuing you there, will perish to utter destruction. The heretics too, and every doctrine contrary to the truth, trust in false accusation and lying, and, according to the Seventy, mutter against their Creator. Therefore the city of their ungodliness, which Cain built, will be destroyed; sudden perdition will come upon it, when it has been taken by churchmen, and so destroyed and broken in pieces that nothing remains in it that could rekindle a dead fire, or offer even a little muddy water to thirsting peoples.
Catechetical Lecture 2:15

Would you know the power of repentance? Would you understand this strong weapon of salvation and the might of confession? By confession Hezekiah routed 185,000 of the enemy. That was important, but it was little compared to what shall be told. The same king's repentance won the repeal of the sentence God had passed on him. For when he was sick, Isaiah said to him, "Give charge concerning your house, for you shall die, and not live." What expectation was left? What hope of recovery was there when the prophet said, "For you shall die"? But Hezekiah did not cease from penitence, for he remembered what was written: "In the hour that you turn and lament, you shall be saved." He turned his face to the wall, and from his bed of pain his mind soared up to heaven—for no wall is so thick as to stifle reverent prayer—"Lord," he said, "remember me." "For it is sufficient for my healing if you remember me. You are not subject to circumstances but are yourself the legislator of life. For not on birth and conjunction of stars, as some vainly say, does our life depend. No, you are the arbiter, according to your will, of life and the duration of life." He whom the prophet's sentence had forbidden to hope was granted fifteen further years of life, the sun turning back its course in witness thereof. Now while the sun retraced its course for Hezekiah, for Christ it was eclipsed, the distinction marking the difference between the two, I mean Hezekiah and Jesus. Now if even Hezekiah could revoke God's decree, shall not Jesus grant the remission of sins? Turn and lament, shut your door and beg for pardon, that God may remove from you the scorching flames. For confession has the power to quench even fire; it can tame even lions.
LETTER 147.9

It is never too late to repent. You may have gone down from Jerusalem and may have been wounded on the way; yet the Samaritan will set you upon his beast and will bring you to the inn and will take care of you. Even if you are lying in your grave, the Lord will raise you though your flesh may stink. At least imitate those blind men for whose sake the Savior left his home and heritage and came to Jericho. They were sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death when the light shone upon them. For when they learned that it was the Lord who was passing by, they began to cry out, saying, "You son of David, have mercy on us." You too will have your sight restored, if you cry to him and cast away your filthy garments at his call. "When you shall turn and repent then shall you be saved, and then shall you know where you have been."
Commentary on Isaiah

For thus says the Lord God, the Holy One of Israel: If you return and are quiet, you shall be saved: in silence and in hope shall be your strength; and you would not, and you said: By no means; but we will flee to horses: therefore you shall flee; and we will mount upon swift ones: therefore swift shall they be who pursue you. A thousand men from before the terror of one: and from before the terror of five you shall flee. LXX: Thus says the Lord God, the Holy One of Israel: When you have returned and groaned, then you shall be saved, and you shall know where you were: because you trusted in vain things, your strength has become vain; and you would not hear, but you said: We will flee upon horses: therefore you shall flee; and we will be upon light riders: therefore light shall they be who pursue you. A thousand shall flee at the voice of one, and at the voice of five many shall flee. The Holy One, he says, whose name I had kept silent above, is himself the Lord God, who speaks to you both through me and through Jeremiah (Jer 12): If you do penance, and abandon either your vices or the error of your evil counsel, and remain in Judea, fearing not the onset of the Babylonians but my precepts, you shall be saved. Be quiet and hope in the Lord, and take hold of the strength of faith in my promises, you who, despising the precepts of life, said in despair: It shall by no means be as you say; but we will flee to the horses of the Egyptians, and go to them with quick and swift step. Since, then, you have said this, you shall indeed flee and enter Egypt at a rapid pace; but swifter will be the Babylonians, who will pursue you even to Egypt, and such terror and dread will seize Egypt that a thousand Egyptians will not be able to withstand one Chaldean, and a very great multitude of fugitives will not withstand five enemies; according to what we read in Deuteronomy: The Lord will cause you to fall before your enemies. You shall go out against them by one way, and flee before them by seven ways, and you shall be scattered through all the kingdoms of the earth (Deut 28:25, 32). According to the anagogy and the edition of the Seventy, the divine word exhorts all sinners to repentance, and especially the heretics: that when they have returned from their vices and groaned, and done penance, they may be saved; and then they will understand where they were before, and that they hoped in vain things to no purpose. And while he exhorts them to repentance, they on the contrary trust in false teachers and in the uncertainty of the world; and, unwilling to hear the words of God, they long for the horses of Egypt and delight in their swiftness, horses which the Lord forbade to be multiplied (Deut 17). Therefore churchmen will swiftly pursue them, and a thousand men, a disorderly crowd of fugitives, will not be able to withstand the voice of one warrior, or of five fighters (which we should refer to the mind and to the five senses).
LETTER 60.17

When Moses fought against Amalek, it was not with the sword but with prayer that he prevailed. Therefore, if we wish to be lifted up, we must first prostrate ourselves.… We do not understand the prophet's words: "One thousand shall flee at the rebuke of one." We do not cut away the causes of the disease, as we must do to remove the disease itself. Else we should soon see the enemies' arrows give way to our javelins, their caps to our helmets, their saddle horses to our chargers.
Commentary on Isaiah

Until you are left like the mast of a ship on the top of a mountain, and like a signal upon a hill. Jeremiah too writes that, when those who had fled into Egypt had been slain by sword and famine, a few remained who returned to Judea (Jer 44). And as, when a ship has been broken and its framework dissolved, only the tree that is called the mast remains, and is set up as a signal on the summit of a mountain or on a lofty hill, so, as a signal and a trace, scarcely one or two would remain, to show the power of God. And then, he says, all the remnant of Judah, who now are entering the land of Egypt to dwell there, will know, when they have returned to the land of Judea, whose word is fulfilled, mine or theirs.
Commentary on Isaiah

Therefore the Lord waits, that he may have mercy on you, and therefore he shall be exalted in sparing you, because the Lord is a God of judgment: blessed are all who wait for him. Great is the clemency of God, that he waits for our repentance, and, until we are converted from our vices, holds back his mighty hand, so as not to be compelled to strike. And he has mercy and spares for this reason, that his mercy may be exalted, and the goodness of the Creator made known to all. Or certainly, according to what he says in the Gospel (John 12:32): When I am lifted up, I will draw all things to myself, he is exalted on the cross for this reason, that he may spare all. For he is the God of judgment; and blessed are all who wait for the Lord, who waits for their conversion. But whose this conversion is, and what it is, the following words will show.
Commentary on Isaiah

For the people of Zion shall dwell in Jerusalem. The Jews refer this to the times of Cyrus, when the people returned from Babylon to Judea under Zerubbabel and Jeshua the high priest. But we, as we have often said already, refer all the promises that exceed the modest measure of that time to the coming of Christ, at which the people once captive, set free by the passion of the Lord, dwelt in Zion and Jerusalem, that is, in the watchtower and the vision of peace, that is, in the Church. Further, as to the word of holiness added in the Seventy, who said: for a holy people dwells in Zion, we can interpret it thus: we say that no one dwells in Zion except one who is holy, and who hears the Lord saying: Be holy, for I too am holy (Lev 11:44).
Commentary on Isaiah

Weeping, you shall by no means weep; showing mercy, he will have mercy on you: at the voice of your cry, as soon as he hears, he will answer you. When you have returned to Zion and dwelt in Jerusalem, you shall by no means weep as you had wept before, but your weeping shall be turned into joy: For blessed are those who weep, for they shall laugh (Luke 6:21). And after you have cried out and said to the Lord: I cried with my whole heart, hear me, O Lord (Ps 118 [119]:145); and again: I cried, have mercy on me, and I will keep your commandments (Ps 85 [86]); and elsewhere: I waited in the morning and cried out (Ps 118 [119]:147); and your voice has been so clear that it pierces the heavens: at once the Lord will answer you, and you will be like Moses, of whom it is written: Moses spoke, and the Lord answered him (Exod 19:19).
Commentary on Isaiah

And the Lord will give you scant bread and short water. If we refer these things to the times of Zerubbabel, the interpretation is easy: that under him there was no perfect joy, as David says: When the Lord turned back the captivity of Zion, we became like those comforted: so that they received not full and perfect comfort, but a likeness of comfort. But if to the coming of the Savior, then by the scant bread and short water, according to the Apostle Paul and this same prophet Isaiah, the word of the Gospel is foretold, which, in place of the long-drawn observances and commandments of the Law, summed up all things in one word: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. For the Lord has made a word completed and cut short upon the earth (Gal 5).
Commentary on Isaiah

And he will no longer make your teacher fly away from you, and your eyes shall see your instructor, and your ears shall hear the word of one admonishing behind your back: This is the way, walk in it, neither to the right nor to the left. LXX: And those who deceive you shall no longer come near you, because your eyes shall see those who led you astray, and your ears shall hear behind you the words of those who deceive, who said: This is the way, let us walk in it, whether to the right or to the left. In this place the Seventy's edition and the Hebrew disagree greatly. First, then, we shall treat of the common edition, and afterward follow the order of the truth. When the eyes of the heart have understood and discerned the truth, and have recognized with the whole reason of the mind those who had deceived them before, and with trained ears have perceived the words of the deceivers behind their back (for they always hasten to deceive the blind part of the body, according to what we read in the psalm: That they may shoot in the dark at the upright of heart (Ps 10 [11]:2)), who assume to themselves such authority that, whether they teach things on the right or on the left, that is, whether good or evil, they do not wish their disciples to examine them by reason, but to follow them as their forerunners: then those who before deceived will no longer be able to approach them, once they perceive that they have been seen through. Further, according to the Hebrew, the explanation is both easy and true. For when the Lord has given believers scant bread and short water, he will no longer make him who teaches man knowledge fly away from them; but their eyes will always see their instructor, and their ears will hear the word of one admonishing behind their back and saying: This is the right way, walk in it, neither to the right nor to the left; according to what is read elsewhere: We will turn aside neither to the right nor to the left; we will go by the king's highway (Num 20:17). For on either side whatever is beyond measure is in vice. And of the right side it is said: Do not be overly righteous (Eccl 7:17). And of the left, there is no doubt that it is placed on the side of the goats and of those who perish.
Forty Gospel Homilies 34

He has seen us sinning and has borne with it. He who forbade us to sin before we did it does not stop waiting to pardon us even after we have sinned. The one we have rejected is calling us. We have turned away from him, but he has not turned away. Hence Isaiah said, "Your eyes shall see your teacher, and your ears shall hear the voice of a counselor behind you." A person is counseled to his face, so to speak, when he is created for righteousness and receives the precepts of rectitude. When he despises these precepts, it is as if he is turning his back to his Creator's face. But he still follows behind us and counsels us that we have despised him, but he still does not cease to call us. We turn our backs on his face, so to speak, when we reject his words, when we trample his commandments under foot; but he who sees that we reject him still calls out to us by his commandments and waits for us by his patience, stands behind us, and calls us back when we have turned away.
Pastoral Care 3.28

God opens the bosom of his loving kindness to us if we return to him after sinning, for he says by the prophet, "If a man puts away his wife, and she goes from him and marries another man, shall he return to her any more? Shall not that woman be polluted and defiled? But you have prostituted yourself to many lovers; nevertheless return to me, says the Lord." Note how the plea of justice is proposed in regard to the wife who commits fornication and is deserted, and yet, for us who return after our fall, it is not justice but loving kindness that is shown. The inference is obvious, namely, that if our sins are spared with such great love, how great would be our wickedness if we sinned but failed to return after our sin, and what pardon can the wicked expect from him who does not cease to call them after they have sinned! This mercy of God in calling us after our sin is well expressed by the prophet, when it is said to him who turns away from him: "And your eyes shall see your teacher, and you ears shall hear the word of one admonishing you behind your back."
Forty Gospel Homilies 34

We are truly repentant if we weep bitterly over the actions we have committed. Let us consider the riches of our Creator's attitude toward us. He has seen us sinning, and has borne with it. He who forbade us to sin before we did it, does not stop waiting to pardon us even after we have sinned. The one we have rejected is calling us. We have turned away from him, but he has not turned away. Hence Isaiah said, "Your eyes shall see your Teacher, and your ears shall hear the voice of a Counselor behind you." A person is counseled to his face, so to speak, when he is created for righteousness and receives the precepts of rectitude. When he despises these precepts, it is as if he is turning his back to his Creator's face. But he still follows behind us, and counsels us that we have despised him but that he still does not cease to call us. We turn our backs on his face, so to speak, when we reject his words, when we trample his commandments under foot; but he who sees that we reject him, and still calls out to us by his commandments, and waits for us by his patience, stands behind us, and calls us back when we have turned away.
Commentary on Isaiah

And you shall defile the plates of your graven images of silver, and the garment of your molten image of gold, and you shall scatter them like the uncleanness of a menstruous woman: Go out, you shall say to it. LXX: And you shall defile the silvered and gilded idols: you shall break them in pieces and scatter them like the water of a menstruous woman, and you shall cast them away like dung. When you have understood the truth, and the deceivers have not come near you, but your eyes have seen your instructor and your ears have always heard: This is the way, walk in it, neither to the right nor to the left: then you will break in pieces and scatter all the errors and idols and likenesses of the truth which an artful tongue had composed in the splendor of eloquence, which is what silver means, and in the reasoning of wisdom, which is what gold signifies; and you will judge them so unclean that you will compare them to the most filthy blood of a menstruous woman, which the Seventy, in other words, translated as the water of a menstruous woman.
Commentary on Isaiah

And rain shall be given to your seed wherever you sow in the land, and the bread of the fruits of the land shall be most abundant and rich. LXX: Then there shall be rain for the seed of your land, and the bread of the fruits of your land shall be plentiful and rich. It is written in the volume of Kings (1 Kgs 18) that after the false prophets had been slain by Elijah, rain was given to the land of Israel; and that the bread of Elisha, and afterward of the Savior, was most abundant and most rich, and had such fullness that many thousands of men were filled from it (2 Kgs 4; John 6). So also in the present place, rain will not be given to the spiritual seed, nor the most abundant and richest bread of the land, until the silvered and gilded idols have been broken in pieces and reckoned as a dunghill. For unless vices depart, virtues do not enter.
Commentary on Isaiah

In that day the lamb shall feed in your possession at large. And your bulls and the foals of asses that work the ground shall eat mingled mash, as on the threshing floor it has been winnowed. LXX: And in that day your cattle shall feed in a rich and spacious place. Your bulls and your oxen that work the ground shall eat chaff mixed with winnowed barley. In the abundance of all things, when the heavenly rain comes down, and that bread which came down from heaven, which whoever eats will never hunger, the lambs shall feed in a most spacious place, those who follow the Lamb wherever he goes and who are always on the right hand. The bulls are the leaders of the flock, of whom we read: The assembly of bulls among the cows of the peoples (Ps 67 [68]:31); and the foals of asses, sitting on which the Lord entered Jerusalem (Matt 21), who work the ground, shall eat from the threshing floor in such a way that it has been winnowed, namely, so that no chaff be mixed in their food; of which chaff it is written in Jeremiah: What has the chaff to do with the wheat, says the Lord (Jer 23)? and which in the Gospel is burned with unquenchable fire (Luke 3). Further, according to the Seventy, the cattle, which are not yet full of reason and wisdom, and one of whom says to God: I have become like a beast before you (Ps 72 [73]:23), shall feed in a most rich and spacious place, which does not bring forth thorns and thistles, but, like the land of Israel, flows with milk and honey and gives full freedom to those who feed there. And the bulls and oxen that work the ground, that is, the Apostles and apostolic men, of whom the apostle Paul too interprets what is written: You shall not muzzle the ox that treads out the grain; and: Is it for oxen that God cares (1 Cor 9:9)? but surely he speaks of those who work their own ground, and of whom he likewise says: We are God's husbandry, God's building (1 Cor 3:9); for the Father is the husbandman, and Christ the vine (John 15): these shall eat chaff mixed with winnowed barley. We read that Isaac sowed barley and, because he was among the foreigners, received a hundredfold harvest of barley (Gen 26). And Hosea hired an adulterous woman for a cor and a half cor of barley (Hos 3). The Savior too had filled with barley loaves five thousand men who still served the senses of the body and followed the Law of Moses (John 6). In another place, breaking the seven loaves of the Law and crushing them into pieces, he filled with wheaten loaves four thousand men who followed the number of the Gospel (Matt 15). Peoples of this kind eat a part of the chaff too, since in certain things they follow the letter; and yet through the chaff and the barley they gradually advance, so as to pass on to the wheat.
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 105: ON THE DARKENING OF THE SUN

HOW THE PROPHECY AGREES WITH THE GOSPEL, CONCERNING THE DARKENING OF THE SUN AND CERTAIN OTHER THINGS. — Since at the Lord’s first coming it was foretold that the sun would be darkened at his passion, at the very hour when it is proved to have happened, that is, at midday, for therefore it is written in the prophet Amos: “And it shall come to pass in that day, says the Lord, I will cause the sun to go down at noon, and I will darken the earth in the clear day” (Amos 8:9). On that day, therefore, from the sixth hour the sun was darkened until the ninth hour, and therefore the prophecy of the aforementioned prophet was fulfilled. The image of this event, which is to occur at the Lord’s second coming, was shown in the Lord’s passion; for at the end, when the Lord begins to come to judge the world, the heavenly lights will be released from their service, as the Lord says: “In those days the sun shall be darkened, and the moon shall not give her light” (Matt. 24:29). Joel the prophet has not omitted this either, so that, being signified by many, it may without doubt be believed to be fulfilled. For therefore he said: “The sun shall be turned into darkness and the moon into blood, before the great and revealing day of the Lord comes” (Joel 2:31). As far as appears, this more fittingly belongs to the second coming; for then it will be openly revealed to all, as Scripture says: “Then every eye shall see him, and all the tribes of the earth shall mourn over him, and those who crucified him” (Rev. 1:7). Therefore, if in both comings it is contained that the sun shall be darkened in those days, what is that day on which Scripture rings that the sun and moon shall be increased? For among other things Isaiah says: “And there shall be upon every high mountain, and upon every high hill, streams running with water in that day, when many shall perish and when the towers shall fall. And the light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, in the day when the Lord shall heal the brokenness of his people” (Isa. 30:25–26), and so forth. What day can be understood, on which the Lord promised to heal the brokenness of his people? I think this is the day which Zacharias, the father of John, pointed out when he said: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and performed the redemption of his people. And he has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of David his servant, as he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets, who have been since the world began, that he would deliver us from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us, to perform mercy with our fathers” (Luke 1:68–72). And Simeon, among other things, said: “This child is set for the fall and for the rise of many in Israel” (Luke 2:34). This fall is that of the scribes and Pharisees and the rulers of the Jews, whom the prophet signified by the towers. These, therefore, falling through unbelief, others rose up by believing, who had previously seemed weak and sick through negligence. Where the Savior says: “For judgment I have come into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (Jn. 9:39); so that those who by the practice and knowledge of the Law seem to be lights may be blinded through unbelief, but the blind, that is, the unlearned or publicans, may see by believing. Their weaknesses the prophet foretold that the Savior would bear (Isa. 53:11). And so at this time of the Savior it came to pass, as we read in the Gospel, that “he took our infirmities and bore our diseases” (Matt. 8:17). All these things indeed were completed and fulfilled in the Savior’s passion: for therefore the salvation of the human race, both in heaven above and in the lower regions, was both redeemed and confirmed, since the prophecy of the aforementioned Zacharias encompasses both. For here above they were freed from the crushing of enemies by the intervention of mercy; and there below, in the underworld, when they were snatched from Tartarus. For all who hoped in the promised Christ were awaiting his coming, that, death having been conquered, they might be freed from Hades. Therefore he said: “To perform mercy with our fathers.” If anyone, however, understands this salvation also to be contained in the second coming, yet in both comings, especially in the second, the sun will be turned into darkness and the moon will not give her brightness: how then shall we perceive the sun and moon to be increased on the day when the Lord will visit his people, when in both times, in which the liberation of the people was begun and completed, we read that the sun and moon are not diminished but darkened? Unless, clearly, we understand the sun and moon to be compared to the saints; just as in another place we read that the saints are made equal to the heavenly lights, with the Apostle Paul preaching that among these men the saints in this world appear as luminaries. And in the Gospel: “Then the righteous shall shine like the sun” (Matt. 13:43). For the Lord calls righteous works “light”: therefore he says, “Let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16). Those, therefore, who, having left all that is theirs, follow the Lord for the sake of righteousness and holiness, are compared to the sun and moon as being honored sevenfold; as the Lord says: “There is no one who leaves house, or wife, or children, or fields, who will not receive seven times as much in this age” (see Luke 18:29–30). Those, then, who are now honored sevenfold can be understood to be believed in the future to become seven degrees brighter than the rest; so that their resurrection is compared to the sun and moon, while that of the others is like the stars. Therefore the brightness of the saints, which is honored sevenfold here, obtains another sevenfold in the resurrection, so that one who here has the brightness of the moon will receive the brightness of the sun in the future; and one who here is compared to the sun will be believed then to receive seven times as much. Therefore the prophet Isaiah foretold that by comparison with the sun and moon the merits of the saints would be increased, and not without reason. For if the Lord himself is called the Sun of righteousness, and the saints will be like him, as the Apostle John says: “When he appears, we shall be like him” (1 Jn. 3:2), then fittingly the saints are signified in the sun, yet the aforementioned prophet shows the sun to be greater than the moon by seven degrees For when it shows that the moon, like the light of the sun, will exist in the future, but the sun will be seven times as great; it certainly means, in the manner of speaking, that the moon will be increased sevenfold more than the sun, so that the moon will then be such as the sun is now: although the reasoning here concerns the saints, under this explanation of the luminaries it has nevertheless partly revealed their measure, so that after the increase of the sun and the moon, a saint will again be as much greater as the sun once was; and as much as one saint now differs from another saint, so much will one differ from another in the future after the reward.
Commentary on Isaiah

And there shall be upon every high mountain and upon every lifted-up hill streams of running waters in the day of the slaughter of many, when the towers have fallen. In this place the Jews refer the many slain and the falling towers to the power of the Roman empire, of which the Apostle too speaks (2 Thess 2:7): Only let him who holds now hold, until he be taken out of the way: namely, that at that time the blessedness of the people of Israel will be so great that not only the valleys and plains but all the mountains and hills will be watered with flowing waters. But let us understand by the mountains and hills those who are lifted on high by virtues, who hunger and thirst for righteousness (Matt 5), whom the Lord invites to drink. For whoever drinks of his waters will never thirst (John 4). Hence in the psalm too we read: Bless the Lord from the fountains of Israel (Ps 67 [68]:27). And in the Gospel it is said that whoever drinks of the waters of Jesus, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly (John 7). And the holy man says to God: For with you is the fountain of life (Ps 35 [36]:10), from which goes forth a most pure river, of which Scripture again makes mention: The stream of the river gladdens the city of God (Ps 45 [46]:5). And in another place: The river of God is filled with waters (Ps 64 [65]:10): that is, he who speaks through Jeremiah: They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water (Jer 2:13). This will happen when very many have been slain, or have perished: for many are called, but few chosen (Matt 20). And when the towers have fallen, whether the powers of the demons, or all the proud and arrogant and great in this world; of whom it is said in the psalms too: I saw the ungodly man lifted up and exalted like the cedars of Lebanon, and I passed by, and behold, he was not; I sought him, and his place was not found (Ps 36 [37]:35-36). Such towers those desired to build (Gen 11) who moved their feet from the East, whose tongues were confounded in Babylon; and those too on whom the tower of Siloam fell (Luke 13).
Commentary on Isaiah

And the light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, as the light of seven days, in the day when the Lord binds up the wound of his people and heals the stroke of its blow. LXX: And the light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun sevenfold, in the day when the Lord heals the crushing of his people and cures the pain of your blow. I wonder how in the present place the same Seventy translated moon and sun, following the Hebrew, when above they translated the Hebrew words LABANA (לבנה) and HAMMA (חמה), which Aquila renders white and heat, and by which he signifies the moon and the sun, as brick and wall, in the place where it is written: And the moon shall blush, and the sun shall be confounded; for which they translated: the bricks shall melt, and the wall shall fall. Hence the suspicion comes to me that they did not err from the beginning, but were gradually corrupted by the fault of copyists. For it cannot be that those who in this place translated the same words well should have erred in the earlier passage. In the day, then, of the slaughter of many, when the arrogant and proud have fallen, and those who set their mouth against heaven have learned that they are earth, the light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun: when the Lord gives a new heaven and a new earth, and the fashion of this world passes away, so that the moon and the sun may obtain the rewards of their labor and their course. For the expectation of the creature waits for the revelation of the sons of God, because the creature itself also will be set free from the bondage of corruption into the liberty of the glory of the sons of God (Rom 8:19); although some, understanding them as instruments of light, contend that they are without sense. The moon, then, will receive the brightness of the sun. Nor is it a wonder to think this of a most bright element, to which the rule of the night has been given, since it is written of the saints too: The righteous shall shine like the sun (Matt 13:43). And the sun will receive a sevenfold light, as was the light of seven days when the world was created in the beginning (although the Seventy did not translate seven days), when the Lord binds up the wound of his people, or heals the crushing of his people: when what is written will be fulfilled: Sorrow and mourning and sighing shall flee away (Isa 35:10): when, the fullness of the nations coming in, all Israel shall be saved; or certainly when the vengeance comes of those whose souls cry out beneath the altar: How long will you not avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth (Rev 6:10)? And consider this too: that he did not say, when he heals the crushing of his people Israel, or Jacob, but absolutely, of his people, so as to signify all who serve God. Some refer this place, and all that is contained in this chapter of promises, to the heavenly Jerusalem and to the return of its people, when what is written will be fulfilled: Heaven and earth shall pass away (Matt 24:35). Others refer it to the times of Elijah, and say that he is the one of whom it is written above: Your eyes shall see your instructor, and your ears shall hear the word of one admonishing behind your back: that then, according to the fables of the poets and the golden age of Saturn, streams of milk will flow from the mountains and hills, and the purest honey will drip from the leaves of the trees. Those who accept these things will also, by a Jewish error, take up the fable of the thousand years and the earthly kingdom of the Savior, not understanding that the Apocalypse of John, under the surface of the letter, weaves together the inmost mysteries of the Church.
On the Gospel of Mark 4:13.24

Moreover, when the day of judgment has been completed and the glory of the future life has become evident with the new heaven and the new earth, then will come to pass what the same prophet announced elsewhere: "The light of the moon will be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun will be increased sevenfold, like the light of seven days."
Commentary on Isaiah

Behold, the name of the Lord comes from afar: his fury is burning and heavy to bear. His lips are filled with indignation, and his tongue is like a devouring fire. His spirit is like an overflowing torrent reaching to the middle of the neck, to destroy the nations unto nothing, and the bridle of error that was in the jaws of the peoples. You shall have a song, like the night of a hallowed solemnity, and gladness of heart, like one who goes with the pipe to enter into the mountain of the Lord, to the Mighty One of Israel. LXX: Behold, the name of the Lord comes after a long time: his fury burning with glory, the utterance of his lips, an utterance full of wrath, and the wrath of his fury shall devour like fire; and his spirit, like water in a valley, dragging, shall come up to the neck, and shall be divided to confound the nations for their vain error, and error shall be cast away, and it shall take them in their sight. Must you always rejoice and enter continually into my holy places, as though celebrating feasts and rejoicing, that you may enter with the pipe to the mountain of the Lord, to the God of Israel? Let us speak first according to the Hebrew. What is said here hangs on what precedes. The prophetic word had rebuked those who, scorning the help of God, were fleeing to the Egyptians for fear of the Babylonians, and it threatened those who went down that they would die there. And again, after the punishments, it promises that those who were willing to listen to him would not only dwell in Jerusalem under Zerubbabel, Ezra and Nehemiah, but it pledges a greater blessedness to all who believe the word of God at the consummation of the world, when rivers of waters will run over all the mountains and hills, and, when many have been slain, the towers will fall. The moon too and the sun will receive a brighter light, when the Lord binds up and heals the wound of his people; although some contend, ὑπερβολικῶς, that these things were fulfilled in the land of Judea in the times of Cyrus, who released the people from captivity. Since, then, rewards were promised to the good and obedient, now, on the contrary, punishments are announced to the wicked and the scorners: that the Lord will fulfill his purpose, and will come after a long time to punish sinners, and will pronounce sentence upon all, and with the breath of his mouth will slay the impious one, whom he calls the bridle of the peoples: not one by which he might govern those subject to him, but one by which he might drag those subjected to him to ruin. He also sets down the likeness of a torrent flooding up to the neck, to testify that the end of all things has come. For as a torrent chokes the one up to whose neck it has reached, so the judgment of God will let no one go away unpunished. And when he has destroyed the bridle that was in the jaws of all the nations, together with the nations subject to it, and has brought it to nothing, then, he says, you, the saints, who obey my commands, shall have a song, like the night of the hallowed solemnity when you went out of Egypt, and in the solemnity of the Passover threw off the yoke of Egyptian slavery, saying at the Red Sea, when Pharaoh had been drowned: Let us sing to the Lord, for he is gloriously magnified (Exod 15:1); and such gladness of heart that you will imitate those who, bringing first fruits to the temple and carrying gifts into the winepresses of God, go with pipes, showing the joys of their heart in song. These things according to the Hebrew I have touched on briefly.
Commentary on Isaiah

But in both editions it must be noted that it is not the Lord, but the name of the Lord, that comes after a long time, of which it is said in the Psalms: Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; the Lord is God, and he has shone upon us (Ps 117 [118]:26). And he himself says in the Gospel: I have come in the name of my Father, and you have not received me (John 5:43). And it is well said that he comes after a long time, since human impatience says: How long, O Lord, will you forget me unto the end? How long do you turn your face away from me? (Ps 12 [13]:1). His burning fury also comes with glory, so that him whom we despised in humility we may fear in majesty. This very thing is written in the psalms too: God manifestly will come, our God, and will not keep silence. Fire will burn in his sight, and round about him a mighty tempest (Ps 49 [50]:3, 4). For he himself says in the Gospel (Luke 12:49): I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and how I wish that it may burn! Again, in another psalm we read: The voice of the Lord cutting off the flame of fire (Ps 28 [29]:7), so that the seizing flame may consume whatever there is in the world of hay, wood and stubble. Hence God is also said to be a consuming fire (Deut 4). And as for what follows: The wrath of his fury shall devour like fire, most of our writers interpret the wrath of the Lord's fury as the devil, to whom we are handed over for punishment, who, according to the book of Samuel, moved David to number the people of God (2 Sam 24). And the Apostle says: to hand such a one over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved (1 Cor 5:5). But this fury itself, and the wrath of the Lord's fury, will do nothing by its own will, but only what it has been commanded. Hence there follows: The utterance of his lips, an utterance full of wrath.
Commentary on Isaiah

His spirit too, like water in a valley, dragging, will come up to the neck, to make punishments overflow upon sinners. It will be divided according to the quality of their deserts, to destroy and confound the nations which vain error had led astray, so that they may understand that they have been overthrown.
Commentary on Isaiah

Hence it is said to men of this kind, who prevailed in the power of this world and took delight in their own error, that they will not always be doing this. And some of our writers think that this passage especially, and the whole tenor of the chapter, is spoken against the heretics and all the doctrines that are contrary to the truth: that when the time of judgment has come, they shall by no means enter his holy places and his mountain, that is, the Church of the Lord, lest under the name of religion they gather riches and abandon themselves to luxury, as though celebrating the feasts of the Lord. The Jews understand these things of the nations Gog and Magog, which they think will come from the North, that is, from the regions of Scythia, of whom Ezekiel speaks more fully (Ezek 38-39).
Commentary on Isaiah

And the Lord will make the glory of his voice heard, and will show the terror of his arm in the threatening of his fury and in the flame of devouring fire: he will dash them down with whirlwind and with hailstone. For at the voice of the Lord Assyria, struck with the rod, will tremble, and the passing of the rod will be founded, which the Lord will make to rest upon him with timbrels and with harps, and in chief battles he will overthrow them. For Topheth has been prepared from yesterday, prepared by the king, deep and wide; its fuel is fire and much wood: the breath of the Lord like a torrent of sulphur kindling it. LXX: And the Lord will make the glory of his voice heard, and will show the fury of his arm with fury and wrath: and with a devouring flame of fire he will strike with lightning vehemently, and like water and hail coming down with violence. For at the voice of the Lord the Assyrians will be overcome by the stroke with which he will strike them, and there will be round about him that from which he had the hope of help, in which he trusted; they themselves with timbrels and harp will fight against him by a change. For you will be deceived before the days: is a kingdom prepared for you too? A deep valley, wood laid, fire and the wood of many; the fury of the Lord, like a valley kindled with sulphur. I could have shown readers in passing what seems right to me according to the Hebrew; but what am I to do about the zeal of certain people, who declare that unless I also discuss the edition of the Seventy Translators, I shall have an imperfect work? I shall therefore follow the order of discussion I have begun. The voice of the Lord and his command will become known to all, and the strength of his arm will be plain to everyone, when the time of retribution has come, and it will be brought down with the greatness of flame and whirlwind and hail, and with the weight of stones. Of this, as we have said, Ezekiel writes at full length in his prophecy of Gog and Magog (Ezek 38 and 39).
Commentary on Isaiah

Further, what is said according to the Seventy: At the voice of the Lord the Assyrians will be overcome by the stroke, when he has struck them, and there will be round about him that from which he had the hope of help, in which he trusted; they themselves with timbrels and harp will fight against him by a change, signifies that those who were once subject to the devil rise up against him, and fight against him with joy and gladness by a sudden change, when, understanding their error, they destroy him by whom they had been deceived. And it is said to him that from the beginning he deceived himself, thinking his kingdom everlasting, he for whom Gehenna and eternal punishments are prepared.
Commentary on Isaiah

At the command of his voice Assyria, struck with the rod, will tremble: every impious man, every imitator of the hostile nation; not that on the day of judgment the Assyrian alone is to be struck, but that by the Assyrian we should understand the devil.
Commentary on Isaiah

Then there follows: And the passing of the rod will be founded, which the Lord will make to rest upon him. And the sense is: the rod will not strike him and then be lifted again, and, in the manner of those who flog, make an end of beating; but he will make it remain in his punishments as if founded and fixed with a deep root. And if it is understood in this way, where will the repentance of the devil be? Especially since it is said to sinners: Go into the eternal fire, which God has prepared for the devil and his angels (Matt 25:41). With timbrels and with harps, and in chief battles, he will overthrow them: that is, the Lord will overthrow the demons and all the impious, to the joy of all.
Commentary on Isaiah

For from yesterday, that is, from time past, Topheth, that is, a broad and spacious Gehenna, has been prepared by the king, the Lord, to burn them with eternal fires. Its nourishment and kindling is fire and much wood, that is, perpetual flame and the punishments of sinners. And since the prophetic word had foretold this as of a furnace and an oven of burning fire, it keeps the metaphor, so that we may know that it is kindled by the breath and spirit and will of the Lord, with sulphur mixed in, which rouses the flames, to make the torments more bitter.

n: Chariots. He continues to inveigh against this practice, chap. xxx. 16. (Calmet) --- Salmanasar will ruin the ten tribes. (Menochius)
Words. The Lord will punish the wicked Jews, (Calmet) after the Egyptians. (Josephus, [Jewish Antiquities?] x. 1.) --- The former would not believe the prophets. (Worthington)
Hand. If God neglect to support empires, they fall of themselves.

Thereof. He will thence hurl destruction on the distant enemy. (Calmet) --- He had destroyed Sennacherib's army, 4 Kings xix. Yet they forgot this and other proofs of God's power and love. (Worthington)
Over. He will protect Jerusalem, notwithstanding the menaces of Sennacherib, as he did his people from the destroying angel.
Revolted. Let your conversion bear proportion (Calmet) with your sins. (Haydock)
Idols. Their worship was afterwards more severely prohibited, chap. xxx. 21.

Flee not. Hebrew, "flee to himself," lo. Septuagint and Vulgate have read la, "not." The angel destroyed the army, and the king was slain at his return. --- Tributaries. Ninive being afterwards subject to the Chaldeans, &c. (Calmet) --- Hebrew, "shall melt." (Vatable)
Strength. Hebrew, "rock," the king. --- Jerusalem, to protect it, (Calmet) and punish the guilty. (Chaldean)

f: Letter 28.8

Let our course take us to regions above, because it is better to ascend. Finally, as was read today, "Woe to them that go down to Egypt." Surely it is not wrong to go to Egypt, but to change to the ways of the Egyptians, to change to the violence of their treachery and to the ugliness of their wantonness—this is wrong. He that changes in this way descends, and one who descends falls. Let us keep away, then, from the Egyptian who is a man, but [let us] not [keep away] from God. Even the king of Egypt himself fell under the dominion of his own vices and in comparison with him Moses was accounted a god, ruling over kingdoms and subjecting powers to himself. So we read that it was said to Moses: "I shall make you a god to Pharaoh."
Commentary on Isaiah

These things, indeed, we can also understand of those who, in a time of persecution and of tribulation and distress, do not trust in the Lord, but in the help of the Egyptians, that is, of worldly men; not knowing that Abraham was endangered in Egypt, and that the people of God served with clay and bricks in that region, which is spiritually called the iron furnace. Hence in the Apocalypse of John too we read: The place in which the Lord was crucified is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt (Rev 11:8).
Commentary on Isaiah

Woe to those who go down into Egypt for help, hoping in horses, and having confidence in chariots, because they are many, and in horsemen, because they are exceedingly strong, and have not trusted in the Holy One of Israel, and have not sought the Lord. But he, being wise, has brought evil, and has not taken away his words; and he will rise up against the house of the most wicked, and against the help of those who work iniquity. Egypt is man and not God, and their horses are flesh and not spirit: and the Lord will incline his hand, and the helper will collapse, and he to whom help is given will fall, and all of them together will be consumed. After the burden of the beasts of the South, and of those who carried their riches into Egypt to a people that could not profit them, who hoped for help in the strength of Pharaoh and had confidence in the shadow of Egypt, the prophetic word had spoken, under the figure of the return to Jerusalem and of the release of the captivity under Cyrus, of the consummation of the age and of the perfect blessedness of the righteous: now it returns to the same people to whom it had spoken above, that they should not go down into Egypt. And this is the difference between the present passage and the earlier one: there the tribe of Judah is commanded not to go down into Egypt; here it is prophesied that, scorning the command of the Lord, they will go down, and that by Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon Israel and the Egyptians alike, the fugitives and their helpers alike, will be slaughtered together. Of this Jeremiah speaks most fully (Jer 42). Woe, then, to those who go down into Egypt and, for fear of the Chaldeans, scorn the precepts of the Lord, hoping in idolaters, while they boast that they hold the worship of God; and, trusting in the help of horses, they do not know that it is written: A horse is a deceitful thing for safety (Ps 32 [33]:17); and they have confidence in four-horse chariots and carriages and horsemen, and do not remember that Song: Horse and rider he has cast into the sea (Exod 15:1). And they have not trusted in the Holy One of Israel, who was promising his help through Jeremiah to those who remained in the land of Judea. And they have not sought the Lord: not that they did not seek him, but that, having sought him, they scorned his words. Hence it is also said of the wicked priests: Who devour my people, they have not called upon the Lord (Ps 52 [53]:5, 6).
Commentary on Isaiah

But he, being wise, that is, the Lord, brought evil upon them, and the worst, namely Nebuchadnezzar; or evil in the absolute sense, signifying a thing, not a person; and he did not take away his words, which he had spoken through the prophets. Wherefore he will rise up against the tribe of Judah, the house of the most wicked, and against the help of the Egyptians, who work iniquity.
Commentary on Isaiah

For Egypt, or the Egyptian, as the Seventy translated, is man and not God, and their horses are flesh and not spirit. Hence it is also written in Jeremiah: Cursed is the man who has his hope in man, and has made firm the flesh of his arm, and whose heart has departed from the Lord. And he will be like a tamarisk in the desert, which will not see when good things come (Jer 17:5, 6). And in another place it is written: Vain is the salvation of man (Ps 59 [60]:13), or, as it stands better in the Hebrew, in man. And when the Lord stretches out his hand to punish, or inclines it, under the metaphor of a charioteer, and slackens the reins of the running horses, the Egyptian helper will collapse, and Israel, to whom help was being given.
Commentary on Isaiah

For thus says the Lord to me: as when a lion roars, and a lion's whelp, over its prey, and a multitude of shepherds comes against it, it will not dread their voice, nor be afraid at their multitude: so will the Lord of hosts come down to fight upon Mount Zion and upon its hill. Like birds flying, so will the Lord of hosts protect Jerusalem, protecting and delivering, passing over and saving. In plain passages we set down one edition, especially where there is no difference of sense. When the Israelites, and the Egyptians in whose help they trusted, have been slain in Egypt, the captives will return to Jerusalem in the reign of Cyrus. And by two likenesses the strength of the Lord, who had promised that he would be their helper, is shown. As a lion and a lion's whelp, when hungry, if it sees a flock of sheep, is not frightened by any voice of the shepherds, and, conscious of its own strength, despises their multitude: so the Lord of hosts will fight, not against Mount Zion and its hill, but upon Mount Zion, against its adversaries.
Commentary on Isaiah

Let us state the other comparison as well: as birds, to defend their young, fly over their nests, and if they see a serpent or a man, or other birds approaching their chicks, forget their own weakness and fight with beak and claws, and redouble the grief of their breast with chattering cries: so the Lord will protect Jerusalem, and will deliver it, passing over, and will save it. For passing over, in the Hebrew it is PHASE; in the three translators, besides the Seventy, ὑπερβαίνων is set down. From this it is plain that Pascha, that is, the Phase of the Lord, signifies not passion but passage. And that the Lord, in the likeness of birds, was a protector over Jerusalem, he himself testifies in the Gospel: Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those who were sent to you (Matt 23:37): how often I wished to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not? And in Deuteronomy it is said of the Lord: He spread his wings, and took them up, and carried them on his shoulders (Deut 32:11).
Commentary on Isaiah

Turn back, as you had withdrawn into the depth, sons of Israel. For in that day a man will cast away the idols of his silver and the idols of his gold, which your hands have made for you for sin. And Assyria will fall by a sword not of a man, and a sword not of a human being will devour him: and he will flee, not from the face of the sword, and his young men will be tributaries. And his strength will pass away from terror, and his princes will flee in fear, said the Lord, whose fire is in Zion, and his furnace in Jerusalem. LXX: Turn back, as you had withdrawn into the depth, sons of Israel. For in that day a man will cast away the idols of his silver and the idols of his gold, which your hands have made for you for sin. And Assyria will fall by a sword not of a man, and a sword not of a human being will devour him, and he will flee, not from the face of the sword; his young men will be overcome: for they will be surrounded by rock as by a rampart, and will be conquered; and whoever flees will be taken. Thus says the Lord: Blessed is he who has seed in Zion, and kinsmen in Jerusalem. While the Lord fights upon Mount Zion against its adversaries, and protects it like birds: Turn back, O sons of Israel; or, as Symmachus translated: Repent, you who by deep counsel and sin have withdrawn from the Lord. For if you do this, casting away the idols of gold and silver which were to you for sin, on account of which your city was taken, Assyria, for fear of whom you now flee, will fall, not by the sword of men, nor by the strength of an army, but by the power of God. And he means the Angel by whom one hundred and eighty-five thousand Assyrians were destroyed in one night. The Assyrian king himself will also flee, not from the sword of men, but from the wrath of God: so that his young and strong men become tributaries to the Medes, of whom it is said above, against Babylon: Behold, I will stir up the Medes against you. And the strength of the Assyrian will pass away and go by through the terror of the Lord, and all his princes will tremble. For the Lord has said it and promised it, for whom to have said is to have done; he who has fire in Zion and a furnace in Jerusalem, so that the flame going out from Jerusalem may consume his adversaries like stubble and wood. Another interprets the words: In that day a man will cast away the idols of his silver, and the rest, in such a way as to testify that after the return from the Babylonian captivity until the coming of Christ the sons of Israel never worshipped idols; and that the Assyrian too is signified in the present place as one to be overcome not by the Angel but by the Medes, because a most ancient and once powerful kingdom, after offending the Lord, was destroyed and served its conquerors. The Nazarenes understand this passage thus: O sons of Israel, who by most wicked counsel denied the Son of God, return to him and to his Apostles. For if you do this, you will cast away all the idols which were formerly to you for sin, and the devil will fall before you, not by your own strength, but by the mercy of God: and his young men, who once fought for him, will be tributaries of the Church, and all his strength and his rock will pass away: the philosophers too, and every perverse doctrine, will turn their backs at the sign of the cross. For it is the sentence of the Lord that this should come to pass, whose fire, or light, is in Zion, and his oven in Jerusalem.
LETTER 122.2

In place of the last clause ["But you have played the harlot with many lovers; yet return again to me, says the Lord."] the true Hebrew text (which is not preserved in the Greek and Latin versions) gives the following: "you have forsaken me, yet return, and I will receive you, says the Lord." Isaiah also speaking in the same sense uses almost the same words: "Return," he cries, "O children of Israel, you who devise a deep and sinful counsel. Return to me, and I will redeem you. I am God, and there is no God else beside me; a just God and a Savior; there is nothing beside me. Look to me, and be saved, all the ends of the earth." Remember this and show yourselves men: bring it again to mind, O you transgressors. Return in heart and remember the former things of old: for I am God and there is none else."
Commentary on Isaiah

Fire and light are written in Hebrew with the same letters, ALEPH, VAU, RES; if it is read UR, it means fire; if OR, light. This is said because for fire, which Symmachus alone translated, Aquila and Theodotion translated light. But what is meant by what we read in the Septuagint: They will be surrounded by rock as by a rampart, and will be conquered: and whoever flees will be taken, I am unable to know. Unless perhaps we can say this: that the young men of the Assyrian king, who are to be conquered and taken, are surrounded by rock, that is, by the strength of the Lord, as a city is surrounded by a rampart. Further, what follows: Blessed is he who has seed in Zion, and kinsmen in Jerusalem, we can interpret so as to say that it fits the sense of the present passage, in that the divine word exhorts those fleeing into Egypt to return to Jerusalem and beget sons. To this city so great a blessedness is promised that it is defended and protected by the help of the Lord; and in another place it is written of it: The glory of this latter house will be greater than that of the former (Hag 2:10). This can also be referred to the Church, the vision of peace and the watchtower, of which it is written: Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God (Ps 86 [87]:2). And elsewhere: The rush of the river makes glad the city of God (ibid. 45 [46]:3). For in her is the fire and the furnace, to devour sinners and to consume wood, hay and stubble; or the light and the oven, so that the brightness of the righteous and the punishment of sinners may be shown.
Homilies on Ezekiel 2.9.10

Of this love that is begun here to be perfected from the sight of the Lord in the eternal kingdom Isaiah rightly speaks, saying, "The Lord lives, whose fire is in Zion, and his furnace in Jerusalem." It is, however, greater to be a furnace than a fire because a fire can also be small, but a larger flame is kindled in a furnace. Zion truly is said to be speculation but Jerusalem the vision of peace. Truly we sometimes catch a glimpse of our peace here in order there later to see it fully. Therefore through the Lord's love the fire is in Zion and his furnace in Jerusalem because here we burn in some measure with the flames of his love when we glimpse him, but there we shall burn totally when we shall fully see him whom we love.
Commentary on Ezra and Nehemiah 3

If the breads of the furnace that were baked in secret signify the interior devotion of the mind of the faithful confirmed by the fire of charity, breads which were also commanded by the law to be offered in the sacrifice of the Lord, it is most fitting that the hearts which were made to burn constantly with the flame of intimate love and virtue and to beget words are symbolized through the furnaces in which the same breads were baked. The prophet spoke beautifully about these things when he referred to "the Lord whose fire is in Zion and whose furnace is in Jerusalem." It is also written: "Did our hearts not burn within us when he spoke along the way and opened the Scriptures to us?"

n: King. Ezechias or Josias, as figures of Jesus Christ, who is meant. (Calmet) --- They and their counsellors only foreshewed the advantages derived from Christ and his apostles in a more abundant manner. (St. Jerome) --- Judgment and justice. These words have a higher meaning than what is assigned to them by philosophers. In God, the former implies the preparation of the means for man's redemption, as the latter does the execution; and in man, judgment denotes the selection of what is right, and justice implies the putting it willingly in practice. Thus Christ will fulfill all that he has graciously purposed, with the two other divine persons; and the princes, his pastors, shall discern what is good for their own and people's eternal welfare. (Worthington)
Land. Ezechias and Josias were both a defence to their subjects.
Dim. True prophets shall speak, while false ones shall be silent. (Calmet)

Plain. Some parts of the prediction relate literally to the Old Testament. But this alludes to the New, when the mysteries of religion are clearly confessed in the Catholic Church. (Worthington) --- Even the most illiterate are guided with security, if they will but hear the Church. (Haydock)
Deceitful. Hebrew, "miser be called liberal," Luke xxii. 25. These good princes are contrasted with Achaz, who had oppressed his subjects.
Vessels. Arms, (Calmet) or all the words and actions of the miser are bent on evil. (Haydock) --- The ministers of wicked princes resemble them. (Menochius)
Women. Great cities. He announces the impending dangers.
Year. After a long time; or the prophet speaks two years before the arrival of Sennacherib, after the vintage was ended, chap. xxx. 20., and 4 Kings xix. 29. (Calmet)

Mourn. Septuagint, "beat." (Haydock) --- Breasts, suckling infants. In mourning, women beat and uncovered their breasts, which, on any other occasion, would have been deemed very indecent. (Calmet) (Ezechiel xxiii. 34.) (Herodotus ii. 84.)
Up. Being uncultivated for two years. This was still more the case during the captivity. (Calmet) --- How. Septuagint, "from every house joy shall be taken away, thou rich city." (Haydock)
Ever. Some palaces had been demolished by Sennacherib, though this seems to refer to the Babylonian captivity.

High, as Ezechiel (xxxvii. 10.) saw the dry bones rise again. Under this idea prosperity is frequently described. The rest of the chapter may very well be explained of the propagation of the gospel. --- Forest. Carmel was a fertile spot. Judea shall flourish, and Assyria shall be laid waste. The synagogue will be rejected, while the Gentiles, (Calmet) formerly so barren, shall embrace the faith and true piety. (Haydock)
Peace. The just shall enjoy peace, under Ezechias.
Hail. God's judgment shall overtake Babylon, or rather Ninive.
Waters. Fruitful soils, abounding with cattle. (Calmet) --- Both Jews and Gentiles shall submit to Christ. (Clement of Alexandria, Strom. vi.) (St. Jerome)

f: Commentary on Isaiah

These things are according to the Hebrew, from which the Seventy disagree in most places not only in words but also in senses. For when the righteous king has reigned, and his princes have ruled with judgment, there will be a man hiding his words, a man who by nature is God, and he will hide his words, speaking to them in parables (Matt 20:21, 23, 24, and 25). And he will hide them as from running water, that is, from the people of the Jews, which, like water, is borne and drawn this way and that at the will of its teachers. This man, hiding his words among the unbelieving, will appear in Zion, that is, in the Church, like a glorious river running down in a thirsty land. For he will appear to the people of the Gentiles, which before suffered thirst for the truth; and the river of God will water the thirsty fields, the river of which it is written: The rush of the river makes glad the city of God (Ps 45 [46]:4). And in another place: The river of God is filled with waters (Ps 64 [65]:10). For he himself says in the Gospel: He who thirsts, let him come to me and drink. He who believes in me, as the Scripture says, out of his belly will flow rivers of living water (John 7:38). Then they will by no means have confidence in their teachers, but will offer their ears to hear the Lord; and both with heart and with tongue they will confess the peace of the Lord, forsaking the foolish princes and their ministers, who imposed silence on those who believed in Jesus.
Commentary on Isaiah

Behold, a king will reign with righteousness, and princes will rule in judgment. And a man will be like one who is hidden from the wind and conceals himself from the tempest: like streams of waters in thirst, and the shade of a jutting rock in a desert land. The eyes of those who see will not be dimmed, and the ears of those who hear will listen diligently. And the heart of the foolish will understand knowledge, and the tongue of stammerers will speak quickly and plainly. He who is senseless will no longer be called a prince, nor will the deceitful man be called great. For the fool will speak foolish things, and his heart will work iniquity, to accomplish pretense, and to speak deceitfully to the Lord, and to empty the soul of the hungry, and to take away drink from the thirsty. The vessels of the deceitful man are most evil: for he has devised schemes to destroy the meek with the word of a lie, when the poor man spoke judgment. But the prince will think the things that are worthy of a prince, and he himself will stand over the leaders. LXX: For behold, a righteous king will reign, and princes will rule with judgment. And there will be a man hiding his words, and he will be hidden as from water that is borne along: and he will appear in Zion like a running river, glorious in a thirsty land; and they will by no means be trusting in men, but they will give their ears to hear, and the heart of the weak will attend to hearing, and the tongues of the stammering will quickly learn to speak peace: and they will no longer tell the fool to be a prince, nor will your ministers any longer say, Be silent. For the fool will speak foolish things, and his heart will understand vain things, to accomplish iniquity and to speak error to the Lord, to scatter the hungry souls and to make the thirsty souls empty. For the counsel of the most wicked will think unjust things: to slay the humble with unjust words, and to scatter the words of the humble in judgment. But the pious have thought wisdom, and this counsel abides. According to the Seventy Translators, who said: For behold, a righteous king will reign, and princes will rule with judgment, what follows must be joined to what precedes, namely to the words with which the previous section ended: Blessed is he who has seed in Zion, and kinsmen in Jerusalem. According to the Hebrew, the former prophecy, concerning those who were going down into Egypt, is finished, and now begins another oracle, namely concerning the coming of Christ and of his Apostles. For this king will reign righteously, not respecting persons in judgment, and his princes will rule with truth, considering causes, not men.
Commentary on Isaiah

And whoever is under his shelter will be as safe in tribulations and distresses, and in the tempest of this world, as one who, fleeing wind and whirlwind, hides himself in a safe place; and as one who finds the purest springs in the desert; and as one who, in fierce heat, when the blaze of the sun scorches everything, rests under a jutting rock. Where we said: like streams of waters in thirst, the Seventy translated: and he will appear in Zion like a running river. For the Hebrew word about which we argued above, BASAION (בציון), which means in thirst, or in dryness, and in a pathless place, the Seventy and Theodotion translated in Zion, reading SION, which is written with the same letters, for SAION, that is, thirst.
Commentary on Isaiah

When, therefore, Christ has reigned, and his princes have ruled in judgment, the eyes of those who believe will not be dimmed, and the ears of those who hear, which before were deaf, will attend diligently, and the heart of those once foolish will understand knowledge, and the tongue of the stammering and the mute, which could not utter Christ, will confess the Lord with full and open speech.
Commentary on Isaiah

He who is foolish will no longer be called a prince (1 Cor 1). For God has made foolish the wisdom of this world. Nor will the deceitful and perverse teacher be called great among the peoples: namely the scribes and Pharisees, to whom the Lord said: Fools and blind, which is greater, the gold or the temple that sanctifies the gold? (Matt 23:17).
Commentary on Isaiah

What follows contains nearly the same sense as the Hebrew, and can be fitted to the heretics. For these speak a lie against the Lord, and pervert the hungry and thirsty souls, and make them go away empty; so that even if they have anything good by nature, they lose it through the fault of their teachers, whose whole counsel is to destroy the humble with unjust words and to scatter the words of the humble in judgment. In which it must likewise be noted that whoever can be deceived by them is humble, and clings to the earth.
Commentary on Isaiah

For the fool will speak foolish things, for which in the Hebrew it is written: NABAL NABALA IDABBER (נבל נבלה ידבר). We say this in order to explain the words of Abigail, who says of Nabal the Carmelite: According to his name he is foolish (1 Sam 25:25). For truly the fool will speak foolish things, and his heart will accomplish iniquity: he who feared where there was no fear, and practiced folly in place of wisdom, saying: If this man were from God, he would not break the sabbath (John 9:16). This the master of the synagogues does to this day, to accomplish pretense, for which in the Hebrew is written ONEPH (חנף), that is, ὑπόκρισις. Hence it is said again and again to the Pharisees: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites (Matt 23:14). And he will speak, he says, deceitfully to the Lord: Master, we know that you are from God, and that you have no concern for men; is it lawful to give tribute to Caesar, or not? (ibid. 22:16, 17). They empty the souls of the hungry people, and take away drink from the thirsty crowds, neither entering themselves nor allowing others to enter.
Commentary on Isaiah

For all the vessels and weapons of the deceitful teacher and prince are most evil; he contrives snares to destroy the simple with the word of a lie, saying to the deceived people: Search and see, that a prophet does not arise from Galilee (John 7:52). When the poor man spoke to them judgment: he who, though he was rich, became poor for our sake (2 Cor 8). For truly Christ spoke judgment and righteousness to them, saying: If I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe me: but if I do them, even if you will not believe me, believe the works (John 10:37).
Commentary on Isaiah

This poor man who speaks judgment, the prince and Lord, will think the things that are worthy of a prince, saying: I came only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt 15:24). And he will be anxious for the unbelieving, desiring to save those who do not believe; and he will stand over his leaders, the Apostles, to one of whom he says: But you, a man of one mind with me, my leader and my familiar friend (Ps 54 [55]:14).
Commentary on Isaiah

After the calling of the nations, when Christ the king has ruled with righteousness, and his princes, the Apostles and apostolic men, have presided over the believers with judgment, the prophetic word will be directed to the wealthy women, whom we must take either as the cities of Judea, or as the synagogues of that time, or, as most think, as the matrons of the rich men of the former people of the Jews, to whom, as to women lying prostrate after their ruin, it is said: Rise; and they are nonetheless called confident daughters, or hoping; and they are commanded to hear the words of the Lord, and to remember the days and the year, of which we shall speak in what follows, as the Savior himself says: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me: he has sent me to preach the gospel to the poor, to proclaim release to the captives and sight to the blind, to call the acceptable year of the Lord (Luke 4:18, 19); and that this very remembrance may become for them, according to the Seventy, grief with hope, so that they may lament that they denied the Lord, and may have hope of salvation if they repent. For he says that the vintage is ended, and that after the last devastation, which happened under Vespasian and Titus and Hadrian, no other captivity will come, nor will clusters remain among the peoples to be gathered afterward.
Commentary on Isaiah

Hence they are summoned to lamentation, and are commanded to bare their breasts and to gird their loins, because the country once desirable, and the fruitful vine, of which it is written: I planted you a fruitful vine, wholly true: how have you turned into the bitterness of a strange vine? (Jer 2:21), has been destroyed by the ravaging Roman.
Commentary on Isaiah

Over the ground, he says, of my people thorns and briers, or grass will come up. And the sense is: if thorns and briers have filled the land of Judea, which is the land of promise, how much more the other cities, which are full of joy, and which that saying of the Gospel will overtake: Woe to you who rejoice now, for you will weep (Luke 6:25)!
Commentary on Isaiah

What was said above according to the LXX: Over the land of my people thorns and grass will come up, can be referred both to the heretics and to all the simple among believers, who do not understand Holy Scripture as befits its majesty. Hence we have fitted each to each: that the land of the people of God brings forth thorns for the heretics, and grass for all the unskilled in the Church.
Morals on the Book of Job 17.23

If those very persons, who amid the darkness of the present life shine bright by virtuous attainments—if they also cannot be void of contagion, with what guilt of wickedness are those bound, who still live after the flesh? If those persons cannot be free from sin who are already walking in the way of heavenly desires, what about those who still lie under the loads of sinful habits, who, abandoned to the gratifications of their fleshly part, still bear the yoke of rottenness?
