So Peter says, "And if the righteous scarcely be saved, where shall the ungodly and the sinner appear?" And it is said by Isaiah, "Upon the land of my people shall come up thorns and briars; how much more upon all the houses of joy in the joyous city." The "house of joy in the joyous city" is the mind of the wicked, which neglects to regard the punishments that are destined to come, in the gratification of the flesh, and going away from itself, it revels in empty mirth.
Commentary on Isaiah

Wealthy women, rise and hear my voice: confident daughters, take in my speech with your ears. After days and a year you too will be troubled, you confident ones: for the vintage is ended; the gathering will come no more. Be astonished, you wealthy women; be troubled, you confident ones: strip yourselves and be confounded. For which Symmachus translated be made naked; there follows: Gird your loins, lament upon your breasts, over the desirable country, over the fruitful vine: thorns and briers will come up over the ground of my people: how much more over all the houses of joy of the exulting city? For the house has been forsaken; the multitude of the city has been left; darkness and groping have come upon the caves for ever: the joy of wild asses, pastures of flocks. Until the spirit is poured out upon us from on high: and the desert will be in Carmel, and Carmel will be counted as a forest. And judgment will dwell in the wilderness, and righteousness will sit in Carmel. And the work of righteousness will be peace, and the service of righteousness silence, and security for ever. And my people will sit in the beauty of peace, and in the tabernacles of confidence, and in wealthy rest. But hail in the descent of the forest, and the city will be brought low with lowliness. Blessed are you who sow upon all waters, sending forth the foot of the ox and the ass. The LXX, for the darkness and groping which have come upon the caves for ever, translated and your villages will be caves for ever: what in the Hebrew is called OPHEL (עפל) and BEEN (בחן), which the Hebrews think were two towers in Jerusalem, lofty and very strong, called by these names. The first of them means darkness, or cloud, because it raised its head up to the clouds; the other, proving and firmness, or, as Symmachus renders it, inquiry: because the eyes were deceived in gazing at its summit.
Commentary on Isaiah

For the Lord, that is, my temple, has been forsaken, as I said to the Apostles: Rise, let us go hence (John 14:31); and to the unbelieving: Your house will be left to you desolate (Luke 13:35). Palpable darkness has taken possession of the inner sanctuaries of the Temple and its secret mysteries, and they have become no longer storerooms for the vessels of the Lord, but caves for ever. For they had heard from the Lord Savior (Matt 21:13): The house of my Father shall be called a house of prayer: but you have made it a den of robbers. The joy, he says, of wild asses, pastures of flocks. This is to be understood either according to the letter, in that all things are deserted; or spiritually, in that, Israel having been driven out, savage men who have no knowledge of God dwell in Judea.
Commentary on Isaiah

And this is to be until the spirit is poured out upon us from on high, which the Savior, ascending to the Father, promised to believers, saying: Behold, I go, and I will send you the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth (John 16). And again: Until you receive power from on high (Luke 24:49). And what he had said above: Yet a little while, and Lebanon will be in Carmel, and Carmel will be counted as a forest: and in that day the deaf will hear the words of the book, and out of darkness and gloom the eyes of the blind will see (above, Isa 29), he now repeats in other words: that the wilderness of the nations is turned into the riches of Israel, and Israel is counted among the nations: at which time judgment will have dwelt in the desert, the Lord and Savior, to whom the Father has given all judgment (John 3). And righteousness will rest in Carmel, of which it was said above: And the desert will be in Carmel: that judgment and righteousness dwell in the desert, and rest in Carmel, which before was called the desert.
Commentary on Isaiah

The work of righteousness too will be peace, which, according to the Apostle, surpasses all understanding (Phil 4). And the service of righteousness silence, so that they may worship the Lord not with the much speaking of the Jews but with the brevity of faith; and may rest secure in eternal peace, and in their tabernacles may be the riches of which the Apostle spoke (1 Cor 1:5): I give thanks to my God through Jesus Christ, because in everything you have been made rich in him, in all speech and in all knowledge.
The Book of Pastoral Rule, Part 2, Chapter 4

He that suffers from a flux of seed is pronounced unclean, because, being addicted to much speaking, he defiles himself by that which, had it been orderly issued, might have produced the offspring of right thought in the hearts of hearers; and, while he incautiously spends himself in loquacity, he sheds his seed not so as to serve for generation, but unto uncleanness.
Morals on the Book of Job, Book 10, Section 2

It is the practice of the impertinent ever to answer by the opposite what is said aright, lest, if they assent to the things asserted, they should seem inferior. And to these the words of the righteous, however small in number they have been heard, are 'much,' in that as they cut their evil habits to the quick, they fall heavy upon the hearing, whence that is even wrested to a crime, which by a right declaration is pronounced against crimes. For the very person, who had delivered strong sentences on grounds of truth, Zophar rebukes and calls full of words, in that, whereas wisdom reprimands sins by the mouth of the righteous, it sounds like superfluity of talkativeness to the ears of the foolish. For froward men account nothing right, but what they themselves think, and they reckon the words of the righteous idle in the degree that they find them differing from their own notions. Nor yet did Zophar deliver a fallacious sentiment, 'that a man full of words could never be justified,' in that so long as anyone lets himself out in words, the gravity of silence being gone, he parts with the safe keeping of the soul. For hence it is written, "And the work of righteousness, silence." Hence Solomon saith, "He that hath no rule over his own spirit in talking, is like a city that is broken down, and without walls." Hence he says again, "In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin." Hence the Psalmist bears witness, saying, "Let not a man full of words be established upon the earth"; but the worth of a true sentence is lost, when it is not delivered under the keeping of discretion. Thus it is a certain truth, that 'a man full of words cannot be justified,' but a good thing is not well said, because there is no heed taken to whom it is spoken. For a true sentence against the wicked, if it is aimed at the virtue of the good, loses its own virtue, and bounds back with blunted point, in proportion as that is strong which it hits. But that the wicked cannot hear good words with patience, and that wherein they neglect the amending of their life, they brace themselves up to words of rejoinder, Zophar plainly instructs us.
Commentary on Isaiah

And when the Christian people sits, or dwells, in beauty, or, as the Seventy translated, in the city of peace, which is without doubt in the Church, then hail and tempest and the raging wrath of the Lord will come down upon the forest, of which it was said above: And Carmel will be counted as a forest; and the city of Jerusalem will be brought low, and, according to another Scripture, will speak from the earth.
The Stromata Book 6
The prophet says, "Blessed is he that sows into all waters, whose ox and donkey tread," [that is] the people, from the law and from the Gentiles, gathered into one faith.
Letter 63.88

Accordingly, like a perfect man learned in the law and made firm in the gospel, accept the faith of both Testaments, for, as we read today, "Blessed is he who sows upon every water, where the ox and the donkey tread," that is, who sows upon the people who follow the teaching of both Testaments. This is the ploughman's ox, wearing the yoke of the law, of which the law says, "You shall not muzzle the ox that treads out your corn," for this ox has the horns of holy Scripture. But in the Gospel the Lord, representing the people of the Gentiles, mounts the colt of a donkey.
LETTER 27.3

Let them take as much pleasure as they please in their Gallican geldings; we will be satisfied with the simple "donkey" of Zechariah, loosed from its halter and made ready for the Savior's service, which received the Lord on its back and so fulfilled Isaiah's prediction: "Blessed is he that sows beside all waters, where the ox and the donkey tread under foot."
Commentary on Isaiah

Do we ask where we have read of the ox and the ass together? In Deuteronomy it is written: You shall not plough with a calf and an ass together (Deut 22:10). And in this same Isaiah: Blessed is he who sows upon every water, where the ox and the ass tread (Isa 32:20). Ebion ploughs with the ox and the ass together, worthy, for the lowliness of his understanding, of the poverty of his name; for he so receives the Gospel as not to abandon the ceremonies of the Jewish superstitions, which went before in shadow and image. But blessed is he who sows in the words of the Scriptures, of the old as well as of the new Instrument, and treads the waters of the letter that kills, so as to reap the fruit of the life-giving spirit.
Commentary on Isaiah
At the end of the section too they translated thus: Blessed are those who sow upon every water, where the ox and the ass tread.
Commentary on Isaiah

Since these things are so, and we have learned from the prophetic oracle how great the goods are that the Church will possess, and how great the evils that Jerusalem will suffer: blessed are you, Apostles, and you other teachers, who sow upon all the waters of Holy Scripture, in which the ox and the ass tread. The ox is a clean animal, on account of the election of the fathers; the ass unclean, on account of the former idolatry of the Gentiles; so that the Church of the Lord may be gathered both from the Circumcision and from the Uncircumcision.
Morals on the Book of Job, Book 19

By water peoples are denoted, as it is said by John, "Now the waters are peoples." By water likewise not only the tide of peoples drifting away, but also the minds of good men that follow the preachings of faith, are denoted, as the Prophet saith, "Blessed are ye that sow upon all waters." And it is said by the Psalmist; "The voice of the Lord is upon the waters."
Morals on the Book of Job, Book 31

What else is meant by 'seed,' but the word of preaching? As the Truth says in the Gospel, "A sower went forth to sow"; and as the Prophet says; "Blessed are ye who sow upon all waters." What else but the Church, ought to be understood by the threshing floor? Of which it is said by the voice of the Forerunner; "And He will throughly purge His floor."

n: Spoilest. This is particularly directed to Sennacherib. (Challoner) --- He was a figure of persecutors of the Church, to which many passages here allude. (Calmet) --- Remota justitia quid sunt regna nisi magna latrocinia? (St. Augustine, City of God iv. 4.) --- Sennacherib plundered Samaria and Juda, and despising God, was himself contemned. (Worthington)
Morning. Speedily. Hebrew, "mornings," or every day. Ezechias thus addresses God.
Them. The neglect of burying these insects has often brought on the plague. (St. Augustine, City of God iii. 31.)
Faith. Sincerity and justice adorn the reigns of Ezechias and Christ.

Without. The people of the country, and the envoys of Ezechias, 4 Kings xviii. 14. Hebrew, "Behold their Ariel, cried they without," insultingly, (Calmet) pointing at Jerusalem, chap. xxix. 1. At which (Haydock) the envoys rent their garments, &c., chap. xxxvi. 22. (Calmet) --- "Behold I shall appear to them." (Aquila) (St. Jerome) --- Angels. Messengers or deputies sent to negotiate a peace, (Challoner) who wept because they could not obtain it. (Worthington)
Void, though Sennacherib had received what he demanded, 4 Kings xviii. 14.
Confounded. Its trees were cut down, chap. xxxvii. 24.
Myself, when all human aid fails.
You, Assyrians, are bringing destruction upon yourselves. (Calmet)

Of you. Hebrew, "of us." (Haydock) --- They are seriously alarmed at the sight of the fires prepared to burn the dead bodies of the Assyrians, (chap. xxx. 33.) and begin to think of hell, (Calmet) which their sins deserve. (Haydock)
Blood. Avoiding revenge, and punishing the guilty, without respect to persons. Such was Ezechias, and therefore his enemies could not hurt him.
Sure. Never failing. (Calmet) --- This was a great advantage in those dry regions. (Haydock)
King Ezechias, or he shall be one of his courtiers. --- Off. Their limits shall be extended. Those who believe in Christ, shall cast their eyes up towards their heavenly country, Hebrews ix. 13.
Ones. These questions were put by the people, when the enemy approached; or they now rejoice that their severe masters were gone.
Shameless, unjust Assyrians, Luke xviii. 2. When shame is gone, people give way to every excess. --- Profound. Unknown to the Jews, 4 Kings xviii. 26. --- No wisdom, manners, or piety.
Broken. It was taken 125 years afterwards. The Church remains till the end of time, (Calmet) whereas both the prophets and history assure us, that Jerusalem was subject to destruction. (Worthington)

Of rivers. He speaks of the rivers of endless joys that flow from the throne of God to water the heavenly Jerusalem, where no enemy's ship can come, &c. (Challoner) --- God keeps all enemies from Jerusalem, like a deep river. (Calmet)

Thy tacklings. He speaks of the enemies of the Church, under the allegory of a ship that is disabled. (Challoner) --- Sennacherib shall attempt invasion no more than a ship without masts would put to sea.
Feeble. All were obliged to collect the plunder, to be afterwards divided. None shall plead illness. The inhabitants of Jerusalem will not feel the effects of sin (Calmet) on this occasion. (Haydock)

f: Commentary on Isaiah

Woe to you who plunder: will you not yourself be plundered? And you who despise: will you not yourself be despised? When you have finished plundering, you will be plundered: when, wearied, you have ceased to scorn, you will be scorned. LXX: Woe to those who make you wretched: for no one makes you wretched. And those who reject you do not reject you: those who reject will be taken, and will be handed over, and like a moth in a garment so will they be overcome. He had spoken of the Apostles and of the teachers of the churches: Blessed are those who sow upon every water, where the ox and the ass tread: now he directs a curse at their persecutors, nay, at their prince, who possesses the hearts of the impious: that whatever they have done they may receive back, and their present power may be the material of future torments. Hence according to the LXX it is said: Woe to those who make you wretched: for no one makes you wretched. And the sense is: as far as lies in them, when they persecute you and afflict you with various tortures, they think you wretched once you have been killed and tortured. But no one can make you wretched, for they have power not over the soul, but over the body. And he who rejects you does not reject you, but him who sent you, according to what the Savior says to the disciples: He who rejects you rejects me: and he who rejects me rejects him who sent me (Luke 10:16). The persecutors, therefore, will be taken, and will be handed over to eternal fires. And as a moth consumes a garment, so will the perpetual flame consume them. This is also written at the end of this prophecy: Their worm will not die, and their fire will not be quenched.
Commentary on Isaiah

O Lord, have mercy on us: for we have waited for you: be their arm in the morning, and our salvation in the time of tribulation. At the voice of the Angel the peoples fled, at your exaltation the nations were scattered. And your spoils will be gathered as the young locust is collected, as when the ditches are full of it. The Lord is magnified, for he has dwelt on high: he has filled Zion with judgment and righteousness. And there will be faith in your times: the riches of salvation are wisdom and knowledge: the fear of the Lord is itself his treasure. LXX: O Lord, have mercy on us, for we trust in you: the seed of the unbelieving has come to perdition, but our salvation is in the time of tribulation: because of the voice of fear the peoples were astonished at the fear of you, and the nations were scattered. But now your spoils will be gathered, small and great: as if someone were gathering locusts, so will they mock you: holy is God who dwells on high. Zion is filled with judgment and righteousness; they will be handed over in the law; in treasures is our salvation: wisdom has come, and discipline, and piety from the Lord; these are the treasures of righteousness. The Hebrews think that the preceding section, in which we read: Woe to you who plunder: will you not yourself be plundered? and the rest to the end, was spoken against Sennacherib king of the Assyrians: that after he had overthrown the cities of the ten tribes, which were called Israel, and had also taken the cities of Judea, except Jerusalem, he himself would be overcome, and his army would be destroyed when the Angel struck. Hence they contend that the things contained in the present section are now spoken in the person of the people giving thanks to God and saying: O Lord, have mercy on us, we have waited for you: that he himself was the arm and the strength of the people hemmed in by the siege, in the morning time, and their salvation in need and distress. For at the voice of the Angel, which Symmachus rendered just as it is written in the Hebrew, AMUN (המון), and whom the Hebrews hold to be Gabriel and to have the etymology of people, the Assyrian fled, and at the exaltation of God the nations that were with him were scattered this way and that. As they fled, the spoils were gathered by the Jews, as a multitude of young locusts and of locusts is usually gathered when they have been heaped up in ditches. In their victory the Lord was magnified, and Zion was filled with judgment and righteousness, and the faith of the besieged people was proven; and they had all their riches in wisdom, and in the knowledge of God and the fear of the Lord, who alone was their treasure. These things they may say according to the history, striving by every means to overthrow the mysteries of Christ and of his Apostles. But we, after the blessedness of the Apostles, of whom it was said above (cf. Isa 32:20): Blessed are those who sow upon every water, where the ox and the ass tread, and after the lamentation and wailing of those who persecuted them, of whom it is said in what follows: Woe to those who make you wretched; but no one makes you wretched: and as a moth in a garment, so will they be worn away, prove that these things are spoken in the person of the same Apostles and of all believers. And the sense is: Lord, we have hoped in your help, and we trust in you: the seed of the unbelieving has perished for ever, and our salvation has appeared in the time of tribulation. For when you gave help, the whole multitude of the nations was scattered, and became a prey and a mockery to the victors. And this came about because the holy Lord dwells on high, and Zion is filled with judgment and righteousness, of which it was written above: Judgment and righteousness will rest in the desert. This, then, is Zion, which before was called the desert; and whoever dwells in her, to him will be handed over the law of the Gospel, in whose treasure is our salvation, and the wisdom of believers, and discipline and piety, or faith, which properly belongs to Christians, and the fear of the Lord, in which the treasures of wisdom are contained.
On the Gospel of Luke 5:16.11-12

But "true wealth" signifies either the joy of eternal life itself, concerning which it is written, "the riches of his inheritance in the saints," or those spiritual virtues with which the fullness of life is attained, about which Isaiah said, "the riches of salvation, wisdom, and knowledge; the fear of the Lord himself is its treasure.""And if you are unfaithful with goods that are not yours, who will give you something of your own?" The resources of this world are alien to us, that is, external to the nature of our habitat, "for we brought nothing into this world and we are without doubt unable to take anything from it." Our possession is the kingdom of heaven, our life is Christ, and our wealth consists in the fruitfulness of spiritual works, about which Solomon said, "The redemption of a man's soul is his wealth."
Commentary on Isaiah

Behold, those who see will cry outside: the Angels of peace will weep bitterly. The ways are laid waste, the one who passed along the path has ceased, the covenant has been made void, he has cast off the cities, he has not regarded men. The earth has mourned and languished, Lebanon is confounded and has become deaf, and Sharon has become like a desert, and Bashan and Carmel are shaken. Now I will rise up, says the Lord: now I will be exalted, now I will be lifted up. You will conceive burning heat, you will bring forth stubble; your spirit, like fire, will devour you. And the peoples will be like ashes from a burning: thorns gathered together will be burned with fire. The Hebrew word ARELLAM (אראלם), for which Aquila and Symmachus and Theodotion translated I will appear to them, dividing the last syllable and reading ARE LAHEM (ארא להם), the Hebrews think signifies Angels, and that this is a prophecy, after the calling of the nations and the riches of the Church, of the overthrow of the Temple: that the Angels will weep, no longer dwelling within, but going outside; and those who before were messengers of peace will weep bitterly. Or the Apostles themselves, who had been sent to announce peace to Jerusalem, to which the Lord said: If you too had known the things that belong to your peace (Luke 19:42), and to whom the Lord appeared, to strengthen them by his sight, will weep for Jerusalem, because it did not receive their preaching, because the ways are laid waste, and the one who passed along the righteous path has ceased, according to what is said in the Lamentations of Jeremiah: The ways of Zion mourn, because there are none who come to the solemnity (Lam 1:4). The covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob has also been made void: He has cast off the cities of Judea: he has not regarded men, who by their own fault chose to be beasts.
Commentary on Samuel 3:16.1

But if you want to see that the ancient prophets were terribly sad and aggrieved about the future blinding of their nation, which was the cause of our illumination, listen to Isaiah, for when he was sent to announce beforehand the grace of the Lord's coming, saying that "a light has arisen upon those who dwell in the region of the shadow of death," he responded immediately to the advent of the same light, saying "you have enlarged the nation; you have not increased its joy." And elsewhere, while commemorating the despondency of this people, Isaiah said, among other things, "the messengers of peace will weep bitterly, referring to the prophetic heralds of the divine word."
Commentary on Isaiah

The earth has mourned and languished for those who dwelt in the land (Gen 15 and 22). Lebanon is confounded and has become deaf: without doubt it signifies the Temple, of which we read in Zechariah: Open your gates, O Lebanon, that fire may devour your cedars (Zech 11:1). Or Jerusalem, which in Ezekiel is called Lebanon, when the Prophet says: A great eagle with great wings, which has the design of entering into Lebanon (Ezek 17:3); which the divine word afterward interprets: when, it says, Nebuchadnezzar came to Jerusalem; plainly explaining the Eagle as the king of Babylon, and Lebanon as Jerusalem. Sharon has become like a desert, and Bashan and Carmel are shaken. For Bashan, the LXX translated Galilee, the province in place of one place of the province. Sharon, moreover, is the name of the whole region around Joppa and Lydda, in which very broad and fertile plains stretch out. Bashan too is a region beyond the Jordan, which the two and a half tribes possessed, and which means most fruitful and fat (Deut 3); and Carmel, of which we spoke above. The once fertile places of Judea, then, will be turned into a wilderness, by which it is shown μεταφορικῶς that all the opulence of the Jews is to be exchanged for want and poverty. Since, then, they would not receive the word of the Apostles, Lebanon is confounded, and Sharon is turned into a wilderness, and Bashan and Carmel are shaken.
Commentary on Isaiah
Therefore the Lord says that he will rise up, either from his very great patience, or from the underworld, and will be exalted among the nations, and lifted up on the cross.
Commentary on Isaiah

And he turns in apostrophe to the Jews themselves: You will conceive burning heat, and you will bring forth stubble, and your spirit will kindle a fire for you, so that the devouring flame may consume what was conceived and brought forth.
Commentary on Isaiah

And the peoples of the Jews, he says, will be like ashes from a burning, showing the greatness of their misfortune by the remnants of the embers. For their thorns, which have been gathered together by the multitude of their sins, will be devoured by the burning; which most refer to the last captivity and overthrow of Jerusalem. Others affirm that it will come about more fully and perfectly at the time of judgment.
The Epistle of Barnabas, Chapter IX

He speaks moreover concerning our ears, how He hath circumcised both them and our heart. The Lord saith in the prophet, "In the hearing of the ear they obeyed me." And again He saith, "By hearing, those shall hear who are afar off; they shall know what I have done." And, "Be ye circumcised in your hearts, saith the Lord." ... Therefore He hath circumcised our ears, that we might hear His word and believe.
Commentary on Isaiah

Hear, you who are far off, what I have done, and you who are near, know my strength. The sinners in Zion are terrified, trembling has seized the hypocrites. Who of you can dwell with devouring fire? Who of you will dwell with everlasting burnings? He who walks in acts of righteousness, and speaks truths, who casts away avarice from calumny, and shakes his hands free of every bribe, who stops his ears lest he hear blood, and shuts his eyes lest he see evil. He will dwell on high; fortresses of rocks are his height: bread has been given him, his waters are faithful. His eyes will see the king in his beauty: they will behold the land from afar. Your heart will meditate fear. Where is the scribe? Where is he who weighs the words of the law? Where is the teacher of little ones? You will not see the imprudent people, the people of deep speech, so that you cannot understand the eloquence of its tongue, in which there is no wisdom. LXX: Those who are far off will hear what they have done: those who draw near will know my strength. The lawless who were in Zion have departed; trembling will seize the impious. Who will announce to you that fire is burning? Who will announce to you the eternal place? He who walks in righteousness, and speaks the right way, and hates impiety and iniquity, and shakes his hands free of gifts, and stops his ears so as not to hear the judgment of blood, and shuts his eyes so that they may not see iniquity, he will dwell in a lofty cave of a very strong rock. Bread will be given him, and his water will be faithful: your eyes will see the king with glory, they will see the land from afar; your soul will meditate fear. Where are the grammarians? Where are the counselors? Where is he who numbers those who nourish both the small and the great people? To whom he did not give counsel: nor did he know his deep voice, so that the despised people did not hear, and there is no understanding for the one who hears. Since the ways are laid waste, the one who passed along the paths has ceased, the covenant with the people of the Jews has been made void, God has cast off their cities and has not counted them among men; therefore you who are far off, hear what I have done, and draw near, that you may know my strength.
AGAINST MARCION 4.34

The Scripture itself … expressly distinguishes between Abraham's bosom, where the poor man dwells, and the infernal place of torment. "Hell" (I take it) means one thing, and "Abraham's bosom" another. "A great gulf" is said to separate those regions and to hinder a passage from one to the other. Besides, the rich man could not have "lifted up his eyes," and from a distance too, except to a superior height, and from the said distance all up through the vast immensity of height and depth.… There is some determinate place called Abraham's bosom, and it is designed for the reception of souls of Abraham's children, even from among the Gentiles (since he is "the father of many nations," which must be classed amongst his family), and of the same faith as that with which he himself believed God, without the yoke of the law and the sign of circumcision. This region, therefore, I call Abraham's bosom. Although it is not in heaven, it is yet higher than hell, and it is appointed to afford an interval of rest to the souls of the righteous, until the consummation of all things shall complete the resurrections of all people with the "full recompense of their reward." This consummation will then be manifested in heavenly promises.… Amos, however, tells us of "those stories towards heaven" which Christ "builds"—of course for his people. There also is that everlasting abode of which Isaiah asks, "Who shall declare to you the eternal place, but he (that is, of course, Christ) who walks in righteousness, speaks of the straight path, and hates injustice and iniquity?" Now, although this everlasting abode is promised, and the ascending stories (or steps) to heaven are built by the Creator, who further promises that the seed of Abraham shall be even as the stars of heaven, by virtue certainly of the heavenly promise, why may it not be possible, without any injury to that promise, that by Abraham's bosom is meant some temporary receptacle of faithful souls, wherein is even now delineated an image of the future and where is given some foresight of the glory of both judgments?
Commentary on Isaiah

The sinners, or the impious, who were in Zion are terrified, or have departed, and trembling has seized the hypocrites, to whom the Lord said in the Gospel: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites (Matt 23:14)! Who of you can dwell with him who is a devouring fire? Who will dwell with everlasting burnings? Or according to the LXX: Who will announce to you that the eternal fire is burning, which God has prepared for the devil and his angels?
Commentary on Isaiah

Who, then, will be able to dwell with God, or to announce the punishments to come? Everyone who is such as the prophetic word describes: who walks in many acts of righteousness, and loves acts of righteousness not once but always, and speaks truths not on one occasion but continually; who casts away avarice, which is the mother of calumny. For money is not heaped up for one man except with another's loss and harm. And he shakes his hands free of every bribe; for bribes blind the eyes even of the wise. He stops his ears lest he hear the judgment of blood. All iniquity and oppression and injustice is a judgment of blood: and though one does not kill with the sword, yet he slays by his will. And he shuts his eyes lest he see evil. Happy the conscience that neither hears nor beholds evil.
40 Homilies on the Gospels, Homily IV

There are some who indeed do not receive rewards of money from ordination, yet bestow sacred orders for human favor, and from that very generosity seek only the recompense of praise. These certainly do not bestow freely what was freely received, because from the service of holiness they have rendered, they seek the coin of favor. Hence the prophet spoke well when describing the just man, saying: Who shakes his hands free from every gift. For he does not say: Who shakes his hands from a gift, but added from every, because one thing is a gift from service, another a gift from the hand, another a gift from the tongue. A gift from service is deference unduly rendered, a gift from the hand is money, a gift from the tongue is favor. Therefore he who bestows sacred orders shakes his hands free from every gift when in divine matters he seeks not only no money, but also no human favor.
Morals on the Book of Job, Book 9

We must bear in mind too that there are three ways in which deceit itself is practised, in that, surely, the object aimed at in it is either the secret interest of our fellow creatures' feelings, or the breath of applause, or some outward advantage; contrary to which it is rightly said of the righteous man by the prophet, "Blessed is he that shaketh his hands clear of every favour." For as deceit does not consist only in the receiving of money; so, no doubt, a favour is not confined to one thing, but there are three ways of receiving favours after which deceit goeth in haste. For a favour from the heart, is interest solicited in the opinion, a favour from the mouth is glory from applause, a favour from the head a reward by gift. Now every righteous man 'shaketh his hands clear of every favour,' in that in whatever he does aright, he neither aims to win vainglory from the affections of his fellow creatures, nor applause from their lips, nor a gift from their hands. And so he alone is not guilty of deceit in doing God's work, who while he is energetic in studying right conduct, neither pants after the rewards of earthly substance, nor after words of applause, nor after favour in man's judgment. Therefore because our very good actions themselves cannot escape the sword of ambushed sin, unless they be guarded every day by anxious fear, it is rightly said in this place by the holy man, I was afraid of all my works.
Commentary on Isaiah

He, then, who is such will dwell on high, that is, in the kingdom of heaven, or in a lofty cave of a very strong rock, in Christ Jesus: the rock that followed the people of Israel, that they might drink from it and be protected by its strength. Bread will be given him, and his waters are faithful: which the fables of the Gentiles understand as ambrosia and nectar. But we shall interpret the bread and the most faithful waters as the law of God.
Commentary on 1 Kings, Book 6, Chapter 3

By the name of bread the teaching of perfection is shown, as Paul attests, who, rousing the weak to conversion, says: "I gave you milk to drink, not solid food. For you were not yet able, nor are you yet able." For if milk belongs to little ones, bread belongs to none but the perfect. Whence also it is said of the strength of the perfect man: "He shall dwell on high, the fortifications of rocks shall be his loftiness, bread has been given to him." Therefore in the house of bread a king is sought for anointing, because those are profitably advanced who are nourished in the order of perfect conduct. For he is able to make others strong who has not been nourished in lax and negligent conduct.
Commentary on Isaiah

He, then, who is such will behold Christ the king in his brightness, of whom it is said above (cf. Isa 32:1): Behold, a righteous king will reign, and princes will rule in judgment. And his eyes will see from afar the land which they had long desired, the land of the meek and gentle, of which it is written in the Gospel: Blessed are the meek, for they will possess the land (Matt 5:4); or, set in heaven, they will look down on earthly things.
Homilies on the Gospels 1:19

Through the sacraments of his humanity with which we have been imbued, we may be able to attain the contemplation of the glory of his divinity, that contemplation which he himself in his faithful benevolence pledged to his faithful servants when he said, "One who has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me. One who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him." He says, "I will manifest myself"—that is, "Not in such a way that everyone can look at me, or in such a way that even the unfaithful can see me and crucify me, but in such a way that only the pure eyes of the saints can see 'the King of ages in his beauty.' " In this way I will show myself to those who love me, so as to reward them for their love. Therefore let us hope, as we have said, that through the visible nature of his humanity we may be able to ascend to see the beauty of his divinity, if we keep these sacraments as we have received them, unblemished in the worthy honor of justice and holiness and truth, if we follow his example in his human way of life, and if we humbly follow the words of the teaching which he ministered to us through his humanity.
Homilies on the Gospels 1:24

The disciples indeed saw him coming in his kingdom, for on the mountain they saw him shining in that brightness with which he will be seen in his kingdom by all the saints when the judgment has been brought to completion. But since the eyes of the disciples were still mortal and corruptible, they were then unable to sustain what the whole church of the saints will have the power to look upon when she has become incorruptible through resurrection. Concerning this it is written, "Their eye will see the king in his beauty."
Commentary on Isaiah

Your heart will meditate fear: so that when you have attained all things, you may say with the Apostle: I who am not worthy to be called an Apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God (1 Cor 15:9). For the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord. Where is the scribe? Where is he who weighs the words of the law? Where is the teacher of little ones? (Prov 9:1). Where, he says, are the scribes and Pharisees, who, weighing the words of the Law in the balance, deceived the unhappy people? whom the Scripture now calls little ones: little in sense, little in understanding.
Commentary on Isaiah

And when the eyes of the believer have beheld the king in his majesty, and his heart has meditated fear, then he will not see the imprudent people, the people of the Jews, or of the philosophers and orators of the world, who applaud themselves for secular learning and eloquence, of whom he now says: A people of deep speech, so that you cannot understand the eloquence of its tongue; whose whole adornment is in words, who have only the leaves and the shade of speech, and do not possess the fruit of truth. Then there follows: In which there is no wisdom; of whom it is also said in another place: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the understanding of the prudent I will reject (1 Cor 1:19). Why? Because God has made foolish the wisdom of this world.
Commentary on Isaiah

Look upon Zion, the city of our solemnity: your eyes will see Jerusalem, a wealthy habitation: a tabernacle that can by no means be moved, nor will its pegs be taken away for ever, and none of its cords will be broken. For only there is our Lord magnificent: a place of rivers, streams very broad and open; no ship with oars will pass through it, nor will a great trireme cross it. For the Lord is our judge, the Lord is our lawgiver, the Lord is our king; he himself will save us. Your cords are loosened, and will not hold: so will your mast be, that you cannot spread out the ensign. Then the spoils of many preys will be divided: the lame will seize the plunder. Nor will the neighbor say, I am faint: the people that dwells in it, iniquity will be taken away from it. LXX: Behold Zion, the city, our salvation: your eyes will see Jerusalem, a rich city, tabernacles that will not be moved: nor will the stakes of its tabernacle be taken away for ever, and its cords will not be torn apart: for the name of the Lord is great to you: your place will be rivers and streams very broad and spacious: no ship driven by oars will go in through it: for my God is great: the Lord will not pass me by, our judge, the Lord our prince, the Lord our king, the Lord himself will save us. Your cords are broken because they did not hold: your mast is bent, so that it lets the sails go: it will not raise the ensign until it is given over to devastation. Many lame, therefore, will take spoils: and they will not say, I shall labor; the people that dwells in them, their sin will be forgiven them. O righteous one, to whom it was said above: your heart will meditate fear; and, the imprudent people you will not see; and who had heard before, your eyes will see the king in his beauty: look upon Zion, the city of our solemnity, see the Church of Christ, in which is the true solemnity: your eyes will behold the vision of peace, and riches beyond hope, which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have they entered into the heart of man, and the tabernacle that can by no means be moved. For the former tabernacle, which the people of the Jews had, was moved and taken away. Nor will its pegs be moved for ever, and all its cords will be firm; so that the Lord dwells in it, which is the place of all the rivers and running streams, through which no one of the opposing side will be able to sail: nor a great trireme, which is interpreted as the devil, will be able to cross it: because the Lord himself is our judge, and prince, and king, and Savior, and under his protection we shall fear the snares of no one. These things are said of Zion, the city of our solemnity, and of Jerusalem, the richest habitation, which the Lord himself will surround and fortify with his rivers.
Morals on the Book of Job, Book 18

For the plainly spoken words of these interpreting have made the sentences of the ancient Fathers henceforth clear to us. Hence the Prophet Isaiah viewing the words plain by the interpretation of Holy Church, not obscured by the darkness of allegories, exclaimed, saying, "The place of rivers, the broadest and open streams." For the sayings of the Old Testament were as narrow and close streams, which bound up the sentences of their lore in the darkest gathering together. But on the other hand the teaching of Holy Church are 'streams both broad and open,' because her declarations are at once many in number to those that find them, and plain to those that seek.
Commentary on Isaiah

But now he speaks to the earthly Jerusalem: that the cords of its tabernacle are loosened, and could not hold up the tent, and its mast, on which the most beautiful sails once hung, has fallen with its ropes broken, so that it is useless not only for sailing but also for an ensign. And after their ship has been broken up and the tabernacle scattered, so that the cords are torn apart on both sides, the plunder will be divided among the victors: who will be so weak in their own strength that they are called lame; and nonetheless, since the wrath of God gives them strength, they will feel no weakness, nor will they say: I have labored. For whoever is among them, iniquity and sin will be taken away from him, because he has carried out the will of God.

n: Come. Both Gentiles and Jews are admonished of the world's end before judgment. (Worthington)

Away. These strong expressions denote great misery, chap. xiii., and Joel ii. 10., and Ezechiel xxxii. 27. (Calmet) --- Book. Hebrew, "roll." (Haydock) --- Some thence foolishly inferred that the destiny of every one might be read in the heavens. (Huet.; Eusebius, præp. vi. 11.; Philoo. xxiii.; Pic. Astrol. viii. 5.) --- The prophet only means that the heavens shall be devoid of beauty, (Calmet) and covered with darkness. (Haydock)

Heaven. Casting down the rebel angels. (St. Jerome) --- The resolution to destroy the Idumeans, for their cruelty to the Jews, has been taken long ago. All these expressions allude to the last judgment. (Calmet) --- Idumea. Under the name of Idumea or Edom, a people that were enemies of the Jews, are here understood the wicked in general, the enemies of God and his Church. (Challoner) --- Assaradon fell upon Edom two years after Sennacherib's death. (Calmet) --- No strong place like Bosra, shall rescue any from destruction at the last day. (Worthington)
The unicorns. That is, the great and mighty. (Challoner)

Recompenses. When the persecutors of Sion, that is, of the Church, shall receive their reward. (Challoner) --- The Idumeans had frequently shown their ill-will towards the Jews, 2 Paralipomenon xxviii. 17., and Amos i. 11. (Calmet) --- Sion shall perish as the wicked in hell shall be tormented. (Worthington)
Pitch. The soil was sulphureous, and became neglected, (ver. 10.) like the territory of Sodom. The people are now no more, and only a few miserable Arabs pitch their tents there.
Line. Intimating entire destruction, Lamentations ii. 8., and 4 Kings xi. 13. (Calmet) --- Yet God will not punish more than people deserve. (Menochius)
Dragons, Thannim, chap. xiii. 22. (Haydock) --- Ostriches, or swans.

Monsters. Literally, "Ass-centaurs." (Haydock) --- Hebrew, "fishermen shall find islands," chap. xiii. 21. --- Ones. Goats. --- Lamia. Hebrew lilith. Chaldean, "owl," the bird of Minerva, or the Moon, which the Arabs style Alilat. (Calmet) --- Dicodorus (20) relates that Lamia was an African queen, who having last her children, was changed into a beast, and destroyed all the children she could catch; and the Jews deal still more in fables, (Calmet0 asserting that Lilith was the first wife of Adam, &c. (Buxtorf. Syn. 2.)
Ericius. Hebrew, "kippoz, (Haydock) hath its nest." It may denote the serpent, acontias. (Bochart) --- All this shews the desolation of the country.
Read what I have written. --- The other. All these beasts will be there, (Calmet) or all these declarations will be verified. (Haydock)

f: Commentary on Isaiah

Come near, you nations, and hear, and you peoples, attend: let the earth hear, and its fullness, the world and all its offspring. For the indignation of the Lord is upon all the nations, and his fury upon all their host: he has slain them and given them over to slaughter. Their slain will be cast out, and from their corpses a stench will rise: the mountains will melt with their blood. And all the host of the heavens will waste away: the heavens will be rolled back (or folded together) like a book: and all their host will fall away, as a leaf falls from the vine and from the fig tree, for my sword has been made drunk in heaven. Behold, it will come down upon Idumea, and upon the people of my slaughter, to judgment. The sword of the Lord is filled with blood, it is fattened with fat: with the blood of lambs and goats, with the blood of rams full of marrow; for the Lord has a victim in Bozrah, and a great slaughter in the land of Edom. And the unicorns will come down with them, and the bulls with the mighty. Their land will be made drunk with their blood, and their ground with the fat of the fat ones. After the overthrow of Jerusalem and the shipwreck of the once most solid ship, and the plundering of all its furnishings, it speaks of the destruction of all the nations, and of the consummation of the world, which is on the future day of judgment. Hence all the nations and peoples, the earth and its fullness, the world and all its offspring, both the places that are inhabited and those that are uninhabitable through excess of cold and of heat, are commanded to hear, and to learn with all trembling of mind what is to come.
Commentary on Isaiah

For the indignation of the Lord is described as coming not upon the one nation of Judea alone, and upon the Assyrians and Chaldeans, the Egyptians, the Moabites and the Ammonites and the Philistines, but against all the nations, and upon all their host, or, as the LXX translated, their number, to slay them and to make the stench of rotting bodies rise on high, signifying the sins of all the nations; so that the mountains are filled with their gore and filth and blood: all the lofty powers and the Angels who presided over the several nations; and all the host or strength of the heavens wastes away: the heavens are rolled back, or folded together, like a book, and all their host and army, and, as the LXX translated, the stars will fall away, in the likeness of leaves which, as the cold draws near, fall withered and shrivelled from the vine and the fig tree. Which indeed the Savior also says in the Gospel: The stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens will be moved, and then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven (Matt 24:29, 30). And this must be considered, that he does not say that the heavens perish, but that they are rolled back, or folded together, like a book: so that after all sins have been laid open and read through, the heavens which before were open are folded together, so that the offenses of many are no longer written in them. Of books of this kind Daniel speaks in his volume: The judgment sat, and the books were opened (Dan 7:10), in which the works of each had been written down. Most think that the stars fall according to the Apocalypse of John (Rev 6 and 8), and according to what is written elsewhere: All the stars, burning, will be dissolved, and heaven and earth will pass away (Luke 10:2). For the form of this world passes away. Some think that this is said of the stars that glitter in the heaven, so that the whole is shown in the part: namely, that through the ruin of the stars the destruction of the heavens too is shown (1 Cor 7). Others, however, think that those stars will fall of which the Apostle Paul also writes: Our struggle is not against blood and flesh, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places (Eph 6:12). Nor is it surprising if the demons who dwell in the air are called heavenly, since the Scripture also names the birds of heaven, which certainly fly not in heaven but in the air. For Satan too transforms himself into an Angel of light (2 Cor 11), pretending to be a star. And the Savior saw him falling like lightning from heaven (Luke 10). And tropologically it is said of him as of a great star: How has Lucifer fallen, who rose in the morning? (Isa 14:12).
Catechetical Lecture 15:3

So, our Lord Jesus Christ comes from heaven, and he comes with glory at the last day to bring this world to its close. For this world will accomplish its course, and the world that once came into being is hereafter to be renewed. For seeing that corruption, theft, adultery and every form of sin has been poured out on the earth, and in the world fresh blood has been ever mingled with previous blood, this astonishing habitation filled with iniquity is not to last. This world passes away that the fairer world may be revealed. Now would you have this proved by the express words of Scripture? Listen to these from Isaiah: "And the heavens shall be rolled together as a scroll; and all the stars shall fall down, as the leaf falls off from the vine, and as a falling fig from the fig tree."
LETTER 22.3

To us this life is a race course: we contend here, we are crowned elsewhere. No one can lay aside fear while serpents and scorpions beset his path. The Lord says, "My sword has drunk its fill in heaven," and do you expect to find peace on the earth? No, the earth yields only thorns and thistles, and its dust is food for the serpent. "For our wrestling is not against flesh and blood but against the principalities, against the powers, against the world rulers of this darkness, against the spiritual hosts of wickedness in the heavenly places." We are hemmed in by hosts of foes; our enemies are upon every side. The weak flesh will soon be ashes: one against many, it fights against tremendous odds. Not till it has been dissolved, not till the prince of this world has come and found no sin therein, not till then may you safely listen to the prophet's words: "You shall not be afraid for the terror by night nor the arrow that flies by day; nor for the trouble which haunts you in darkness." … When the hosts of the enemy distress you, when your body is hot with fever and your passions roused, when you say in your heart, "What shall I do?" Then Elisha's words shall give you your answer, "Fear not, for they that be with us are more than they that be with them." He shall pray, "Lord, open the eyes of your handmaid that she may see." And then when your eyes have been opened, you shall see a fiery chariot like Elijah's waiting to carry you to heaven, and you shall joyfully sing, "Our soul has become free like a bird out of the snare of the fowlers: the snare is broken and we have been set free."
Commentary on Isaiah

All these things will come about because his sword has been made drunk in heaven: the punishment and sentence and vengeance upon sinners which is pronounced by the Lord. This sword and blade is sharpened against the impious in Ezekiel (Ezek 21), and, when very many have been slain, is commanded to go back into its sheath. And when it has been made drunk and filled in heaven, that is, in the air, which by the usage of the Scriptures is called heaven, then it will come down to Idumea too, that is, to earthly things: so that after the punishment of the demons the souls of men too may be judged. For Idumea in our language means earthly.
Commentary on Zechariah
And because God did not spare the angels who sinned, who by their own fault lost their heavenly dwelling, therefore he himself says through Isaiah: My sword has been made drunk in heaven.
Commentary on Isaiah

And it is filled with blood and fattened with the fat of lambs and goats, and of rams full of marrow, and of bulls: so as to signify that princes and people alike are to be punished. For the Lord has a victim in Bozrah, and a great slaughter in the land of Edom. Of this Bozrah and Idumea the same Prophet also testifies in what follows (cf. Isa 63:1), saying: Who is this who comes from Edom, with his garments red from Bozrah? And some think that, because Bosor means flesh, the torments of all in the flesh are shown by the Lord's victim in Bozrah: they fall into a pious error. For in the present place it is written not with the letter SIN, which is set in BOSOR (בשר), that is, flesh, but with SADE, and it is called BOSRA (בצרה), which according to Joshua and Jeremiah is found not in Edom, that is, Idumea, but in the land of Moab (Jer 48). And Bosra in our language means fortified and surrounded, or strengthened: to teach that the world has been made firm by the will of the Lord, according to what is sung in the psalm: He has founded it upon the seas, and established it upon the rivers (Ps 23 [24]:2); and of the firmness of the earth it is said in the person of God: I have made firm its pillars (Ps 74 [75]:3). And when the Lord's victim has been in Bozrah, and his slaughter in Idumea, the unicorns will come down with the mighty bulls, namely the kings and princes of the earth; and all things will be filled with slaughter and blood, and with the fat of those once rich and mighty. By these words, which, after the manner of human speech, strike terror into the hearers, torments are shown against all princes and mighty men, and against peoples and small ones. By Bosra, that is, fortified and strengthened, and by Edom, or Dumah, and Idumea, the teachers of the Jews want Rome to be understood, and all the things contained in the following section to be said of it.
Commentary on Isaiah
What we have said is prophesied of Jerusalem, and what the Jews suspect is said of the Roman empire, some refer to the whole world, so as not to seem to disagree with what precedes.
Commentary on Isaiah

For it is the day of the Lord's vengeance, the year of the recompenses of the judgment of Zion. And its torrents will be turned into pitch, and its ground into sulphur: and its land will become burning pitch. Night and day it will not be quenched, for ever: its smoke will go up: from generation to generation it will be desolate; for ages of ages there will be none passing through it. And the pelican and the hedgehog will possess it, and the ibis and the raven will dwell in it, and the measuring line will be stretched over it, to bring it to nothing, and the plummet unto desolation. Its nobles will not be there: they will rather call upon the king, and all its princes will be as nothing. And thorns will spring up in its house and nettles, and the thornbush in its fortresses: and it will be the lair of dragons and the pasture of ostriches. And demons will meet with onocentaurs, and the hairy one will cry out one to another: there will lie down the lamia, and will find rest for herself. There the hedgehog has had its hole, and has reared its young, and has dug round about, and cherished them in its shade: thither the kites have gathered, one to another. Search diligently in the book of the Lord, and read: not one of them was missing, one did not seek the other: for what proceeds from my mouth, he has commanded, and his spirit, he himself has gathered them. And he himself has cast the lot for them and his hand has divided it to them by measure; they will possess it for ever: from generation to generation they will dwell in it. The Hebrews, as we said above, contend that these things were prophesied of the Roman empire, and that the devastation of a once most powerful kingdom is foretold in vengeance for Zion; and most of our writers think that this, according to the letter, is also written in the Apocalypse of John. But we, from what is said, the day of the Lord's vengeance, the year of the recompenses of the judgment of Zion, judge this to be the year of which the Savior himself speaks: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach the gospel to the poor, to proclaim release to the captives, and to the blind that they may see, to call the acceptable year of the Lord, and the day of recompense for our God: to comfort all who mourn, and to give glory to those who lament for Zion (Luke 4:18, 19; Isa 61:1-3); and of which it was said above: Wealthy women, rise (Isa 32:9), and remember the days of the year in grief with hope;
Homilies on Ezekiel, Book 1, Homily 6

Sacred Scripture has stature, because it directs conduct toward standing, so that the minds of hearers may not be bent toward earthly desire. It has height, because it promises the joys of eternal life in the heavenly homeland. It also has a horrible appearance, because it threatens all the reprobate with the punishments of hell. Therefore it shows its stature in the building of conduct, it shows its height in the promise of rewards, it shows its horrible appearance in the terrors of punishments. For it is upright in precepts, lofty in promises, horrible in threats. ... It has a horrible appearance when, describing hell, it says: "The day of vengeance of the Lord, the year of retribution for the judgment of Zion; and its torrents shall be turned into pitch, and its soil into sulphur; and the land shall be burning pitch, day and night it shall not be extinguished forever."
Commentary on Isaiah

and therefore we judge that after the general consummation of the whole world the Scripture returns to Jerusalem, to which it was speaking at that time, and describes its devastation at full length: namely, that after the time of the Roman siege has come, all things will be filled with pitch and sulphur and burning flames, and its smoke will remain for ever, and the pelican and the hedgehog and the ibis and the raven will dwell there, animals which are accustomed to dwell in desert places; and that this will come about because the line and the plummet of the Lord, that is, his sentence, cannot be changed.
Commentary on Isaiah

But those who follow tropology affirm that, once the people of the Jews has been driven out, idolaters and those who serve various superstitions will dwell in Jerusalem under the names of beasts and monsters; and that these are the pelicans and hedgehogs, the ibis and the raven, the dragons and ostriches, and the onocentaurs, and the demons, and the hairy ones, and the lamia, which in Hebrew is called LILITH (לילית), and was translated lamia by Symmachus alone, and which some of the Hebrews suspect to be ἐριννὴν, that is, a fury. And indeed, if we consider that colonies brought from various nations were settled in Jerusalem, and that according to the rite of their own provinces the several households worshipped the monstrous forms of their own demons, we shall affirm that all these dwelt in Jerusalem.
Commentary on Isaiah

Its nobles, that is, the Apostles and the believers, will not be there, nor will they be joined to the number of the lost, but will rather call upon Christ the king. But all its princes, namely the scribes and Pharisees, will be brought to nothing, and in the once most adorned houses thorns and nettles and the thornbush will spring up. And it will be the lair of dragons and the pasture of ostriches, which are themselves also signs of utter desolation.
Morals on the Book of Job, Book 33

Which conduct the Lord by the Prophet well reproves, under the character of Babylon, saying; "Thorns and nettles shall spring up in her houses, and the bramble in the fortresses thereof." For what do we understand by 'nettles,' but the irritations of thoughts, and what by 'thorns,' but the piercings of sins? Nettles therefore and thorns spring up in the houses of Babylon, because in the disorder of a reprobate mind there arise longings of thoughts which exasperate, and sinful deeds which wound. But they who act thus have others also more wicked than themselves as their defenders. Whence he there fitly subjoined immediately, "And the bramble in the fortresses thereof." For the bramble is crowded with such a circle of thorns, that it can hardly be touched from its roughness. The nettle and the thorn therefore spring up within, but both of them are fortified without by the bramble: because, namely, smaller offenders commit any kinds of evil, but greater and most abandoned ones defend them.
Commentary on Isaiah

And there will meet one another in it, according to the LXX, various phantoms of demons, or, as all the others translated according to the Hebrew, SIIM (ציים) and IIM (איים), onocentaurs and hairy ones and the lamia, which the fables of the Gentiles and the fictions of the poets describe.
Commentary on Isaiah

The hedgehog too rears its young there, and has a most secure lodging: thither the kites are gathered, a most rapacious bird, which in Hebrew is called DAJOTH (דיות), or, as the LXX translated, stags, of which we shall speak below.
Commentary on Isaiah

And what the LXX translated: There the stags met one another, and saw one another's faces: they passed by in number, not one of them perished, nor did one seek the other. For the Lord commanded them, and his spirit gathered them: and he himself gave them lots, and his hand will divide for them, that they may feed for ever, and possess it from generation to generation, and rest in it: this we shall interpret allegorically, to teach that the stags, that is, the Apostles and all holy teachers, of whom it is written: As the stag longs for the springs of waters, so my soul longs for you, O God (Ps 41 [42]:1); and elsewhere: The voice of the Lord perfecting the stags (Ps 28 [29]:9); and again: Let the stag of friendship and the foal of your graces speak with you (Prov 5); and in Job: But you have watched the months of the stags, and you will bring forth their young (Job 39:2); and in the Song of Songs it is said: My kinsman is like a roe, or a young stag upon the mountains of spices (Song 2:9); met one another in Jerusalem and saw each other's faces, and passed through it and left it, and went on to various provinces, because the Lord commanded them: Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matt 28:19); and that his spirit gathered them, and gave them lots and divided them, so that one went to the Indians, another to the Spains, another to Illyricum, another to Greece, and each rested in the province of his own Gospel and teaching.
The Book of Pastoral Rule, Part 3

Hence it is rightly said through the prophet, under the similitude of Judah, to the soul that sins and excuses itself, "There the urchin had her nest." For by the name of urchin is denoted the duplicity of a mind that is insincere, and cunningly defends itself; because, to wit, when an urchin is caught, its head is perceived, and its feet appear, and its whole body is exposed to view; but no sooner has it been caught than it gathers itself into a ball, draws in its feet, hides its head, and all is lost together within the hands of him that holds it which before was all visible together. So assuredly, so insincere minds are, when they are seized hold of in their transgressions. For the head of the urchin is perceived, because it appears from what beginning the sinner has advanced to his crime; the feet of the urchin are seen, because it is discovered by what steps the iniquity has been perpetrated; and yet by suddenly adducing excuses the insincere mind gathers in its feet, in that it hides all traces of its iniquity; it draws in the head, because by strange defences it makes out that it has not even begun any evil; and it remains as it were a ball in the hand of one that holds it, because one that takes it to task, suddenly losing all that he had just now come to the knowledge of, holds the sinner rolled up within his own consciousness, and, though he had seen the whole of him when he was caught, yet, illuded by the tergiversation of dishonest defence, he is in like measure ignorant of the whole of him. Thus the urchin has her nest in the reprobate, because the duplicity of a crafty mind, gathering itself up within itself, hides itself in the darkness of its self-defence.
Commentary on Isaiah

Among these things the Prophet speaks to his hearers: O men who hear me speaking, what I announce as to come will all be fulfilled in deed. For they are written in the book of the Lord, and his sentence is fixed, and not even one will be void. For what proceeds from my mouth, he has commanded; that is, I indeed speak, but the words are the Lord's, and by his spirit whatever has been said will be accomplished. By his decree and measure each thing will be fulfilled, and they will not abandon their order unto everlasting generations. Let these things be said according to the Hebrew and the historical explanation.

n: Lily. Judea flourishes under Ezechias: but the Church does more so after the coming of Christ, to whom these expressions conduct us. (Calmet) --- The Gentiles shall be converted and flourish, as this text shews. (Worthington)
Joy. The primitive Christians rejoiced in a good conscience, and in suffering for the truth.
Knees. Ye prophets, comfort the people with these promises. (Calmet) --- The apostles taught the Gentiles to do good. (Menochius)

Recompense. Christ will satisfy the justice of his Father. (Haydock) --- He will redeem the world, and refute the false interpretations of the Bible. (Calmet) --- He will bring the devil into subjection. (Menochius)

Free. Our Saviour healed both soul and body, (Calmet) shewing by his works (John x.; Worthington) that he had fulfilled this prediction, Luke vii. 22., and Matthew xi. 5. --- Waters. Baptism has sanctified the most wicked.
Dragons. Sea monsters, chap. xxxiv. 13. (Calmet) --- All shall be in proper order, neither too dry nor too wet. (Haydock)

Way, leading to Jerusalem. Idolaters, &c., shall not be there, chap. lii. 1. This was only verified (Calmet) in the Catholic Church, where, though some wicked may be found, the truth still prevails; and holiness can be obtained no where else. (Haydock) --- This Church is unspotted, Ephesians v. 27. (Calmet) --- Fools. The most simple may learn what is necessary for salvation, (Menochius) which will never be done by consulting Scripture alone. (Haydock)
Lion. The devil's power shall be repressed, so that none will be deluded except by their own fault. (Menochius)
Sion. Before the defeat of Sennacherib, the roads were unsafe, chap. xxxviii. 8. (Calmet)

f: ON THE BAPTISM OF CHRIST

And where shall we place that oracle of Isaiah, which cries to the wilderness, "Be glad, O thirsty wilderness: let the desert rejoice and blossom as a lily: and the desolate places of Jordan shall blossom and shall rejoice"? For it is clear that it is not to places without soul or sense that he proclaims the good tidings of joy: but he speaks, by the figure of the desert, of the soul that is parched and unadorned, even as David also, when he says, "My soul is unto Thee as a thirsty land," and, "My soul is athirst for the mighty, for the living God."
ON THE BAPTISM OF CHRIST

And "the excellency of Carmel" is given to the soul that bears the likeness to the desert, that is, the grace bestowed through the Spirit. For since Elijah dwelt in Carmel, and the mountain became famous and renowned by the virtue of him who dwelt there, and since moreover John the Baptist, illustrious in the spirit of Elijah, sanctified the Jordan, therefore the prophet foretold that "the excellency of Carmel" should be given to the river.
ON THE BAPTISM OF CHRIST

And "the glory of Lebanon," from the similitude of its lofty trees, he transfers to the river. For as great Lebanon presents a sufficient cause of wonder in the very trees which it brings forth and nourishes, so is the Jordan glorified by regenerating men and planting them in the Paradise of God: and of them, as the words of the Psalmist say, ever blooming and bearing the foliage of virtues, "the leaf shall not wither," and God shall be glad, receiving their fruit in due season, rejoicing, like a good planter, in his own works.
Commentary on Isaiah

The desert and the pathless land will be glad, and the wilderness will exult, and will flower like the lily. Budding, it will bud forth, and will exult, joyful and praising. The glory of Lebanon has been given to it, the beauty of Carmel and Sharon. They will see the glory of the Lord, and the beauty of our God. LXX: Rejoice, thirsty desert, and let the wilderness exult, and let it flower like the lily. The deserts of the Jordan will flower and exult: the glory of Lebanon has been given to it, and the honor of Carmel: and my people will see the glory of the Lord, and the height of our God. Since Jerusalem has been turned into pitch, and its everlasting smoke has gone up, and the pelican and the hedgehog, the ibis and the raven, dragons and ostriches, demons and onocentaurs, the lamia and the hairy ones dwell in it, and the sentence of the Lord has been fulfilled upon it: Your house will be left to you desolate (Luke 13:35): therefore she who before had been deserted, of whom it is said in the psalm: The voice of the Lord shaking the wilderness, and the Lord will shake the desert of Kadesh. The voice of the Lord preparing the stags; and he will lay bare the thickets of the forests (Ps 28 [29]:8, 9), will be changed into an abundance of all things; and, as the stags fight, the beasts which formerly possessed all the forests of the nations will be driven out of them, so that what is said in this same Prophet may be fulfilled: Rejoice, barren one, who do not bear: break forth and cry, you who do not travail; for more are the children of the desolate than of her who has a husband (Isa 54:1). She who before was thirsty, or pathless, not having life-giving waters, and through whom the Lord did not walk, will now flower into a lily, or, as Aquila expressed it more significantly, καλύκωσις, which we can call a swelling rose whose petals have not yet opened. And she will flower, so as to declare with the Apostle: We are the good fragrance of Christ in every place (2 Cor 2:15); and that saying of the Song of Songs: Flowers have appeared in the land: the mandrakes have given their fragrance (Song 7:12, 13).
On the Gospel of Luke 3:9.10

After John was killed, the Lord saw the time drawing near and withdrew to a deserted place called Bethsaida. This teaches mystically that a deserted Judah, which had beheaded its prophets by not believing them, would later become fruitful in the desert of a church that possessed no man of the Word. Hence, the beautiful Bethsaida means "house of fruitfulness." For it was about it that Isaiah said, "The desert and the dry land will rejoice, and the wilderness will exult and bloom like the lily," and again, "they will see the glory of the Lord and the beauty of our God."
Commentary on Isaiah

And what is set down in the LXX, and the deserts of the Jordan will exult, is indeed not found in the Hebrew; but we can say that by the river Jordan John's baptism of repentance is shown, which the Lord sealed and confirmed by his own washing. And since this is said figuratively of the wilderness, which refers to the nations, and in which John was, the Jordan can fittingly be joined to it, so that through the desert of the nations we may come to the baptism of the Savior. And what follows, the glory of Lebanon has been given to it, and the beauty of Carmel and Sharon, we must take according to the earlier explanation, in which we said that by Lebanon the Temple or Jerusalem is understood, as Zechariah says: Open your gates, O Lebanon (Zech 11:1); and Ezekiel: A great eagle with great wings, full of talons, which has the design of entering into Lebanon and Carmel (Ezek 17:3); and that Carmel signifies the former people, of which it was said above: And the desert will be in Carmel, and Carmel will be counted as a forest (Isa 32:15); and that Sharon has the same meaning, since the Scripture says: Sharon has become like a desert. All the brightness, then, the worship of God, and the knowledge of circumcision, and the most fruitful and level places, which are called Sharon, for which Symmachus translated plains, will be given to the once deserted Church, and its inhabitants will see the glory of the Lord, and the beauty, or height, of our God.
Commentary on the Song of Songs 5:8.4-5

Because a multitude of Gentiles followed it after Judah came to faith in the Lord's incarnation and an astonished partaker of the same grace hastened its own unexpected conversion, Judah exclaimed in surprise, "Who is this that ascends from the desert, flowing with delights, leaning upon my beloved?" The church of the Gentiles ascends from the desert because the one who was deserted by its Creator for a very long time now arrives at his grace by the incremental steps of faith and good works, thus fulfilling what the prophet Isaiah said: "The desert and the dry land will rejoice, and the wilderness will exult and bloom like the lily." Indeed, she is truly flowing with those delights about which the spouse spoke above: "How beautiful you are, and how lovely, my dear, with delights," that is, with the delights of heavenly life. "Leaning upon my beloved" means leaning upon him without whose assistance she would be able neither to ascend above nor to rise again, for we are unable to possess either advancement in the virtues or the beginning of faith itself unless the Lord bestows them upon us.Therefore, Judah was even more awestruck by this grace of the Gentiles' new conversion, a grace that it believed pertained only to itself and to those who were received in its rite through the mystery of circumcision, as the Acts of the Apostles made abundantly clear.
AGAINST MARCION 4.10.1

The sick of the palsy is healed, and that in public, in the sight of the people. For, says Isaiah, "they shall see the glory of the Lord and the excellence of our God." What glory, and what excellence? "Be strong, you weak hands and feeble knees" refers to the palsy. "Be strong; fear not." "Be strong" is not vainly repeated, nor is "fear not" vainly added; because with the renewal of the limbs there was to be, according to the promise, a restoration also of bodily energies: "Arise, and take up your couch"; and likewise moral courage not to be afraid of those who should say, "Who can forgive sins, but God alone?"
On Joseph the Patriarch 3.17

Therefore the traders came from Gilead, that is, from their possessions of or dwelling in the law, and brought their wares to the church, so that that balm might heal the sins of the nations. Of them it is said, "Be strong, you hands that are feeble and you knees that are without strength." The balm is unspoiled faith. Such a faith Peter exhibited when he said to the lame man, "In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, arise and walk." And he arose and walked, as was right. Such a faith Peter had when he said to the paralytic, "Aeneas, the Lord Jesus heals you; get up and make your bed." And he got up and made his bed. Such a faith he had when he said to the dead woman, "Arise in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ." And the departed woman arose. With the mortar made from this cement those stones are fastened together from which God is able to raise up children to Abraham.
Flight from the World 7.37

Then let us flee the wickedness of this world, in which "the very days are evil," and flee it relentlessly. On that account Isaiah cries out, "Be strong, you hands which are feeble and you knees which are without strength." This means: Be strong, you knees, not of the body but of the soul, so that the footstep of the spirit can rise up straightway to the heights of heaven. Thus conduct will be more stable, life more mature, grace more abundant and discretion more guarded.
Commentary on Isaiah

Strengthen the slackened hands, and make firm the feeble knees. Say to the faint-hearted (or to the fearful), Be strengthened, and do not fear; behold, your God will bring the vengeance of recompense: God himself will come and will save you (or, as the LXX translated, us). Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped (or will hear). Then the lame man will leap like a stag, and the tongue of the dumb will be opened, for waters have broken out in the desert, and torrents in the wilderness, and what was dry ground will become a pool (or marshes), and the thirsty land springs of water. In the lairs in which dragons dwelt before, the green of reed and rush will spring up (for which the LXX translated: There will be the gladness of birds, and folds of flocks). And there will be a path there, and a way (or a clean way), and it will be called the holy way; the polluted will not pass through it. And this will be for us a straight way, so that fools may not go astray in it (or, as the LXX translated, nor will there be an unclean way there, but those who have been scattered will pass through it, and will not go astray). There will be no lion there, he says, and no evil beast will go up by it, nor will one be found there, but those who have been set free will walk in it. And the redeemed of the Lord will return, and will come to Zion with praise, and everlasting gladness will be upon their head. They will obtain joy and gladness, and sorrow and groaning will flee away. We have mingled both editions, lest, by setting out each one, the size of the books be stretched, which already exceeds the measure of brevity.
