The Apostles, of whom it was said above: They will see the glory of the Lord and the beauty of our God, are commanded to strengthen the hands that had grown slack among the nations, and to make firm the feeble knees; so that those who before could not do the work of God with slackened hands, and had a withered right hand, may stretch it out to good works; and those who long limped among idols with various errors may walk with firm step upon the truth; and that, strengthening the faint-hearted or timid by faith in the Lord, they may make them not fear, and the fear of the one God may drive out the fears of all error. And the cause of their security and constancy is that Christ is to come, to whom the Father has given all judgment, and he will render to each according to his works (John 5). He himself will come and will save you, you to whom it is said, Do not fear; or us, so that the Apostles may say that salvation is common to them with the believers.
AN ANSWER TO THE JEWS 9

The actions of Christ must be seen alongside the rule of the Scriptures. Unless I am mistaken, we see that Christ's work consisted of two actions: preaching and power. Let us look at each of these in the order we have just listed them. First, Christ was announced as a preacher. Isaiah said, "Cry out loud, and do not hold back. Lift up your voice as a trumpet, and declare to my people their crimes and to the house of Jacob their sins. Then seek me day by day and desire to learn my ways, as a nation that has done righteousness and has not forsaken the judgment of God," and so forth. Second, it was announced that Christ would do acts of power from the Father. Isaiah said, "Behold, our God will come with judgment; he will come and save us. Then the sick will be healed, the eyes of the blind will see, the ears of the deaf will hear, the mute will speak, and the lame will leap as a deer."
SERMON 293:8

This is the divine arrangement, as far as any human being can investigate it, better minds in a better way, lesser minds less effectively; this divine arrangement is giving us hints of a great and significant mystery. Christ, you see, was going to come in the flesh, not anyone at all, not an angel, not an ambassador; but "he himself will come and save you." It wasn't anyone who was going to come; and yet how was he going to come? He was going to be born in mortal flesh, to be a tiny infant, to be laid in a manger, wrapped in cradle clothes, nourished on milk; going to grow up, and finally even to be done to death. So in all these indications of humility there is indeed a pattern of an extreme humility.
Commentary on Isaiah

Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped. Then the lame man will leap like a stag, and the tongue of the dumb will be opened. And although this was fulfilled by the greatness of signs, when the Lord said to the disciples of John who had been sent to him: Go and report to John what you have heard and seen: the blind see, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise again, the poor have the gospel preached to them (Luke 7:22); yet it is fulfilled daily among the nations, when those who before were blind, and stumbled against wood and stones, behold the light of truth. And those who with deaf ears could not hear the words of the Scriptures now rejoice at the precepts of God; when those who before were lame, and did not keep the right way, leap like stags, imitating their teachers; and the tongue of the dumb is opened, whose mouths Satan had shut, so that they could not confess the one Lord.
The First Apology, Chapter XLVIII

And that it was predicted that our Christ should heal all diseases and raise the dead, hear what was said. There are these words: "At His coming the lame shall leap as an hart, and the tongue of the stammerer shall be clear speaking: the blind shall see, and the lepers shall be cleansed; and the dead shall rise, and walk about." And that He did those things, you can learn from the Acts of Pontius Pilate.
ON THE RESURRECTION OF THE FLESH 20

Let me dispel at once the … assertion that the prophets make all their announcements in figures of speech. Now, if this were the case, the figures themselves could not possibly have been distinguished, inasmuch as the verities would not have been declared, out of which the figurative language is stretched. And, indeed, if all are figures, where will be that of which they are the figures? How can you hold up a mirror for your face, if the face nowhere exists? But, in truth, all are not figures, but there are also literal statements; nor are all shadows, but there are bodies too. We have prophecies about the Lord himself even, which are clearer than the day. For it was not figuratively that the Virgin conceived in her womb.… Not even of his mighty works have [the prophets] used parabolic language. Or else, were not the eyes of the blind opened? Did not the tongue of the mute recover speech? Did not the relaxed hands and palsied knees become strong, and the lame leap like a deer? No doubt we are accustomed also to give a spiritual significance to these statements of prophecy, according to the analogy of the physical diseases that were healed by the Lord. But still they were all fulfilled literally, thus showing that the prophets foretold both senses, except that very many of their words can be taken only in a pure and simple signification and free from all allegorical obscurity.
AGAINST CELSUS 2:48

That [Jesus] healed the lame and the blind, and that therefore we hold him to be the Christ and the Son of God, is manifest to us from what is contained in the prophecies: "Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened."
On the Incarnation of the Word 38

Now what can they [i.e., those who deny the incarnation] say to this, or how can they dare to face this at all? For the prophecy not only indicated that God is to sojourn here but also announces the signs and the time of his coming. For they connect the blind recovering their sight, and the lame walking, and the deaf hearing, and the tongue of the one who stammers being made plain, with the divine coming which is to take place. Let them say, then, when such signs have come to pass in Israel, or where in Judah anything of the sort has occurred. Naaman, a leper, was cleansed, but no deaf man heard nor lame walked. Elijah raised a dead man; so did Elisha;64 but none blind from birth regained his sight. For in good truth, to raise a dead man is a great thing, but it is not like the wonder wrought by the Savior. Only, if Scripture has not passed over the case of the leper and of the dead son of the widow, certainly had it come to pass that a lame man also had walked and a blind man recovered his sight, the narrative would not have omitted to mention this also. Since, then, nothing is said in the [Old Testament] Scriptures, it is evident that these things had never taken place before. When, then, have they taken place, save when the Word of God himself came in the body? Or when did he come, if not when lame men walked, and those who stammer were made to speak plainly, and deaf men heard, and men blind from birth regained their sight?
Commentary on Isaiah

And for this reason the eyes will be opened, the ears will hear, the lame will leap, and the tongue of the dumb will be opened: because in the once deserted Church the waters of saving baptism have broken out, or burst forth, and torrents and streams in the wilderness, namely the various spiritual graces; and what was dry ground has been turned into a pool and marshes, so that it is not only free from the burning of thirst, but is navigable and well watered, and has very many springs, which the stag longs for, and of which whoever has drunk can bless the Lord, according to what is written: Bless the Lord from the springs of Israel (Ps 67 [68]:27).
Dialogue with Trypho, Chapter LXIX

But since I have not quoted to you such Scripture as tells that Christ will do these things, I must necessarily remind you of one such: from which you can understand, how that to those destitute of a knowledge of God, I mean the Gentiles, who, 'having eyes, saw not, and having a heart, understood not,' worshipping the images of wood, [how even to them] Scripture prophesied that they would renounce these [vanities], and hope in this Christ. It is thus written: 'Rejoice, thirsty wilderness: let the wilderness be glad, and blossom as the lily: the deserts of the Jordan shall both blossom and be glad: and the glory of Lebanon was given to it, and the honour of Carmel. And my people shall see the exaltation of the Lord, and the glory of God. Be strong, ye careless hands and enfeebled knees. Be comforted, ye faint in soul: be strong, fear not. Behold, our God gives, and will give, retributive judgment. He shall come and save us. Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall hear. Then the lame shall leap as an hart, and the tongue of the stammerers shall be distinct: for water has broken forth in the wilderness, and a valley in the thirsty land; and the parched ground shall become pools, and a spring of water shall [rise up] in the thirsty land.' The spring of living water which gushed forth from God in the land destitute of the knowledge of God, namely the land of the Gentiles, was this Christ, who also appeared in your nation, and healed those who were maimed, and deaf, and lame in body from their birth, causing them to leap, to hear, and to see, by His word. And having raised the dead, and causing them to live, by His deeds He compelled the men who lived at that time to recognise Him.
Commentary on Isaiah

In the lairs of the Gentile souls, in which dragons dwelt before, there will be the reed and the rush, with which the faith of the Lord may be written, and on which limbs once weary may rest; or there will be the gladness of birds, and folds of flocks: so that they may take the wings of a dove, and, leaving lowly things, hasten to the heights, and be able to say with the Psalmist: The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing: in a place of pasture, there he has set me: beside the waters of refreshment he has brought me up.
Homilies on Ezekiel 2.1

The Lord promises concerning holy Church through another prophet, saying: "There shall spring up in her the greenness of the reed and the rush." I remember having explained this in another place, that by the reed we should understand writers, and by the rush, hearers. But since both rush and reed are accustomed to grow near the moisture of water, and both spring forth from one and the same water, and the reed indeed is taken up for writing, while with the rush one cannot write, what should we understand by the rush and the reed, except that there is one doctrine of truth which irrigates many hearers? But some who are irrigated advance in the word of God even to the point that they also become writers, that is, like reeds; but others hear the word of life, maintain the greenness of good hope and right works, yet cannot advance to writing at all. What are these in the water of God except certain rushes, so to speak? They indeed advance by growing green, but they cannot express letters at all.
Commentary on Isaiah

There will be a path there, and a most clean way, which will be called holy, and which says of itself: I am the way (John 14:6), through which he who is polluted will not be able to pass. Hence it is also said in the psalm: Blessed are the undefiled in the way (Ps 118 [119]:1). And this way, that is, our God, will be for us so straight and level and plain that it has no error: and fools and the senseless may be able to walk in it, to whom Wisdom speaks in Proverbs: If anyone is a little one, let him come to me. And to the unwise she said: Come, eat my bread, and drink the wine which I have mixed for you. Leave childishness, and live, and walk in the ways of prudence (Prov 9:4-6). For God has chosen the foolish things of the world (1 Cor 1): the prince of which fools speaks in the psalm: O God, you know my foolishness. And the foolishness of God is wiser than men (Ps 68 [69]:6). Hence the LXX translated: And those who had been scattered (1 Cor 2), and separated from the fellowship of the Lord, will by no means go astray.
Commentary on Isaiah

There follows: There will be no lion there: our adversary the devil, who goes about roaring, seeking how he may enter the sheepfold of the Lord (1 Pet 5). And the evil beasts, his attendants, will not go up by it. For the track of a serpent cannot be found upon a rock. But those will walk in it who have been set free from the chains of sins, and redeemed by the blood of the Savior, and have repented, and have come to Zion, of which we have often spoken: You have come to Mount Zion, and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem (Heb 12:22); lest after the Jewish fashion we seek a golden Zion and a jewelled Jerusalem, which, according to the prophecy of Daniel, has been dissolved into everlasting ashes (Dan 9).
ON THE RESURRECTION OF THE FLESH 58

"Everlasting joy," says Isaiah, "shall be upon their heads." Well, there is nothing eternal until after the resurrection. "And sorrow and sighing," he continues, "shall flee away." The angel echoes the same to John: "And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes," from the same eyes indeed which had formerly wept and which might weep again if the loving kindness of God did not dry up every fountain of tears. And again: "God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death," and therefore no more corruption, it being chased away by incorruption, even as death is by immortality.
Commentaries on the Twelve Davidic Psalms 38.16

[God] is the same one who said to Jeremiah, "Behold, I place my words in your mouth as a fire." David, therefore, also received this tongue of fire, so that he could speak of divine knowledge while enkindled with zeal: "Make known to me my end, O Lord." He was not here asking about his own death or about the final resurrection. He was inquiring into that end of which the apostle spoke: "For the end will come when the Lord Jesus hands over the kingdom to God the Father and when he destroys every principality and power and when death is the last of all things to be destroyed," such that evil is defeated and eternal goodness is ignited. Therefore it was said, "Pain and wailing will flee."
Commentary on Isaiah

And the everlasting gladness of those who praise the Lord will be upon their head, so that after they have conquered the world they may be able to say with the Apostle and with the Prophet: I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; for the rest, there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness (2 Tim 4:7, 8); and, O Lord, as with the shield of your good will you have crowned us (Ps 5:13). Then, as joy and gladness take their place, sorrow and groaning will flee away, when he comes out of Zion who will deliver. All these things we, following the apostle Paul, interpret of the first coming of the Savior: but the Jews, and our Judaizers, refer them to the second, on the strength of a single little verse, They will return and come to Zion with praise, longing for the blood of victims, and the servitude of all the nations, and the beauty of wives.
SERMON 158:8.8

What about hope? Will that be there [i.e., in heaven]? Hope will not continue when the thing hoped for is there. Certainly hope is very necessary for us in our exile. It is what consoles us on the journey. When the traveler, after all, finds it wearisome walking along, he puts up with the fatigue precisely because he hopes to arrive. Rob him of any hope of arriving, and immediately his strength for walking is broken. So the hope also which we have here is part and parcel of the justice of our exile and our journey. Listen to the apostle himself. "Awaiting the adoption," he says, "we cannot yet say there is the bliss of which Scripture says, 'Toil and groaning have passed away.' "

f: Commentary on Isaiah

I have read in someone's Commentary that this Sennacherib is the same who also took Samaria, which is altogether false. For the sacred history relates that first Pul king of the Assyrians, under Menahem king of Israel, laid waste the ten tribes; second, that Tiglath-pileser came to Samaria under Pekah son of Remaliah of Israel; third, that Shalmaneser under Hoshea king of Israel took all Samaria (2 Kgs 15, 17); fourth, that it was Sargon who stormed Ashdod (Isa 20); fifth, Esarhaddon, who, when Israel had been carried away, sent the Samaritans into the land of Judea as guards (2 Kgs 17); sixth, Sennacherib, who under Hezekiah king of Judah, having taken Lachish and the other cities of Judea, besieged Jerusalem (2 Kgs 18). Others, however, think that one and the same king is called by many names.
Commentary on Isaiah

And it came to pass in the fourteenth year of king Hezekiah, Sennacherib king of the Assyrians came up against all the fortified cities of Judah and took them. And the king of the Assyrians sent Rabshakeh from Lachish to Jerusalem to king Hezekiah with a heavy hand, and he stood at the aqueduct of the upper pool, in the way of the fuller's field. And there went out to him Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was over the house, and Shebna the scribe, and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder; and Rabshakeh said to them: Say to Hezekiah: Thus says the great king, the king of the Assyrians: What is this confidence in which you trust? Or with what counsel and strength are you planning to rebel? In whom do you have confidence, that you have withdrawn from me? Behold, you are trusting in this broken staff of reed, in Egypt: on which if a man leans, it will enter into his hand and pierce it: so is Pharaoh king of Egypt to all who trust in him. But if you answer me, We trust in the Lord our God, is it not he whose high places and altars Hezekiah has taken away, and has said to Judah and Jerusalem: You shall worship before this altar? And now deliver yourself to my lord the king of the Assyrians, and I will give you two thousand horses, and you will not be able on your part to furnish riders for them. And how will you withstand the face of the judge of a single place, one of the lesser servants of my lord? But if you trust in Egypt, and in chariots, and in horsemen: and now, have I come up without the Lord against this land to destroy it? The Lord said to me: Go up against this land, and destroy it. The history is plain and needs no interpretation; and these same things are related, written more fully, in the volumes of Kings and of Chronicles: that in the third year of Hoshea son of Elah, king of Israel, Hezekiah son of Ahaz king of Judah began to reign. He was twenty-five years old, it says, when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem, and he did what was good before the Lord, according to all that David his father had done. And a little after: He hoped in the Lord God of Israel, and after him there was none like him among all the kings of Judah, nor among those who were before him: he clung to the Lord and did not depart from his footsteps, and he did his commandments which the Lord had commanded Moses: whence also the Lord was with him, and in all things to which he went forth he conducted himself wisely (2 Kgs 18:2, 7). And he rebelled against the king of the Assyrians and did not serve him: in the sixth year of whose reign Shalmaneser king of the Assyrians took Samaria and the ten tribes which were called Israel, and carried them away to the Assyrians, and settled them in Halah and in Habor, the rivers of Gozan, in the cities of the Medes (2 Kgs 17 and 18). And after seven years, that is, in the fourteenth year of Hezekiah, Sennacherib king of the Assyrians entered Judea and besieged its fortified cities, wishing to take them. And when he was besieging Lachish, Hezekiah sent messengers to him, saying: I have sinned; withdraw from me, and whatever you lay upon me I will bear. And when he had paid three hundred talents of silver and thirty of gold at the king's command, having broken off the doors of the Temple of the Lord and stripped off its plates, which he himself had fastened on, the king of the Assyrians sent Tartan and Rabshakeh from Lachish to king Hezekiah with a strong hand to Jerusalem: and when they had gone up, they came to Jerusalem and stood by the aqueduct of the upper pool, which is in the way of the fuller's field, and called the king to them. And there went out to them Eliakim son of Hilkiah, the overseer of the house, and Shebna the scribe, and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder; and Rabshakeh said to them: Speak to Hezekiah: Thus said the great king, the king of the Assyrians, and the rest that is contained in the history. In this the arrogance of Rabshakeh is to be considered: that, like some opposing power, he imitates the custom of the Prophets, so that what they are accustomed to put in their prologues, Thus says the Lord, to show the authority and greatness of the speaker, this man now said: Thus says the great king, the king of the Assyrians. And there went out to him Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was overseer of the house, and Shebna the scribe, and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder. This is the Eliakim son of Hilkiah of whom we read above, in the Vision of the valley of Zion (cf. Isa 22:20, 21): I will call my servant Eliakim son of Hilkiah, and I will clothe him with your tunic, and strengthen him with your girdle, and give your power into his hand, and he shall be as a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem and to the house of Judah, and the rest. Now these things are said to Shebna, who before him was overseer of the Temple, of whom it is written in the same vision: Go and enter in to him who dwells in the tabernacle, to Shebna the overseer of the Temple (ibid., 15); and the Hebrews relate that he, terrified by Rabshakeh's threats, surrendered to the Assyrians and betrayed the lower part of Jerusalem to the enemy, so that, apart from the citadel of Zion and the Temple, nothing else remained that the Assyrian did not hold. Hence those err who think that the Shebna who now goes out with Eliakim and Joah to Rabshakeh is the same as the one above. For there Shebna is set down as overseer of the Temple, who is said to be destined for capture by the Assyrians; but here Shebna is a scribe, that is, γραμματεὶς, which in Hebrew is called SOPHER סופר, and he is ὁμώνυμος with the former. As for Rabshakeh, who spoke in the Hebrew tongue, the Jews suppose him to have been a son of the prophet Isaiah, who was himself also a traitor; and that the other son of Isaiah, who was left, was called Jasub, which in our language means left. Others, again, think that he was a Samaritan, and that for this reason he knew the Hebrew speech and blasphemed the Lord so boldly and impiously.
Commentary on Isaiah

Let us then consider the words of Rabshakeh; and first, what he says: You are trusting in this broken staff of reed, in Egypt, is false: for no history relates that Hezekiah sent to the Egyptians and asked for Pharaoh's help. And what he adds: If you answer me, We trust in the Lord our God, is true. But again he joins a lie to the truth: that Hezekiah had taken away His high places and altars. For he had done this not against God but for God, so that, idolatry and the old error being destroyed, he might command God to be worshiped in Jerusalem, where his Temple was; although we read that by a very bad custom the people sacrificed victims to God on the mountains and hills, even when the altar had already been built. And his promising two thousand horses, wishing to show the fewness of the besieged, for which Hezekiah could not furnish riders, does not come from the weakness of the people of the Jews, as if it lacked the skill of riding, but from the observance of the commandments of God, who through Moses had commanded concerning the king of Israel: He shall not multiply horses for himself, and he shall not have very many wives (Deut 17:16, 17). But if, he says, you cannot withstand me, the servant of Sennacherib, who am the least of his servants, how will you withstand the so great might of the king? And to what he had said, If you answer me, We trust in the Lord God, he replied cunningly and shrewdly that he had come not by his own will but by the Lord's commands: The Lord said to me: Go up against this land and destroy it. And the argument is: certainly I could not have come here without the Lord's will. But since I have come and taken many cities, and only part of Jerusalem remains untouched, it is clear that I came by his will.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Of a reed staff of this kind Rabshakeh too vainly reproaches Hezekiah king of Judah, saying: Behold, trusting in this reed rod, and a broken one, upon Egypt; whoever leans on it, it goes into his hand: so is Pharaoh king of Egypt and all who trust in him; and he indeed was lying about a righteous king in recalling these things — he who is interpreted as 'much with a kiss': for he was drunk from the golden cup of Babylon, and therefore he was thrusting his own things upon the people, while it was confessing the Lord —; here, however, Pharaoh is reproached for having been to the house of Israel a rod or reed staff, promising them help that was vain and fragile and soon to be shattered.
Commentary on Isaiah

And Eliakim and Shebna and Joah said to Rabshakeh: Speak to your servants in the Syrian tongue, for we understand it: do not speak to us in the Jewish tongue in the ears of the people who are on the wall. And Rabshakeh said to them: Has my lord sent me to your lord and to you to speak all these words, and not rather to the men who sit on the wall, that they may eat their own dung and drink the urine of their feet with you? And Rabshakeh stood and cried out with a loud voice in the Jewish tongue, and said: Hear the words of the great king, the king of the Assyrians. Thus says the king: Let not Hezekiah deceive you, for he will not be able to rescue you; and let not Hezekiah give you confidence in the Lord, saying: The Lord will surely deliver us; this city will not be given into the hand of the king of the Assyrians. Do not listen to Hezekiah. For thus says the king of the Assyrians. The accusation of Rabshakeh is a testimony to Hezekiah: that when all the cities of Judea had been taken he trusted in the Lord and said to the people: Do not fear, nor be afraid of the king of the Assyrians and of all the multitude that is with him; for there are many more with us than with him. With him is an arm of flesh; with us is the Lord our God, who is our helper and fights for us. And the people, it says, were strengthened by such words of Hezekiah king of Judah. Hence Rabshakeh wishes to destroy what the other had built up, and he speaks to the people: Let not Hezekiah deceive you; and let him not give you confidence in the Lord God. And the humble entreaty of Eliakim and Shebna and Joah, Speak to your servants in the Syrian tongue, for we understand it; and do not speak to us in the Jewish tongue in the ears of the people who are on the wall, has this sense: What need is there for the people to be stirred by false terrors, and for you to boast of a vain strength? Speak a language which the people do not understand. For we have knowledge of your language, and we know the Syrian speech, which is common to both. To which Rabshakeh arrogantly: Has, he says, my lord sent me to your lord and to you, and not rather to the men who sit on the wall? And again, increasing the terror with a threat, that they may eat, he says, their own dung, and drink the urine of their feet with you? By this he shows that they will be taken by hunger and want and thirst. And at the same time he joins enticement to fear, so that those whom he had not conquered by terror he might deceive by promises and persuasion, saying, in the words of the king of the Assyrians:

In order then that both our houses may be continually open to the one, and our ears to the others, let us purge away the filth from the ears of our soul. For as filth and mud close up the ears of our flesh, so do the harlot's songs, and worldly news, and debts, and the business of usury and loans, close up the ear of the mind, worse than any filth; nay rather, they do not close it up only, but also make it unclean. And they are putting dung in your ears, who tell you of these things.
