Commentary on Isaiah

Make a blessing with me, and come out to me, and eat each one of his vine, and each one of his fig tree, and drink each one the water of his cistern: until I come and take you away to a land that is like your land: a land of grain and wine, a land of bread and vineyards. Let not Hezekiah trouble you, saying: The Lord will deliver us. Have the gods of the nations delivered each one his land from the hand of the king of the Assyrians? For which in the volume of Kings one reads: Do with me what is profitable, and come out to me (2 Kgs 18:31). So the sense is the same. Do, he says, what may benefit you and turn to your blessing. Or he says this: Bless the Assyrian king and praise him, and confess him your lord, so that you may obtain rewards; and until I return from Egypt, or, having taken Libnah, come back, dwell in your city and enjoy your goods. But afterward I will come and transfer you to a land which is like your land, of grain, wine and olives. And he does not say the name of the region, because he could not find one equal to the land of promise; but he promises a likeness. For this is what each one desires: the land in which he was born. Some think that Media was promised them, which had a likeness to the land of Judea both in situation and in its crops. And what he adds:
Commentary on Isaiah

Where is the God of Hamath and Arpad? Where is the God of Sepharvaim? Have they delivered Samaria out of my hand? Who is there among all the gods of these lands that has rescued his land out of my hand, that the Lord should rescue Jerusalem out of my hand? And they were silent and answered him not a word. For the king had commanded them, saying: Do not answer him. This shows that Samaria served all these gods, and was taken for that reason. But if, he says, with so many gods presiding, we easily overcame the ten tribes, how much more easily shall we conquer you, nay, Jerusalem alone, with one God as its guardian?
Commentary on Isaiah

And all the people kept silent and answered him nothing; for they had received the king's command not to answer him. Truly righteous was Hezekiah, doing all things faithfully and everything with counsel. And he had commanded that the blaspheming Assyrian not be answered for this reason: lest he provoke him to greater blasphemies. Hence it is written: Do not kindle the coals of the sinner (Sir 8:13); and in the psalm we read: When the sinner stood against me, I was dumb, and was humbled, and kept silent from good things (Ps 38 [39]:2-3); and again: Set, O Lord, a guard to my mouth, and a fortified door to my lips: incline not my heart to words of malice (Ps 140 [141]:3).
Commentary on Isaiah

And Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was over the house, and Shebna the scribe, and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder, came in to Hezekiah with their garments torn, and reported to him the words of Rabshakeh. And it came to pass, when king Hezekiah had heard, he tore his garments, and was covered with sackcloth, and went into the house of God. And he sent Eliakim, who was over the house, and Shebna the scribe, and the elders of the priests covered with sackcloth, to Isaiah, the son of the prophet Amos, and they said to him: Thus says Hezekiah: This day is a day of tribulation and of rebuke and of blasphemy, for the children have come to the birth, and there is no strength to bring forth. If by any means the Lord your God may hear the words of Rabshakeh, whom the king of the Assyrians his master sent to blaspheme the living God and to reproach him with words which the Lord your God has heard. Lift up therefore a prayer for the remnant that is found. And the servants of king Hezekiah came to Isaiah; and Isaiah said to them: Thus shall you say to your master: Thus says the Lord: Do not be afraid before the words that you have heard, with which the servants of the king of the Assyrians have blasphemed me. Behold, I will give him a spirit, and he shall hear a report, and shall return to his own land, and I will make him fall by the sword in his own land. Leaving aside what is plain, let us discuss only those things in which a hidden sense lies. They tear their garments because they hear Rabshakeh blaspheming. The king himself also tears his garments, because he believed it was owing to his own sins and the people's that Rabshakeh had come up to the gate of Jerusalem and had spoken such things against the Lord. Hence the high priest, because he believed the Savior had blasphemed, tore his garments (Matt 26); and Paul and Barnabas, when the Lycaonians offered them the worship due to God, tore their garments (Acts 14). In place of royal attire, then, he was covered with sackcloth; and going from the palace to the Temple, he sent Eliakim the high priest, and Shebna the scribe, and the elders of the priests to Isaiah, the son of the prophet Amos. In this the humility and prudence of the king is to be considered. He himself goes to the Temple; the princes of the people and the elders of the priests, covered not with priestly stoles but with haircloth, he sent to Isaiah, the son of the prophet Amos. For which in the volume of Kings one reads: He himself was covered with sackcloth and entered the house of the Lord, and he sent Eliakim the overseer of the house, and Shebna the scribe, and the elders of the priests covered with sackcloth, to Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amos (2 Kgs 19:1, 2). Here, because Isaiah was writing the history about himself, he did not call himself a Prophet but the son of a Prophet; there, however, because the writer of the history was another, he writes that he himself was a Prophet. This we read also of Matthew the Evangelist: that Matthew himself called himself a publican (Matt 9), while the other Evangelists were silent about the name of publican and set down only the apostolic dignity; and that in the pairings of the Apostles he is second in his own list and first in the others'.

n: Sackcloth. Emblems of repentance. Sennacherib's boasting (ver. 13.) was chastised, ver. 36. (Worthington)
Spirit. Angel, or a different design, 2 Thessalonians ii. 8. (Calmet)
Lands. Hebrew, "all the lands and their land." The parallel text is more correct, "the nations and their land." (Kennicott)
Carmel. See 4 Kings xix. (Challoner)
Shut, &c. Hebrew matsor, (Haydock) "of Egypt," where Sennacherib had been. (Calmet)
Lips, and treat thee like some ungovernable beast. (Haydock) (Ezechiel xxix. 4., and xxxviii. 4.) (Calmet)
Thee. He directeth his speech to Ezechias.

Servant. Hence it plainly appears that God protects the living for the sake of the saints departed. To evade this proof, Protestants (Bible 1603) explain, "for God's promise sake made to David." But God never made any such promise to him; otherwise the city would never have been destroyed. (Worthington)
They. The people of Jerusalem, or rather the soldiers of Ezechias, who saw those who had been slain, near Pelusium. (Calmet)

f: Commentary on Isaiah

And they said, it says, to him: Thus says Hezekiah, not 'the king', not swelling with the title of empire: This day is a day of tribulation and of rebuke and of blasphemy: of our tribulation, of God's rebuke, of the enemies' blasphemy. And he sets down the likeness of a woman in labor and in pain, who has come up to the birth and cannot bring forth, nor say: From fear of you, O Lord, we have conceived, and have been in pain, and have brought forth the spirit of salvation.
Commentary on Isaiah

There follows: If by any means the Lord your God may hear the words of Rabshakeh (Isa 26:18 LXX). For we do not dare to call the Lord of all our Lord, since through his anger we suffer so much; but we call him your Lord. And we have this confidence of vengeance: that the living God is blasphemed by a worshiper of dead idols. And they have reproached with words which the Lord your God has heard. Lift up therefore a prayer, our prayer, which lies prostrate: not for the whole people, which has already perished, but for the remnant, which is besieged.
Commentary on Isaiah

And when the servants of king Hezekiah had come to Isaiah: again he was silent about the name of Prophet, in order to keep the humility he had begun. And Isaiah anticipated them: for by the same spirit by which he knew things to come, he had heard the king too, though absent; and he tells them what they should answer to their master, humbled in this confidence of conscience. Say, he says, to your master, who is your lord; for my Lord says this: Do not fear the words with which not you but I have been blasphemed. Nor do I tell all that I am going to do to the king of the Assyrians, lest I seem to boast of my power; but only that a spirit is to be given him, not of God but an adverse one. And having heard a report, let him return to his own land and fall in it by the sword: so that Hezekiah might hear both things he desired together, that he was to be freed from siege and danger, and that the hostile and angry king would die in his own land. If anyone asks why in a book of Prophecy the history written in the volumes of Kings and Chronicles seems to be mixed in, let him consider that prophecy is coupled with the history, as much concerning the liberation of the city as concerning the destruction of the Assyrian, and the turning back of the sun by ten hours, and the prolonging of life by a space of fifteen years, which belongs both to prophecy and to history.
Commentary on Isaiah

And Rabshakeh returned and found the king of the Assyrians fighting against Libnah: for he had heard that he had departed from Lachish. And he heard concerning Tirhakah king of Ethiopia, people saying: He has come out to fight against you. And when he heard it, he sent messengers to Hezekiah, saying: Thus shall you say to Hezekiah king of Judah, speaking: Let not your God, in whom you trust, deceive you, saying: Jerusalem will not be given into the hand of the king of the Assyrians. Behold, you have heard all that the kings of the Assyrians have done to all the lands which they overthrew, and will you be able to be delivered? Have the gods of the nations rescued them, whom my fathers overthrew, Gozan and Haran, and Rezeph, and the sons of Eden who were in Telassar? Where is the king of Hamath, and the king of Arpad, and the king of the city of Sepharvaim, Ana and Ava? In the same words and with the same sense it is written in the volume of Kings and of Chronicles that Rabshakeh, according to the will of the Lord, abandoned the siege of Jerusalem and went on to his master, who, as he had learned, was going to attack Libnah, Lachish having been either abandoned or taken. Sennacherib himself too, hearing that Tirhakah king of the Ethiopians was bringing war against him, went to meet him as he came, and nonetheless sends messengers and letters to Hezekiah, so that those whom he had not yet taken by force he might terrify by words. And just as he had said to the people, Let not Hezekiah deceive you (2 Kgs 18:29), so he speaks the same blasphemy to the king: Let not your God deceive you (2 Kgs 19:10). And he sets out the examples of his forefathers: that just as their gods could not deliver the other lands out of their hands, so neither would Jerusalem be delivered.
Commentary on Isaiah

We pass quickly over the plain things in order to dwell on the doubtful ones. That Sennacherib king of the Assyrians fought against the Egyptians and besieged Pelusium, and that, when the mounds had already been built to take the city, Tirhakah king of the Ethiopians came to its help, and that in one night near Jerusalem one hundred and eighty-five thousand of the Assyrian army fell by pestilence, is related by Herodotus, and most fully by Berosus, the writer of Chaldean history, whose credibility must be sought from their own books.
Commentary on Isaiah

In the enumeration of the other nations he sets down ANA (הנע) and AVA (ועוה), which the Seventy ran together, saying anavegava; and the conjunction and, that is, vau, between the two nations Ana and Ava, they set down in the Hebrew tongue, so that to the ignorant it seems one nation or city.
Commentary on Isaiah

And Hezekiah took the books from the hand of the messengers and read them; and he went up into the house of the Lord and spread them out before the Lord, and prayed to the Lord, saying: O Lord of hosts, God of Israel, who sit upon the Cherubim, you alone are God of all the kingdoms of the earth: for you made heaven and earth. Incline, O Lord, your ear and hear; open, O Lord, your eyes and see, and hear all the words of Sennacherib which he sent to blaspheme the living God. For truly, O Lord, the kings of the Assyrians have made desolate the lands and their regions, and have given their gods to the fire: for they were not gods, but works of men's hands, wood and stones; and they broke them in pieces. And now, O Lord our God, save us from his hand, and let all the kingdoms of the earth know that you alone are God. Against the blasphemies of king Sennacherib Hezekiah seized his accustomed weapons. And again he goes to the Temple and spreads out his letters before the Lord. Before, he had been silent: for, terrified by fear of the Lord, he did not dare to open his mouth in the Temple or to pour out free prayers to God. But now, because he had already heard Isaiah saying: Do not be afraid before the words that you have heard, with which the servants of the king of the Assyrians have blasphemed me, and the rest, he boldly entreats the Lord and asserts that God alone is living; whereas the idols we understand as images of the dead.
Commentary on Isaiah

And what he adds: For truly, O Lord, the kings of the Assyrians have made desolate the lands and their regions, and have given their gods to the fire: for they were not gods, but works of men's hands, wood and stones; and they broke them in pieces, is proved by many histories, which write that the kings of the Persians came into Greece and overthrew and plundered the temples of the Greeks.
Commentary on Isaiah
And he asks for vengeance, so that through his occasion all kingdoms may know that he alone is God, who can deliver his own from danger.
Commentary on Isaiah

And Isaiah son of Amos sent to Hezekiah, saying: Thus says the Lord God of Israel: As to what you have asked me concerning Sennacherib king of the Assyrians, this is the word which the Lord has spoken concerning him: The virgin daughter of Zion has despised you and mocked you; behind you the daughter of Jerusalem has shaken her head. Whom have you reproached, and whom have you blasphemed, and against whom have you raised your voice and lifted up the height of your eyes? Against the Holy One of Israel? By the hand of your servants you have reproached the Lord and have said: With the multitude of my chariots I have gone up to the height of the mountains, the ridges of Lebanon, and I will cut down its lofty cedars and its choice fir trees, and I will enter the height of its summit, the forest of its Carmel. I dug, and drank water, and dried up with the sole of my foot all the streams of the embankments. Because Hezekiah had entreated the Lord so boldly and did not send to Isaiah as he had sent before, the Prophet himself does not go to him, but sends messengers to tell him in the words of God: Concerning Sennacherib, against whom you pray, this is the Lord's sentence: The virgin of Zion and daughter of Jerusalem (who is called virgin and daughter for this reason, that while all the nations worship the images of dead men, she alone preserves the chastity of the religion of God and the worship of the one Godhead) has mocked you and despised you; and she who, lest she provoke you to greater blasphemy, had not answered you when you were present, has shaken her head behind you as you go away, sure of vengeance, secure about punishment.
Commentary on Isaiah

And she has said this: Not against me, but against the Lord you have been proud; and not you yourself, but through your servants, so that the arrogance of the blasphemer might be the greater. For you said that with the multitude of your chariots you would climb the height of the mountains and the ridges of Lebanon, and cut down its lofty cedars and fir trees. This we ought to take either μεταφορικῶς of all the nations and their princes, or of Jerusalem, which is what Lebanon means, so that we refer its cedars and firs to all its powerful and noble men, and the height of its summit and the forest of Carmel to the Temple. For he himself had said above: Have you not heard what the kings of the Assyrians have done to all the lands which they overthrew? Therefore neither will you be able to be delivered.
Commentary on Isaiah

And what he adds: I dug and drank water, and dried up with the sole of my foot all the streams of the embankments, can be understood according to the history: that because of the multitude of his army he dried up all the streams, so that he was compelled to dig wells for himself; according to the metaphor: that he laid waste with his army all the peoples, who are sometimes described under the name of waters. For which the Seventy alone translated: and I have set a bridge, and I have made desolate the waters, and every gathering of waters: that is, that no nation was impassable to him, but he trod with his foot upon all the waters of the peoples.
Commentary on Isaiah

Have you not heard what I did to it long ago? From the days of old I formed it, and now I have brought them, and it has come to be for the uprooting of the hills that fight together, and of fortified cities. Their inhabitants, with shortened hand, trembled and were confounded: they became like the hay of the field, and the grass of the pasture, and the herb of the housetops, which withered before it ripened. Your dwelling, and your going out, and your coming in I have known, and your madness against me, when you raged against me. Your pride has come up into my ears; I will therefore put a ring in your nostrils, and a bridle in your lips, and I will lead you back by the way by which you came. These things are to be understood as spoken in the person of God against the words of the Assyrian: that the Lord answered his blasphemy thus: Do you not know that these things which you have done, you did by my will, and that I foretold them as to come, and commanded that they be done through you? So what I decreed long ago has been fulfilled in its time: that the hills, that is, the princes who formerly fought among themselves, and the most fortified cities, when I drew back my hand and did not furnish my accustomed help, should be uprooted and tremble and perish, and be compared not to the olive and the vine and fruitful trees, but to hay and grass and the herbs of the housetops, which are a hindrance to the crops and wither before they come to maturity.
Commentary on Isaiah

So I knew beforehand your sitting, and your going out, and your coming in, and I spoke of the madness with which you were going to rage against me, through the Prophets as they prophesied (above, on Isa 14:13): through whom I had long ago known that you would say: I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will set my throne, and I will be like the Most High.
Commentary on Isaiah

So your fury and your pride have reached my ears, and I will by no means bear with you any longer, so that you may understand that what you were able to do, you were able to do not by your own strength but by my decision. For the impious nations and the unfruitful trees deserved to be cut down and to fall through you, as through my axe and saw. So I will put a ring, or a muzzle, in your nostrils, to bind fast your blaspheming mouth, so that you may by no means dare to speak such things any more; and I will put a bridle on your lips, to tame your ferocity and lead you back to the Assyrians. This figure Scripture also uses in the Psalms against the impious: With bridle and muzzle bind fast the jaws of those who do not draw near to you (Ps 31 [32]:9).
Commentary on Isaiah

But this shall be a sign to you: Eat this year what springs up of itself, and in the second year feed on fruits; but in the third year sow and reap, and plant vineyards, and eat their fruit. And what has been saved of the house of Judah, and what is left, shall send down root downward and bear fruit upward: for out of Jerusalem shall go forth a remnant, and salvation from mount Zion. The zeal of the Lord of hosts shall do this. All these things the Prophet speaks to Hezekiah through messengers: what Sennacherib said, what the Lord answered him. Now he addresses his speech to the king himself, lest perhaps he doubt that the things spoken will come. And it was for this reason above all that the Prophets had credit for their words among the people: because they told not only of things that were to come many ages later, but also of things to be fulfilled at once and after no great space of time; and that within two years both the Assyrian king would perish and security would be restored to the city of Jerusalem. This, he says, will be the sign of the things to come that I foretell: that this year you will eat what springs up of itself; or, according to the Seventy, what you sowed before. And in the second year, according to Symmachus, feed on fruits; or, according to the same Seventy, on what has sprouted from the former crops and from seed falling to the ground. But in the third year, the Assyrian now put to flight and the siege lifted, sow and reap, and plant vineyards, and eat their fruits.
Commentary on Isaiah

For the remnant of this small city, which is now walled in by a hostile army and does not believe it will escape, will receive such abundance and happiness in all things that, like a tree founded on a deep root, they will be filled with the thickest fruits. For out of Jerusalem and out of mount Zion a remnant shall go forth and fill the land of Judea, not by its own merit but by the mercy of God, nay by the zeal with which he was jealous for his people against the impious.
Commentary on Isaiah

Therefore thus says the Lord concerning the king of the Assyrians: He shall not enter this city, and he shall not shoot an arrow there, nor shall a shield seize it, and he shall not cast up a mound around it. By the way by which he shall come, by it he shall return, and he shall not enter this city, says the Lord; and I will protect this city and save it for my own sake and for the sake of David my servant. He returns to his subject, and after the hope of things to come he shakes off the present fear. For there was not as much gladness over the things he had promised would come long afterward as there was anxiety about those that were imminent. And when he says that the Assyrian will withdraw, and will not raise a shield against Jerusalem nor shoot darts, nor is the city to be walled in with siege works and a mound, and that the adversary will return by the way he came, and the city will be freed from the present siege, and at the end adds: for my own sake and for the sake of David my servant, this signifies that they are preserved not by their own merit but by God's clemency, nay by the memory of their father David. In this they are reminded both of their own negligence and of his faith and righteousness: that God so loves righteousness that he protects even the descendants of holy men, not by their own merit but by the virtue of their forefathers.
Commentary on Isaiah

And the Angel of God went out and struck in the camp of the Assyrians one hundred and eighty-five thousand; and they arose in the morning, and behold, all were corpses of the dead. And Sennacherib king of the Assyrians went out and departed and returned, and dwelt in Nineveh. And it came to pass, while he was worshiping in the temple of Nisroch his god, Adrammelech and Sharezer his sons struck him with the sword; and they fled into the land of Ararat; and Esarhaddon his son reigned in his place. One hundred and eighty-five thousand of the bravest men are slain by one Angel in one night, and without wounds on the slain a cruel death runs through them, driving the souls out of the bodies by the will of God. Concerning which one reads in Chronicles: And the Lord sent an Angel, who struck every strong man and warrior and the commander of the army of the king of the Assyrians; and he returned with disgrace to his own land (2 Chr 32:21). He was preserved for this reason, that he might know the power of God and restrain his blaspheming mouth, and become a witness of that majesty which a little before he had despised. As for what he added, And they arose in the morning, let us take it either of the Israelites or of the rest of his army: although it is written in the volume of Kings that when the king himself had risen at daybreak, he saw all the bodies of the dead (2 Kgs 19).
Commentary on Isaiah

Pharaoh too is preserved through the ten plagues of Egypt, so as to perish last: which this man also suffered. For when he had returned to Nineveh, the chief city of his kingdom, and was worshiping in the temple of Nisroch his god, as though bringing back a victory over his enemies, and was entering the shrine of his idol triumphant and giving thanks, the despiser of the true God is slaughtered in the sanctuary of a false deity: and he perishes not by the Angel's sword, which would have been a fate shared with many, but by the parricide of his sons. And when they had fled into the land of Ararat, which is understood as Armenia, Esarhaddon succeeded to his father's place, who, as Scripture testifies, sent inhabitants to Samaria, so that the land should not remain uncultivated. Ararat is a level region in Armenia, through which the Araxes flows, of incredible fertility, at the roots of mount Taurus, which extends as far as there. So the Ark too, in which Noah was delivered with his children when the Flood ceased, was carried not to the mountains of Armenia in general, which is called Ararat, but to the highest mountains of Taurus, which overhang the plains of Ararat.

n: Ezechias. Sanchez groundlessly thinks it was composed by Isaias. (Calmet) --- Ezechias was afflicted lest he should give way to dangerous joy. (Worthington)

Hell. Sheol, or Hades, the region of the dead. (Challoner) --- He was afraid to die without issue. (St. Jerome; ver. 12.) --- Manasses was born three years later. (Calmet) --- The king would naturally have died. (St. Augustine, de Gen. ad lit. vi. 17.) (Worthington)
Living. I shall not assist at the festivals of the Lord in the temple.
For me. He represents his disease, as an inexorable creditor.
Truth. He speaks only of the body.

Lord. The answer is given, (4 Kings xx. 9.) which seems to evince that this is only an extract. (Calmet) --- The prophet prescribed the medicine, and the king asked for a sign before he sung the canticle. (Worthington)

f: St. Jerome, Commentary on Daniel, CHAPTER FOUR

[Daniel 4:27] "'Wherefore, O king, let my counsel meet with thy favor, and make up for thy sins by deeds of charity, and thine iniquities by showing mercy to the poor. Perhaps God will forgive thy transgressions.'" Since he had previously pronounced the sentence of God, which of course cannot be altered, how could he exhort the king to deeds of charity and acts of mercy towards the poor? This difficulty is easily solved by reference to the example of King Hezekiah, who Isaiah had said was going to die (Isaiah 38:1); and again, to the example of the Ninevites, to whom it was said: "Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be destroyed" (Jonah 3:4). And yet the sentence of God was changed in response to the prayers of Hezekiah and the city of Nineveh, not by any means because of the ineffectualness of the judgment itself but because of the conversion of those who merited pardon. Morever in Jeremiah God states that He threatens evil for the nation (Jeremiah 18:7-8), but if it does that which is good, He will alter His threats to bestow mercy. Again, He affirms that He directs His promises to the man who does good; and if the same man thereafter works evil, He says that He changes His decision, not with regard to the men themselves, but with regard to their works which have thus changed in character. For after all, God is not angered at men but at their sins; and when no sins inhere in a man, God by no means inflicts a punishment which has been commuted. In other words, let us say that Nebuchadnezzar performed deeds of mercy toward the poor in accordance with Daniel's advice, and for that reason the sentence against him was delayed of execution for twelve months. But because he afterwards while walking about in his palace at Babylon said boastingly: "Is this not the great Babylon which I myself have built up as a home for the king by the might of my power and the glory of my name?" therefore he lost the virtue of his charitableness by reason of the wickedness of his pride.

"It may be that God will forgive thy sins." In view of the fact that the blessed Daniel, foreknowing the future as he did, had doubts concerning God's decision, it is very rash on the part of those who boldly promise pardon to sinners. And yet it should be recognized that indulgence was promised to Nebuchadnezzar in return, as long as he wrought good works. Much more, then, is it promised to other men who have committed less grievous sins than he. We read in Jeremiah also of God's direction to the people of the Jews, that they should pray for the Babylonians, inasmuch as the peace of the captives was bound up with the peace of the captors themselves (Jeremiah 29:7).
Commentary on Isaiah

In those days Hezekiah was sick unto death; and Isaiah son of Amos, the Prophet, came in to him and said to him: Thus says the Lord: Set your house in order, for you shall die and not live. And Hezekiah turned his face to the wall, and prayed to the Lord, and said: I beseech you, O Lord, remember, I pray, how I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart, and have done what is good in your eyes: and Hezekiah wept with a great weeping. Whom the Lord loves he rebukes, and he chastises every son whom he receives (Prov 3). Lest the heart of Hezekiah be lifted up after his incredible triumphs and the victory won out of the midst of captivity, he is visited with infirmity of body and hears that he is going to die, so that, turning to the Lord, he may bend his sentence. This indeed we read also in the prophet Jonah, and in the threats against David, which are said to be coming and were not done: not because God changes his sentence, but because he calls mankind to the knowledge of himself. For the Lord repents over evils.
Commentary on Isaiah

And Hezekiah turned his face to the wall because he could not go to the Temple: to the wall of the Temple, that is, next to which Solomon had built the palace. Or simply to the wall, lest he seem to display his tears to those sitting by. Or certainly, according to Jeremiah, to his heart; who calls CIR (קיר), that is, wall, the heart: so that he entreated the Lord with his whole mind.
Catechetical Lecture 2:15

Do you want to know the power of repentance? Do you want to understand this strong weapon of salvation and the might of confession? By confession Hezekiah routed 185,000 of the enemy. That was important, but it was small compared with what else happened. The same king's repentance won the repeal the sentence God had passed on him. When he was sick, Isaiah had said, "Give direction for your household, for you will surely die, and not live." What expectation was left? What hope of recovery was there? The prophet had said, "You will surely die." But Hezekiah remembered what was written: "In the hour that you turn and lament, you will be saved." He turned his face to the wall, and from his bed of pain his mind soared up to heaven (for no wall is so thick as to stifle fervent prayer). He said, "Lord, remember me." … He whom the prophet's sentence had forbidden to hope was granted fifteen further years of life, the sun turning back its course as a witness.
Commentary on Isaiah

And he says: I beseech you, O Lord, remember, I pray, how I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart, and have done what is good in your eyes. And hearing that he is going to die, he does not pray for life and many years, but leaves to God's judgment what he wishes to grant. For he knew that Solomon had pleased God for this reason, that he did not ask for more years of life; but as one about to go to the Lord, he recounts his works, how he walked before him in truth and with a perfect heart. Happy the conscience that in time of affliction remembers its good works: For blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God (Matt 5:8). And what of its being written elsewhere: Who shall boast that he has a pure heart (Prov 20:9)? This is solved thus: perfection of heart is ascribed to him here because he destroyed the idols, overturned the vessels of the temple of Baal, broke the bronze serpent in pieces, and did the other things which Scripture records. And he wept with a great weeping because of the Lord's promise to David, which he saw would perish in his death. For at that time Hezekiah had no sons; for after his death Manasseh began to reign in Judea when he was twelve years old. From which it is clear that Manasseh was begotten after the third year of the life granted to him. So all this weeping is because he despaired that the Christ would be born of his seed. Others assert that even holy men are terrified by death, because of the uncertainty of judgment and their ignorance of God's sentence as to what abode they will have. And at the same time the question of fate is solved, and of the chains of necessity and of causes: that the day of death is by no means fixed beforehand for each person, but that by the will of God and by causes unknown to mortals one either lives or dies; especially since the necessity of death, once set, is here postponed, and we have read that very many were raised up after death.
Commentary on Isaiah

And the word of the Lord came to Isaiah, saying: Go and say to Hezekiah: Thus says the Lord, the God of David your father: I have heard your prayer, I have seen your tears. Behold, I will add to your days fifteen years, and I will deliver you and this city out of the hand of the king of the Assyrians, and I will protect it. And this shall be a sign to you from the Lord, that the Lord will do this word which he has spoken: Behold, I will make the shadow of the lines, by which it had gone down on the dial of Ahaz in the sun, go back ten lines: and the sun went back ten lines by the steps by which it had gone down. Here, as in a prophecy, the history is related in reversed order, which in the volume of Kings is read in better sequence. While Hezekiah was weeping with a great weeping, before Isaiah had gone out of the middle part of the court, the word of the Lord came to him, saying: Go back and say to Hezekiah, the leader of my people: I have heard your prayer and seen your tear: Behold, I have healed you. And Hezekiah said to Isaiah: What will be the sign that the Lord will heal me (2 Kgs 20:4 and 5)? To him the Prophet answered: This shall be the sign from the Lord that the Lord will do the word which he has spoken: Do you wish the shadow to advance so many lines, or to go back as many steps? And Hezekiah said to him: It is easy for the shadow to increase by ten lines, and I do not wish this to be done; but that it go back ten steps. And when, at Isaiah's calling upon the power of the Lord, the sign had been accomplished, Isaiah commanded that a lump of fresh figs be brought: and when they had brought it and laid it upon his wound, he was cured. The Prophet returns to the king at the Lord's command, so that he who had struck might himself heal; and Hezekiah is called the leader of his people, and son of David, whose works he followed, for he had done what was right according to all that David his father did: and his prayer is heard and his tears are seen, because he had walked before the Lord in truth and with a perfect heart, and had wept with a great weeping, and had done what was pleasing in his eyes. Fifteen years are added to his life, which he had not asked for, and besides, the security of the kingdom during his lifetime is promised. But if, as some think, to live in the body is a condemnation, and, according to what is said: Return, my soul, to your rest (Ps 114 [116]:7), and in another place: Bring my soul out of prison (Ps 141 [142]:8), death is to be desired, that we may be freed from prison: how does the Lord now grant it as a benefit that one who was about to be freed should live yet fifteen years in prison?
Hippolytus Exegetical Fragments

When Hezekiah, king of Judah, was still sick and weeping, there came an angel, and said to him: "I have seen thy tears, and I have heard thy voice. Behold, I add unto thy time fifteen years. And this shall be a sign to thee from the Lord: Behold, I turn back the shadow of the degrees of the house of thy father, by which the sun has gone down, the ten degrees by which the shadow has gone down," so that day be a day of thirty-two hours. For when the sun had run its course to the tenth hour, it returned again. And again, when Joshua the son of Nun was fighting against the Amorites, when the sun was now inclining to its setting, and the battle was being pressed closely, Joshua, being anxious lest the heathen host should escape on the descent of night, cried out, saying, "Sun, stand thou still in Gibeon; and thou moon, in the valley of Ajalon," until I vanquish this people. And the sun stood still, and the moon, in their places, so that day was one of twenty-four hours. And in the time of Hezekiah the moon also turned back along with the sun, that there might be no collision between the two elemental bodies, by their bearing against each other in defiance of law. And Merodach the Chaldean, king of Babylon, being struck with amazement at that time-for he studied the science of astrology, and measured the courses of these bodies carefully-on learning the cause, sent a letter and gifts to Hezekiah, just as also the wise men from the east did to Christ.
Commentary on Isaiah

And a sign is given, that the sun should go back ten steps, which we, following Symmachus, have rendered as lines and dial; for he understood the steps as lines, to make the sense clearer to readers. Or else the steps had been built by mechanical art in such a way that the shadow, descending through each one, marked off the spaces of the hours. This sign was a type both of the present time and of the future: that as the sun went back to its beginning, so Hezekiah's life too returned to years already unwoven; and that for us, who live in the hebdomad and the ogdoad, the spaces of life are prolonged through the resurrection of Christ. The guides to the holy Places in this province are accustomed to show, within the enclosure of the Temple, the steps of the house of Hezekiah, or of Ahaz, down which the sun descended. But I will never believe that the house, I do not say of Ahaz, who was an impious king, but of any righteous king whatever, was in the Temple of God: since Solomon is said, among other things, to have offended God for this reason, that he built Millo on high, from which, walking in the tower of his palace, he used to look down on the court of the Temple (1 Kgs 9).
Hippolytus Exegetical Fragments

We find in the commentaries, written by our predecessors, that day had thirty-two hours. For when the sun had run its course, and reached the tenth hour, and the shadow had gone down by the ten degrees in the house of the temple, the sun turned back again by the ten degrees, according to the word of the Lord, and there were thus twenty hours. And again, the sun accomplished its own proper course, according to the common law, and reached its setting. And thus there were thirty-two hours.
Catechetical Lecture 2:15

For Hezekiah's sake the sun turned back, but for Christ the sun was eclipsed. The sun did not simply retrace its path for Christ but was completely eclipsed. This shows the difference between Hezekiah and Jesus. The former's prayer resulted in the canceling of God's decree. But does not Jesus forgive sins? Repent, shut your door, and pray to be forgiven. Pray that Christ may remove you from the burning flames, for confession has power even to quench fire, power even to tame lions.
Commentary on Isaiah

The writing of Hezekiah king of Judah, when he had been sick and had recovered from his infirmity. LXX: The prayer of Hezekiah king of Judah, when he was sick and rose up from his infirmity. I wonder how the Seventy alone put prayer for writing, since prayer is called THEPHELLATH (תפלת), and not MACHTHAB (מכתב), which is what is written in the present place; otherwise prayer would fittingly be said if it concerned the present time and not the past. For it is clear that after his health was restored, rising from his infirmity, he wrote these things down; from which it follows that it is not a prayer but a thanksgiving for the benefit he had received.
Commentary on Isaiah

I said: In the half of my days I shall go to the gates of hell: I sought the remainder of my years. I said: I shall not see the Lord God in the land of the living: I shall not behold man any more, and the dweller of rest. My generation has ceased: it is taken away and rolled up from me like a shepherds' tent. My life is cut off as by a weaver: while I was yet beginning, he cut me off: from morning to evening you will make an end of me. I hoped until morning: like a lion, so he has broken all my bones. From morning to evening you will make an end of me. LXX: I said: In the height of my days I shall go to the gates of hell: I will leave the remaining years. I said: I shall by no means any more see the salvation of God in the land of the living, nor shall I see man any more with the inhabitants: I have failed from my kindred. It has gone out and departed from me, as one takes down a tent who had pitched it: like a web my spirit has departed, when it is cut off by the weaver. In that day I was given up until morning: like a lion, so he has broken all my bones. From day to night I was given up. He relates what he thought silently in the time of pressing distress and imminent sickness. I said, he says, in my heart, in the half of my days, or, as Aquila and Symmachus and Theodotion translated, in the infirmity and silence of my days; for which the Seventy translated height, because of the likeness of a letter, reading RAME (רמי) for DAME (דמי): although some have rendered DAME as blood, so that the sense is, In the blood of my days, when my blood and my death were being sought. So in despair I said: I shall go to the gates of hell, either by the common law of nature, or those gates from which the Psalmist sings that he was freed: You who lift me up from the gates of death, that I may announce all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion (Ps 9:15). These I think are the gates of hell which do not prevail against Peter (Matt 16), because he slept in the fullness of his days. The saints fill up their days, as Abraham did, who died full of days in a good old age (Gen 25). But sinners and the impious die in the half of their days, of whom the Psalmist also speaks: Men of blood and deceitful men shall not live out half their days (Ps 54 [55]:25). For they do not fulfill the works of virtue, nor are they eager to amend their faults by penance. Hence in the middle of life's course and in the darkness of their errors they will be led to Tartarus. I sought, he says, the remainder of my years, thinking that he would live no longer.
Commentary on Isaiah

There follows: I shall not behold man any more, and the dweller of rest. This we had formerly joined to the following verse because of the ambiguity of the word; for the Hebrew word HOLED, if it is read or written ELED (חלד), means rest; if EDEL (חדל), it means setting. So he fears that he may not dwell in rest with the saints and the men of God, that he may not see the Lord in the land of the living, that his generation may be dissolved like a tent, that like a web it may be cut off at the very beginning of the light, and that the Christ may by no means arise from his seed. And that our body is called a tent the Apostle too teaches, saying: We who are in this tent groan, being burdened (2 Cor 5:4).
Commentary on Isaiah

I said: I shall not see the Lord, the Lord in the land of the living. For Lord and Lord, IA (יה) is set twice in the Hebrew, which sounds in the last syllable of ALLELUIA (הללויה); for which the Seventy translated: I shall by no means any more see the salvation of God in the land of the living. Of which it is written in another place: I will please the Lord in the region of the living (Ps 114 [116]:9). And again: I will please the Lord in the light of the living (Ps 55 [56]:9). The region of the Saints, then, is the very one that is called the light of the living. For he is not the God of the dead but of the living (Matt 22). And this is all that he fears: that, led down to hell, he may by no means deserve to behold the salvation of God.
Commentary on Isaiah

From morning, he says, to evening you will make an end of me: I hoped until morning: which Job too says he endured in his distress and in the torments of his body (Job 4), when in the day he awaited the night, and in darkness looked for the light, thinking that with the change of the times his torments could change. That this is true he knows who burns with high fevers, whose inner fire, like a lion, consumes all his bones, and who, for the greatness of his pain, does not think he will live any longer.
Commentary on Isaiah

Like the young of a swallow, so will I cry: I will meditate like a dove: my eyes are worn thin looking upward. O Lord, I suffer violence; answer for me: what shall I say, or what will he answer me, since he himself has done it? LXX: Like a swallow, so will I cry; like a dove, so will I meditate. For my eyes have failed with looking to the height of heaven, to the Lord, who has rescued me and taken away the pain of my soul, and he himself has done it. Imminent death and the pressing pain of sickness, like a lion, were breaking all the bones of my body; but I, like the swallow and the dove, joined days and nights with weeping and groaning; and from God alone, who could help, with my eyes lifted on high, I awaited aid. And I said to him: I suffer more than my deserts require; but even if I have erred in anything, I will turn to the better; do you answer for me: For it is not of him who wills nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy (Rom 9:16). And again he turns back into himself: What shall I say, or what shall I plead against you, my maker? Or what will he answer me, who himself has done what he willed? Whatever he has decreed, then, must be endured. For young of a swallow, or swallow, as the Seventy translated, in the Hebrew is written SUS AGOR (סוס עגור), which Aquila translated the horse Agor; Theodotion, SIS AGUR (סיס עגור); for the middle vowel-letter, if vau is put between two Samec, is read sus and means horse; if jod, it is read sis and is called swallow. Symmachus translated thus: Like a shut-in swallow, so will I sing. This word agor is also read in Jeremiah, where it is written: The kite in heaven has known its time: the turtledove and the swallow and the stork have kept their times (Jer 8:7).
Commentary on Isaiah

I will reckon up all my years in the bitterness of my soul. O Lord, if one lives thus, and if in such things is the life of my spirit, you will rebuke me and you will give me life. Behold, in peace my bitterness is most bitter. But you have rescued my soul, that it should not perish: you have cast all my sins behind your back. For hell will not confess to you, nor will death praise you: those who go down into the pit will not await your truth. The living, the living, he will confess to you, as I also do today. The father will make your truth known to the children. O Lord, save me, and we will sing our psalms all the days of our life in the house of the Lord. LXX: O Lord, concerning it, it was announced to you: and you have raised up my spirit, and, having comforted me, you have given me life. Behold, in peace is my bitterness: for you have delivered my soul, that it should not perish, and you have cast all my sins behind me. For in hell they will not praise you, nor will the dead bless you. Nor will those who are in hell hope for your mercy: the living will bless you, as I also do. For from today I will make sons, who will announce your righteousness, O Lord of my salvation, and I will not cease blessing you with the psaltery all the days of my life before the house of God. Nothing belonging to mortals is long-lasting, and all the happiness of the world is lost even while it is held. For when the time of tribulation has come, all that is past is no help to the one who endures it. Hence the foolish opinion of Epicurus, who asserts that present evils are softened by the remembrance of past goods. So Hezekiah says that he reckons up all the years of his reign, and of his past happiness, as he thought it, in his present bitterness.
Commentary on Isaiah

And because he is now secure and no longer suffers what he relates, he philosophizes on the human state and says: O Lord, if one lives thus: if we have been born in such a condition, you have rebuked me, but you have given me life, and you have granted peace, the Assyrian being put to flight; but my peace was more bitter to me than all bitterness, because, when tranquillity was restored to the peoples and the city was secure, I alone entered the threshold of death. But you have rescued my soul, that it should not perish, either for the present life or for the future. For you have cast all my sins behind your back, lest I should look upon them in sadness, but that I might contemplate your mercy.
Commentary on Isaiah

For hell and death will not confess, nor will they praise you, according to what is written: But in hell who will confess to you (Ps 6:6)? And confession in this place is taken not for penance but for glory and praise, as we read also in the Gospel: I will confess to you, O Lord, Father of heaven and earth (Matt 11:25). Those who go down into the pit, he says, will not await your truth: better than mercy in the Seventy. For he who is in hell does not await the truth of judgment but the mercy of God: especially since the Savior descended into hell to free the prisoners from the lower world. For pit the same translators more plainly rendered hell.
Commentary on Isaiah

The living, the living, he will confess to you, as I also do today. Here too confession is put for praise. For he does not confess his crimes, but gives thanks to God: and praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner (Sir 15). And while hell and death do not confess nor praise God, on the contrary life and the living glorify the Lord. And what follows: The father will make your truth known to the children, signifies what is said in Deuteronomy: Ask your father, and he will declare it to you; your elders, and they will tell you (Deut 32:7), so that through the successions and each generation the clemency of God may be proclaimed to posterity. For which the Seventy set: For from today I will make sons, who will announce your righteousness. And the causal conjunction joins what follows to what precedes: namely, that the living, and he himself living, bless God for this reason, that from this day he would make sons who would announce his truth, which certainly was not in his own power. For those children were not promised him through the Prophet; only the present life was granted. Especially since he begot a most impious son, Manasseh, who filled Jerusalem with blood from gate to gate, and did not bless but cursed God, persecuting his saints. We can therefore say this according to the Seventy: that he did not say I will make sons, but παιδία, which we understand either as little ones, or boys, or little infants, and descendants, so that from the fact that he himself obtained mercy, all posterity to come, knowing this, might praise his incredible clemency.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 3:4.38

"For from this day I shall beget children who will announce your righteousness." Some say that he promises to institute a choir [chorostasia] and to appoint chanters of psalms with good voices in the temple. Others, who pay attention to more esoteric things, say that Hezekiah, since he thought on a high plane, was of the opinion that he would have a kingdom without end and unceasing life. For he was persuaded that the writings concerning the son of David destined to be the Christ were said about himself. Hence they say, although he was in the fifteenth year of his reign he does not seem to have procreated children. Accordingly, on learning that his end was near, he pays attention to the question of his successors and adds with reference to his children that they will announce the righteousness of the Lord. However, this statement was not verified since. Manasseh was wicked and impious.
Letter 10.3

At no time should one freely praise God more than when one has passed through afflictions. Nor again should one at any time give thanks more than when he finds rest from toil and temptations. As Hezekiah, when the Assyrians perished, praised the Lord and gave thanks, saying, "The Lord is my salvation, and I will not cease to bless you with harp all the days of my life, before the house of the Lord."
Commentary on Isaiah
Save me then, O Lord; and all of us who believe in you and have been delivered by your help will sing to you in the Temple all the days of our life.
Commentary on Isaiah

And Isaiah commanded that they take a lump of figs and plaster it upon the wound, and he would be healed. And Hezekiah said: What will be the sign that I shall go up into the house of the Lord? This is to be read before the prayer of Hezekiah, or Writing, which we have now interpreted: for the plaster was laid on the wound, and the sign of future health was asked by him, before he gave thanks to the Lord, which he is said to have done when healed. The Hebrews say that the word SIIN (שחין), which the Seventy passed over, means ulcer, not wound. For Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion also translated ἕλκος, by which they wish the royal disease to be understood, to which whatever is sweet, whether taken as food or applied to the body, is thought to be contrary. So, that the power of God might be shown, health was restored through things harmful and contrary. Others suppose SIIN to be not ulcer but abscess: when the swelling body is filled with ripened and putrefying pus. And according to the art of physicians, all matter is drawn out to the surface of the skin by dried and pounded figs: and hence a medicine established by use and experience is not to be despised, since God too made this one. So the prayer and thanksgiving is written up to this point. As for the sign that was given, the earlier order of the history has narrated it.

n: And. Septuagint add, "ambassadors and presents." See 4 Kings xx. 12. (Calmet)
Days. He is not unconcerned about his children, but dares not request more. Having given way to immoderate joy and vanity, he was informed that all his treasures should be taken away. (Worthington)

f: AGAINST MARCION 4.28

In the parable of the rich man, he flattered himself about the increase of his fields. But God said to him, "Fool! This night your soul is required of you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?" It was the same way when King Hezekiah heard from Isaiah the sad doom of his kingdom after he had gloried before the envoys of Babylon in his treasures and the deposits of his precious things.
Commentary on Isaiah

At that time Merodach-baladan, son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent books and gifts to Hezekiah: for he had heard that he had been sick and had recovered. And Hezekiah was glad over them, and showed them the storehouse of spices, and of silver, and of gold, and of perfumes, and of the best ointment, and all the storerooms of his furnishings, and all that was found in his treasuries: there was not a word that Hezekiah did not show them in his house and in all his dominion. Above we read that in the fourteenth year of king Hezekiah, Sennacherib king of the Assyrians came up against all the fortified cities of Judah and took them, and afterward besieged Lachish, passed on to Libnah, and sent part of his army to Jerusalem; and that, when one hundred and eighty-five thousand of his army had been slain by the Angel, he himself fled to Nineveh and was killed by his sons in the shrine of his god, and Esarhaddon his son reigned in his place; that Hezekiah fell sick and recovered his health at the Prophet's message; that an incredible sign was done, so that the sun went back by the space of ten hours toward its rising, and the day became almost double. Now we read that at that time, that is, in the same year in which all these things were done, Merodach-baladan, son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent books and gifts to Hezekiah; not Esarhaddon, who had succeeded his father Sennacherib in the kingdom among the Assyrians, about whose death or life Scripture is silent. From which it is clear that the kingdom of the Assyrians was then one thing, and that of the Babylonians another. Indeed, the Assyrians took Samaria, that is, the ten tribes; but Judah and Jerusalem, we read, were taken later by the Chaldeans, whose king was Nebuchadnezzar. And because among them there is the observation of the heavenly bodies, and the course of the stars is known by long practice and exercise, as is shown also at the Lord's nativity, they understood that the sun had gone back and the spaces of the day had been doubled, in the service of him whom they thought the only God. And when they inquired into the causes and reason of this miracle, as the report flew through all the nations, they learned that because of the sickness of the king of Judah even the course of the brightest sign had been changed. That this is not my opinion but the faith of holy Scripture, the words of Chronicles testify, which say after other things: This is Hezekiah who stopped the upper spring of the waters of Gihon, and turned them down to the west of the city of David. In all his works he accomplished prosperously what he wished; but in the embassy of the princes of Babylon, who had been sent to him to inquire about the portent that had happened on the earth, God left him, that he might be tested, and that all that was in his heart might be made known (2 Chr 32:30, 31). And he was left to temptation for this reason, because after so great a victory, and the sun's going back, and the congratulation of a most powerful kingdom, his heart was lifted up. Indeed, in the same volume it is written: Many brought victims and sacrifices to the Lord in Jerusalem, and gifts to Hezekiah king of Judah: and he was exalted before all the nations. In those days he was sick unto death, and he prayed to the Lord; and he heard him and gave him a sign; but he did not make return according to the benefits he had received: for his heart was lifted up, and there was wrath against him, and against Judah and Jerusalem (2 Chr 32:23, 24). And again holy Scripture says that the lifting up of his heart was softened by penance, adding: And afterward he was humbled because his heart had been lifted up, both he and the inhabitants of Jerusalem: and therefore the wrath of the Lord did not come upon them in the days of Hezekiah.
The Book of Pastoral Rule, Part 1, Chapter 4

Often the care of government, when undertaken, distracts the heart in divers directions; and one is found unequal to dealing with particular things, while with confused mind divided among many. Whence a certain wise man providently dissuades, saying, "My son, meddle not with many matters;" because, that is, the mind is by no means collected on the plan of any single work while parted among divers. And, when it is drawn abroad by unwonted care, it is emptied of the solidity of inward fear: it becomes anxious in the ordering of things that are without, and, ignorant of itself alone, knows how to think of many things, while itself it knows not. For, when it implicates itself more than is needful in things that are without, it is as though it were so occupied during a journey as to forget where it was going; so that, being estranged from the business of self-examination, it does not even consider the losses it is suffering, or know how great they are. For neither did Hezekiah believe himself to be sinning, when he shewed to the strangers who came to him his storehouses of spices; but he fell under the anger of the judge, to the condemnation of his future offspring, from what he supposed himself to be doing lawfully. Often, when means are abundant, and many things can be done for subordinates to admire, the mind exalts itself in thought, and fully provokes to itself the anger of the judge, though not breaking out in overt acts of iniquity. For he who judges is within; that which is judged is within. When, then, in heart we transgress, what we are doing within ourselves is hidden from men, but yet in the eyes of the judge we sin.
Commentary on Isaiah

He was glad, then, at the coming of the envoys of Merodach, whom the Hebrews suppose to have been the father of Nebuchadnezzar, and at the offering of gifts and the congratulation on his recovery. And he showed them, according to the Seventy, the house NECHOTHA (נכתה), for which Symmachus translated of his spices; and the treasuries of silver, and of gold, and of perfumes, and of the best ointment, which in the Hebrew is written of good oil; and all the treasuries of the vessels of his gaza, or, as is read there, of his vessels. Now in the language of the Persians riches are called gaza; nor is it a Hebrew word, but a Barbarian one. There was not, he says, a word (which according to Hebrew usage is frequently taken for thing) that he did not show them in his house and in all his dominion. Hence the most just wrath of God, because he showed not only his own treasures and those of the palace but also those of the Temple, which certainly was within his dominion, and from whose doors he had already earlier taken the plates of gold.
Commentary on Isaiah

Then Isaiah the Prophet came in to king Hezekiah and said to him: What did these men say, and from where did they come to you? And Hezekiah said: From a far country they came to me, from Babylon. And he said: What did they see in your house? And Hezekiah said: They saw all that is in my house: there was not a word, or thing, that I did not show them in my treasuries. And Isaiah said to Hezekiah: Hear the word of the Lord of hosts. Behold, the day will come, and all that is in your house, and what your fathers have stored up until this day, shall be carried away to Babylon: nothing shall be left, said the Lord. And of your sons who shall come forth from you, whom you shall beget, they shall take away: and they shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon. And Hezekiah said to Isaiah: Good is the word of the Lord which he has spoken. And he said: Only let there be peace and truth in my days. The Hebrews relate that Hezekiah fell sick for this reason, because after the unheard-of victory of the Jews and the destruction of the Assyrian king he did not sing praises to the Lord, as Moses sang when Pharaoh was drowned (Exod 15), and Deborah when Sisera was killed (Judg 4), and Hannah when Samuel was born (1 Sam 2); and that hence he was reminded of his frailty. And again, after the health of his body and the greatness of the sign, another occasion of pride was offered him, which, as a prudent man and a worshiper of God, he ought to have avoided; nor ought he to have shown to foreigners his riches, which he possessed by God's gift. From which, according to the laws of tropology too, we learn that pearls are not to be cast before swine, nor what is holy given to dogs (Matt 7). For he who is of a faithful spirit hides matters; and whoever does not do this, all his strength is unnerved, and his posterity perishes, and, its manly vigor lost, is reduced to womanly softness (Prov 11:13-15). So Isaiah goes in to the king and, as though not knowing, inquires: What did these men say, and from where did they come? He asks two things: what they said, and from where they came. The king answered one, passing over the other, which is to be read with ἐμφάσει and a lifted brow: From a far country they came to me, from Babylon: meaning that the farther the land from which they came, the more glorious is he on whose account they came. And they came, he says, to me, when he ought to have said: they came to glorify God for the greatness of the sign; from Babylon, which is the most powerful city in the whole world.
Commentary on Isaiah

And again Isaiah: What, he says, did they see in your house? And he answered with part of the truth: that they saw everything in his house, and there was nothing that he did not show them in his treasuries. But he is silent about the other thing, for which he feared offense: that he showed them all that he had in his dominion; no doubt the furnishings of the Temple as well.
Commentary on Isaiah

For these reasons Isaiah pronounces the sentence in the word of God: Hear the word of the Lord of hosts: The time will come when all these things which are in your house, acquired not by your labor but by your fathers', will be carried over to Babylon, and of your seed eunuchs will be made in the royal court.
St. Jerome, Commentary on Daniel, CHAPTER ONE

Verse 3. "And the king said to Ashpenaz the overseer of his eunuchs, that he should out of the number of the children of Israel and, of the royal seed and (the seed of) the rulers bring in some young lads who were free from all blemish." Instead of Ashpenaz ("Asphanez") I found Abriesdri written in the Vulgate edition. For the word phorlhommin which Theodotion uses, the Septuagint and Aquila translated "the chosen ones," whereas Symmachus rendered "Parthians," understanding it as the name of a nation instead of a common noun. This is in disagreement with the Hebrew edition as it is accurately read; I have translated it as "rulers," especially because it is preceded by the words "of the seed royal." From this passage the Hebrews think that Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah were eunuchs, thus fulfilling that prophecy which is spoken by Isaiah regarding Hezekiah: "And they shall take of thy seed and make eunuchs of them in the house of the king of Babylon" (Isaiah 39:7). If however they were of the seed royal, there is no doubt but what they were of the line of David. But perhaps the following words are opposed to this interpretation: "...lads, or youths, who were free from all blemish, in order that he might teach them the literature and language of the Chaldeans." Philo supposes that Chaldee is the same thing as the Hebrew language, because Abraham came from the Chaldeans. But if we accept this we must ask how the Hebrew lads could now be bidden to be taught a language which they already knew; unless, perchance, we should say, as some believe, that Abraham was acquainted with two languages.
Commentary on Isaiah
From this the Hebrews hold that Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah, who were of the royal seed, were made eunuchs; that they were in the service of king Nebuchadnezzar there is no doubt.
Commentary on Isaiah

So Hezekiah said: Good is the word of the Lord which he has spoken. In this he is reproached by the Hebrews for not imitating the goodness of Moses, who spoke to the Lord: Either forgive them this offense; or if you do not, blot me out of your book which you have written (Exod 32:32). Hence the apostle Paul too wishes to be anathema from Christ for his brethren who are Israelites (Rom 9); and they say that for this reason Hezekiah was not approved by the words of God, who in what follows says: Comfort, comfort, O my people, says your God, so that those for whom he had not prayed might be comforted by the Lord's clemency.

n: Be. Septuagint, "comfort my people." Let them not be dejected. (Haydock) --- The end of the captivity, and still more the coming of the Messias, afford consolation, (Calmet) and to this the prophet chiefly alludes. (Worthington)

God, that he may conduct his people from Babylon. (Sanchez) --- Yet the prophet speaks chiefly of John the Baptist, (Matthew iii. 3.; Calmet) who is evidently foretold. (Worthington)

Dust. Hebrew caddak, (Haydock) "as dok fallen." (Symmachus) --- It may signify an atom. (St. Jerome) --- If all nations be only like a drop, what portion of it do I occupy? (Calmet; ver. 17.)

Image. Catholics never pretend to represent the Deity, when they depict the Father as a venerable old man, &c. They do not adore pictures, as our adversaries would insinuate.
