f: Commentary on Isaiah

Comfort, comfort, O my people, says your God: Speak to the heart of Jerusalem, and call to her; for her evil is fulfilled, her iniquity is forgiven. She has received from the hand of the Lord double for all her sins. LXX: Comfort, comfort my people, says God; ÷ O priests ⁚ speak to the heart of Jerusalem: comfort her: for her humiliation is filled up. Her sin is loosed, for she has received from the hand of the Lord double her sins. According to the other translators, others are commanded to comfort the people of God and Jerusalem alike; according to the Hebrew, the people itself is commanded to comfort, and to speak to the heart of Jerusalem, and to call to her. To speak to the heart of Jerusalem is an idiom of the Scriptures. For he who speaks to one who mourns, and comforts with soothing words, is said to speak to the heart. Let Shechem son of Hamor teach us, who, after he had violated Dinah, spoke to her heart and comforted her (Gen 34). And wherever you find anything similar, it has this sense. And the cause of the comfort is the remission of sins; and the cause of the remission, that she has received from the hand of the Lord double for all her sins. For he who knows the will of his Lord and sins will be beaten with many stripes (Luke 12). And everyone who has the Holy Spirit dwelling in him, whom the Savior promised to the Apostles, saying: I will ask my Father, and he will give you another comforter, to be with you for ever, the Spirit of truth (John 14:16); and again: But when the comforter, the Holy Spirit, has come, whom my Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things (ibid., 26); and again: When the comforter has come, whom I shall send you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness of me (John 15:26); and: It is to your advantage that I go: for if I do not go away, the comforter will not come to you (John 16:7); he is a comforter, and he is now commanded to comfort the people of God. Hence the Apostle Paul too said to the believers: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our tribulation, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any tribulation, through the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God: for as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so through Christ our comfort also will abound (2 Cor 1:1-6); and again: And our hope for you is firm: knowing that as you are partakers of the sufferings, so you will be also of the comfort (2 Cor 1:7). But who this people is that is comforted through the Apostles and churchmen, not Israel and Jacob and Judah, as Scripture records in other places, but the people of God, the prophet Zechariah testifies, saying: Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Zion: for I will come and dwell in the midst of you, says the Lord. And many nations shall flee to the Lord in that day, and shall be his people, and they shall dwell in the midst of you, and they shall know that the Lord almighty has sent me to you (Zech 2:10, 11). By this testimony it is clearly shown that very many nations are to be turned into the people of God. And these things the Lord says, sent by the Lord whose name is Almighty. And this is to be noted, that our sins are not loosed unless we have received them from the hand of the Lord. Nor is it the same for sins to be loosed and to be forgiven. For he to whom they are forgiven does not need loosing, as he hears in the Gospel: Take heart, son, your sins are forgiven you (Matt 9:2). But he for whom they are loosed, for him they are loosed for this reason, that they have been purged and paid off through punishments. According to the history, Jerusalem received from the hand of the Lord double her sins: once from the Babylonians, the second time from the Romans. And what is added by the Seventy, O priests, is to be marked beforehand with an obelus.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 3:4.40:1

Hezekiah was at a loss for a defense. Since he could offer no excuse for his crimes, he said that God's word was good, even though it foretold things that should have made him shed tears. Then he asks for peace in his own days, bidding goodbye, as it were, to those who were to come after him and thereby neglecting his native land, his own city and his own race. But it would have been better for him to be sorry for the things that had been predicted and to ask God for mercy and happiness (not temporary and restricted) on behalf of those to come after him.
Exposition On Psalm 118, Sermon 18

There is also another type of consolation for those who have paid heavy penalties, as it is written in the book of Isaiah: 'Comfort, comfort my people,' says the Lord. 'Speak tenderly to Jerusalem, and cry to her that her warfare is ended, that her iniquity is pardoned, that she has received from the Lord's hand double for all her sins.' Even if faith was lacking, punishment was satisfied. The penalties are mitigated for those who are acquitted by commendation of their merits.
AGAINST MARCION 4.33

Since even then by Isaiah it was Christ, the Word and the Spirit of the Creator who prophetically described John as "the voice of one crying in the wilderness to prepare the way of the Lord." And [he] was about to come forth for the purpose of terminating from that point onwards the course of the law and the prophets: by their fulfillment and not their extinction.
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 21

But this very thing, which is now set down from the old instrument, we read written in the prophet Isaiah. For there it is said: "The voice of one crying in the desert: prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight". The Lord wishes to find ways in you—he who, that he may be able to enter into your souls and make his journey, prepare for him the path of which it is said: "make his paths straight". "The voice of one crying in the desert". "The voice" cries: "prepare the way"; for first "the voice" reaches the ears, then after the voice—rather, together with the voice—the word penetrates the hearing. According to this sense Christ was announced by John. Let us see, therefore, what "the voice" announces concerning the word. "Prepare", it says, "the way for the Lord". What "way for the Lord" are we to prepare? Surely not a bodily one? Or can the word of God travel by such a road? Or is the way to be prepared for the Lord within, and straight and even paths to be laid out in our heart? This is the way by which the word of God enters, which consists in the capacity of the human heart. Great is the heart of man, and spacious and capacious, if only it be clean. Do you wish to know its greatness and breadth? See how great a magnitude of divine perceptions it can contain. It itself says: "he gave me true knowledge of the things that are: to know the constitution of the world and the operations of the elements, the beginning and the end and the middle of the ages, the changes of the seasons and the transitions of the months, the circuits of the years and the positions of the stars, the natures of living creatures and the ragings of beasts, the violences of spirits and the thoughts of men, the diversities of trees and the power of roots". You see that the heart of man is not small, which can contain so much. And understand its greatness not in the quantity of the body, but in the strength of perception, which can contain so great a knowledge of the truth. But that I may also lead the simpler folk by everyday examples to believe that the heart of man is great, let us look at what follows. Whatever cities we have passed through, we have them in our mind, and the qualities and situations of the streets and the walls and the buildings are turning over in our heart. The road that we have entered upon we retain in the picture and description of memory; the sea that we have sailed we embrace in silent thought. It is no small thing, as I have said, the heart of man, which can contain so much. But if it is no small thing, containing so much, consequently in it the way of the Lord is prepared and a straight path is made, so that the word of God and wisdom may walk in it. Prepare the way for the Lord through good conduct, and by outstanding works wear smooth the path, so that the word of God may walk in you without any stumbling and may grant you the knowledge of his mysteries and of his coming: to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 6:103

Now the way of the Lord is made straight in two ways: by contemplation, which is clarified by truth unmixed with falsehood, and by activity, which follows sound contemplation of the appropriate action to be taken, which is conformed to the correct sense of these things to be done.
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 57: WHY MARK ATTRIBUTES MALACHI'S WORDS TO ISAIAH

WHAT DOES THIS MEAN, THAT ALTHOUGH IT IS WRITTEN IN THE PROPHET MALACHI, “BEHOLD, I SEND MY ANGEL BEFORE YOUR FACE, WHO WILL PREPARE YOUR WAY BEFORE YOU,” THE EVANGELIST MARK CLAIMS THAT THIS IS WRITTEN IN THE PROPHET ISAIAH (Mal. 3:1; Mark 1:2)? — Mark could not have been unaware of what he was writing; for he was not lacking in learning, since from childhood he had been immersed in the divine Scriptures and trained in the Law, especially as he had followed the Apostles. Knowing that all sayings must be referred back to their original author, he attributed these words to Isaiah, who had first conveyed this meaning when he said, “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord, make straight the paths of our God” (Isa. 40:3). Accordingly, after the words from Malachi, the Evangelist immediately added, “The voice of one crying in the wilderness,” so that he might unite the words of both prophets, which relate to one and the same sense, under the name of the earlier prophet.
Catechetical Lecture 3:1

While the heavenly powers rejoice, let the souls that are to be united to the spiritual bridegroom make themselves ready. For the voice is heard of one crying in the wilderness, "Prepare the way of the Lord." For this is no light matter, no ordinary and indiscriminate union according to the flesh but the all-searching Spirit's election according to faith.
Exposition of the Christian Faith 5.7.98

God, indeed, never descends from any place, for he says, "I fill heaven and earth." But he seems to descend when the Word of God enters our hearts, as the prophet has said, "Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight." We are to do this, so that, as he himself promised, he may come together with the Father and make his abode with us.
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 10:3

Thus the prophet saith that he shall come saying, "Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make his paths straight." And he himself when he was come said, "Bring forth fruits meet for repentance," which corresponds with, "Prepare ye the way of the Lord." Seest thou that both by the words of the prophet, and by his own preaching, this one thing is manifested alone; that he was come, making a way and preparing beforehand, not bestowing the gift, which was the remission, but ordering in good time the souls of such as should receive the God of all?
LETTER 119.10

In that the Word has now become flesh and dwelled among us, now there will not be in any way the voice of a prophet in the desert but the voice of the archangel, preparing the way for the one coming not in the humility of the flesh but for him who is with the Father. And in those days they were going out into the desert, so as to hear the forerunner of the assumed man and to see the sand perturbed by the wind.
Commentary on Matthew

For this is he who was spoken of through the prophet Isaiah, saying: The voice of one crying in the desert: Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight. He was preparing the souls of believers, in which the Lord was going to walk, so that he, the pure one, might walk in most pure ways, saying: I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. Porphyry compares this passage with the beginning of the evangelist Mark, in which it is written: The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God; as it is written in the prophet Isaiah: Behold, I send my angel before your face, who shall prepare your way; the voice of one crying in the desert: Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight. For since the testimony is woven together from Malachi and Isaiah, he asks how we can think the example was taken as from Isaiah alone. To him churchmen have answered most fully. We, however, think either that the name of Isaiah was added through the fault of copyists, which we can prove in other places as well, or at any rate that one body has been made out of different testimonies of the Scriptures. Read Psalm 13 (14) and you will find this same thing.
Commentary on Isaiah

The voice of one crying in the desert: Prepare the way of the Lord, make straight in the wilderness the paths of our God. Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low: and the crooked shall become straight, and the rough ways plain; and the glory of the Lord shall be revealed, and all flesh together shall see that the mouth of the Lord has spoken. LXX: The voice of one crying in the desert: Prepare the way of the Lord: make straight the paths of our God. Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low; and the crooked shall become straight, and the rough ways plains. And the glory of the Lord shall appear, and all flesh shall see the salvation of God, for the Lord has spoken. Mindful of this voice, the Scribes and Pharisees and the princes of the Jews, when they heard that John was preaching in the wilderness a baptism of penance and teaching the people, send men to ask him whether he was the Christ, or Elijah, or the Prophet; and when he had answered that he was none of these, they ask again: Tell us then, who are you? that we may give an answer to those who sent us. What do you say of yourself? And he answered: I am the voice of one crying in the desert: Prepare the way of the Lord; as Isaiah the Prophet said (John 1:22, 23). In this it is to be noticed that the straight ways of the Lord and the paths of our God, the filling of the valleys, and the lowering of the mountains and hills, and the correction of the crooked, and the level plains made of rough places and rocks, and the glory of the Lord and the salvation of our God, are proclaimed not in Jerusalem but in the wilderness of the Church and in the deserted multitude of the nations, of which we read above (cf. Isa 35:1): Rejoice, thirsting desert: let the wilderness exult and flower like the lily. For this multitude was deserted of the knowledge of God, and was held by idols: low in confession, lifted up in pride, rough and intractable in savagery. But after the glory of the Lord appeared, and all flesh saw the salvation of God, all things were suddenly changed and the way of the Lord prepared, so that the glory of God appeared in the wilderness: when the Lord was baptized in the Jordan, and the heavens were opened, and the Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove and remained on him; and the voice of the Father thundering from above was heard: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased: hear him (Matt 3:17). And all flesh saw the salvation of God. It was called flesh for this reason, that before it did not have the Holy Spirit. Of it the Lord also says: My spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh (Gen 6:3). But that flesh will see the salvation of God of which the same Lord spoke through Joel: I will pour out of my spirit upon all flesh, and they shall prophesy (Joel 2:28). This was cried out not only at that time by John, who, as the forerunner and precursor of the Word of God, is rightly called a voice (Matt 3); but to this day in the desert of the Gentiles the teachers of the Churches cry out: that we should make straight ways and paths for God in our hearts, and be filled with virtues, and be bowed down by humility; that we should change the crooked into straight and turn the rough into smooth: and so deserve to see the glory of the Lord and the salvation of God.
Enchiridion 14:49

They were not reborn, those who were baptized by John's baptism, by which Christ himself was baptized. Rather, they were "prepared" by the ministry of a forerunner, who said, "Prepare a way for the Lord"—for him in whom alone they could be reborn.
SERMON 289

There it is written, "a voice of one crying in the wilderness," the Word is conceived in the virgin's womb. If the voice is not the Word, it is then a loud clanging of metal. For one then would not be able to say that every word is a sound but not every sound is a word. For it is not unfitting to take "the way" as that which came up to the very heart and filled us inwardly. Indeed, the heart became his place to which he comes and remains.
Forty Gospel Homilies, Homily 7

"I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Make straight the way of the Lord, as Isaiah the prophet said." You know, dearest brothers, that the only-begotten Son is called the Word of the Father, as John testifies when he says: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." And from your own manner of speaking you recognize that the voice sounds first, so that the word may afterward be heard. Therefore John asserts that he is the voice, because he precedes the Word. And so, going before the coming of the Lord, he is called a voice, because through his ministry the Word of the Father is heard by men. He also cries out in the wilderness, because he announces the comfort of the Redeemer to abandoned and forsaken Judea. But what he cries out he indicates when he adds: "Make straight the way of the Lord." The way of the Lord is made straight to the heart when the word of truth is humbly heard. The way of the Lord is made straight to the heart when one's life is prepared according to his commandment.
Forty Gospel Homilies, Homily 17

It is well said that he sent them before his face into every city and place where he himself was about to come. For the Lord follows his preachers, because preaching comes first, and then the Lord comes to the dwelling place of our mind, when words of exhortation run ahead, and through these truth is received in the mind. For thus Isaiah says to these same preachers: Prepare the way of the Lord, make straight the paths of our God.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 3:4.40:3-5

And this is the Lord of glory, and we too have come to know his glory. However, those of old did not see it when he showed himself during the dispensation in which he was made man, equal to God the Father in strength, operation and glory, bearing all things by the word of his power and with great tranquillity performing godly works, enhancing creation, raising the dead and performing other deeds of wonder effortlessly. For the glory of the Lord appeared, and all flesh saw the salvation of God, that is, of the Father. For he has sent us his Son from heaven to salvation and redemption. For the law brings no one to perfection, for the sacrifices in prefigurative form were unable to deal with sin. But we have been perfected in Christ and reconciled from every fault as we have been honored with the spirit of sonship.
40 Homilies on the Gospels, Homily 20

"And all flesh shall see the salvation of God." Because by "all flesh" is meant every person, not every person was able to see the salvation of God, namely Christ, in this life. Where then does the prophet direct the eye of prophecy in this statement except to the day of the last judgment? When, with the heavens opened, angels ministering, apostles seated alongside, Christ shall appear on the throne of His majesty, all—both the elect and the reprobate alike—will see Him, so that the just may rejoice without end in the gift of recompense, and the unjust may groan perpetually in the vengeance of punishment.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 11:3

And [Christ] commanded all the multitudes to sit down on the grass because of what is said in Isaiah, "All flesh is grass." That is to say, he commanded them to subjugate the flesh and to keep in subjection "the mind of the flesh," so that one might be able to partake of the loaves that Jesus blesses.
HOMILIES ON PSALMS 37, HOMILY I

Do you wish also to be fortified by the authority of another prophet's admonitions concerning such men? Hear what Isaiah too pronounces concerning all carnal glory: "All flesh", he says, "is grass, and all its glory as the flower of grass". Do you wish also to see through particular cases how the glory of the flesh is the flower of grass? See who ruled thirty years ago, how his rule flowered: but straightway like the flower of grass it withered; then afterward another after him, then another and another, who thereafter were leaders and princes: and all their glory and honor not only withered like a flower, but even, like dry dust scattered by the wind, left not even a trace of itself. Others too, lifted up by riches and swollen with honors, striving either to be held praiseworthy through feigned goodness, or execrable through untamed cruelty. If anyone thinks their vain pursuits are to be envied, let him now go to the remains of their corpses, if indeed even these can be found; for to some not even this has been granted: and then he will find how "all flesh is grass, and all its glory as the flower of grass. The grass has withered and its flower has fallen away". But whoever does not love the little flowers of the flesh, nor lives carnally, but loves the word of God, and advances in it, hear what he may hope for: "The word", he says, "of the Lord abides forever".
Discourses Against the Arians 1.12.48

What advancement, then, was it to the Immortal to have assumed the mortal? Or what promotion is it to the Everlasting to have put on the temporal? What reward can be great to the everlasting God and King in the bosom of the Father? Do you not see that this too was done and written because of us and for us, that the Lord, having become a human being, might make immortal us who are mortal and temporal and bring us into the everlasting kingdom of heaven? Do you Arians not blush, speaking lies against the divine oracles? For when our Lord Jesus Christ was among us, we indeed were promoted, as rescued from sin; but he is the same, nor did he change when he became man, but, as has been written, "the Word of God abides forever." Surely as, before he became human, he, the Word, dispensed to the saints the Spirit as his own, so also when made human, he sanctifies all by the Spirit and says to his disciples, "Receive the Holy Spirit."
Commentary on Isaiah

The voice of one saying: Cry. And I said: What shall I cry? All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field. The grass is withered, the flower has fallen; because the spirit of God has blown upon it: truly the people is grass. The grass is withered, the flower has fallen; but the word of our Lord shall stand for ever. LXX: The voice of one saying: Cry: and I said: What shall I cry? All flesh is grass, and all the glory of man is like the flower of grass. The grass has dried up, and the flower has fallen ※ because the spirit of God has blown upon it ※ truly the people is grass ※ the grass is withered, the flower has fallen ⁚ but the word of our God abides for ever: What is marked with asterisks, because the spirit of God has blown upon it: truly the people is grass: the grass has dried up, the flower has fallen, has been added from the Hebrew and the edition of Theodotion. From which it is clear that it was either passed over by the Seventy or gradually lost by the fault of copyists, since both the former and the following verse end in flower. Above we read, the Prophet saying: And I heard the voice of the Lord saying: Whom shall I send, and who will go to this people? And I said: Behold, here am I, send me; and he said: Go and say to this people: With the ear you shall hear and not understand: and seeing you shall see and not see, and the rest. Having suffered hard things for that preaching, now, when the Lord's voice says Cry, fearing the like, he asks what he ought to cry; and beginning from the general, All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass, he comes to the particular, so as to say none the less of the people: Truly the people is grass. And indeed, if anyone looks at the frailty of the flesh, how from moment to moment we grow and decline and do not remain in the same state, and how the very time in which we speak, dictate and write flies away from the portion of our life, he will not hesitate to call flesh grass, and its glory like the flower of grass, or the meadows of the fields. He who was lately an infant is suddenly a boy; he who was a boy, suddenly a young man; and up to old age he is changed by imperceptible stages; and he perceives himself an old man before he wonders that he is no longer young. A beautiful woman who drew flocks of young men after her is shrunk with a furrowed brow; and she who before was an object of love is afterward one of disgust. This the distinguished orator among the Greeks also writes: that the beauty of the body either fails with time or is consumed by sickness. So the flesh has withered and its beauty has fallen, because the spirit of the fury and sentence of God has blown upon it (to return from the general discussion to the order of Scripture): the flesh of him who bears the image of the earthly and serves vices and luxury; and it is grass and a passing flower. But he who has and keeps the image of the heavenly, he is the flesh that sees the salvation of the Lord, that is renewed daily unto knowledge according to the image of the Creator, and, receiving an incorruptible and immortal body, changes its glory, not its nature. But the word of our Lord, and those who are joined to the word, abide for ever.

And what is said in Psalm 67 (68): The Lord will give the word to those who bring good tidings with great power, they understand thus: The Lord will give the word to those women who bring good tidings with great power (Ps 122 [123]:3): namely, to those souls which have obtained the Holy Spirit. And also the verse: As the eyes of a maidservant are on the hands of her mistress: they interpret the soul as the maidservant and the Holy Spirit as the mistress. But also in the Gospel written according to the Hebrews, which the Nazarenes read, the Lord says: just now my mother, the Holy Spirit, took me. No one ought to be scandalized in this matter, that spirit is said among the Hebrews in the feminine gender, while in our language it is called in the masculine gender, and in the Greek speech in the neuter. For in the Godhead there is no sex. And therefore in the three principal languages in which the title of the Lord's passion was written, it is called by three genders, so that we may know that what is diverse is of no gender.

Hence also in the same Ezekiel it is written: I will raise up over them one shepherd, and he shall feed them, my servant David; and he shall be their shepherd, and I the Lord will be their God, and David a prince in their midst. Because we come upon difficult passages, I would wish to inquire whether somewhere in the Scriptures we find any such thing, from which that which seems obscure could be opened up more plainly. From which let whoever is the more prudent of the hearers consider, through the several passages, the differences of the measures, how the part of life which is heavenly, of those indeed who merit to be called heaven, is said to be measured with the span of God, whatever that span of God is: and of those whose life is still earthly, their life is measured with the fist of God. But to inquire now the difference of the divine fist would perhaps exceed both our speech and your hearing. Nevertheless just as there he measured the water with his hand, the heaven with a span, and all the earth with his fist, and weighed the mountains in a balance, and the hills in a scale; so also here, according to the same consequence, this measure is to be understood, since to God nothing is without measure, nothing without weight, but all things stand for him in number and measure.

For such an indication of God's infinity the words "I Am that I Am" were clearly adequate; but, in addition, we needed to apprehend the operation of His majesty and power. For while absolute existence is peculiar to Him Who, abiding eternally, had no beginning in a past however remote, we hear again an utterance worthy of Himself issuing from the eternal and Holy God, Who says, "Who holdeth the heaven in His palm and the earth in His hand," and again, "The heaven is My throne and the earth is the footstool of My feet. What house will ye build Me or what shall be the place of My rest?" The whole heaven is held in the palm of God, the whole earth grasped in His hand. Now the word of God, profitable as it is to the cursory thought of a pious mind, reveals a deeper meaning to the patient student than to the momentary hearer. For this heaven which is held in the palm of God is also His throne, and the earth which is grasped in His hand is also the footstool beneath His feet. This was not written that from throne and footstool, metaphors drawn from the posture of one sitting, we should conclude that He has extension in space, as of a body, for that which is His throne and footstool is also held in hand and palm by that infinite Omnipotence. It was written that in all born and created things God might be known within them and without, overshadowing and indwelling, surrounding all and interfused through all, since palm and hand, which hold, reveal the might of His external control, while throne and footstool, by their support of a sitter, display the subservience of outward things to One within Who, Himself outside them, encloses all in His grasp, yet dwells within the external world which is His own. In this wise does God, from within and from without, control and correspond to the universe; being infinite He is present in all things, in Him Who is infinite all are included.

Who has measured the waters in his fist, and weighed heaven with his palm? Who has poised the mass of the earth with three fingers, and weighed the mountains in a weight, and the hills in a balance? Who has helped the spirit of the Lord, or who was his counselor and showed him? With whom did he take counsel, and who instructed him, and taught him the path of righteousness, and schooled him in knowledge, and showed him the way of understanding? Behold, the nations are like a drop of a bucket, and are counted as the tipping of a balance: behold, the islands are like a little dust. And Lebanon is not enough for burning, and its beasts will not be enough for a burnt offering. All the nations are before him as if they were not, and they are counted to him as nothing and void. LXX: Who has measured the water with his hand, and heaven with his palm, and all the earth with his fist? Who has set the mountains in a weight, and the rocks in a balance? Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who was his counselor? Who taught him, whose counsel did he receive, and who instructed him? Or who showed him judgment, and who showed him the way of understanding? If all the nations are counted like a drop of a bucket, and as the tipping of a balance, they are counted also as spittle. Lebanon is not enough for burning, and all the four-footed beasts are not enough for a burnt offering, and all the nations are as nothing, and are counted to him as nothing. Lest anyone should think the calling of the nations difficult, and that all flesh should see the salvation of God, that those who bring good tidings to Zion should be commanded to climb a high mountain, and that the Lord himself should come in strength and render to each according to his work, and like a shepherd cherish the lambs in his bosom and himself carry the ewes with young, his greatness is described: that nothing is impossible to him; and that he who founded all things and is the Creator of all can accomplish also these things, which are small in comparison with those. In calling it fist and palm, he uses the words and measures of human custom, so that we may learn the power of God through our words. Where the Seventy translated: Who has measured the water with his hand? or, as we rendered: Who has measured the waters in his fist? Aquila translated: Who has measured the waters with his smallest finger? For this is what λιχὰς means: that, namely, not with the whole hand but with the little finger, which is commonly called the taster, the whole vastness of the waters is weighed; while σπιθαμὴ, that is, the palm, signifies the hand stretched out from the thumb to the tip of the last finger. But if we close the hand, it becomes a fist: so that through the palm and the fist we may know the outstretched heavens and the globe of the earth. For fist, which the Seventy translated in the grasping of the earth, in the Hebrew is written SALIS (שליש), which Symmachus translated τρίτον, Aquila τρίσωμον: and we, to make it plainer, rendered it three fingers; namely, that he weighed the mass of the earth and the heights of the mountains and hills as if with three little fingers and with the small tipping of a balance: by which the majesty of God and the power of the Creator is shown.

Who, he says, has helped the spirit of the Lord, or who was his counselor and showed him? etc. For which Symmachus translated: Who has prepared the spirit of the Lord, and who has shown him the man of his counsel? By this he shows more plainly that the spirit was prepared, or established, the one of whom one reads in the Apostle: Now the Lord is the Spirit. And: Upon whom the Spirit of God rested, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, and the rest. Who says in what follows: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me: because he has anointed me (Isa 61:1). Isa 9:6): Wonderful, Counselor. And in Proverbs it is written: God founded the earth by wisdom, and prepared the heavens by understanding (Prov 3:19). All the nations that did not know their Creator, or the whole race of mortals, are in comparison with God like a drop of a bucket, and like the tipping of a balance, which with a light weight inclines to one side. And just as, if a small drop flows from a bucket, it is disregarded by the one who carries it, so the whole multitude of the nations, compared with the heavenly ministries and the multitude of the Angels, is counted as nothing. The islands too are counted as spittle, or, as Symmachus and Theodotion have it, setting down the Hebrew word itself, as DOC (דק), which falls off: for which Aquila translated λεπτὸν βαλλόμενον. And the Hebrews say that this word signifies the finest dust, which, snatched up by the wind, is often thrown into the eyes and is felt rather than seen. The tiniest and almost invisible particles of dust, then, are called by this word: what perhaps Democritus with his Epicurus calls atoms. And there are many words which are read in the Greek just as they are set down in the Hebrew, because of the difficulty of translating, and because of the poverty of both the Greek and the Latin speech in comparison with the Hebrew language.

And at the same time he mocks the folly of the nations, that a craftsman or bronze-smith, or goldsmith or silversmith, should make a god for themselves, and fasten it together with plates and nails and set it firmly, lest it be pushed over by the blasts of the winds. And what he added: the wise craftsman has chosen strong and incorruptible wood, in the Hebrew is said AMSUCHAN (המסכן); which is a kind of incorruptible wood from which idols are especially made. He says these things so that, idols being rejected, he may prepare the way for the teaching of the Gospel, and all crooked things may be directed into straight; the valleys exalted and the hills brought low; and the glory of the Lord revealed, so that all flesh may see the salvation of God. According to tropology we can say that the chiefs of the heretics are rebuked, who fashion various idols from their own heart: whether by the charm of eloquence, which silver signifies; or by the splendor of gold, which is referred to the understanding; or by incorruptible wood, which are the baser doctrines: and these are thought perpetual by those who fashion them, and are strengthened by the dialectical art, so that they may not be moved and fall, but stand on a solid root.

Will you not know? Will you not hear? Has it not been announced to you from the beginning? Have you not understood the foundations of the earth? He who sits upon the circle of the earth, and its inhabitants are like locusts; who stretches out the heavens like nothing, and spreads them out like a tent to dwell in; who makes the searchers of secrets as though they were not; he has made the judges of the earth as void. Indeed, their stock was neither planted, nor sown, nor rooted in the earth: suddenly he blew upon them and they withered, and the whirlwind will carry them off like stubble. And to whom have you likened me and made me equal? says the Holy One. Lift up your eyes on high, and see who has created these things: who brings out their host by number, and calls them all by name. Because of the greatness of his might and strength and power, not one was left behind. LXX: Will you not know? Will you not hear? Has it not been announced to you from the beginning? Have you not known the foundations of the earth? He who holds the circle of the earth, and its inhabitants as locusts; who has set up the heaven as a vault, and stretched it out as a tent to dwell in; who makes princes reign as nothing, and has made the earth as nothing. For they shall not be planted, nor sown, nor shall their root be made firm in the earth. He blew upon them, and they were dried up, and the tempest will take them up like stubble. Now therefore to whom have you likened me? Shall I be made equal to them? said the Holy One. Lift up your eyes on high, and see who has shown all these things. He who brings out his array by number, he will call them all by name, from much glory and in the strength of might: nothing is hidden from you. From the beginning, he says, I taught you by the natural law, and afterward through Moses I testified by the written Law that idols were nothing, and that the Creator of the world was himself God, who had founded so great a mass of earth upon the seas and set it upon the rivers, so that the heaviest element hangs over thin waters at the will of God, who like a king sits upon the circle of the earth: from which some contend that it is like a point and a globe; and its inhabitants are like locusts. For if we consider the various nations in the whole world, from Ocean to Ocean, that is, from the Indian sea to the British, and from the Atlantic to the frozen North, where the waters congeal and beautiful amber grows solid, we see the whole race of men in between dwelling like locusts. Why then is earth and ashes proud? As for their other assertion, that God's knowledge cannot comprehend things infinite, it only remains for them to affirm, in order that they may sound the depths of their impiety, that God does not know all numbers. For it is very certain that they are infinite; since, no matter of what number you suppose an end to be made, this number can be, I will not say, increased by the addition of one more, but however great it be, and however vast be the multitude of which it is the rational and scientific expression, it can still be not only doubled, but even multiplied. Moreover, each number is so defined by its own properties, that no two numbers are equal. They are therefore both unequal and different from one another; and while they are simply finite, collectively they are infinite. Does God, therefore, not know numbers on account of this infinity; and does His knowledge extend only to a certain height in numbers, while of the rest He is ignorant? Who is so left to himself as to say so? Yet they can hardly pretend to put numbers out of the question, or maintain that they have nothing to do with the knowledge of God; for Plato, their great authority, represents God as framing the world on numerical principles: and in our books also it is said to God, "Thou hast ordered all things in number, and measure, and weight." The prophet also says, "Who bringeth out their host by number." And the Saviour says in the Gospel, "The very hairs of your head are all numbered." Far be it, then, from us to doubt that all number is known to Him "whose understanding," according to the Psalmist, "is infinite." The infinity of number, though there be no numbering of infinite numbers, is yet not incomprehensible by Him whose understanding is infinite. And thus, if everything which is comprehended is defined or made finite by the comprehension of him who knows it, then all infinity is in some ineffable way made finite to God, for it is comprehensible by His knowledge. Wherefore, if the infinity of numbers cannot be infinite to the knowledge of God, by which it is comprehended, what are we poor creatures that we should presume to fix limits to His knowledge, and say that unless the same temporal thing be repeated by the same periodic revolutions, God cannot either foreknow His creatures that He may make them, or know them when He has made them? God, whose knowledge is simply manifold, and uniform in its variety, comprehends all incomprehensibles with so incomprehensible a comprehension, that though He willed always to make His later works novel and unlike what went before them, He could not produce them without order and foresight, nor conceive them suddenly, but by His eternal foreknowledge.

But that it did not originate with the Apostle that Christ is "righteousness", and a living and subsisting "righteousness", but rather that, finding it in the prophetic words, he set forth this mystery for us, is certain from the chapter at which our reading has now come to rest. And the Father "called" Christ, because for our salvation he had made his way to us and had "come down from heaven" to us: "for no one has ascended into heaven except him who came down from heaven, the Son of man". The great Isaiah thus speaks of the Divine nature with reference to these doctrines, in his exalted utterance,—who speaks in the person of the Deity, "I am the first, and hereafter am I, and no God was before Me, and no God shall be after Me." … Since, then, neither is that God which was before God, nor is that God which is after God, (for that which is after God is the creation, and that which is anterior to God is nothing, and Nothing is not God;—or one should rather say, that which is anterior to God is God in His eternal blessedness, defined in contradistinction to Nothing;)—since, I say, this inspired utterance was spoken by the mouth of the prophet, we learn by his means the doctrine that the Divine Nature is one, continuous with Itself and indiscerptible, not admitting in Itself priority and posteriority, though it be declared in Trinity. Since, then, the saying is the saying of God, whether you grant that the words are the words of the Father or of the Son, the orthodox doctrine is equally upheld by either. For if it is the Father that speaks thus, He bears witness to the Son that He is not "after" Himself: for if the Son is God, and whatever is "after" the Father is not God, it is clear that the saying bears witness to the truth that the Son is in the Father, and not after the Father.
