And you, Israel my servant, Jacob whom I have chosen, seed of Abraham my friend. In whom I took hold of you from the ends of the earth, and called you from its far places, and said to you: You are my servant; I have chosen you and have not cast you off. Do not fear, for I am with you; do not turn aside, for I am your God; I have strengthened you and have helped you and the right hand of my righteous one has upheld you. Behold, all who fight against you will be confounded and will blush; they will be as though they were not; and the men who contradict you will perish. You will seek them and will not find them; the men who rebel against you will be as though they were not; and the men who war against you, as a thing consumed. For I the Lord your God have taken hold of your hand, saying to you: Do not fear, I have helped you. Do not fear, worm Jacob, you who are dead out of Israel. I have helped you, says the Lord, and your redeemer is the Holy One of Israel. I have made you like a new threshing wagon, having sawing teeth. You will thresh the mountains and crush them, and you will make the hills like dust. You will winnow them, and the wind will carry them off, and the whirlwind will scatter them; and you will exult in the Lord, you will rejoice in the Holy One of Israel. LXX: But you, Israel my child, Jacob whom I have chosen, seed of Abraham whom I loved, whom I took up from the ends of the earth, and from its heights I called you, and said to you: You are my child; I have chosen you and have not forsaken you. Do not fear, for I am with you, lest you go astray; for I am your God, who have strengthened you, and I have helped you, and have made you firm with my righteous right hand. Behold, all your adversaries will be confounded and will blush; for they will be as though they were not; and all your enemies will perish. You will seek them and will not find them, the men who will rage against you. For they will be as though they were not, and those who fight against you will not be. For I am the Lord your God, who hold your right hand, who say to you: Do not fear, Jacob, little Israel. I have helped you, says God, I who redeem you, the Holy One of Israel. Behold, I have made you like the new wheels of a threshing wagon, in the manner of saws; and you will thresh the mountains and crush the hills, and you will make them like dust and winnow them, and the wind will carry them off, and the tempest will scatter them. But you will rejoice in the Lord and in the holy ones of Israel. That there is a fleshly Jacob and Israel and a spiritual one, the Apostle Paul teaches: Behold Israel according to the flesh (1 Cor 10). From this we understand that there is also another according to the spirit; and to the fleshly Israel it is said: If you were sons of Abraham, you would do the works of Abraham. To them also it is said above (cf. Isa 40:27): Why do you say, Jacob, and speak, Israel: My way is hidden from the Lord, and my judgment has passed away from my God? Now, on the contrary, God speaks to the spiritual Israel, which received the coming of its Lord, which he calls first servant, then chosen, and finally the seed of Abraham. For first we received the spirit of bondage in fear (Rom 8); and afterward, being chosen, we are joined in friendship with God. So after the calling of the nations, when the islands saw and feared, the ends of the earth were astounded, drew near and came, the remnant according to the election of grace is called, of whom the Gospel also writes: These twelve Jesus chose, whom he also named Apostles (Luke 6); who, after the bondage of the Law as tutor, were chosen in the Gospel, and were found worthy to be the seed of Abraham the friend of God.
Commentary on Isaiah

For in him he took hold of them from the end of the earth, and from its far-off borders he called Israel out of all the nations, gathering first the people of the Jews, of whom the Apostle Paul also says: It was necessary that the word be preached first to you; but since you turn us away, we go to the nations (Acts 13:46).
AGAINST EUNOMIUS 2:15

For to none other than to God does it belong to implant courage in the fearful, saying to the faint-hearted, "Fear not, for I am with thee, be not dismayed," as says the Psalmist, "Yea though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death I will fear no evil, for Thou art with me." Nay, the Lord Himself says to the fearful,—"Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid," and, "Why are ye fearful, O ye of little faith?" and, "Be of good cheer, it is I, be not afraid," and again, "Be of good cheer: I have overcome the world."
Commentary on Isaiah

To you, therefore, who are both my servant and my chosen one, who are to preach among the nations and to suffer very many persecutions, I say: Do not fear, for I am with you, to whom I speak in the Gospel: Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age (Matt 28:20). Do not go astray, nor turn aside from the truth, nor deceive yourself with a false persuasion that by your own strength, unskilled and naked, you will penetrate the forest of the nations and call the fiercest peoples to gentleness. It is I who have strengthened you and have helped you; and the right hand of my righteous one has upheld you, or protected you, that is, of the Lord the Savior; or my right hand, as the Seventy translated.
Commentary on Isaiah

For behold, your adversaries, the people of the Jews, and all who fight against you, and your persecutors, will be turned into nothing, and you will seek your adversaries and will not find them. And the reason is given why he does not find his adversaries: Because they will be as though they were not. These adversaries are said to rage against the Apostles, or, according to the Hebrew, to be consumed.
Commentary on Isaiah

And for this reason you ought not to fear, because I have taken hold of your hand, I who say to you: Do not fear, I have helped you; do not fear, worm Jacob, you who are dead out of Israel, or, as the Seventy have it, very few out of Israel. What we have set down, I have helped you: do not fear, worm Jacob, is not found in the Seventy. Now the worm, which in Hebrew is called THOLATH (תולעת), is the name given, for its lowliness and contempt, to the choir of the Apostles, imitating the Savior, who speaks in the psalm: I am a worm, and no man, a reproach of men, and the outcast of the people (Ps 21 [22]:7). For as a worm penetrates the earth, so the apostolic word penetrated the cities of the nations, and entered first into the hardest hearts. And rightly they are called few out of Israel, because in comparison with the whole world very few of the Jewish nation believed, to whom the Lord says in the Gospel: Do not fear, little flock (Luke 12:32). Or, according to the Hebrew, dead out of Israel, who say with the Apostle: I die daily (1 Cor 15:31); and elsewhere: I am crucified with Christ. Yet I live, not I; but Christ lives in me (Gal 2:20).
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 3:5.41:11-14

There are many who think of the holy mysteries and the saving message in disrespectful ways, but they amount to nothing, and such impious adversaries will perish. For those who oppose the divine agents of preaching are doing no less than fighting against the teachings of godliness.… For thousands will make war against God's ministers, but these will end up as though they never existed and will clearly be brought low, falling under the machinery of the wrath of God. [Isaiah] tells them to quit relying on human strength and their own foolhardiness, saying, "I am your God who strengthens your arm," that is, I am the one who supports you and makes you prevail in any test. I say to you, "Do not be afraid, O little Israel."
Commentary on Isaiah

And what follows, I have made you like a new threshing wagon, having sawing teeth, signifies this: that the preaching of the Gospel crushes the adverse powers and the spiritual wickedness that lifts itself up against the knowledge of God, which, according to the variety of their pride, are called mountains and hills; and when these are carried off and scattered after the manner of a whirlwind, let Israel exult and rejoice in the Lord, the Holy One of Israel. We can also say that the churchman, having the sawing teeth of the Gospel preaching on a new wagon, which works not in the oldness of the letter but in the newness of the spirit, crushes the hardest hearts of unbelievers, separating the wheat from the chaff and crushing the mountains and hills, that is, all the chiefs of the heretics, so that, crushed and ground down, they are reduced to dust and are taught that they are nothing, so that those who had been wrongly gathered together may be divided for their own good.
Commentary on Isaiah

The needy and the poor seek water, and there is none; their tongue is parched with thirst. I the Lord will hear them; I the God of Israel will not forsake them. I will open rivers on the sloping hills, and fountains in the midst of the plains. I will make the desert into a pool of waters, and the trackless land into streams of waters. I will put in the wilderness the cedar and the thorn, and the myrtle, and the olive tree. I will set in the desert the fir, the elm and the box together, that they may see and know and consider and understand together that the hand of the Lord has done this, and the Holy One of Israel has created it. LXX: And the poor and the needy will exult; for they will seek water, and there will be none; their tongue has dried up for thirst. I the Lord God will hear them, the God of Israel, and I will not forsake them; but I will open rivers on the mountains, and fountains in the midst of the plains; I will make the desert into marshes, and the thirsty land into watercourses. I will put in a land without water the cedar, and the box, and the myrtle, and the cypress, and the poplar, that they may see and know and think and understand together that the hand of the Lord has done these things, and the Holy One of Israel has shown it. The people of the nations, poor and meager, which did not have the knowledge of the truth, seeks wholesome waters through various teachers and the diverse doctrines of the philosophers, and does not find them, because there are none; their tongue is parched with thirst, without the Law and the Prophets. For, according to the faith of the Gospel, it had spent all its substance on physicians (Luke 8), and could not be freed from the gore of idolatry and the blood of victims.
AGAINST MARCION 3.5
God is not offering his services as a water manager or a farmer when he says, "I will open rivers in a dry land; I will plant in the wilderness the cedar and the box tree."
Commentary on Isaiah

Therefore the Lord, the God of Israel, did not wholly forsake them, nor let them perish for ever, but opened rivers on the sloping hills, or on the mountains, and fountains in the midst of the plains. These rivers took their beginning from that river which is read of in the Psalms: The rush of the river gladdens the city of God (Ps 45 [46]:4); and in another place: The river of God is filled with waters. These waters and fountains flowed from that fountain who speaks through Jeremiah: They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water (Jer 2:13). And above in this same Prophet it is said: They will drink waters from the fountains of the Savior. Of these also it is sung in the Psalms: Bless the Lord God from the fountains of Israel (Ps 67 [68]:27). And he made, he says, the desert into a pool of waters, and the trackless land into streams of waters. Of these waters the Savior too spoke in the Gospel in mystical language (John 4:13-14): Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will not thirst for ever; but the water that I shall give him will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life. And again: If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him, out of his belly will flow rivers of living water (ibid. 7:37-39). But this, says the Evangelist, he spoke of the Holy Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive.
Commentary on Isaiah

Since, then, the multitude of the Church, once a desert, had been watered with life-giving waters, therefore, according to the Seventy, there spring up in it the cedar, and the box, and the myrtle, and the cypress, and the poplar; according to the Hebrew and the other translators, the cedar, the setta, and the myrtle, and the olive tree, and the fir, and the elm, and the box together. These varieties of trees signify the diversity of spiritual grace. And because the nature of the others is known to all, let us discuss only the Hebrew SETTA (שטה), which Theodotion translated thorn. It is a kind of tree growing in the desert, resembling the white thorn, of which all the wood of the ark and the furnishings of the tabernacle were made, which are called Settim (Exod 37): a wood that does not rot and is very light, and that surpasses all woods in solidity and beauty, as much in strength as in sheen. The cedar, too, and the cypress and the myrtle are of the finest fragrance and do not rot. The elm also and the poplar, or the box, are either joined to vines to wed them, or are most fit for various works. And all these are set together in the wilderness, so that not even one string of the Lord's lyre, and no power of the graces of the Church, may seem to be lacking: so that all may understand, and together know in their mind, that the hand of the Lord has accomplished all these things, so that in the dryness of the nations streams of virtues should be found, and in a land once deserted and full of salt the cedar and the cypress and other trees should spring up, whose loftiness and crown hastening toward heavenly things the olive tree should illuminate, which is the nourishment of light and the rest of those who labor.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 3:5.41:16-20

The water was not life-giving. For they were not able to satisfy those who longed for truth from their teachings. Their tongues remained parched from thirst. But I will hear them, says the God of Israel, and I will not abandon them. For he had mercy on the mass of those who strayed and did not leave them without gifts from above, but rather he gave to them in fullness, and this in such a way as is finely described in the verses that follow.… The desert and the land short of water is the region of the Gentiles. The desert that will run dry and barren of any flowering growth, meaning spiritual growth, is the way of shriveling, where the wild trees are those useful only for burning in fire. The water allows the nations to bear fruit. To those who were once thirsty he says, "I will make rivers flow on the mountains," that is, holy people who are enriched by the divine word from above and pour out like flowing streams to the thirsty.
Commentary on Isaiah

Bring your judgment near, says the Lord; bring forward whatever you may have, said the king of Jacob. Let them approach and tell us whatever things are to come; tell the former things that have been, and we will set our heart on them and we will know their last end; and show us the things that are to come. Declare the things that are to come hereafter, and we will know that you are gods. Do good also, or evil, if you can, and let us speak and see together. Behold, you are of nothing: and your work is of that which is not; an abomination is he who has chosen you. LXX: Your judgment is near, says the Lord God; your counsels have come and drawn near, says the king of Jacob. Let them draw near and declare to us the things that are to come; or tell the former things that were, and we will apply our mind, and we will know what the last things are. Tell us also the things to come, and declare the things that are to come at the last, and we will know that you are gods. Do good and evil, and we will marvel, and we will see together whence you are and whence your work is: from a land of abominations they have chosen you. As we said above that there are two Jacobs and two Israels, of those who do not believe and of those who believe in the Lord the Savior, so, when the nations have been called, and rivers and fountains have burst forth in the once desert Church, and it is wonderfully leafy with a variety of trees, all of them full of abundance, those of the nations who refused to believe in Christ are summoned to judgment, to answer why they refused to see and know and consider and understand that the hand of the Lord has done these things and the Holy One of Israel has created all things. Let your idols approach, he says, which you think most mighty. Or bring forward whatever you may have in yourselves, and lay open your counsels: on what ground, with what mind, you refused to receive the manifest truth.
Commentary on Isaiah

And at the same time an apostrophe is made to the idols themselves, which are without sense and possess the faculty neither of hearing nor of answering. Tell us, he says, either things past or things to come, and show your power by the outcome of events. Now this signifies that after the coming of Christ all the idols fell silent. Where is Delphic Apollo, and Loxias, and the Delian, and the Clarian, and the other idols that promised knowledge of the future, which deceived the most powerful kings? Why could they foretell nothing of Christ, nothing of his Apostles, nothing of the ruin and abolition of their temples? If, then, they could not foretell their own destruction, how could they announce what concerned others, whether evil or good? But if anyone says that many things were foretold by idols, it must be known that they always joined falsehood to truth, and so tempered their sentences that whether something good or something evil happened, either could be understood. Such is that oracle to Pyrrhus king of the Epirotes: I say that you, son of Aeacus, the Romans can conquer. And to Croesus: Croesus, having crossed the Halys, will destroy the greatest kingdoms. There is also another sign that idols are not gods: that they can do neither good nor evil. Not that idols, or the demons that sit by idols, have not often done evil; but that, unless power has been granted to them by the Lord, they cannot do it. Indeed, in the Gospel they beg to have power over the herd of swine (Matt 8). And in Job we read that without the Lord's command he [the devil] could not destroy even the beasts and possessions of the holy man (Job 1). Nor is this to be wondered at in God's case, since even the Apostle Paul delivers some to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme (1 Tim 1).
Commentary on Isaiah

Or else it must be said that mute images of men, without sense, can do neither good nor evil, nor know things past nor things to come, because they are of nothing and of that which is not, and it is not so much they as he who worships them that is worthy of abomination. For the idols of the nations are silver and gold, the works of men's hands. They have a mouth, and will not speak (Ps 113 [115]:13). How then can they know and announce things to come, or relate things past, and do good or evil, when they have neither the sense of men nor that of brute animals? Nor does it matter of what material they seem to be made, since all are earthly.
Commentary on Isaiah

The Hebrews interpret the one raised up from the North and coming from the rising of the sun as the Assyrian and the Persian, who came to Jerusalem and trod down all its princes; and none of the idols which they worshiped knew that this would come, but the Lord alone, who punished them for their sins.
Commentary on Isaiah

I have raised up from the North, and he will come from the rising of the sun; he will call upon my name, and he will bring on rulers as mud, and as a potter treading the ground. Who has announced it from the beginning, that we may know; and from the first, that we may say: You are righteous? There is none announcing, nor foretelling, nor hearing your words. The first will say to Zion: Behold, they are here; and to Jerusalem I will give a bearer of good tidings. And I looked, and there was not even any of these who would enter into counsel, and, when asked, would answer a word. Behold, all are unrighteous, and their works are vain; their images are wind and emptiness. LXX: But I have raised up him who is from the North, and him who is from the rising of the sun; they will be called by my name. Let princes come, and as the clay of the potter, and as a potter treading clay, so you will be trodden down. For who will announce to you the things that are from the beginning, that we may know the things that are in the future, and we will say that it is true? There is none who foretells , nor who hears your words. I will give a beginning to Zion, and I will comfort Jerusalem on the way; for of the nations there is none, and of their images there was none who announced; and if I ask them, Where are you from? they will not answer me; for they are your makers, and they lead you astray in vain. He still speaks against the idols, and against those who after the coming of Christ refused to forsake them. And while they remain in error, he says that he himself has raised up the people of the nations from the North. For from the North evils will blaze forth upon all the inhabitants of the earth. And to Jeremiah it is said: What do you see, Jeremiah? And he answered: A pot set on fire, and its face from the face of the North (Jer 1:13). But they are raised up from the North, so that they may believe in him who has come from the rising of the sun, of whom we read above: Who raised up the righteous one from the East, or righteousness? And in another place: Behold a man, the Dayspring is his name (Zech 6:12). He will call them by my name, so that, forsaking their images, they may worship the one God. For he himself says in the Gospel: I have come in the name of my Father, and you did not receive me; another will come in his own name, and you will receive him (John 5:43). He will tread down the princes and rulers and all the pride of the world, and they will be made subject to him as clay to the potter, so that from them he may make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor (Rom 9).
Commentary on Isaiah

These things, which, according to prophetic custom, I say that I have done as though they were already past, or, according to Symmachus, which I promise as future, none of the demons and idols can foretell. Hence all the oracles fell silent, because there is no one who announces, no one who hears, while the once brutish hearts of the Gentiles have understood their error and forsaken false prophecies.
Commentary on Isaiah

And the Lord will speak first to Zion, that is, to his Church, and will say to her: Behold, here are your sons, whom I have given to you through faith in me. And he means the Apostles, who preached the Gospel in the whole world. Zion and Jerusalem differ in name; but as there is one city, so also there is one Church.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 3:5.41:27-28

"I will give a leader to Zion, and I will console Jerusalem as I go." … Again the multitude of those going astray is promised the revealing of the Savior, through whom each one under heaven has been saved and is summoned to the recognition of the truth. So that we could have a guide who would be able and skilled to lead us along the path of salvation, the only-begotten Son of God became a human being. And though he was King by nature in that he is considered to be God and from God the Father and ruler of all things with all creation under his feet, he is said to be elected king among us.
Commentary on Isaiah

Let all the nations, therefore, which follow the error of idols, be questioned by us, so that they may answer whence they are. And this will be the answer of them all: that all follow vanity and the winds, and worship the works of their own hands. Whatever we have said of the idols and the nations, let us refer to the doctrines of perversity, and to their chiefs, the heresiarchs: that while Christ announces the peace of the Church and shows them the way of truth, they follow error and are likened to wind and whirlwind.

n: My servant. Christ, who, according to his humanity, is the servant of God, (Challoner) and Redeemer of others; none else being able to satisfy for themselves. (Worthington) (Philippians ii. 7.) (Calmet) --- This passage clearly refers to the Messias, (Chaldean; Kimchi) who was prefigured by Cyrus, ver. 6. (Calmet) (Hugo.) --- It is quoted by St. Matthew (xii. 18.) who has some variations both from the Hebrew and the Septuagint, (Calmet) particularly the first part of ver. 4., which the Septuagint renders, "He shall shine, and shall not be broken."
Islands. Septuagint and St. Matthew, "the Gentiles shall hope in his name." (Haydock)
Gentiles. This was literally verified in Christ. Cyrus is also styled the just, (chap. xli. 26.) and gave liberty to many nations.
House. The Jews out of captivity, prefigured the redemption of mankind. These miracles proved that Jesus was the Messias, Luke vii. 22.
Things. They shall not partake of my divinity. Our Saviour was truly God, Philippians ii. 6.
Them. The completion of former predictions enforces the belief of those which are yet to come. (Calmet)
All. Literally, "its fullness," (Haydock) sailors, (Calmet) and fishes. (Haydock) --- He concludes with a canticle.
Cedar, or the Jews in exile in the desert Arabia, Psalm cxix. 5. (Calmet) --- The people dwell in tents. (Roger. ii. 5.) --- Petra. A city that gives name to Arabia Petræa. (Challoner)
Enemies. The Chaldeans, (Calmet) by the hand of Cyrus.

Pools. Cyrus deluged the country about Babylon, chap. xiii., and xxi. 1. (Haydock) --- The proud and covetous, who expected Christ to give them kingdoms, were deceived. He came to teach humility, and to grant eternal rewards. (Worthington)
Blind captives, or converts to Christianity.
Deaf Jews, who would not listen to the prophets, ver. 19. (Calmet)
Sold. Hebrew Cimshullam, (Haydock) the perfect, or favoured. The Turks call "believers" Musselmans. (Calmet)
Men, whom they corrupt by their bad example. (Haydock) --- Hebrew, "their young men are in chains," during the last wars, and the captivity of Juda. (Calmet)
We. Septuagint, "they have sinned," which seems preferable. (Haydock)

f: Life of St. Anthony 35

It is possible, with the help of God, easily to distinguish the presence of the good and the bad; a vision of the holy ones is not agitated. "He shall not protest and cry out; none will hear his voice." It occurs so quietly and gently that joy and gladness and confidence are at once born in the soul.… The soul's thoughts remain untroubled and calm, so that, enlightened of itself, it contemplates those who appear. LIFE OF ST.
Commentary on Isaiah

Behold my servant, I will uphold him; my chosen one, in him my soul is well pleased. I have put my spirit upon him; he will bring forth judgment to the nations. He will not cry out, nor will he accept a person, nor will his voice be heard outside. A bruised reed he will not break, and smoking flax he will not quench; in truth he will bring forth judgment. He will not be sad nor troubled, until he sets judgment in the earth; and the islands will wait for his law. LXX: Jacob my child, I will take him up; Israel my chosen one, my soul has received him. I have put my spirit upon him; he will bring forth judgment to the nations; he will not cry out, nor will he let go, nor will his voice be heard outside. A broken reed he will not break, and smoking flax he will not quench; but in truth he will bring forth judgment. He will shine and will not be broken, until he sets judgment upon the earth; and in his name the nations will hope. Jacob and Israel are not found in the present passage, which the Evangelist Matthew too did not set down, following the Hebrew truth. We say this to the shame of those who despise our work. This has been discussed more fully in the little Commentaries on Matthew, and in the book which we recently wrote to Algasia. Meanwhile it must be noted that where it is written of the choir of the Apostles, they are called both Jacob and Israel and the seed of Abraham, to whom, as to men and servants, it is said accordingly: Do not fear, worm Jacob, and Israel small in number. But where the prophecy is of Christ, it is read without Jacob and Israel: Behold my servant, I will uphold him; my chosen one, in him my soul is well pleased. And in what follows: I have given you as a covenant of the race, as a light of the nations, to open the eyes of the blind, and to bring the bound out of their chains, and those who dwell in darkness out of the prison house. Nor is it to be wondered at if he is called a servant, made of a woman, made under the law (Gal 4); he who, though he was in the form of God, humbled himself, taking the form of a servant, and was found in fashion as a man (Phil 2). In him the soul of God was well pleased, seeing that all virtues were in him; nay rather, that he himself was the power and wisdom of God. I have put, he says, my spirit upon him: the Spirit who descended in the form of a dove. He will bring forth judgment to the nations, which before they did not know.
Commentary on Matthew

Behold my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved, and the rest. This is said through the prophet Isaiah in the person of the Father: I will put my Spirit upon him. The Spirit is put not upon the Word of God and upon the Only-begotten who came forth from the bosom of the Father, but upon him of whom it was said: Behold my servant.
Letter 121, Chapter 2

What does it mean that it is written in Matthew: 'A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench' (Matthew 12:20). For the explanation of this passage, the whole testimony that Matthew takes from the Prophet Isaiah must be set forth, even the words of Isaiah (Isaiah 42): according to the Septuagint interpreters and the Hebrew itself, to which Theodotus, Aquila, and Symmachus agree. Thus of the four Evangelists, only Matthew relates: "And Jesus knowing it, retired from thence: and many followed him, and he healed them all. And he charged them that they should not make him known. That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Isaias the prophet, saying: Behold my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved in whom my soul hath been well pleased. I will put my spirit upon him, and he shall shew judgment to the Gentiles." (Chapter 12, verses 15-18) He will not strive, nor cry out, nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets. A bruised reed he will not break, and smoking flax he will not extinguish, until he brings forth judgment unto victory. And in his name the Gentiles will hope" (Matthew 12:15 and following). For which in Isaiah, according to the Septuagint interpreters, it is thus written: "Jacob my servant, I will uplift him. My chosen one, my soul has received him. I have given my spirit upon him, he shall bring forth judgment to the Gentiles. He shall not cry, nor have respect to person, neither shall his voice be heard abroad. The bruised reed he shall not break: and smoking flax he shall not extinguish: but he shall bring forth judgment unto truth. He shall shine, and shall not be broken, until he set judgment in the earth: and the countries shall wait for his law." However, we translate it from Hebrew like this, "Behold my servant, I will uphold him; my chosen, my soul has delighted in him. I have given my spirit upon him: he shall bring forth judgment to the Gentiles. "He will not cry out, nor raise his voice, nor make it heard in the street. A bruised reed he will not break, and a smoldering wick he will not snuff out. In truth he will bring forth justice. He will not grow faint or be discouraged till he has established justice on the earth; and the islands will put their hope in his law." This shows that the Gospel writer Matthew, not bound by authority of the old interpretation, dismissed the Hebrew truth and brought forth to the nations, educated in the Law of the Lord, the things he had read in Hebrew as if he were a Hebrew among Hebrews. For if it is to be taken thus, as the Seventy Interpreters have given it: Jacob is my servant, I will receive him; Israel is my chosen, my soul has received him, how do we understand that it has been fulfilled in Jesus, what has been written concerning Jacob and Israel? We read that Blessed Matthew did this not only in this testimony, but also in another place: Out of Egypt I called my son (Hosea 11:2): for which the Seventy translated: Out of Egypt I called his sons. Certainly, if we do not follow the Hebrew truth, it is evident that it does not pertain to the Lord and Savior. For it follows: but they sacrificed to Baalim. And that which is less in the assumed testimony in the Gospel: it shall shine and not be shaken, until he shall place judgment upon the earth, seems to have happened by the error of the first writer who, reading the higher sentence to be finished in the word judgment, thought that the final word of the lower sentence was judgment, and he omitted a few words which were in the middle, that is, between judgment and judgment. And again, that which is read among the Hebrews: And in his law shall the islands hope, Matthew, interpreting the sense rather than the words, put for law and islands, a name and nations. And not only in the present place, but wherever the testimonies of the Evangelists and Apostles from the old Instrument have been brought forth, it should be observed more diligently: not that they followed words, but the sense: and where they differ from the Hebrew in the Septuagint, they expressed the Hebrew sense in their own words. Therefore, the Child of the almighty God, according to the dispensation of assumed flesh, which is sent to us, is called the Savior. To whom and in another place the Father says: It is great for you to be called my child, to gather the tribes of Jacob (Isai. 49.3). This is the vineyard of Sorec, which is interpreted as chosen. This is the beloved son, in whom the soul of God is pleased; not because God has a soul, but because every affection of God is shown in the soul. And it is not surprising if the soul is named in God, when all the members of the human body, according to the laws of tropology, and various intelligences, are said to have it. He also placed his spirit upon him: the Spirit of Wisdom and Understanding, the Spirit of Counsel and Strength, the Spirit of Knowledge and Piety, and the Spirit of the Fear of the Lord (Isaiah 11): He who descends upon him in the form of a dove, about whom John the Baptist narrates having heard from God the Father: "The One upon whom you see the Holy Spirit descending and remaining upon, He is" (John 1:33). And He will announce judgment to the Gentiles; concerning whom it is also written in the Psalms: "Give the king your justice, O God, and your righteousness to the son of a king" (Psalm 71:1). He Himself speaks about it in the Gospel: "For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son" (John 5:22). He will not contend: like a lamb led to the slaughter: He will not argue in the hearing. Nor will he cry out, in accordance with what the Apostle Paul writes: Let all clamor, and anger, and bitterness be taken away from you (Ephesians 4:31). He will not cry out: because Israel did not do justice, but cry out. Nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets or outdoors. For all the glory of the daughter of the king is within (Psalm 44:14): And, Narrow, and cramped is the way that leads to life (Matthew 7:14). Therefore his voice is not heard in the streets, where wisdom confidently acts, not entering a broad and spacious way, but accusing and condemning. And so he spoke to those who were outside, not in his own voice, but in parables: 'The reed, he said, shaken does not break; or, as the Septuagint translated, the broken reed not to be crushed. The broken reed that was once vocal, and sang in praise of the Lord, is called Israel, who, because he stumbled on a corner stone and fell on it, was broken in it; therefore it is said of him: Rebuke, O Lord, the beasts of the reed (Ps. 67. 31): and in the volume of Jesus he is called the torrent of the cane, that is, of the reed; who has turbid waters, which Israel chose, despising the purest streams of the Jordan: and turning his mind back to Egypt, and desiring the marshy and swampy region, and pumpkins, and onions, and garlic, and cucumbers, and the pots of Egyptian flesh, is rightly called a broken reed by Isaiah: he who wants to lean on which, his hand will be pierced. For whoever, after the advent of the Lord and Savior and leaving behind the spirit of interpreting the Gospel, rests in the death of Jewish literature, all the works of that person are harmed. Even smoking linen will not extinguish a people gathered from the nations who, with the ardor of natural law extinguished, are wrapped in the bitter smoke, which is hurtful to the eyes, and enveloped in the darkness of errors. He who not only did not restrain and reduce to ashes, but on the contrary, from a small spark, and almost dying, raised the greatest fire; so that the whole world burned with the fire of the Lord and Savior, whom he came to send upon the earth, and in all desires to burn (Luke 12:49). According to the tropology, what we see in this place, we have briefly noted in the Commentaries of Matthew. But he who has not broken the bruised reed, and has not extinguished the smoking flax, has also brought judgment unto victory (Isai. 42:3), whose judgments are true, justified in themselves (Psalm 18), so that he may be justified in his words and may overcome in judgment (Psalm 50), and so that the light of his preaching may shine in the world, not be crushed by anyone, and may overcome all snares, until he establishes judgment on earth and that which is written may be fulfilled: 'Thy will be done on earth, as it is in heaven' (Matthew 6:10). Behold, ye sons of men! behold, all ye people, these new wonders! They suspended Him on the tree, who stretches out the earth; they transfixed Him with nails who laid firm the foundation of the world; they circumscribed Him who circumscribed the heavens; they bound Him who absolves sinners; they gave Him vinegar to drink who hath made them to drink of righteousness; they fed Him with gall who hath offered to them the Bread of Life; they caused corruption to come upon His hands, and feet who healed their hands and feet; they violently closed His eyes who restored sight to them; they gave Him over to the tomb, who raised their dead to life both in the time before His Passion and also whilst He was hanging on the tree.
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 1: WHAT IS GOD?

WHAT IS GOD? — [God is] good, just, merciful. Good, because He brought into existence things that were not; just, because whatever He made to advance He left to the free judgment of their own liberty; yet because they are not so perfect that they cannot fall, He decreed that seeds of law should naturally exist in them, adding the help of revealed law, so that His authority might be complete for humankind; merciful, because He does not quickly repay those who sin, but bears with them so that He may forgive the repentant. He is also severe, so that, through fear, the things well created by Him may be preserved, lest negligence give rise to the downfall of life. And, lest we omit what is more wondrous, His mercy is so great that He endures insults from those He has made and Himself first calls them to peace. Is this not an act of greater power than having created the creature? Yet if His excessive goodness remained without limit in this, it would harm the creature. Therefore He wills that He be at times loved, at times feared, lest those who stray from Him perish. Therefore it is that, lest His patience be thought something to be despised, not indeed to His loss, but altogether to ours, He says: I have kept silence; shall I always keep silence? (Isa. 42:14).

He will also shout and cry aloud against his enemies, openly rebuking their unbelief and declaring with a loud cry: I have held my peace, I have always kept silent, I have been patient, or, as the Seventy translated: I have held my peace; shall I always hold my peace (Eccl 3:7)? So that what is said through Solomon may be fulfilled: A time to keep silence, and a time to speak. And when I have dried you up and destroyed you from head to foot, then I will make the rivers of my teaching run in the islands of the nations, and I will reduce your pools or marshes to dryness, so that among the nations there may be the knowledge of the Scriptures, and among you the dryness of teaching.

Which same truth he conveys by the Prophet in few words, saying, "I have long time holden my peace, I have been still and refrained myself; now will I cry like a travailing woman." In the section we examined and read previously, he delivered a prophecy of the covenant in Christ and the graces bestowed by him, for he said that he would "make a way in the desert and rivers in the dry land," and because of this he would be blessed by "all the wild animals of the field." The praise-giving is to be understood as a spiritual sacrifice and fruit of the new covenant in Christ. In the present passage, however, he tries to assure Israel that they had been redeemed from Egypt, rescued from the slavery that they endured there and freed from such intolerable labors, not so that they would offer him calves and thus secure access to him through blood and smoke—for such things are repugnant to God, and shadow rather than reality.That is why he says: "I have not called you now, O Jacob." The word "now" ought to be understood to mean, "Not when you were offering sacrifices," that is, "I have not called you when you were sacrificing oxen and slaughtered sheep, so that you should not think that you had been redeemed as a reward for the offerings." Rather, it was when you were still in sin and guilty of defilement, for you had worshiped the gods of the Egyptians, that I deemed you worthy of mercy and love. So the gift is one of gentleness, and the fruit of loving-kindness is mercy, and the redemption came from love. The sheep of your burnt offering are nothing to me, he says, nor did you glorify me with your sacrifices. After all, how can that which is wholly unacceptable and offered in vain contribute to my glory? You did not serve me with your sacrifices. The one who pursues any good deed, he says, who achieves the character that leads to virtue, who bends his neck in submission to my decrees, who puts the teachings of the prophets into practice, could be said to serve the God who is over all. As for the one who fills the holy tent with incense, who offers oxen or sheep, or who performs successfully any of the other fine actions, that one will not genuinely glorify me. Such a person, in fact, has done nothing at all that pleases me. So then, service does not consist in offering sacrifice, but in being prepared to submit a tender neck, that willingly submits to his wishes. … Everywhere he rejected worship in shadows, leading them away from types, and drawing them to the justification which is in Christ, and teaching them to be refashioned according to the way of life taught by the gospel, by which alone it is possible to do what is pleasing to God, and come to truly blameless and sincere worship—that is, worship that is spiritual. For it says, "God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and in truth."

Thus says the Lord, the King of Israel, and his redeemer, the Lord of hosts: I am the first and I am the last, and besides me there is no God. Who is like me? Let him call and declare, and set out the order for me, since I established the ancient people; let them declare to them the things to come and the things that shall be. Do not fear, nor be troubled: from that time I have made you hear, and I have declared; you are my witnesses. Is there a God besides me, and a former whom I have not known? The makers of an idol are all nothing, and their most beloved things will not profit them. They themselves are their witnesses, that they do not see nor understand, so that they may be confounded. Who has formed a god, and cast a graven image that is profitable for nothing? Behold, all its partners will be confounded; for the craftsmen are of men; they will all assemble, they will stand, and they will be afraid, and they will be confounded together. The ironsmith has worked with the file; with coals and with hammers he has formed it, and he has worked with the arm of his strength. He will hunger and faint, he will not drink water, and he will grow weary. The carpenter has stretched out the rule he has formed it with the plane; he has made it with the corner tools, and turned it with the compass; and he has made the image of a man, like a handsome man dwelling in a house. He cut down cedars, he took the holm oak and the oak that had stood among the trees of the forest. He planted a pine, which the rain nourished; and it became fuel for men; he took from them and was warmed; he kindled it and baked bread. But of the rest he has made a god, and has worshiped it; he has made a graven image, and has bowed down before it. Half of it he burned in the fire, and on half of it he ate flesh. He cooked a stew and was filled, and was warmed, and said: Aha! I am warm, I have seen the fire. But the rest of it he made into a god and a graven image for himself; he bows down before it and worships it, and prays to it, saying: Deliver me, for you are my god. They have not known, nor understood; for they have forgotten, so that their eyes may not see, so that they may not understand with their heart. They do not consider in their mind, nor know, nor perceive, so as to say: Half of it I burned in the fire, and on its coals I baked bread; I cooked flesh and ate, and of the rest of it shall I make an idol? Shall I fall down before the trunk of a tree? Part of it is ash; a foolish heart has worshiped it; and he has not delivered his soul, nor will he say: Perhaps there is a lie in my right hand. After the preaching of the Apostles, the calling of the nations, the coming of the Savior, and the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, whom he promised he would give to all believers, when, according to the variety of their merits, one will say, I am the Lord's; another will call in the name of Jacob; another will write with his hand that he is the Lord's, and, though sprung from the unbelieving crowd of the Gentiles, will be likened in the name of Israel, so that, forsaking idols, he may be a worshiper of the one God, another περικοπὴ begins, which we have set out whole at once, so as not to divide the continuity of a single sense. And because the Seventy in this passage, except for a few words, do not differ from the Hebrew, we have been content with our own edition, and when it has been understood, the others too will be known. The discourse is against the idolaters of that time when the prophet Isaiah was announcing things to come to the peoples, and it reproves those who, despising the religion of Almighty God, bow down to wooden images and worship the works of their own hands. Let us run through it, then, point by point. Thus says the Lord, the King of Israel, which is to believe in me, and his redeemer, which will receive the coming of my Son: the Lord of hosts, and of powers, and the Almighty. For this is what SABAOTH (צבאות) means in Hebrew. I am the first, and I am the last, I am the Α and the Ω; and besides me there is no God, because the child whom I have chosen is God in me. Of him I said above: Behold my child, whom I have chosen; my chosen one, whom my soul has received; he will bring forth judgment to the nations; and in his name the nations will hope. Nor does he say that he is alone, but that besides his own power and wisdom there is no outside God; and condemning the opinion of many gods, and images, he says: Who, he says, is like me?

And when the prophet says concerning the creation, "That stretches forth the heavens alone," and when God says, "I only stretch out the heavens," it is made plain to everyone that in the "Only" is signified also the Word of the Only, in whom "all things were made" and without whom "was made not one thing." Therefore, if they were made through the Word, and yet he says, "Only," and together with that Only is understood the Son, through whom the heavens were made, so also then, if it is said, "One God," and "I Only," and "I the First," in that "One" and "Only" and "First" is understood the Word co-existing, as in the Light the Radiance. And this can be understood of no other than the Word alone. For all other things subsisted out of nothing through the Son and are greatly different in nature, but the Son himself is natural and true offspring from the Father. And thus the very passage that these insensate have thought fit to adduce, "I the First," in defense of their heresy, does rather expose their perverse spirit. For God says, "I the first, and I the last"; if then, as though ranked with the things after him, he is said to be first of them, so that they come next to him, then certainly you will have shown that he himself precedes the works in time only; which, to go no further, is extreme irreligion. But if it is in order to prove that he is not from any, nor any before him, but that he is Origin and Cause of all things and to destroy the Gentile fables that he has said, "I the first," it is plain also that when the Son is called firstborn, this is done not for the sake of ranking him with the creation but to prove the framing and adoption of all things through the Son. For as the Father is first, so also is [the Son] both first, as image of the First, and because the First is in him, and also offspring from the Father, in whom the whole creation is created and adopted into sonship.
Commentary on Isaiah

Thus says the Lord, your redeemer, and your former from the womb: I am the Lord who makes all things, who alone stretches out the heavens, who establishes the earth, and there is none with me; who makes void the signs of the diviners, and turns the soothsayers to madness; who turns the wise backward, and makes their knowledge foolish; who raises up the word of his servant, and fulfills the counsel of his messengers; who say to Jerusalem: You will be inhabited , and to the cities of Judah: You will be built, and I will raise up its deserts; who say to the deep: Be desolate, and I will dry up your rivers; who say to Cyrus: You are my shepherd, and you will fulfill all my will; who say to Jerusalem: You will be built; and to the temple: You will be founded. LXX: Thus says the Lord who redeemed you, and who forms you from the womb: I am the Lord who accomplish all things; I alone stretched out the heaven, and made firm the earth. Who else has scattered the signs of the pythons, and divinations from the heart? I who turn the prudent backward, and make their counsel foolish; and I establish the word of my child, and prove true the counsel of his angels; who say to Jerusalem: You will be inhabited; and to the cities of Judah: You will be built, and its deserts will spring up; who say to the abyss: You will be made desolate, and I will dry up your rivers; who say to Cyrus that he should be wise, and do all my wishes; who say to Jerusalem: You will be built; and I will lay the foundations of my holy house. When the idols and the iniquities of Israel have been destroyed and its sins blotted out, when the whole creation will rejoice together, and, according to the faith of the Gospel (Luke 15), the angels in heaven will rejoice over the repentance of sinners, the power of God is described: that it is in no way a great thing for him to redeem Jacob and to restore an upright heart in Israel, whom he formed from the womb. And if this should seem no small thing to anyone, let it not be difficult for him who alone stretched out the heavens; according to what is read elsewhere: Who stretches out the heaven like a skin (Ps 103 [104]:2). Not that the Son is excluded from the stretching out of the heavens, For all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made (John 1:3); but that, as we have often said, the idols are excluded by this sentence. For in the Proverbs of Solomon too it is said in the person of Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God: When he was preparing the heaven, I was with him (Prov 8:27). For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created (Ps 148; Ps 32 [33]:9); and: By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and all their power by the spirit of his mouth (Ps 32 [33]:6). We press these points frequently, so that no occasion may be left to the heretics for blaspheming Christ. In the establishing of the earth too, when he was making its foundations solid, there was no one with God except him who was in him.

And he who restores Jerusalem and destroys Babylon also says to Cyrus, king of the Persians, who first destroyed Babylon and the Chaldeans: You are my shepherd, or, as the Seventy translated, that he should be wise. The cause of this difference is plain. For if we read the Hebrew word ROI with the letter RES (רעי), it is understood as my shepherd; if with DALETH (דעי), as knowing or my understanding one; and the likeness of these letters is distinguished by a small stroke, and for this reason they are often confused. It is written at the beginning of Ezra that at the edict of Cyrus, king of the Persians and Medes, the captivity of the people of Israel was loosed, and those who wished to return were sent back to Jerusalem under Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, and Jeshua son of Jozadak, the high priest. For the Lord inspired him to do his will and to fulfill his commands. And significantly he added, who say to Jerusalem: You will be built; and to the Temple: You will be founded. For under Cyrus it was ordered that Jerusalem and the Temple be built, but while he lived only the foundations of the Temple were laid. For the rest, under Darius, in his second year, when Haggai and Zechariah prophesied, the Temple began to be built.

"Thus says the Lord God to my Christ [the] Lord, whose right hand I have held, that the nations may hear him, 'the powers of kings will I burst asunder; I will open before him the gates, and the cities shall not be closed to him.' " This very thing we see now fulfilled. For whose right hand does God the Father hold but Christ's, his Son? All nations have heard of him, that is, people of all nations have believed. Their preachers, the apostles, are pointed to in the psalms of David: "Into the entire earth," he says, "is gone out their sound, and to the ends of the earth their words." For on whom else have nations the world over believed but on the Christ who has now already come?… In all these places the name of the Christ has already come to reign. He is the one before whom the gates of all cities have been opened and to whom none are closed, before whom iron bars have been crumbled and brazen gates opened. There is a spiritual sense affixed to these expressions. The hearts of individuals, having been blockaded in various ways by the devil, are now unbarred by the faith of Christ. This promise has already been evidently fulfilled, inasmuch as in all these places there are people who live believing in the name of Christ.

Thus says the Lord to my anointed, Cyrus, whose right hand I have taken hold of, to subdue nations before his face, and I will turn the backs of kings, and I will open doors before him, and the gates will not be shut. I will go before you, and I will humble the glorious ones of the earth; I will break the gates of bronze, and I will shatter the bars of iron. And I will give you hidden treasures and the secrets of hidden places, that you may know that I am the Lord, who call your name, the God of Israel. For the sake of my servant Jacob, and Israel my chosen, I have also called you by your name; I have likened you, and you have not known me. I am the Lord, and there is none besides; apart from me there is no God; I girded you, and you have not known me; that they may know, those who are from the rising of the sun and those who are from the west, that besides me there is none. I am the Lord, and there is no other. I form light and create darkness; I make peace and create evil. I am the Lord who does all these things. I know that in this passage very many, not only of the Latins but of the Greeks, err badly, thinking that it is written: Thus says the Lord to my anointed, the Lord; so that it may be understood according to what we read elsewhere: The Lord rained from the Lord (Gen 19:24); and: The Lord said to my Lord (Ps 109 [110]:1). For it says not κυρίῳ, which means Lord, but Cyrus, who in Hebrew is called CHORES (כרש), the king of the Persians, who overcame Babylon and the Chaldeans; and, joined with the Medes, he is read of above as the driver of a two-horse chariot, that is, of the camel and the ass. He was called Christ, that is, the anointed of the Lord, because this was the mark of royal power among the Hebrews; so that, as among us the diadem and the purple are given to emperors alone, so among the Hebrews those who were to reign were anointed with ointment. Hence Saul too is called the Lord's anointed (1 Sam 6). And in the Psalms we read: Do not touch my anointed ones, and do no harm to my prophets (Ps 104 [105]:15).

QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 97: REFUTING THE WICKEDNESS OF ARIUS FROM THE LAW

BY WHAT REASONING CAN THE WICKEDNESS OF ARIUS BE SIMPLY REFUTED FROM THE LAW? — If we grant authority to reason, the very meaning of the names “Father” and “Son” shows their unity. You ask, how? For the true Son of God would not be so called unless He had come forth from the substance of God the Father. Truth and justice in God would not permit Him to call someone “Son” truly if that Son were not from Himself. He is not truly the Son of God if He is not from Him. But Scripture says He is true; therefore He is from Him. Whoever denies that Christ was born of God does an injustice to Scripture, which calls Him the true Son of God precisely in order to signify that He was born of God. For if He is not from God, and yet is called the true Son of God, then Scripture is deceitful. But if Scripture does not deceive, then whoever does not confess that Christ came forth from God both nullifies Scripture and denies Christ to be the true Son of God. It is not will that makes a true Son, but birth. “But,” they say, “this falls under the power of God, that He can make what is false into true.” On the contrary, this is the power of God, for which He is worthy of all praise: that what is true with Him is true, and what is false is false. That is the mark of a liar, to call the false true; this does not apply to God. For God can indeed do all things, but He does nothing except what accords with His truth and justice. It is, then, clear that Christ is called the true Son of God so that He may be understood as His own Son, that is, born of His substance. Therefore the Apostle says: “He who did not spare His own Son” (Rom. 8:32); and in another Epistle: “Who, though He was in the form of God, did not count it robbery to be equal with God” (Phil. 2:6). If then He did not consider it robbery to declare Himself equal with God, He thereby showed Himself to be the true Son of God. For He could not be equal with God unless He were from Him. Those are equal who are either both true or both false. Beginning and eternal being, or unity, do not admit equality. By saying that He is one with the Father, Christ makes Himself equal to God. “For not only,” it says, “was He breaking the sabbath, but He also called God His Father, making Himself equal with God” (Jn. 5:18), that is, His peer. Is it not clear that this equality comes down from the property of His birth? In calling Himself God’s own Son, that is, His true Son, He made Himself equal with God. Therefore He says: “He who sees Me, sees also My Father” (Jn. 14:9). Because they are of one substance, he who sees one sees both. “For as the Father has life in Himself, so He has granted to the Son to have life in Himself” (Jn. 5:26); that is, the Father begot the Son equal to Himself; and “all that is the Father’s is the Son’s, and what is the Son’s is the Father’s” (Jn. 17:10); and “no one can snatch anything out of the Father’s hand, nor out of the Son’s hand” (cf. John 10:29). And He adds: “I and the Father are one” (Jn. 10:30); and, “The words that I speak to you, I do not speak from Myself; but the Father who dwells in Me, He Himself speaks; and the works that I do, He does. Believe Me that I am in the Father and the Father in Me; or else believe for the very works’ sake” (Jn. 14:10–12). Since generation is not from oneself but from the One who begets, therefore whatever He does, He calls it the Father’s work, so that by all these things it may be confirmed that Christ is called the true Son of God so that He may be believed to be born of Him, lest His substance be thought to lie outside the nature of the one God. His great humility is therefore His greatest praise. For when He appears to place Himself in subjection, saying, “The words that I speak to you, I do not speak from Myself; but the Father who dwells in Me, He Himself speaks; and the works that I do, He does,” (Jn.14:10) He proves that He has His origin from God and shows that He is His Power, since He says that what He is, is not from Himself but from Him. By this Christ is praised, not lowered. For one who speaks from himself is not a true Son. You see, then, that the Arians misunderstand Christ precisely where He ought to be rightly understood; and they reject Him and call Him false precisely where He is proved to be the true Son of God: for He asks to be glorified by the Father, and promises to glorify the Father whom He asks; and where He seems to humble Himself, He exalts Himself. For when the Father gives testimony to His Son, He bears witness to His own praise; and when the Son proclaims the Father, He reveals His own glory. The majesty and nobility of the Father are the nobility of the true Son. Therefore whatever is said to belong to the Father undoubtedly belongs also to the Son; and whatever is said to belong to the Son belongs also to the Father. For the Spirit is called the Spirit of God, and the same Spirit is called the Spirit of Christ. The Church is called the Church of God, and is called the Church of Christ. God is adored, and Christ is adored. Service is rendered to God, and service is rendered to Christ. The saints are called priests of God, and they are called priests of Christ. The temple of the holy city is said to be God’s, and likewise Christ’s. The holy city is said to be enlightened by the light of God, and in the same way by the light of Christ. It is the throne of God, and also of Christ. God is Judge, and Christ is Judge: for the prophet Isaiah saw the Lord of hosts seated on the throne of majesty, that is, Christ (Isa. 6:1), which the Arians do not deny. Of God the Father it is read that He is King of kings and Lord of lords (1 Tim. 6:15), and the same is read of Christ, the true Son of God (Rev. 17:14; 19:16). Therefore everywhere Father and Son are equated in divinity, so that the number of persons does not go beyond the measure of one God. Between Father and Son there is no difference except this alone: that the Father is unbegotten, but the Son begotten; that is, the Father is from no one, but the Son is from the Father, this, indeed, is sublime in the Son. For from this we learn the eternity of His nobility, and that He is the true Son of the true Father. From where comes that which is read in Genesis, where God says, “Let us make man in Our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26)? Therefore, if their image and likeness are one, how are they not also one in nature? In spiritual realities, where there are, of course, no outward forms, nothing will be similar except by substance; so where the image of two is one, how will their substance not be one as well? Therefore, we read that their image and likeness are one and the same, so that we might believe that the one is in no way different from the other; that is, that Christ is truly the Son of God, because His birth is not unlike that of the One who begets Him. Finally, the Jews, understanding that He called God His own Father, said to Pilate, “We have a Law, and according to the Law He must die, because He made Himself the Son of God” (Jn. 19:7). The Jews understood, and Christians claim they do not understand? Those who did not believe, understood; and those who claim to believe, act so that they may not understand? At least let them admit this: the prophet Isaiah, in order to show that Christ is God, not from Himself indeed, but God from God, says among other things: “After you they shall come, bound in chains, and they shall worship you, and shall pray in you, for in you is God, and there is no God besides you. For you are God, and we did not know it; the God of Israel, the Savior” (Isa. 45:14–15). As far as an upright mind is concerned, these things are clear. By them the Father is shown to be in the Son, and the Son is shown to be God of the same substance as the Father. In Him in whom God is, and besides Him God is not, and He Himself is God, what else can He be said to be, but what God the Father is, and in no respect different? This is what it is for the two to be one. For God is in Him, because although He is God, He is not God from Himself. He is from the Father, because He is the Son. And besides Him there is no God, because He is the only-begotten Son of the Father. But He Himself is God, because the substance of God and of Christ is one and the same. Therefore no uncertainty is left, so that the substance of the Father and of the Son may be believed to be one. For He is the true Son of a true Father. So also is that saying of the prophet Jeremiah; for he says among other things: “This is our God, and another shall not be reckoned with Him. He found out every way of knowledge, and gave it to Jacob His servant, and to Israel His beloved. Afterward He was seen upon the earth and lived among men” (Baruch 3:36–38). Can this be said of one who is of inferior stock, with whom no other can be reckoned? Or can anything be said to be God other than the Father, such that it would advance to God as an insult to the Father? For if no other god can be reckoned with Him, and He is apart from God the Father, see whether what follows ought to be said, for it is dangerous. He would be said to be greater than the Father. Thinking that they are showing reverence to God the Father if they separate the Son from Him, they reduce from Him; so that Him whom they wish to make lesser, with wicked and blinded mind, they set above the One to whose authority they think He ought to bow. But Scripture, in order to teach that the Son differs in nothing from the Father (He would differ if He were not true), says that no other is to be reckoned with Him; because no other substance can be found similar to the substance of God, which is also that of Christ. For it could not teach in any other way that Christ is from God, than by saying that no other can be reckoned with Him. Knowing that the Son of God could in no way be called subject to God the Father, so as to show Him to be equal, it says, “No other shall be reckoned with Him”; because He is equal to God the Father, since He is God: for He is His true Son. Therefore the prophet says, “This is our God”; that is, the God of Israel. If this is He, He Himself is the one God. Of Him Scripture says, “Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. 6:4); and surely this is not the Father, but His Son. You see then that the person of the Son does not prejudice the one God, if He also is called one God: since Scripture bears witness to this. Where does this come from, unless because the Father and the Son are one, since unity is signified not by persons but by nature? Or they are not two in substance, but one; nor two in divinity, but one God: so that whether the Father speaks or the Son speaks, it is said that one God has spoken. For if the Lord Himself, among other things, concerning male and female, says, “They are no longer two, but one flesh” (Mark 10:8); how much more are the Father and the Son not two gods, but one substance? Now that Father and Son are said to be two, the cause is birth; but that they are not again two gods, the cause is the unity of divinity. With what dullness then do they preach that Christ is created, that is, made, when it is read that God made nothing without Christ (Jn. 1:3)? If therefore nothing was made without Him, He Himself will not be a thing made. For if He is a thing made, something was made without Him. But far be it; for nothing was without Him. Being born of God, He did not begin to exist, but has always existed. For birth is nothing else than proceeding forth; and proceeding forth is revealing. Therefore He was not made, but brought forth. And in order that Christ might be shown to have gone forth or proceeded from the essence of God, His birth was called a proceeding forth; so that, because His birth is not unlike the Begetter, Christ’s consubstantiality with God might be beyond doubt, and that mind which says, “There was a time when He was not,” might be condemned. For He who is read to have proceeded from God, in order that He might be shown to have always been with God, cannot at some time not have been. No one proceeds from God in a place where he was not. The Arians are accustomed to interpret therefore about the Son of God, saying, “Therefore Christ is called the true Son of God, because God made Him in such a way that He is true.” As though there were something false that God makes. And all those things which we said above about the unity of the Father and the Son, what will they be, when they have been so strengthened and confirmed, if it is thought that one must feel differently here? Will many things solidified by divine visions be able to be torn apart by the single testimony of one degenerate? Nevertheless this must be cut off, lest iniquity flatter itself even about this very point. “So,” they say, “He made Him in such a way that He is true, so that will was put in place of birth, and making in place of begetting. For so much must be granted,” they say, “to the power of God, that He can make things which are not, as though they were. Since they rely on this cunning trickery against the Son of God, we must answer them from those very points on which they believe, because they are already convicted in other matters, so that they may appear convicted in the whole sum. For this proposition, as far as its meaning is concerned, has no weight; but as far as the words are concerned, it creates obscurity so that the issue does not quickly appear. For it is as if an Egyptian were placed in the dark, because a bad cause cannot be defended with a good meaning. Therefore, to defend their wickedness, they use sacrilegious words. If, then, this is the power of God, that He could make it true that Christ is His Son, though He was not born from His own being; then He made Him such as He Himself is, so that what generation was going to bestow, the making has accomplished. If, therefore, you say there is no difference between God and Christ, it might perhaps be doubted whether this is not asserted by you unkindly, so that what is said in word might also be in meaning: that because He is called true Son, He may be understood as true, through the fact that He is of one substance with the Father, though not by generation but by making; since, as you say, God can do everything, so that what is made may be as though it were not made. But if, following the rule of reason, you say that what has a beginning cannot be equal and consubstantial with that which is eternal, you lay bare the deceit of your hatred: for, in order to evade the meaning of the word, you falsely say that Christ is truly the Son of God, while denying Him equality with God the Father. For He is not true if He is unequal. Can He be called a true Son, if the Father is not also called true? For if the Son is true, the Father will also be true; and equality proves this truth. But if they are unequal, neither of them is true. Yet since the witness of the Scriptures, by which Christ is approved as the true Son of God, cannot be made void, He must be believed to be born of God the Father: because, in order that this truth might be established, He is read as both equal to and on a par with God. But you, who proclaim the immeasurable power of God, say that God cannot beget, because His nature is simple; and by this you also do an insult to God the Father Himself. For you call Him a liar, since you deny the Son whom He declares to be His own and true; and you betray your hypocrisy, because you falsely proclaim God to be powerful. For if you proclaim the power of God in that which you assert to have been made true out of what was false, so as to mock what is true, how much more ought you to accept this, if you were of sound mind, whereby what is called true is proved true, and the testimony that God the Father gave about His Son is confirmed as true? For the Lord said, “With God,” He says, “all things are possible” (Matt. 19:26), so that whatever seems impossible to men may be possible to God. For if the reasoning of the flesh is followed, neither did a Virgin give birth, nor did Jonah live in the belly of the whale (Jonah 2:1), nor will the dead rise, nor did God beget a Son, because a simple nature cannot beget, since in this world nothing is generated without mixture. All these things must either be believed together or refuted together. For if the reasoning of the world must be maintained, it should have authority in all these matters. But if there is some reasoning proper to spiritual things, he must be called carnal who, infected with the reasoning of the world, denies that anything can be done otherwise than he knows. They are also accustomed to propose something else with their usual evasion. They say, “Did the Father beget the Son by will, or not?” so that when they hear, of course, that it was by will, they may at once, as enemies of the Son of God, reply, “Therefore the will is before the Son,” so that from this He may appear not eternal, since He did not receive a beginning by birth, but came into existence. And yet if they think this, not only will the will be before the Son, but also before the Father; because the cause of generation is the Father and the Son. Unbelief follows carnal notions in everything. For it introduces the cause of God as if He were a man, as though He had first considered and devised that He should beget, as if subject to weakness; whereas in God neither was there generation without will, nor will without generation. For the will itself is generation. Indeed, it is a common expression, “God made,” “man made”; but God makes in one way, man makes in another; and so also in other causes. Therefore must we speak of God as is worthy of Him. They also raise another question about God the Father Himself, saying, “Did it come to Him that He should beget, or is it of His nature always to beget?” They bring this forward so that they may also assert that God is a liar, who testifies that He has begotten Christ, and that they may make Christ not true, but adopted. For, they say, if He has begotten, He must always beget; so that, because He does not always beget, He may not be believed to have begotten Christ: as though it were denied that He made the world, because He does not make others. What disrespect, what lack of discipline it is, to lay down a law for God, so that if He has begotten, He must either have begotten many, or could not have begotten one; not even believing the Lord Himself, who declared Himself the only-begotten Son of God. After these things which have been shown above to be equal in the Father and the Son, let us see whether what is written about the Holy Spirit agrees with them, so that the Trinity which we hold in our saving profession may not admit a difference of nature, just as it has no diversity of faith. For although there is no salvation without any one of these, yet their power appears to be one, which gives salvation to those who believe in it. Since we have brought forward the words of the Father as testimony to the Son, now, as testimony to the Holy Spirit, let us use the words of the Son, by which he declares that the Holy Spirit does not differ from himself: so that, as the Father is witness with the Son, and the Son is witness to the Holy Spirit, the Trinity may be understood to be of one nature. The Lord therefore says among other things: I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, that he may be with you forever, the Spirit of truth (Jn. 14:16–17). When he says that another Paraclete is to be sent, he clearly shows that he himself is a Paraclete. For this is read also in the Epistle of John; he says: We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ, who intercedes for our sins (1 Jn. 2:1). And again the Lord says, I am the truth (Jn. 14:6). Behold the clear unity of the Holy Spirit and the Son of God. For what the Son says about himself, he says likewise about the Holy Spirit. Now we must set forth what Scripture arranges in this sense. It is read in Isaiah that he saw the Lord of hosts seated on a throne of majesty (Isa. 6:1), whom John the Evangelist understood to be Christ, saying among other things, These things said Isaiah when he saw his majesty, and spoke about him (Jn. 12:41). The Apostle says that this one is the Holy Spirit. For he says in the last part of the Acts of the Apostles, Well did the Holy Spirit speak to your fathers, saying, With hearing you shall hear and shall not understand, etc. (Acts 28:25–26). These words were spoken by the Lord of hosts. This is the one God, who, whether he be understood as the Father, or the Son, or the Holy Spirit, is not contrary to himself, because one is their divinity and one their power. For if, in an decree from the praetorium of one captain, the other captains also are said to command, because of the authority of a single power, how much more, under the rule of one God, if one of the three has spoken, will it not be unsuitable to say that the three have spoken? For their nature and will are one. They are also accustomed to prejudice the Holy Spirit by claiming that he must therefore be considered inferior, because he is placed third in order; though there is such simplicity in the divine Scriptures that you sometimes find the third placed first. As the occasion requires, so they are set down. For it is no injury to any of them, because one is their divinity. Indeed we read in Isaiah, with the Lord saying, I am the first, and I am forever: and my hand founded the earth, and my right hand established heaven. And in what follows: I have spoken, I have called, I have brought him, and I have made his way prosperous. Come near to me, and hear these things: I have not spoken in secret from the beginning: from the time that they came to be, I was there, and now the Lord has sent me and his Spirit (Isa. 48:12–13, 15–16). Whom do you suppose to be the one who founded the earth? For it is he who says that he has been sent. Is it the Father? Far from it. It is therefore the Son who says that he has been sent by God and by the Holy Spirit. Behold the equality between the Son and the Holy Spirit.
