For just as the Holy Spirit is read to have been sent by the Father and the Son, so Christ is sent by God and by the Holy Spirit. For this is proper to the Father alone, that he should not be said to be sent. Consider the words of the Apostle, who in another order embraces the Trinity: for he says among other things in the second Epistle to the Thessalonians, May the Lord direct your hearts into the love of God and into the patience of Christ (2 Thess. 3:5). Whom do you think he calls “the Lord,” if not the Holy Spirit? And what is strange in this, since he whom Isaiah saw seated on the throne of majesty, this same one he calls the Holy Spirit, the Lord of hosts, as we showed above. And the Apostle John signifies that God is understood in the Holy Spirit, saying among other things, In this we have known that God remains in us, by the Holy Spirit whom he has given us (1 Jn. 4:13). If therefore it is through his Spirit that he himself remains in us, it is not in doubt that the Holy Spirit is of God. And there is no question that whatever is of God is God. From this the Apostle says, No one knows the things that are in God except the Spirit of God (1 Cor. 2:11). How can he know the things that are in God unless he is of the same divinity? For a lower nature cannot know what is in a higher; how much less could a creature know what was in its Creator? And to the Corinthians, in the first Epistle, departing from the usual order which is in the tradition of the faith, he begins with the Holy Spirit when he recalls the workings of graces and mysteries; and he adds the Lord Jesus; and in the third place he sets God, whom he says to be working in the Holy Spirit and in the Lord (ibid. 12:4–6): just as the Lord also says, The Father, remaining in me, he himself does the works (Jn. 14:10). For through that by which the Holy Spirit and Christ are “of God the Father,” their working is the work of God. In fact he calls the Holy Spirit also “Lord,” and he calls the Lord also “God,” because of the unity of nature. Therefore, since in this place he says that the same one who is God and Lord works all things in all, he concludes below, saying, But all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each as he wills (1 Cor. 12:11). What is more evident, that the three have one operation? For when one works, the three are said to work; why, except because they are of one divinity? For there is no doubt that the gift of graces is properly worked by the Holy Spirit. But in order to teach that God and Lord and the Holy Spirit are one because of the sameness of nature, he shows that the work of the Holy Spirit is the work of the three. And to make clear that, as far as person is concerned, this work is the Holy Spirit’s alone, he says, But all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each as he wills. Therefore he acts as he wills, because his will is the will of God. For he does not say “as God wills,” but “as the Spirit wills.” A creature compels itself to do the will of God; but the Holy Spirit wills this by nature. And in order that it may clearly shine forth that the Holy Spirit works all things, the Lord says among other things: “If I by the finger of God cast out devils,” etc. (Luke 11:20). He calls the Holy Spirit the finger of God, to prove that He is from God. Finally, He testifies that the Jews, who said that He cast out devils by Beelzebub, the prince of devils, blasphemed against the Holy Spirit. Moses also, because he worked signs through the Holy Spirit, is acknowledged by the magicians, who say, “This is the finger of God” (Exod. 8:19). For in the Acts of the Apostles we read: “As they were ministering to the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said: Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them” (Acts 13:2). Behold, service is rendered to the Lord, and the Holy Spirit claims this for Himself. From this it plainly appears that He is Lord, just as God the Father is. And Christ called Saul from heaven and sent him to preach (Acts 9:4); and in like manner the Holy Spirit claims this for Himself, saying, “for the work to which I have called them.” For no one is ignorant that the Savior appointed bishops for the Churches. Indeed, before He ascended into heaven, laying His hand upon the Apostles, He ordained them as bishops. The Apostle attributes this to the Holy Spirit when he says: “Take heed to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you bishops, to rule the Church of the Lord Jesus” (Acts 20:28). And among other things Peter says to Ananias: “Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart, that you should lie to the Holy Spirit?” And further on, he says: “You have not lied to men, but to God” (Acts 5:3–4). It is clear that the Holy Spirit is called God, since Ananias, who lied to the Holy Spirit, is said to have lied to God. If he had in no way wished the Holy Spirit to be understood as God, he would have said, “You have not lied to men, but to the Holy Spirit,” so that he would indicate Him as neither God nor man. And what is surprising in this? For the Apostle at one time calls a man the temple of God (2 Cor. 6:16), and at another time the temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Cor. 6:19), because by nature they are one. For if the Holy Spirit were in no way understood to be God, with what boldness would he later say, “The temple of God is holy, and that temple are you” (2 Cor. 3:17)? For one God is proclaimed in all the Scriptures; but His mystery is adored in the Trinity. Therefore Scripture so speaks, that under the profession of one God, the things which are of Him, that is, His Son and His Holy Spirit, are understood to be in the same honor in which God Himself is. For the mystery of God has been revealed in order that His glory might be signified in the Trinity. Wherefore, what is from God is not called God with full authority, lest it be believed that another is made apart from Him who is the One. But understanding is given, so that we may believe that in this manner the salvation of the creature consists in the Trinity, because one is their divinity. For neither could the Creator and the creatures, the Lord and the servants, eternity and those things that are under a beginning, be joined together and placed in the same order, since without one of them salvation is for none. For everything that is God, whether the Son or the Holy Spirit, is called so to its injury, if it is reckoned outside the honor and glory of the one God. Therefore the Scriptures show Christ to be God, they show the Holy Spirit to be God, so that, seeing, they may know what He is who is shown. It is as if someone were to show a gem without crying out that it is a gem: just because he does not cry out, will that which is seen not be a gem? In the same way, through the things discussed above, the Scriptures show what we ought to believe, enclosing our understanding within the faith of the one God, in the mystery of the Trinity.
Catechetical Lecture 11:16

Would you receive yet a third testimony to Christ's godhead? Hear Isaiah saying, "Egypt has labored, and the merchandise of Ethiopia," and soon after, "In you shall they make supplication, because God is in you, and there is no God except you. For you are God, and we knew it not, the God of Israel, the Savior." You see that the Son is God, having in himself God the Father, saying almost the very same which he has said in the Gospels. … And again he has not said, "I and the Father am one" but "I and the Father are one," that we should neither separate them nor make a confusion of Son-Father.
Commentary on Isaiah

That Egypt, and the Ethiopians, and the Sabaim, lofty and exalted men, served him, no one doubts, since one sees the world subjected to him, and perceives that, under the name of a few nations which dwell at the furthest ends of the earth, all the hinges of the heavens and all the shores of the earth are to believe in him. Hence it is beautifully said, as to men laboring in the error of idolatry, that the labor of Egypt ceases. For no nation was so given over to idolatry, and venerated such innumerable monstrosities, as Egypt, of which we read above (Isa 19:1): Behold, the Lord will ascend upon a light cloud, and will enter Egypt, and the idols of Egypt will be moved at his presence, and the heart of Egypt will melt in its midst.
Commentary on Isaiah

Thus says the Lord: The labor of Egypt, and the merchandise of Ethiopia, and the Sabaim, men of stature, will pass over to you, and will be yours: they will walk behind you, they will go bound in manacles: and they will worship you, and make supplication to you: only in you is God, and there is no God apart from you. Truly you are a hidden God, the God of Israel, the Savior. They are confounded and have blushed, all of them: together the makers of errors have gone off into confusion. Israel is saved in the Lord with an eternal salvation: you will not be confounded, and you will not blush, for ever and ever. LXX: Thus says the Lord Sabaoth: Egypt has labored, and the merchandise of the Ethiopians and of the Sabaim: lofty men will pass over to you, and they will be your servants, and they will follow you bound in manacles, and they will pass over to you, and will worship you, and will pray in you: because God is in you, and there is no God apart from you. For you are God, and we did not know it: the God of Israel, the Savior: let all his adversaries be confounded and blush, and let them walk in confusion. ÷ Be renewed unto me, islands ⁚ Israel is saved by the Lord with an eternal salvation: they will not be confounded nor blush for ever. In this passage too, those who follow the history say that Egypt, and the Ethiopians, and the nations of the Sabaim, which are beyond Ethiopia, served Cyrus, and that the furthest nations were subjected to him; and that from his wondrous victory they understood that the Lord was in him, and that there was no other God besides him who dwelt in him. But how what follows: Truly you are a hidden God, the God of Israel, the Savior, can fit the person of Cyrus, I do not understand. Unless perhaps they use the edition of Theodotion, who translated: In you is the strong one, and there is no other God besides him: therefore you are the strong, hidden God of Israel, the Savior. Whithersoever they turn, they will not be able to escape the snares of the truth. For grant that God is in Cyrus, and that there is no other God besides him who is in Cyrus: how will it be fitting to say to the person of Cyrus, Truly you are a hidden God, the God of Israel, the Savior? Therefore the God in whom God is, is more rightly and more truly understood as our Lord Jesus Christ, who says in the Gospel: I and the Father are one (John 10:30). He is called a hidden God because of the mystery of the body he assumed, and the God of Israel, Savior, which means Jesus. For he, according to the angel Gabriel, will save his people (Luke 1).
Commentary on Isaiah

The Hebrews strive with foolish contention to assert that, up to the place where we read: Only in you is God, and there is no God apart from you, it is said either to Jerusalem or to Cyrus; but that what follows: Truly you are a hidden God, the God of Israel, the Savior, is suddenly an apostrophe made to the almighty God; though it is plain even to fools that the texture of the discourse is one, and that a sense which is joined together in the very order and reasoning of the narration cannot be divided.
Commentary on Isaiah

They are confounded and have blushed, all together, namely the Scribes and Pharisees. And the makers of error have gone off into confusion, who spread a lie through the whole world, saying that he had been stolen away by the Apostles (Matt 28). But Israel, saved in the Lord with an eternal salvation, is understood as the choir of the Apostles, and those who believed through the Apostles. Hence it is said to them: You will not be confounded nor will you blush, not only in the present age but also in the one to come.
Commentary on Isaiah

Further, what is added in the Seventy: Be renewed unto me, islands, we can expound thus: we may say that the Churches gathered from the nations are renewed in Christ, and are called islands because they endure the rage and the storms of persecutors, and, founded upon the rock, are shaken by no mass of whirlwinds.
Commentary on Isaiah

For thus says the Lord, who creates the heavens, God himself who forms the earth and makes it, he himself its fashioner: he did not create it in vain; that it might be inhabited he formed it: I am the Lord, and there is no other. I have not spoken in secret, in a dark place of the earth. I did not say to the seed of Jacob: Seek me in vain. I am the Lord who speaks righteousness, who declares right things. Gather together, and come, and draw near together, you who have been saved from among the nations: they have not known, who lift up the wood of their graven image, and pray to a god that does not save. Declare, and come, and take counsel together: who has caused this to be heard from the beginning, has foretold it from that time? Is it not I the Lord, and there is no God besides me? A righteous God and one who saves, there is none besides me. Be converted to me, and you will be saved, all the ends of the earth: for I am God, and there is no other. By myself have I sworn: the word of righteousness will go forth from my mouth, and will not return: for to me every knee shall bow, and every tongue shall swear. Therefore he will say in the Lord: Mine are righteousnesses and dominion: to him they will come, and all who resist him will be confounded. In the Lord all the seed of Israel will be justified and will be praised: LXX: Thus says the Lord who made the heaven: this God who showed the earth and made it, he himself prepared it: he did not make it for emptiness, but formed it to be inhabited. I am the Lord, and there is no other. I have not spoken in secret, nor in a dark place of the earth. I did not say to the seed of Jacob, Seek vanity: I am the Lord who speak righteousness, I declare truth. Gather together and come, and take counsel together, you who are being saved from the nations; they have not known, who carry the wood of their graven image: they pray to gods that do not save. If they declare, let them draw near, that they may know together who has made these things heard from the beginning; then it was declared to you. Am I not the Lord God, and there is no other besides me: a righteous one and a savior, there is none besides me. Be converted to me, and you will be saved from the ends of the earth. I am God, and there is no other. By myself I swear: unless righteousness shall go forth from my mouth: my words will not be turned back, for to me every knee will bend, and every tongue will swear and will confess to God, saying: Righteousness and glory will come to him, and all who separate themselves from the Lord will be confounded: all the seed of the sons of Israel will be justified and will be glorified in God. Having called Egypt, and Ethiopia, and the Sabaim, lofty men, by which the salvation of all the barbarian nations and the conversion of the whole world to God is shown, God shows his righteousness: that he is the Lord not of the Jews only, but also of the nations. For he, the maker of heaven and earth, is equally the God of all, and he created the earth for no other reason than to be the dwelling place of men, who should worship and understand their Creator, and despise all idols.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 4:3.45:18-19

For it says, "thus says the Lord" and not simply an earthly "lord," for there are many in heaven and earth that ruin this name [the Lord] by overusing it. But he is the one who by nature and in truth is just—he is what he is said to be and derives no false glory from what he has ordained.… For if he who made heaven and earth did not make it in vain but to be inhabited, … then who else other than him can be considered God?
Commentary on Isaiah

For on Mount Sinai too, from its lofty summit, he spoke these things in the hearing of the peoples: You shall have no strange gods besides me, nor shall you make yourself an idol (Exod 20:3, 4). But it is better that we believe this was said of the preaching of the Gospel: for Moses spoke in a hidden wilderness to one people only. But the sound of the Apostles went out into the whole world, and their words reached to the ends of the earth (Ps 18 [19]). I did not say, he says, to the seed of Jacob, Seek me in vain. For I promised them the kingdoms of heaven, and I spoke to them first: I came only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt 15:24). And therefore I spoke righteousness and declared right things, or truth, so that, leaving behind the images and ceremonies of the Law, they might follow the truth of the Gospel.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 4:3.45:18-19

I drew up laws about these things for them and did not speak in riddles, nor did I speak in a weighty tone but lightly and clearly. As a result, the Lord came down on Mount Sinai in the form of fire. There were darkness, storms, smoke and the piercing sound of trumpets.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 4:3.45:18-19

"I speak righteousness and proclaim truth." Righteousness, as I take it, means the law, for the law is the arbitrator of righteousness. And truth is the discipline of Christ. For there is a form of truth in the law, and the mystery of Christ lies concealed in its shadows, for Moses wrote about this. So, in speaking of righteousness, truth and power are proclaimed along with it, since it is true that the law is a shadow—and yet in it there remains a form of the truth.
Commentary on Isaiah

But because they would not believe, and judged themselves unworthy of salvation, therefore I say to the nations: Gather together from the whole world; and come and draw near to me together, you who have been saved from among the nations. By this he shows that not all the nations will believe at once, but gradually and in parts. Finally he rebukes those who remained in their former error, saying: They have not known, who lift up the wood of their graven image, and pray to a god that does not save. And the sense is: They did not understand my words, weighed down by the burden of their idols, and hoping in those in whom there is no salvation.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 4:3.45:20

But Emmanuel appeared who led with courage those who were snared. He endured for us the death of the flesh so that as Isaiah says in an evangelical way, the scattered children of God would be gathered into one … to gather, that is, to be bound together in one faith and like-mindedness. [They are] gathered by God the ruler of all through holiness and righteousness … and "brought near through the blood of Christ." … For it is through faith that understanding grows so that it is not in doubt. Even though faith might be undermined by deceit of ill counsel or led astray into ruin by ancient wickedness, we can quickly return to God and receive the light of the true divine knowledge and with a deliberation that comes from an upright mind constantly pursue the better things. Consider then and take counsel, all who have been saved from among the nations.
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 114: AGAINST THE PAGANS

AGAINST THE PAGANS. — By what reasoning the pagans dare to confront us or attack our faith, while thinking themselves innocent, I do not see. For they have no evidence for their assertions, of their superstition, I would rather say, than of religion. Whatever they have without safeguards they put forward, so that they may themselves be regarded as authors and defenders of novelties. First of all, they claim to worship gods, yet those gods give no marks, no testimonies. They call those beings gods who did not dare to be called by that name, so that men are made the authors of gods, though God ought to be the author of men; and therefore their assertion is vain and empty. Whatever is without God cannot be stable. That what I say is clear is proved by their books, in which nothing divine is read as established by God’s command, but they claim that various sacrifices to their deities were instituted by individual men for certain reasons, so that those who appear to have no merit may at least be seen to have rightly established the very things they decreed. Since, therefore, those whom they call gods are nowhere read to have commanded any of these things, by what authority do these men act, or think their actions accepted, when they cannot show any command? And even if a command were shown, it ought first to be examined whether it was fitting or right to obey those whose deeds show no signs or wonders recommending them as divine. But when they are driven from this, they usually take refuge in the elements, saying that they worship these, by whose governance human life is ruled. From them, as above, we ask whether there is any mandate or command from God, whom even they confess to be great and supreme, and yet they neglect Him. For if such worship ought to be done, it should have been commanded by Him who is said to be their author. If, however, it is not commanded by Him, it is mere presumption and will lead to punishment, not reward; for it is an insult to the Creator when, despising the Lord, men worship His servants, and, scorning the Emperor, adore his nobles. How will this go unpunished, when we see that even in this life such conduct is avenged, and indeed harshly? But if perhaps they say that the mandate has come from the elements themselves, let them show a precept somewhere; let them at some time read anything that those elements have spoken. If they cannot show this, what penalty do they deserve who are exposed as authors of a presumed and fabricated religion? The elements are free from this wickedness. For the very luminaries of the world will accuse them before God the Judge, because in this vain counsel they in no way present themselves as authors. In like manner those whom they call gods, though it is certain that they were men, when they begin to be tormented for their sins, will by no means defend themselves as guilty in this matter, but will shift this charge onto those who, though they had not commanded it, began to worship them as gods. With what sense of shame, then, can they criticize our faith or think it deserves ridicule, when they read our law supported by testimonies of virtues, and also the voice of our Lord and God saying: “I am God, and there is none other besides me” (Isa. 45:21–22)? If He said this in bare words, He would not deserve belief, lest we appear like the pagans, who, seeing no signs of majesty in their gods, began to worship them, and, what is worse, in shameful ways. For disgraceful things are done there, which it is shameful to reveal; and they call themselves wise, because in regard to their law they are mocked like an imposter. But our God, with virtue as witness, has commanded that He be worshipped, and, so as to leave no room for suspicion, has given a law that is upright and holy, as befits God. We, indeed, who are called foolish by the pagans, would not have believed in our God had He not satisfied us also by testimonies of power; nor would we have accepted His law if we had not recognized it as pure and worthy of its own profession. Therefore it is that nothing among us is done in darkness or in secret. For whatever is known to be honorable does not fear to be made public; but that which is shameful and dishonorable cannot be made public because modesty forbids it. For this reason the pagans celebrate their mysteries in darkness, wise at least in this: they are ashamed to be mocked openly. The immoral rites that function in place of law there they do not wish to reveal, lest those who call themselves wise appear dull to those whom they call fools. Yet lest, perhaps on this account, we seem fools to them, because our law proclaims chastity, mercy, devotion, self-control: among them these things are foolish, since every good man is bad to the wicked, and the wise man senseless to the fool. But in the presence of the sign of the cross, paganism falls silent. And if that forethought which they call wisdom is present, it does not dare answer the sacred things of those whom they call foolish. Pagans even profess in writing that they worship gods and goddesses; and what they say is true, since they worship both males and females. Christians, however, as poor people, whom they call fools, worship one God in mystery, from whom are all things; nor do they venerate anything that has been created by Him. For they know that He alone is sufficient and abundant for their salvation, not ignorant that if they assign His glory and name to others, they offend Him; since no emperor allows tribunes and counts to be adored together with his name. Let the laws now be compared, that it may be seen where forethought lies: with the one who worships the Creator, or the one who worships the creature; the one who worships the Lord, or the one who worships servants? Can it be that in some household, besides one, another should be called lord, just as pagans, trained in forensic writings, who seem to themselves wise, in one world created by one God, worship many gods and goddesses? For they call the stewards and managers of the world gods and by the name of God, while they are exposed as foolish. To proclaim that which brings destruction is the mark of the foolish and the irresponsible. For it is necessary that God should avenge His injury upon those who have shared the name and glory of the Lord God with their fellow-servants. But the irrational crowd began to worship as gods either apparitions of shadows, or demons, or images of the dead; and this practice, having been drawn into the custom of antiquity, thinks that it can defend the truth of reason for itself; whereas the rule of truth comes not from custom, which arises from antiquity, but from God, who is not proved to be God by antiquity, but by eternity. Wherefore faith is not something begun, but is without beginning. For to believe in God is the beginning on our side. For that which is believed is eternal. How then do the pagans suppose themselves to be prior, when that which they worship is after God? Is not a work after its maker? Pagans worship the works, we the Maker; they the creature, we the Creator. Surely God made the world; did He not, when He had made it, show His own knowledge? Or did He make man and not wish to be worshiped by him whom He had made? But this is absurd. Therefore man, once made, began to venerate his Creator, because this is fitting and the very cause required it. When this had grown obsolete through the negligence of men, God restored it in Abraham, so that the knowledge of God which had existed in Adam might begin again in Abraham; that those born from him might be brought up under this knowledge, and that through transmission it might not fail, nor be lacking in one who worshiped God; others also from a foreign nation being called to this knowledge of God. Therefore, the one who has come to know is under a beginning; but the one who is known is above beginning.
Commentary on Isaiah

Hence the Apostles are commanded to proclaim the truth in season and out of season (2 Tim 4), and to enter on counsel for the salvation of the nations. And this, that is, that very many from the nations should be gathered and come and be saved, God spoke from the beginning, and the mouths of all the Prophets sang it, who spoke by the word of the Lord, besides whom there is no other. For the Son is God not apart from him, but in him.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 4:3.45:21-22

There is among them no true knowledge of the things to come, but rather they prophesy falsely, and with clownish talk and deception and trickery and nothing else. The God of the universe responds: If they prophesy rightly, they will come close and will know at the same time. For if they are able to prophesy rightly, then they will all be brought together as one. For their oracles came from many places. But some worked others into a frenzy and honored the unclean demons who were speaking falsehood. If they had been able to prophesy rightly, they would all be aware of what is to come and who from the very start made these things to be heard.
Commentary on Isaiah

And beautifully he joins: A righteous God, not of one nation at all, but of the whole world, to which he says: Be converted to me, and you will be saved, all the ends of the earth; fulfilling what the Father promised the Son: Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession (Ps 2:8).
Commentary on Isaiah

And he swears by himself that the sentence of his mouth, and the word he has once uttered concerning the salvation of the nations, will by no means be made void; but that the promise of him who said above: Be converted to me, and you will be saved, all the ends of the earth, will be fulfilled in deed. And he swears, according to the Apostle (Heb 6), so that through two immovable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we may have firm consolation; but he also swears this: that, idols abandoned, every knee should bow to him, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue of mortals should swear by him (Phil 2). In this the Christian people is plainly signified. For it is the custom of the Church to bend the knee to Christ: which the Jews, displaying the pride of their mind, do not do at all. And every tongue too of all the barbarian nations confesses God, not in synagogues but in the Churches of Christ.
Commentary on Isaiah

And every tongue that confesses Christ will speak in the Lord, and will say: Mine are righteousnesses, and mine is the dominion, not the Jewish people's. To him all the nations will come, and those who formerly resisted his Gospel will be confounded; and all the seed of Israel will be justified and praised, whose preaching and most fertile sowing has borne the richest fruits throughout the whole world. Or, according to the Seventy, every tongue that swears by and confesses God will say that the righteousness and glory of the whole world comes to him, and that the Jews, who separate themselves from him, are confounded. But those who have sprung from the stock of the sons of Israel, and who have sprouted from the seed of the Apostles, and have believed in Christ, may they have righteousness and everlasting glory.

n: Bel; perhaps Nimrod, (Calmet) or Saturn, to whom they sacrificed their children. (Worthington) --- Nabo, "the oracle" of Belus. The Chaldeans adored statues and beasts. But the Persians worshipped the elements. (Calmet) --- Xerxes destroyed the tomb of Belus, after his expedition into Greece. (Arrian vii.) He had there demolished the temples, (Herodotus viii. 109.) pretending (Haydock) that "the world is the house of the gods." (Cicero, Leg. ii.) --- Weariness. The priests affected to be weighed down, as if the god were present. (Baruch vi. 25.) (St. Cyril)

They. Literally, "their soul." (Haydock) --- The pagans must have supposed they had one. (Calmet) --- Captivity. "There are as many triumphs over the gods as over men." (Tertullian) --- The former shared the fate of their adorers. Their statues were plundered.
By my. Vulgate may have read a me ab, (Calmet) instead of a meo. Hebrew and Septuagint, "taken from the womb," (Haydock) and treated with the utmost tenderness. (Calmet)
Ashamed. Septuagint, "groan." Protestants, "shew yourselves men." (Haydock)

Bird; Cyrus, whose rapid conquests are thus denoted. (Calmet) --- He chose a golden eagle, with wings expanded, for his standard. (Xenophon vii.) --- Christ came from heaven to redeem the world, Psalm xviii. 6., and Malachias iv. 2. (Calmet) --- He was the orient, adored by the eastern sages, to whom the prophet refers. (St. Jerome) (Worthington)

Israel. It shall no longer be a reproach. Cyrus shall restore my people to their own country. But Christ more full accomplished what is here declared respecting the establishment of his Church. (Calmet)

f: Commentary on Isaiah

Bel is broken, Nebo is crushed: their idols are made over to beasts and cattle, your burdens with heavy weight even to weariness. They have wasted away and are crushed together: they could not save the one who carried them, and their soul shall go into captivity. LXX: Bel has fallen, Dagon is crushed: their graven images are made into beasts and cattle; you carry them bound together like a burden for one who labors, and faints, and hungers, and has no strength besides, who will not be able to save from war: but they themselves have been led captive. After the calling of the nations, and the election of believers from Israel, he testifies that the idols have collapsed. Bel has fallen, has fallen, or is broken: whom the Greeks call Belus, the Latins Saturn. So great was his worship among the ancients that they sacrificed to him not only human victims, captives and mortals of low birth, but even their own children. Nebo, too, is itself an idol, which means prophecy and divination, which he signifies fell silent throughout the whole world after the truth of the Gospel. Or, according to the Seventy, Dagon, which, however, is not found in the Hebrew. And it is the idol of Ascalon, of Gaza and of the other cities of the Philistines. And he passes from the particular to the general: Their idols are made over to beasts and cattle. Not that the idols of the Gentiles were exposed as prey to beasts and cattle: but that the religion of the nations consists in images of beasts and of brute animals, which above all in Egypt were consecrated to divine worship. Of which Virgil says (Aen. 8.698): Monsters of gods of every kind, and barking Anubis.

For most of their towns too have names from beasts and cattle: κυνῶν from dog, λέων from lion; θμοῦϊς, in the Egyptian tongue, from the he-goat; λύκων from wolf; to say nothing of the dreadful and horrible onion, and the noise of the puffed-up belly, which is the religion of Pelusium.
Commentary on Isaiah

These idols, he says, which cannot save those who carry them, are nothing else but burdens for the priests, weighing them down even to weariness. And when captivity comes, they are the first to be led captive, for the value of the metals of which they are made, and they cannot set free their own soul, or that of those who carry them. Not that dumb idols, which are without sensation, have a soul and some sense of pain; but that soul and members are spoken of καταχρηστικῶς in things that are without sense and members. Otherwise, too, we read in Proverbs: In the hand of the tongue are death and life. Or else this must be said: that the heaviest burden among the nations was the error of idolatry, which weighed its worshipers down to the earth, and could not save them, and made their souls captives of the devil and of demons.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 4:3.46:1

But Bel was also honored in other cities. For they say that Bel was the mythical figure Chronos among the godless Greeks, one who was reputedly cruel and bloodthirsty and loved to slaughter humans … whereas the God of the universe is not pleased with such terrible impieties and through one of the holy prophets he said to those who were accustomed to doing this, "You sacrifice humans, for you have run out of cattle." … The expression "cast down" is apt, since the prophet here speaks of a time near to his own. For we can read in the books of the Kings that when the former people carried the divine ark to the temple of Dagon, as those worshiping the idol went in, they saw Dagon fallen down in front of the ark.
Commentary on Isaiah

According to the Seventy, who said: Who are carried from the womb, and are instructed from infancy even to old age, this signifies that they meditate on the law of God day and night in vain, having no knowledge of God, but venerating images of men and beasts: so much so that they need prophetic rebuke, through which God speaks to them: To whom have you likened me, and made me equal? and the rest: that they lavished gold and silver, and, hiring a sculptor, made idols, and worshiped the works of their own hands, which are carried on shoulders, and, fixed and set firm, cannot move themselves, nor profit those by whom they are worshiped. We pass quickly over what is plain, so that by the mercy of Christ we may unlock what is closed.
Commentary on Isaiah

Hear me, house of Jacob, and all the remnant of the house of Israel, who are carried from my womb, who are borne from my matrix. Even to old age I myself, and even to gray hairs I will carry you: I have made, and I will bear: I will carry, and I will save. To whom have you likened me, and made me equal, and compared me, and made me like? You who lavish gold from the purse, and weigh silver on the scales, hiring a goldsmith to make a god: and they fall down and worship. They carry it on their shoulders, bearing it and setting it in its place, and it will stand, and will not move from its place. But when they cry to it, it will not hear: it will not save them from tribulation. LXX: Hear me, house of Jacob, and all the remnant of Israel, who are carried from the womb, and are instructed from a little child even to old age. I am, and until you grow old I am: I sustain you: I have made, and I will carry: I will take you up, and I will save you. To whom have you likened me? See, consider, you who err and lavish gold from the purse, and weigh out silver on the scales, and hire a goldsmith: they have made the works of their hands, and bowing down they have worshiped: they carry it on their shoulders, and go. But if they set it in its place, it stays, and will not move: and whoever cries to it, it will not hear him, and will not deliver him from evils. He by no means calls him Jacob, nor Israel, which itself, we explained above, is said in reproach of the people when it is without the addition of servant, and child, and chosen: but, much more meanly, house of Jacob, and remnant of Israel, because of the nearness of flesh and blood, and as it were the dregs of the remnant of Israel. And he teaches them that they were carried by God out of Egypt like children and sucklings, as it were from a mother's womb and the matrix of one with child. Not that the ineffable and incomprehensible majesty of God has either a womb or a matrix, or feet and hands and the other members of the body; but that we may learn God's affection through our own words. Otherwise, in Psalm 109 (110) too, this same thing is sung in the person of God. For in the place where the Seventy translated, from the womb before the morning star I begot you, the Hebrew has written MEREHEM מרחם, which means from the matrix. But in the present passage it is written not only from the womb and from the matrix, that is, MEBETEN מבטן and MEREHEM מרחם, but MENNI מני, a preposition which signifies from my womb, or from my matrix. And the sense is: I who begot you from infancy, and bore you in my womb and matrix, will myself protect you even to old age, not mine but yours; so as to teach them that they are to be saved by the divine mercy. For the Creator of all spares his creature, and the good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep (John 10). But he who is a hireling, whose own the sheep are not, flees when he sees the wolf. Since, then, I made and begot children, I will bear them and I myself will carry them.
Confessions 4.15.31

O Lord our God, under the shadow of your wings let us hope; defend us and support us. You will bear us up when we are little, and even down to our gray hairs you will carry us. For our stability, when it is in you, is stability indeed; but when it is in ourselves, then it is all unstable. Our good lives forever with you, and when we turn from you with aversion, we fall into our own perversion. Let us now, O Lord, return that we be not overturned, because with you our good lives without blemish—for our good is you yourself.
Confessions 6.16.26

Woe to the audacious soul that hoped that by forsaking you it would find some better thing! It tossed and turned, on back and side and belly, but the bed is hard, and you alone give rest. Yet you are near. You deliver us from our wretched wanderings and establish us in your way. You comfort us and say, "Run, I will carry you. I will lead you home, and I will set you free."
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 4:3.46:8-11

But since their heart was not responsive to his promptings, he predicted the evils to come so that they would be gradually troubled by these terrors and would cease their irregular and foul way of life.
Commentary on Isaiah

Remember this, and be grounded, and return, transgressors, to heart. Recall the former age, for I am God, and there is no God beyond, nor is there any like me. Declaring from the start the last things, and from the beginning things not yet done, saying: My counsel shall stand, and all my will shall be done. Calling a bird from the East, and from a far land the man of my will; and I have spoken, and I will bring it about; I have created, and I will do it. LXX: Remember these things, and groan: repent, you who err. Return in heart, and remember the former things from of old; for I am God, and there is no other besides me. I who declare beforehand the last things before they happen and are fulfilled, and I have said, all my will shall stand, and all that I have planned I will do. I who call a bird from the East, and from a far land, those concerning whom I have planned: I have spoken, and I have brought it about: I have created and I have done it. Because I myself begot you, I myself carried you, and from infancy even to old age you are saved not by your merit but by my compassion: forsake the idols you have made, and return to the worship of the one God. Repent, groan for the error that held you; nay, be grounded, lest the sudden whirlwind of idolatry overturn you again: and return to heart, that is, to your mind, you who, venerating images, dashed yourselves like madmen against wood and stones.
Confessions 4.12.18

Behold, there he is, wherever truth is known. He is within the inmost heart, yet the heart has wandered from him. Return to your heart, O you sinners, and hold fast to him who made you. Stand with him, and you shall stand firmly. Rest in him, and you shall be at rest.
SERMON 102:2

"Go back, therefore, to the heart," and if you are believers, you will find Christ there. He himself is speaking to you there. Yes, here am I, shouting my head off—but he, in silence, is doing more teaching. I am speaking by the sound of these words; he is speaking inwardly by the awe you feel in your thoughts.
Commentary on Isaiah

Consider from the beginning of the world that there is no God besides me, and that no other could know things to come, except me, who announce through the Prophets what I am going to do: so that, when I have fulfilled what was foretold, I may prove my divinity by divination. For I now say that the mystery which in times past was unknown to all generations, or rather my counsel, will stand; so that, when you see it brought to pass, you may know no God but him who knew that these things would be, nay, commanded them to be done.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 4:3.46:8-13

For he says "I am the one possessing knowledge of all, and whatever happens, I give notice of it beforehand." That which is announced, I execute … for what the holy God wills, who will thwart it? And who will avert his hand when it is raised?… We take the bird that is called from the east and from a far land to be the Babylonian, who scorched all the territory of the Jews, took Jerusalem and ruined the temple. They removed both ordinary flock and the leading birds among them and forced them into the region of the Persians. They also subjected them to a yoke of harsh imprisonment.…This work was done not by Israel's own hand, as if God would need a helper. For "it is I alone who save," guard and lead him on the right road, so that those who have made little progress in godliness will help the righteous ones and the humble. By these means, glory and honor are finally given to me alone, even from among wood and stones.
Commentary on Isaiah

I am he who calls a bird from the East: as the Hebrews think, Cyrus king of the Persians, or Darius prince of the Medes; and from a far land the man of my will, to fulfill all my will against Babylon and the Chaldeans. Or, as we prove to be true, the Lord Savior, of whom Balaam too prophesies: A star shall rise out of Jacob, and a man out of Israel (Num 24:17), whose name is the East (Zech 6), whom the Magi coming from the East worshiped. For he it is who speaks in the Psalms: O God, I have willed to do your will (Ps 39 [40]:9), of whom the Father spoke: and he proved his pledge by deed. In place of what we have rendered from the Hebrew, the man of my will, the Seventy put, those concerning whom I have planned. According to them, then, by the birds called from the East we can understand the ministries of the angels, which run to and fro through the whole world at the Lord's command; who are ministering spirits, and are sent for the salvation of believers. Of whom it is also sung in the psalm: You who make your angels spirits, and your ministers a burning fire (Ps 103 [104]:4).
DIALOGUE WITH HERACLIDES

The inner man possesses a heart. "Listen to Me, you who have lost heart!" Those to whom the prophet is speaking have a heart by the flesh: it cannot be lost. But when a man is careless about the cultivation of his intellectual being, then, on account of much idleness, the faculty of thought evaporates from him, he loses his heart, and it is precisely of such people that it is said: "Listen to Me, you who have lost heart!"
Commentary on Isaiah

Hear me, you hard of heart, who are far from righteousness. I have brought my righteousness near: it shall not be far off, and my salvation shall not delay: I will give salvation in Zion, and in Israel my glory. LXX: Hear me, you who have lost heart, who are far from righteousness. I have brought near my righteousness, and the salvation that is from me I will not make to tarry. I have given salvation in Zion, and to Israel glory. Those to whom he had said above: Hear me, house of Jacob, and all the remnant of the house of Israel, and again: Return, transgressors, to heart, even now he calls, according to the Hebrew, hard of heart because of their unbelief, and, according to the Seventy, men who have lost heart and mind. Following this, the most learned man Stephen the martyr, worthy of his name, says in the assembly of the Jews: Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in hearts and ears, you have always resisted the Holy Spirit, as your fathers did (Acts 7:51). These, then, are far from the righteousness of God, because they did not believe in it; which God, in his clemency, made to be near, and wishes by no means to tarry or to be far off in coming to the earth. For he has given Zion his salvation, and Israel his glory. Let this be said of the prophecy of things to come, and of the coming of the Lord Savior. But according to the history, salvation is given to Zion, and glory to Israel, because God made his righteousness to be near, so that he called a bird from the East, and from a far land the man of his will, to avenge the wrongs of Israel and of overthrown Jerusalem, and, with the Medes and Persians victorious, to destroy Babylon and the Chaldeans, as the following words of the Prophet testify.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 4:3.48:5-11

Again we perceive the depth of God's loving kindness, in that God mixes with the evils also the wonders, so that they are not wiped out. For he has saved them from the hand of their enemies. When Israel fell into the marsh of judgment, God dragged them out.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 4:3.46:12-13

See how he once again announces salvation to them and does not allow them to despair, lest they be overwhelmed by unrestrained sorrow and be moved too far away from the hope that they will be saved, if only they stop running. For having strayed, they were disconsolate. This described their situation accurately. For what else would they feel, they who worshiped the things they themselves had made, setting up trees and stones for worship and seeking salvation from them?

n: Virgin; delicate. (Menochius) --- Cyrus overthrew this empire, (Calmet) which now felt its share of misery. (Worthington)

Shame. Hebrew tsammathec, Canticle of Canticles iv. 1, 4. Protestants, "thy locks, make bare the legs, uncover the thigh, pass," &c. (Haydock) --- Thou shalt be reduced to a state of the most abject slavery, Exodus xi. 5., and Supra[Isaias] iii. 17., and xx. 4. The Barbarians sold their slaves naked.
Polluted; deemed or declared unclean. But thou hast sought to gratify thy vindictive temper, in punishing my people. (Calmet) --- The sins of both called down vengeance. (Worthington)
Lady. Pride goes before ruin, Proverbs xvi. 18.
Two. The empire and the people shall be removed at once. --- Enchanters; princes or magicians, who gave them evil counsel, ver. 12.
Know. All this shews the vanity of magic, which cannot announce future events to do any good. (Calmet)
Months, to tell which would prove lucky, Esther iii. 7.

Thereat, to warm themselves, (Haydock) or to adore. (Calmet) --- In Cappadocia are to be seen "Pyratheia,...in which the magi keep a perpetual fire, and sing hymns about the space of an hour." (Strabo xv.) --- These were a sort of open temples. (Calmet)
Merchants. The city was well situated for trade, chap. xiii. 20. (Diodorus ii.)

f: Commentary on Isaiah

Go down, sit in the dust, virgin daughter of Babylon: sit on the ground, there is no throne for the daughter of the Chaldeans, for no more shall you be called soft and tender. Take the millstone, and grind meal: lay bare your shame, uncover your shoulder, reveal your legs, pass over the rivers. Your disgrace shall be revealed, and your reproach shall be seen: I will take vengeance, and no man shall withstand me. LXX: Go down, sit upon the ground, virgin daughter of Babylon, sit on the ground. There is no throne for the daughter of the Chaldeans, for no more at all shall you be called soft and tender. Take the millstone, grind meal. Reveal your covering, lay bare your gray hairs, uncover your shins, pass over the rivers: your disgrace shall be revealed, your reproaches shall appear. What is just I will take from you, no more at all will I hand you over to men. As in Ezekiel the adornment of Tyre, which is given over to trading, is set forth under the figure of a ship and all its equipment (Ezek 26), and the king of Egypt, because of the abundance of waters, is called a dragon, and his scales, and the rush and papyrus and little fishes are described, and the likeness of harlots and of a brothel bears witness to Jerusalem's fornication with idols: so in the present passage the servitude of Babylon is shown under the person of a captive woman who was once a queen: and she is told to come down from the pride of her kingdom and sit in the dust. And she is called a virgin and a daughter: either because all of us men are God's creation, and Babylon is not, as the heretics hold, of a damnable nature; or because of the luxury and adornment of a city once most powerful, which, when she had grown old and was near her setting, boasted that she was a little virgin and a girl. Although from what is written according to the Seventy, daughter of Babylon, some interpret it not of Babylon itself but of the city of Rome, which in the Apocalypse of John (Rev 14) and in the Epistle of Peter (1 Pet 5) is specifically called Babylon, and they maintain that all that is now said to Babylon fits its ruin, against which the bird and the righteousness of God are to be called: so that, after Zion, that is, the Church, has been saved, she may perish for ever. It is said, then, to Babylon, queen and daughter of the Chaldeans (for she was founded by the Chaldeans), that she will no more at all be called soft and tender and overflowing with delights, she who was carried in the hands of all the nations, so that she scarcely pressed the soles of her feet to the ground: and she is commanded to take the millstone and grind meal, which is a sign of harsh captivity and the utmost servitude; so that she who was once a queen afterwards serves at the work of grinding meal.
LETTER 77.5

As Fabiola was not ashamed of the Lord on earth, so he shall not be ashamed of her in heaven. She laid bare her wound to the gaze of all, and Rome beheld with tears the disfiguring scar that marred her beauty. She uncovered her limbs, bared her head and closed her mouth. She no longer entered the church of God but, like Miriam the sister of Moses, she sat apart, outside the camp, till the priest who cast her out should himself call her back. She came down like a daughter of Babylon from the throne of her daintiness, she took the millstones and ground meal, she passed barefoot through rivers of tears.
Commentary on Isaiah

But because there follows: Lay bare your shame, the millstone too is understood figuratively by the Hebrews, namely that, after the manner of a harlot, she lies open to the lust of the victors. And what is written in the book of Judges about Samson (Judg 16), that he was condemned by the Philistines to the mill, they wish to signify this: that, being the strongest of men, he was compelled, for the sake of offspring, to do this with foreign women. In the place where we have translated, lay bare your shame, for which the Seventy translated, reveal your covering, Theodotion put the Hebrew word itself, SAMTHECH (צמתך); Aquila SEMMATHECH; Symmachus τὸ σιωπηλόν σου: which we can express as your silent part, because it ought to be kept silent for modesty. This indeed we also read in the Song of Songs, where the beauty of the bride is described: at the end he adds: Apart from your silent part (Song 4): the translators being unwilling to render a word which in holy Scripture would sound shameful. And rightly he uses immodest names against Babylon (though there is nothing shameful in calling a member of the human body by its own name), she who is commanded to bare her breasts, and to uncover her legs and thighs, and to go into captivity, and to have her disgrace seen, and to lie open to everlasting reproach. And the Lord says he has done this to take vengeance on her who oppressed his people, and that he will hear no intercessor on her behalf who might try to soften the Lord's anger by coming before him. And he means the angel who presides over the Babylonian nation, who says with the other angels: We have cared for Babylon, and she is not healed. And as for what the Seventy translated, what is just I will take from you, no more at all will I hand you over to men, Babylon is understood: or certainly, that which is just, and taken away from Babylon. The Stoics argue that many things shameful in reality are, by the depraved custom of men, decent in words, such as parricide, adultery, homicide, incest, and other things like these. And again, that things decent in reality seem shameful in their names, such as begetting children, relieving the swelling of the belly by breaking wind, easing the bowels of excrement, loosing the bladder by pouring out urine: and finally, that we cannot, as from ruta we say rutula, so make a ὑποκοριστικὸν of menta. Therefore SEMMATHEC (צמתך), which Aquila put, as we have said, is the name for the private parts of a woman. Its etymology among them sounds your thirsty one; so as to show the insatiable lust of Babylon.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 4:3.47:1-3

"Bare your legs and cross the rivers. Your shame will be uncovered and your disgrace shown." For she was once led into captivity. She was taken from her own land into that of the victors. Being between the two rivers, they had to cross on their feet and uncover themselves. What decorum the women had was lost, and out of necessity even the private parts of their bodies were exposed to many.
Commentary on Isaiah

Our Redeemer, the Lord of hosts is his name, the Holy One of Israel. Sit silent, and go into darkness, daughter of the Chaldeans; for no more shall you be called mistress of kingdoms. I was angry with my people, I defiled my inheritance, and I gave them into your hand: you showed them no mercies. Upon the old man you made your yoke exceedingly heavy, and you said, For ever I shall be mistress: you did not lay these things to heart, nor did you remember your latter end. LXX: He who delivered you has said, the Lord Sabaoth, his name is the Holy One of Israel. Sit pierced with grief, enter into darkness, daughter of the Chaldeans: no more at all shall you be called the strength of the kingdom: I was angry against my people, I defiled my inheritance. I gave them into your hand, but you gave them no mercy: on the old man you made the yoke exceedingly heavy, and you said, For ever I shall be mistress: you did not understand these things in your heart, nor did you remember the last things. According to the Seventy, the first verse is joined to what precedes, so that the sense is: And these things will he do who delivered you, the Lord Sabaoth, his name is the Holy One of Israel. But according to the Hebrew, the Prophet speaks in the person of the people, saying that the Lord of hosts, whose name is the Holy One of Israel, has done these things against Babylon.
Commentary on Isaiah

And again the discourse is directed to Babylon itself. Sit silent, or pierced with grief, and remember your crimes. Enter into darkness: because for confusion and disgrace you cannot bear the light: no more at all shall you be called mistress, not of one kingdom, nor even of all kingdoms.
Commentary on Isaiah

And at the same time, because a hidden question arose, why God should be angry against the Chaldeans whom he himself had sent to take Israel, he answered that, being angry against his people, he had wished to chastise them, not to destroy them; to scourge them, not to kill them. But they had given free rein to their own cruelty, and had laid on more stripes than God's vengeance demanded: and it is a great sign of Babylonian cruelty that they did not spare even old men, whose age is venerable even among enemies. And this too is a sign of pride, that, deceived by present prosperity, she did not consider the uncertainties of the future. We ought therefore always, in prosperity, to beware of what is to come, and not to oppress those handed over to us, who are being instructed for this purpose, that they may become better.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 4:3.47:5-7

Out of love God disciplines, then, those who were thoughtless.… They were made docile through their trials. He did this by delivering them into the hands of their enemies or by the affliction of other pains, just as fire and iron often heal a wound where medicine fails. In the same manner our God, a lover of virtue, when he sees a soul rushing onto the rocks with the force of vast waves and getting mixed up in the ways of wickedness, restores that person through harsh punishments.
Commentary on Isaiah

And now hear these things, you delicate one, who dwell confidently, who say in your heart: I am, and there is none besides me any more: I shall not sit as a widow, and I shall not know barrenness. And these two things shall come upon you suddenly in one day, barrenness and widowhood: all things have come upon you, because of the multitude of your sorceries, and because of the hardness of your enchanters, exceedingly. And you trusted in your wickedness, and you said: There is none who sees me: your wisdom and your knowledge, these have deceived you, and you said in your heart: I am, and besides me there is no other. Evil shall come upon you, and you shall not know its rising, and calamity shall rush upon you which you shall not be able to expiate, misery shall come upon you suddenly which you shall not know. Two things will come upon Babylon together, barrenness and widowhood, so that she has neither sons, that is, peoples subject to her, nor a husband, whom we can understand as the king: which she suddenly endured while she did not expect them. For she could not suppose that the Persians, of no strength before, would, in the reign of Cyrus, overcome her and subject her to their power.
Commentary on Isaiah

What you have suffered, he says, is not only because of your pride and the abundance of all wealth and your delights, but also because of the multitude of your sorceries, and of your enchanters, in whom you trusted. And evil shall come upon you which you did not know before, and whose rising you did not know. Or, as the Seventy translated: Destruction shall come upon you, and you shall not know it: a pit, and you shall fall into it: so that you who were preparing the evil of captivity for all the nations may yourself fall into the pit that you prepared. What is plain we pass over in brief speech.
Commentary on Isaiah

Stand with your enchanters, and with the multitude of your sorceries, in which you have labored from your youth, if perhaps anything may profit you, or if you can become stronger. You have failed in the multitude of your counsels: let the augurs of the heaven stand and save you, who gazed at the stars and reckoned the months, that from them they might announce to you things to come. Behold, they have become as stubble, fire has burned them: they shall not deliver their souls from the hand of the flame: there are no coals to warm them, nor a hearth to sit by: so have they become to you, all those things in which you had labored: your traders from your youth have gone astray, each in his own way: there is none to save you. LXX: Stand now in your enchantments and in your many sorceries, which you learned from your youth, if they can profit you: and you have labored in your counsels: let the astrologers of the heaven, who gaze at the stars, stand and save you: let them announce to you what is to come upon you. Behold, they shall all be burned as brushwood in the fire: and they shall not rescue their soul from the flame; because you have coals of fire, you shall sit upon them. These shall be a help to you. You have labored in your exchange from your youth: man has gone astray in himself: but for you there shall be no salvation. That Babylon and all Chaldea pursued the arts of enchanters and augurs, and soothsayers and Gazarenes, whom we call haruspices, is proved by the reading of Daniel the Prophet, who records that the kings of Babylon did everything on their counsel. And in place of what we have translated, following Symmachus and Theodotion: Let the augurs of the heaven stand and save you, the Seventy translated more plainly, Let the astrologers of the heaven stand and save you; who are commonly called mathematicians, and think that human affairs are ruled by the course of the stars and the motion of the heavenly bodies. Hence the Magi too came from the East, saying they had seen the Lord's star, either from the knowledge of their art, or from the prophecy of Balaam, their own Prophet, who had said in Numbers: A star shall rise out of Jacob, and a man from Israel (Num 24:17).
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 19

So also His Father makes great account of prophecy, when He sets Himself against the honor paid to idols: "Let them declare to you," saith He, "what shall come upon you"; and again, "I have declared, and have saved, and there was no foreign God amongst you"; and He brings this forward through all prophecy. Because prophecy is especially the work of God, which devils cannot even imitate, though they strive exceedingly. For in the case of miracles there may be delusion; but exactly to foretell the future belongs to that pure Nature alone. Or if devils ever have done so, it was by deceiving the simpler sort; whence their oracles are always easily detected.
Commentary on Isaiah

Let these, then, who reckon the months and count up the years, and, weighing the moments of the hours, promise knowledge of the future, tell you what the Lord has planned against you; and, since they are silent about what is to come, the Prophet answered: Behold, they have become as stubble, fire has devoured them; so that those who promised salvation to others did not know their own punishments: and there is no doubt that, when the city was burning, the devouring flame consumed its inhabitants. And what follows: There are no coals to warm them, nor a hearth to sit by, the Hebrews explain thus: They have no knowledge of warmth, nor an enlightening sense that could dispel their darkness and drive out the cold of error. For which the Seventy, meaning I know not what, translated: You have coals of fire, you shall sit upon them: these shall be a help to you; unless perhaps we can say this, that fire and burning are much more useful to Babylon than the magi and Gazarenes, the astrologers and enchanters, were. For the one calls them to repentance through penalties and punishments; the others lead them through error to pride.
Commentary on Isaiah

Let us ask those who assert that there are different natures whether Babylon is of an evil nature or a good one. If they say of an evil one, which there is no doubt they will answer, how is she called to repentance, and told: Sit pierced with grief, enter into darkness, daughter of the Chaldeans? And then, after the enumeration of her sins and crimes: You have coals of fire, you shall sit upon them: these shall be a help to you? And what is meant by what is added according to the same Seventy: You have labored in exchange from your youth? What is this exchange? Surely from good to evil. From which it is plain that men are good by nature, and become evil by will. Finally it is added: Man has gone astray in himself, not by nature, but by the choice of the mind.
ON FIRST PRINCIPLES 2:5.3

And when God afflicts those who deserve punishment, how else is it intended except for their good? It is he who says to the Chaldaeans, "You have coals of fire; sit on them. They shall be a help to you." Further, let them hear what is related in the seventy-seventh psalm, which is ascribed to Asaph, about those who fell in the desert. It says, "When he slew them, then they sought him." It does not say that some sought him after others had been killed but that those who were slain perished in such a manner that when put to death they sought God. From all these illustrations it is plain that the just and good God of the Law and the Gospels is one and the same and that he does good with justice and punishes in kindness, since neither goodness without justice nor justice without goodness can describe the dignity of the divine nature.
Commentary on Isaiah
All her labor and her traders, whom we understand as the magi, achieved this: that each went astray in his own way; and, himself lost, could not offer salvation to another.

n: Waters; people, (Apocalypse xvii. 15.; Haydock) or from the stock of Juda, Proverbs v. 15. (Calmet) --- He claimed the sovereign power, but had not the fortitude or wisdom of Israel. (Worthington)
City: citizens of Jerusalem, Daniel iii. 28., and Matthew iv. 5.
Suddenly, when there was no human appearance of the event, as when I foretold the exploits of Cyrus and the ruin of Babylon so long before.
Brass; unblushing, Jeremias iii. 3. (Calmet) --- Os tuum ferreum. (Cicero, contra Pis.)
Them. Could you have believed them? --- Knowest not. He upbraids their ignorance and indocility.
Knew. Therefore I did not speak of the liberation from Egypt, but from Babylon, which is represented as just taking place. (Calmet)

Opened; docile, (Theodoret) or acquainted with these things. Isaias first made known the captivity of Babylon, and its end; and he insists so much, that people may discern the truth of his predictions, and of religion. No atheist can, with a good conscience, hold out against his arguments, chap. xl., &c.
Bridle thee, like a headstrong beast, (Calmet) running to its own ruin. (Haydock) --- God pardons freely, that people may be saved if they will. (Worthington)

Poverty, at Babylon. I have not treated thee with the utmost rigour, nor attempted to render thee free from every imperfection. (Calmet) --- Septuagint, "Lo, I have sold thee, but not for silver; I have snatched thee from the," &c. (Haydock)
Things, as I have done respecting Cyrus? (St. Cyril, &c.) who was a figure of Christ, ver. 15.

Spirit. The Fathers here find the three Persons of the blessed Trinity specified. Isaias was not from the beginning, though the text may also speak of him (Calmet) as he spoke long before the event, by divine inspiration. (Chaldean) (St. Jerome)
Name. The Jews were not forgotten, till they had rejected the Messias.
Out. Their return was facilitated. This may easily be applied (Calmet) to the conversion of the Gentiles. (St. Jerome)
Peace. Septuagint, "rejoicing," or prosperity for the Chaldeans or wicked Jews, ver. 18. (Calmet) --- It is promised only to the penitent. (Worthington)

f: Commentary on Isaiah

Hear these things, house of Jacob, you who are called by the name of Israel, and have come forth from the waters of Judah: who swore in the name of the Lord, and make mention of the God of Israel, not in truth nor in righteousness. For they are called after the holy city: and upon the Lord of Israel they are established: the Lord of hosts is his name. These things I foretold would come upon the Chaldeans and Babylonians, and what I have spoken through my Prophets must be fulfilled in deed. But you, house of Jacob, and you who are called by the name of Israel, and who have come forth from the water of Judah, and the rest that follows, hear more attentively what I am about to say. And it is to be noted that he by no means calls them Jacob, but the house of Jacob; nor Israel, since they are falsely called by this name, not having the work of the name. And from the waters, he says, of Judah you have come forth, σεμνοτερῶς calling it waters in place of seed, so as to show that they are by no means sons of the virtues of the Patriarchs, but of their flesh. And rightly he called them the waters of Judah, because that tribe alone was still then remaining in the land of Judea; and at that time the royal seed of David was being preserved. Who, he says, swore in the name of the Lord, not that you might honor the Lord; but that, having taken up his name, you might do him wrong, while you want him to be the witness of your lie, and you rest in the holy city, and lean upon the Lord of Israel; so that you may boast that you are inhabitants of the city of Jerusalem, and have the privilege of the Lord Sabaoth, while you take up the empty names of Jacob, of Israel and of the holy city, and of the almighty God.
Commentary on Isaiah

The former things I declared from of old, and they went forth from my mouth, and I made them heard: suddenly I worked, and they came to pass. For I knew that you are hard, and your neck is a sinew of iron, and your brow is bronze. I foretold it to you from of old: before they came, I made it known to you, lest perhaps you should say: My idols have done these things, and my graven images and my molten images have commanded them. What you have heard, see it all: but you have not declared it. I have made you hear new things from that time: and things kept in store which you do not know: they are created now, and not from of old: and before the day, and you did not hear them, lest perhaps you should say: Behold, I knew them. You have neither heard, nor known, nor from of old was your ear opened: for I know that you will deal very treacherously, and I have called you a transgressor from the womb. For my name's sake I will put my fury far off: and with my praise I will bridle you, lest you perish. Behold, I have refined you, but not as silver: I have chosen you in the furnace of poverty. For my own sake, for my own sake I will do it, that I be not blasphemed: and my glory I will not give to another. LXX: The former things I declared still: and they went forth from my mouth: and it was made heard: suddenly I did them, and they came to pass, I know that you are hard: and your neck is a sinew of iron, and your brow is bronze: and I declared it to you long ago, before they came upon you. I made it heard to you: lest perhaps you should say that idols have done it for me, that graven and molten images have commanded me. You have heard all things, and you have not known: but I have made you hear new things, those which are now to be. And you did not say, They are being done now, and not long ago: and not in former days. Do not say either, I knew them: you neither know, nor understand, nor from the beginning did I open your ears. For I know that you will deal very treacherously: and you will be called wicked even from the womb. For my name's sake I will show you my fury: and I will bring my glorious things upon you, that I may not kill you. Behold, I have sold you, not for silver: but I have rescued you from the furnace of poverty: for my own sake I will do it, because my name is profaned: and my glory I will not give to another. I foretell to you that the Babylonians are to be overcome by the Medes and Persians, and I will suddenly do what I have threatened, lest, when the things foretold have come, you should think they happened either by the nod of the gods you worship or by chance. Nor do I boast of knowledge of the future, but I speak because of your unbelief, you whose heart I knew from the beginning to be unbelieving, and your neck of iron, and your brow of bronze.
Commentary on Isaiah

Most of our writers, to touch briefly on a few things according to the Seventy Translators, hold that the coming of Christ is prophesied: that he comes suddenly, unhoped for, and shows his presence to a most hard people, whose ears God never opened, because its heart had grown fat, and it heard heavily with its ears. And that, as soon as the Lord was poured forth from the virginal womb, it was called transgressor and wicked, seeking to kill him. And as for what he joins: For my name's sake I will show you my fury, and my glorious things I will bring upon you, he draws on the sense of the Apostle, or rather the apostle Paul (Rom 1) takes his testimony from this passage, that the wrath of God is revealed to terrify those who sin, and afterwards glory is offered to those who have turned: Behold, he says, I have sold you, not for money, but I have sold you in your sins, and I have rescued you from the furnace of poverty. For which reason Solomon too (Prov 30) does not wish to have riches or poverty, but asks only for necessaries, lest either by the former his heart be lifted up into pride, or in the latter he be compelled to do what he does not wish and, pressed by want, to blaspheme God. Hence the Apostle too says: Having food and clothing, he says, let us be content with these (1 Tim 6:8).
Commentary on Isaiah

Behold, you have heard all the things that are to come, and yet you hide the truth in silence. Nor do I recount the past things by which my power has often been proved: how I led the people out of Egypt, drowned the Egyptians in the Red Sea, handed over the land of promise, subjugated various nations to you. But I announce the new things that I am going to do against Babylon, so that the shameless lie of your mouth may be refuted, you who claim to know what you do not know.
Commentary on Isaiah

For from the beginning you have been a transgressor of my commandments; and God called you a transgressor from the womb, when, set free from Egypt, you were, as it were, conceived in my womb, and brought up, and instructed. You longed for the ox's head of Egypt, saying: These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.
AGAINST CELSUS 5:15

But we say that God brings fire on the world, not like a cook [pace Celsus] but like a God who is the benefactor of those who stand in need of the discipline of force. This is confirmed by the prophet Isaiah.… Now the Scripture is appropriately adapted to the multitudes of those who are to peruse it, because it speaks obscurely of things that are sad and gloomy, in order to terrify those who cannot by any other means be saved from the flood of their sins, although even then the attentive reader will clearly discover the end that is to be accomplished by these sad and painful punishments on those who endure them. It is sufficient, however, for the present to quote the words of Isaiah: "For my name's sake will I delay my anger, and my glory I will bring on you, that I may not destroy you."
Commentary on Isaiah

Not for your merit, then, but by my mercy I have put off my fury, lest you should perish utterly, and for the praise of my name I will bridle you, so that, like a beast of burden and a horse in bridles, you may follow me against your will.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 4:3.48:5-11

It is a work that is necessary, and it is the fruit of admirable foresight to avoid these things that are announced and not to wait for the end of the unhappy times but to stand outside of all wrath and judgment.… "I have restrained my wrath for the sake of my name," and I will establish my glorious deeds over you lest you be destroyed.… We see in this the greatness of God's love; he mixes in with unhappy events glorious things lest they be totally destroyed.
Commentary on Isaiah

Behold, I have refined you, that is, I have tested you, as silver is smelted. Or, I wished to test you not in riches but in the furnace of poverty. From this it is shown that most men are tempted both by riches and by poverty, if they either badly abuse the former or by no means bear want with virtue.
Commentary on Isaiah

For my own sake, then, I will do it, lest my name be blasphemed among the nations, and they think that you were overcome not by my anger but by the help of their idols. And what he adds, my glory I will not give to another, signifies this: lest the idols be thought to have crushed the people of God. Or certainly, when he says, I will not give to another, he shows that he has already given it to another; for 'to another' is said to distinguish it from the former.
Commentary on Isaiah

Hear me, Jacob, and Israel, whom I call. I myself, I am the first, and I am the last. My hand also founded the earth, and my right hand measured the heavens: I called them, and they will stand together. Gather together, all of you, and hear: who among them has declared these things? The Lord has loved him: he will do his will in Babylon, and his arm upon the Chaldeans. I, I have spoken and called him: I have brought him, and his way is made straight. Draw near to me, and hear these things: not from the beginning have I spoken in secret: from the time before it came to be, there I was. And now the Lord God has sent me, and his spirit. LXX: Hear me, Jacob and Israel, whom I call. I am the first, and I am for ever: and my hand founded the earth, and my right hand made firm the heaven. I will call them, and they will stand together: and all will be gathered, and will hear: Who has announced these things to them? Loving you, I have done your will upon Babylon: to take away the seed of the Chaldeans. I have spoken and I have called. I have brought him and have made his way prosper. Bring them to me, and hear these things: Not from the beginning have I spoken in secret: when it was being done, there I was. And now the Lord God has sent me, and his spirit. To those to whom he had already said before: Hear these things, house of Jacob, you who are called by the name of Israel, and have come forth from the waters of Judah, he now speaks: Hear me, Jacob and Israel, whom I call.
