For many are called, and few chosen (Matt 22). Hence he names them not chosen, because they had not yet received the Savior; but called. I am, he says, α and ω, the first and the last, who live, and was dead (Rev 22); so that you may refer life to the first, and the last to him who died. Who emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and became obedient to the Father; he humbled himself even to death, even the death of the cross (Phil 2).
AGAINST HERMOGENES 45
He is the Lord's right hand, indeed his two hands, by which he worked and constructed the universe.
Commentary on Isaiah

My hand founded the earth. Hence in Proverbs too he says: God by his wisdom founded the earth, and his right hand measured (Prov 3:19), or made firm the heavens, or the heaven, as the Seventy translated. And he calls the heavens, that they may obey his command and tell forth his glory. But if the heavens obey the will of the Lord and run in their order, why does earth and ashes glory (Sir 10), and not know its own frailty?
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 4:3.48:12-13

Now the hand and the right arm is what God the Father calls his Son. And we often find him so called throughout Scripture. The divine Moses said, "Your right hand has been glorified in might, your right hand has shattered the enemies," and David the blessed said, "May your hand be strengthened, may your right arm be lifted up."
Commentary on Isaiah

Gather together, all of you, and hear: either heavens, or the whole creation, or the whole multitude of Israel. What are the things they are bidden to hear? That the Lord has loved him: there is no doubt that he means Cyrus and Darius, who did the will of the Lord against Babylon, and exercised his arm upon the Chaldeans. And he himself spoke and called him by his name, and brought him, and his way was made straight, so that none dared to resist his might.
Commentary on Isaiah

But according to Symmachus, who translated: Who has announced these things to him? whom the Lord has loved, who does his will in Babylon: and according to the Seventy, to take away the seed of the Chaldeans, it is referred to the person of the Lord: who is truly beloved by the Father, and who did all the will of the Father, and who overthrew in Babylon, that is, in the confusion of this world, all the seed of the Chaldeans, who are interpreted as demons. He himself spoke, and heard the Son, and brought him, who says to believers: Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened (Matt 11:28).
AGAINST CELSUS 1:46

Did the Father and the Holy Spirit send Jesus, or did the Father send both Christ and the Spirit? The latter is correct. For, because the Savior was sent, afterwards the Holy Spirit was sent also, that the prediction of the prophet might be fulfilled.
COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 2:79.81

According to Isaiah the Lord has sent Christ and his Spirit.… It is also possible there to allege of the Spirit that sent the Christ that he does not excel him in nature but that the Savior was made to seek greater lowliness because of the plan of the incarnation.
Commentary on Isaiah

Hence he summons them to draw near and hear, and, as the Lord foretells it, to know that the king of the Persians and Medes will come, to overthrow Babylon and destroy the Chaldeans. And to announce these things, the Prophet says that he has been sent by the Lord and by his spirit. This is according to the Hebrews and their opinion.
Commentary on Isaiah

And hear these things which from the beginning I have spoken in secret, that is, through the riddles and mysteries of the Prophets, which had been unknown to all past generations. When all things were being made by the Father, he himself was with him, who rejoiced with him, who even now says: I, who was always with the Father, and in the Father, and was never without the Father, even now speak (John 14): and according to the frailty of the flesh I assumed, I say that the Lord God has sent me, and his spirit: and in one short verse the mystery of the Trinity is shown to us.
City of God 20.30

Now it is Jesus Christ who is speaking here as the "Lord God"; yet this would not have been obvious if he had not added the final words, "And now the Lord God has sent me and his Spirit." These words were spoken by Christ in his "form" as a "servant." He used a verb in the past tense to indicate a future event.
ON THE TRINITY 2:2.8

Moreover, He could not be sent by the Father without the Holy Spirit, not only because the Father, when He sent Him, that is, when He made Him of a woman, is certainly understood not to have so made Him without His own Spirit; but also because it is most plainly and expressly said in the Gospel in answer to the Virgin Mary, when she asked of the angel, "How shall this be?" "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee." And Matthew says, "She was found with child of the Holy Ghost." Although, too, in the prophet Isaiah, Christ Himself is understood to say of His own future advent, "And now the Lord God and His Spirit hath sent me."
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 4:3.48:15-16

Those who look toward the Savior do not attribute grace for salvation to other gods but to him. For it is said about him that he was moved by love, that is, he was most loving and kind to them in that he was prepared to go all the way to the very end, to the uprooting of the seed of the Chaldeans, that is, those who fought against them and perpetrated all sorts of inhuman acts.… I am spurred by love for you that I will do what is your pleasure in the land of the Babylonians, so that the seed of the Chaldeans will be removed. For [Isaiah] speaks here about Cyrus.
Commentary on Isaiah

Thus says the Lord, your redeemer, the Holy One of Israel: I am the Lord your God, who teach you profitable things, who guide you in the way in which you walk. Would that you had heeded my commandments; your peace would have been like a river, and your righteousness like the whirlpools of the sea. And your seed would have been like the sand, and the offspring of your womb like its pebbles: they would not have perished, and his name would not have been worn away from before my face. Since he has promised Israel things to come, he gives the reasons why he afflicted them before: if they avoid these, they will by no means suffer the like. If, he says, you had heeded my commandments, as the Seventy translated: or certainly, with the feeling of one who wishes, would that you had heeded my commandments: if you had done them, your peace would have been like rivers, and your righteousness like the whirlpools of the sea: signifying abundance and plenty of all things.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 4:3.48:17-19

He says, "I AM your God." This "I AM" means "I am the beginning." He explained all this to the all-wise Moses saying "I am the one who is." For he as Lord is truly the God of everything. Those things that are brought into being by him are said to be "beings" also and to share in the source of being.… Again he works in them a steadfast thinking and a well-established mind that they can see God to be truly existing in nature. To these he reveals his glory so that they are not carried away by deceitful voices.
On the Holy Spirit 1.16.180-81

Set before yourself any river. It springs from its fountain but is of one nature, of one brightness and beauty. And you assert rightly that the Holy Spirit is of one substance, brightness and glory with the Son of God and with God the Father. I will sum up everything in the oneness of the qualities without any dispute over degrees of greatness. For in this point also Scripture has provided for us. For the Son of God says, "Whoever shall drink of the water that I will give him, it shall become in him a well of water springing up unto everlasting life." This well is clearly the grace of the Spirit, a stream proceeding from the living Fountain. The Holy Spirit, then, is also the fountain of eternal life.You observe, then, from his words that the unity of the divine greatness is pointed out and that Christ cannot be denied to be a fountain even by heretics, since the Spirit, too, is called a fountain. The Spirit is called a river, too, just as the Father said, "Behold, I come down on you like a river of peace, and like a stream overflowing the glory of the Gentiles." And who can doubt that the Son of God is the river of life from whom the streams of eternal life flowed forth?
On the Holy Spirit 1.16.182-84

This water is good, then. I mean here the grace of the Spirit. Who will give this Fountain to my heart? Let it spring up in me, let that which gives eternal life flow on me. Let that Fountain overflow on us and not flow away. For Wisdom says, "Drink water out of your own vessels and from the fountains of your own wells, and let your waters flow abroad in your streets." How shall I keep this water so that it does not seep out or glide away? How shall I preserve my vessel, lest any crack of sin penetrating it should let the water of eternal life exude? Teach us, Lord Jesus, teach us as you taught your apostles, saying, "Lay not up for yourselves treasures on the earth, where rust and moth destroy and where thieves break through and steal."8Our rust is wantonness, our rust is lust, our rust is luxury, which dim the keen vision of the mind with the filth of vices. Again, our moth is Arius, our moth is Photinus, who rend the holy vesture of the church with their impiety, and desiring to separate the indivisible unity of the divine power, gnaw the precious veil of faith with sacrilegious tooth. The water is spillled if Arius has imprinted his tooth, it flows away if Photinus has planted his sting in anyone's vessel.…
If you seek Jesus, forsake the broken cisterns, for Christ did not make it his custom to sit by a pool but by a well. There that Samaritan woman found him, she who believed, she who wished to draw water. Although you ought to have come in early morning, nevertheless if you come later, even at the sixth hour, you will find Jesus wearied with his journey. He is weary, but it is because of you, because he has long looked for you, your unbelief has long wearied him. Yet he is not offended if you only come now. He asks to drink who is about to give. But he drinks not the water of a stream flowing by, but your salvation. He drinks your good dispositions. He drinks the cup, that is, the passion that atoned for your sins, that you, drinking of his sacred blood, might quench the thirst of this world.
Commentary on Isaiah

And as for what follows: and your seed would have been like the sand, and the offspring of your womb like its pebbles: it seems indeed to hold good in the people of the Jews, who to this present day sprout sons and grandsons like little worms; but how is this to be taken as a promise, when they have neither peace nor righteousness? For either he is angry with them, or appeased. If angry, how is his seed multiplied daily? If appeased, how are they in servitude, and do not possess peace and righteousness? From this it is plain that he now speaks of the Apostolic seed, of which we also read above (cf. Isa 1): Unless the Lord Sabaoth had left us a seed, we should have been like Sodom. Since this is by no means seen fulfilled at that time, it is fulfilled in the coming of Christ: and the seed of Israel remains before his face.
Commentary on Isaiah

But those who, more truly and more rightly, refer these things to the Savior's coming (cf. below, Isa 61:1), of which it is said: He has sent me to announce good news to the poor, to preach release to the captives (Luke 4:18, 19), understand it to be an exhortation of those who announce the Gospel of the Lord Savior himself, that we should go forth from Babylon, that is, from the confusion of this world, and flee the Chaldeans, of whom it has often been spoken. For the Lord redeemed his servant Jacob with his most precious blood, and led him through the desert of the world, and split water from the rock. Concerning which the Apostle too says: And the rock was Christ (1 Cor 10:4). And the divine word is split, and divided into many parts, so that what we cannot receive whole we may take in parts. And lest this preaching should be thought to be spoken to all the seed of Jacob, and not only to those who were to believe through the Apostles, there is added and joined: There is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord: that is, to those who remained in their former error; who did not deserve to drink from the rock. Whose side, to speak in a new way, wounded by the lance, flowed with water and blood (John 19), consecrating for us baptism and martyrdom.
Commentary on Isaiah

Go forth from Babylon, flee from the Chaldeans: declare it with a voice of exultation, make this heard, carry it to the end of the earth, and say: The Lord has redeemed his servant Jacob. They did not thirst in the desert when he led them out; he brought forth water from the rock for them, and he split the rock, and the waters flowed. There is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord. Those who understood the place above, where it is written: I, I have spoken, and called him: I have brought him, and his way is made straight, of Cyrus and Darius, refer these things too to his times, when the people went forth from Babylon, and fled from the Chaldeans, and was redeemed by the Lord its God.
City of God 18.18

"Come forth out of Babylon." If we take the command of the prophet in a spiritual sense, it means that we should fly from the city of this world, from the fellowship of wicked angels and wicked [people], with the feet of that faith that works through love, and we should press onward unceasingly toward the living God.
Commentary on Isaiah

This also that is said: They did not thirst in the desert when he led them out, he brought forth water from the rock for them; and he split the rock, and the waters flowed, although they cannot show it fulfilled according to the history (for under Zerubbabel and Ezra they did not come through a desert, nor did a split rock furnish them waters, as is related to have happened to those going out of Egypt), they nevertheless maintain was fulfilled hyperbolically, in the likeness of the former happiness, when they came into Judea through the desert of the nations, and were set free from captivity.
Commentary on Isaiah

And so that we may know, they say, that it was prophesied not of Christ but of Cyrus, there is joined: There is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord: and the sense is: Perfect happiness will not be except under Christ, which is reserved for the last time.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 4:3.48:20-22

No one found that this happened when they came out of Babylon and went into Judah. For this is said with reference to the economy of salvation so as to show that God, who was formerly able and is still now able, being of undiminished power, to perform similar miracles with great strength, now, as if calling out, proclaims a universal law, that "there is no peace for the wicked."

n: Give. This fresh discourse continues to chap. lvi. 9., relating to the Messias, who is introduced speaking to all the world, Acts xiii. 47., and 2 Corinthians vi. 2. Some apply a part to Cyrus, Isaias, or John the Baptist, as to his figures. (Calmet) --- The prophet has foretold the conversion of the Gentiles, as he now does, like an evangelist. (St. Jerome) --- Many Jews will embrace the gospel at the end of time. (Worthington)

Sword, penetrating the very soul, (Hebrews iv. 12.) and slaying the wicked, Apocalypse i. 16., and 2 Thessalonians ii. 8. Without Christ, his ministers can apply this sword to little purpose. Cyrus cut asunder the bonds of the captives by his decree. (Calmet) --- Grotius improperly explains all of Isaias. (Houbigant)
Glory. In the Church, God is adored in spirit and truth. Isaias is ordered thus to address the Israelites.
God. He will reward the labours of his ministers, though the people be obstinate. The prophets and our Saviour frequently complain, chap. lxv. 2., and Mark ix. 18.

Will not. Hebrew, Septuagint, &c., "to be gathered." (Haydock) --- The original text, independent of the Masorets, may have the sense of the Vulgate. Yet there are other proofs of the synagogue's rejection. (Calmet) --- Protestants, "though Israel be not gathered, yet," &c. Marginal note, or "that Israel may be gathered, and I may," &c. (Haydock)
Earth. St. Paul, explains this of Christ, (Acts xiii.) who said, Go teach all nations, Matthew xxviii. Isaias was one of his first preachers.
Despised, Christ, Cyrus, or Isaias; though it refer chiefly to our Saviour.
Ways. The captives shall find every convenience. (Calmet)
South. Hebrew Sinim; (Haydock) China, (St. Jerome) or rather Sin, or Pelusium, and Sinai, in Egypt and Arabia. Septuagint, "Persians." (Calmet)
Sion, the Jews, who will at last be converted in great numbers. (Houbigant)

Hands, which were nailed to the cross. Septuagint, "I have delineated thy walls on my hands, and thou art before me always." (Haydock) --- The Assyrians wore such characters on their hands or necks. (Lucian) (Leviticus xix. 28.) (Calmet) --- Christ will always love his Church, which is of all times and nations. (Worthington)
Of thee. Sanballat, &c., shall yield to Zorobabel, Nehemias, &c.
Inhabitants. The country was better peopled, (Calmet) and Jerusalem enlarged under the Machabees. (Josephus, Jewish Wars v. 6.)
Barrenness, of which thou complainest. He alludes to the captives who returned, and to Christian converts. (Menochius)
Shoulders. Thus the Syrians commonly carried children astride. (Cotovic. xiv.)

Nurses. The Persian kings favoured the captives. The greatest monarchs bow before the prelates of the Church, (Menochius) and kiss the Pope's toe. They venerate relics, (Haydock) and greatly enrich the Church. (Calmet)
Strong. Can I force the Babylonians to yield? Surely, and the devil also, Luke xi. 21. --- Mighty. Hebrew, "just," in lawful war. Septuagint, "unjustly."

Flesh. They shall attack one another. (Calmet) --- Neriglissor slew Evil-merodac. (Berosus, apud Josephus, contra Apion i.) --- Gobrias and Gadatas betrayed and killed Baltassar. (Xenophon iv. 5, 7.) (Calmet) --- In their fury they shall tear their own flesh. (Menochius)

f: Catechetical Lecture 10:12

Consider how he who was not yet born could have a people, unless he were in being before he was born. The prophet says this in his person, "From my mother's womb he gave me my name"; because the angel foretold that he would be called Jesus. Again, concerning the plots of Herod, he says, "He … concealed me in the shadow of his arm."
Commentary on Isaiah

Hear, islands, and give heed, peoples from afar: the Lord called me from the womb, from the belly of my mother he remembered my name. And he made my mouth like a sharp sword: in the shadow of his hand he protected me. And he made me like a chosen arrow: in his quiver he hid me; and he said to me: You are my servant, Israel, for in you I will glory. And I said: I have labored in vain, without cause and vainly I have spent my strength: therefore my judgment is with the Lord, and my work with my God. LXX: Hear me, islands, and give heed, nations. After a long time it shall stand, says the Lord. From the belly he called me, and from the womb of my mother he called my name. And he made my mouth like a sharp sword, and under the protection of his hand he hid me. He made me like a chosen arrow, and in his quiver he hid me. And he said to me: You are my servant, Israel: and in you I will be glorified. And I said, I have labored without cause, in vain, and I have given my strength for nothing. Therefore my judgment is with the Lord, and my labor before my God. I know that both these things and those further on that we are going to speak of belong to the knowledge or understanding of a single chapter, and that all must be taken in the person of Christ. But I did not wish, by setting everything out together, to burden the reader's mind, and to confound by its magnitude what can more easily be said in parts. Hence I have also set down both editions, so that what seems obscure in the one may be unlocked by the reading of the other. After the calling of the remnant of Israel, then, and the casting off of the people that remained in unbelief, of whom he had said: There is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord (Isa 48:22), he passes over to the Churches gathered from the nations, and speaks to them under the name of islands. These lie open to the ambushes of persecutors as to the waves of the sea, and, with shipwreck raging on every side, are beaten rather than moved. And lest anyone think that our exposition is forced, and that what is said belongs not to the nations but to the Synagogues of the Jewish people, there follows: And give heed, peoples, or nations, from afar, that is, from the furthest ends of the earth. Or, as the Seventy translated, after a long time it shall stand, that is, not at this time in which they are spoken; but they will come to pass after many times. The Lord, he says, called me from the womb, and from the belly of my mother he remembered my name. Which for the present seems obscure to the hearers, but afterwards will become known to all the nations, when Gabriel will have said to Joseph of the virgin birth: And you shall call his name Jesus: for he will save his people (Matt 1:21).
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 4:4.49:1-3

He calls to "the islands," which we take to be the churches of Christ, just as they are lying in the sea or the waves of this present existence and surrounded by the insulting attacks of "the waves," or the persecutions and afflictions that the enemies of the truth inflict on the churches as they war against the divine call. Concerning these islands the divinely inspired Scripture often speaks. There the blessed David sang a psalm and said, "The Lord reigns, and let the earth be glad and many islands rejoice." So when Christ taking all things in his hands reigned over it from heaven and ejected the demons' tyranny, then did they rejoice, that is, the churches over all the earth were filled with happiness.… [Isaiah] promised that our Savior Jesus Christ would be revealed to everyone and that God as the Word would come on the earth among them in a form "after our likeness." … That this is so, the person of the Savior himself attests, "Out of my mother's womb he called my name." Mixed into these words is a deep and great mystery that requires mystical understanding from above.… For he was and is God the Word, equal and sharing the throne with God the Father, coexisting and coeternal.
COMMENTARY ON THE SONG OF SONGS, PROLOGUE

Therefore, if anyone can with a capacious mind conceive and consider the beauty and comeliness of all these things which were created in Him, being struck by the very loveliness of things and pierced by the magnificence of their splendor as by a chosen arrow, as the prophet says, he will receive from Him a saving wound, and will burn with the blessed fire of His love.
The Six Days of Creation, 5.80

Make for yourself, O man, a case; stripping off the old man with his actions, put on the new. Your case, your sheath, is Christ, who protects and hides you in the evil day. Do you want to know why the case is protection? My quiver, He says, protected him. Therefore, your case is faith: fill it with the good scents of your virtues; that is, chastity, mercy, and justice, and in it, enter completely fragrant with the sweet scent of excellent deeds of faith.
Commentary on Isaiah

He also made his mouth like a sharp sword, so that with the spirit of his mouth he may slay the wicked one. Of which sword he himself also speaks in the Gospel: I came not to send peace upon the earth, but a sword, separating the evil from the good: For I came to divide a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law (Matt 10:34, 35). And in the shadow, he says, of his hand he protected me, so that the lowliness of the flesh might be covered by the power of the divinity, as the angel announced to the Virgin: The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you (Luke 1:35). He made me, he says, like a chosen arrow, in his quiver he hid me. When he says, a chosen arrow, he shows that God has very many arrows, but not chosen ones: which arrows are the Prophets and the Apostles, who run through the whole world. Of whom it is sung in another place too: Your arrows are sharp, O most mighty; peoples will fall beneath you (Ps 44 [45]:6); and again: The sharp arrows of the mighty, with desolating coals (Ps 119 [120]:4). But Christ, out of many arrows and very many sons, is the one chosen arrow, and the Only-begotten Son: whom he hid in his quiver, that is, in a human body, so that the fullness of the divinity might dwell in him bodily. And rare is the faith of believers: to whom it is also said above (Isa 45:15): You are a hidden God, and we did not know it. Receiving a wound from this arrow, the bride too speaks in the Song of Songs: I am wounded with love.
Commentary on Zechariah

According to tropology this place can be explained thus: Judah is stretched as a bow when the Lord and Savior is sent by the Father into this world, he who is himself both the bow and the archer and the arrow. The bow, as in the present place. The archer, as in Psalm 44 (45): Your arrows are sharp, most mighty; and when someone has been wounded by them, he says: I am wounded with love. And the arrow is he himself who speaks through Isaiah: He has set me as a chosen arrow, and in his quiver he has hidden me. The chosen arrow is the Word of God; the quiver in which the arrow is hidden is the dispensation of the flesh he assumed.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 4:4.49:1-3

The name Christ is not appropriate for God the Word before the generation that, as I said, was according to the flesh. If he was then not yet anointed, how could he be called "Christ"? But when the man came forth from his mother's womb, then he received the name at the same time as the generation according to the flesh. For it says that he "set his mouth like a sharp sword" … for no one can overcome his all-powerful right hand, but the Word is kept distinct from the dimensions of the humanity. For he is the Word from the Father and himself is the Lord of hosts. When he became man, the Father did not remove the power of the mystery but confirmed him in the economy of salvation.… There have been several arrows of God hidden in his quiver, in his foreknowledge, and brought out at the time prepared for each, but the chosen arrow above all others is the Christ hidden in the quiver or foreknowledge of God. For he was known before the creation of the world and brought forth in the middle of time when it was necessary that the earth be visited as it was falling into destruction.… This chosen arrow, as I said, got rid of Satan and the evil powers with him … yet he wounds in another way, for benefit and salvation. Thus it says in the Song of Songs, "I am wounded with love."
Commentary on Isaiah

And he said to me: You are my servant, Israel: for in you I will be glorified (Song 4:9). A servant, because, though he was in the form of God, he deigned to take the form of a servant (Phil 2), and Israel, because he was born of the seed of the Jews. And, what can be understood of no other of the servants, there is joined: For in you I will glory. For he himself also says in the Gospel, Father, glorify your name (John 12:28). He it is who in the psalm says to the Son: Arise, my glory, and arise, psaltery and harp (Ps 56 [57]:9), that is, the choir of all the virtues.
Commentary on Isaiah

And when the Father said to me these things that I have related, I answered him: How are you glorified in me, Father, since I have labored in vain, and could not call back to you a great part of the Jewish people? And all these things are said to show the free will of man. For it is God's to call, and ours to believe: nor, if we do not believe, is God at once powerless; but he leaves his power to our choice, so that the will of the righteous may obtain its reward. Since, then, they would not believe in you through me, my judgment is with you, that I have done all things that I ought to have done for them, saying in the Gospel: I have glorified you on the earth, having completed the work which you gave me to do (John 17:4); and again: I have manifested your name to men. And my work, or my labor and pain (for this is what πόνος signifies), is in your sight. For in the Gospel too he wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19), and in the psalm, because of the multitude of unbelievers, he says that in a certain way he suffered in vain: What profit is there in my blood, while I go down to corruption (Ps 29 [30]:10)? And according to the Hebrew, hanging on the cross, he says: Far from my salvation are the words of my lamentations (Ps 21 [22]:1).
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 4:4.49:4

For it was a labor for the Word to come among us and to surrender himself to human fragility. But "my judgment" is the punishment of the Father that I [the Savior] have turned into a feast for their salvation. For that reason the judgment was taken away from him [the servant]. Just what sort of judgment was that? [Sinners] have been cast out of his company, to be placed outside the people of God, no longer sharers in the salvation wrought by him, and they have no longer any taste of the hope of the saints, to which many of the nations have been called in their place.
Commentary on Isaiah

And now says the Lord, who formed me from the womb to be his servant, that I might bring Jacob back to him, and Israel will not be gathered: and I am glorified in the eyes of the Lord, and my God has become my strength. And he said: It is a small thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to turn back the dregs of Israel. I have given you as a light of the nations; that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth. LXX: And now thus says the Lord, who formed me from the womb to be his servant, that I might gather Jacob to him, and Israel: I shall be gathered and glorified before the Lord, and my God shall be my strength. And he said to me: It is a great thing for you to be called my child, and to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to turn back the dispersion of Israel. Behold, I have set you for a covenant of the race, for a light of the nations, that you may be salvation to the end of the earth. When I said, I have labored in vain, without cause and vainly I have spent my strength, because the Jews would not believe, and my judgment is with the Lord, and my work, which with his help I have fulfilled, is with the Lord: the Lord, who formed me from the womb to be his servant, answered me. By this he shows that he is called servant who was formed from the womb. He also says in the psalm: From the belly of my mother you are my God (Ps 21 [22]:11). What, then, does the Lord say to him? That he should bring back to him Jacob, who had wandered off, who, having forsaken his Creator, was serving idols. Hence he himself says to the disciples: Do not go into the way of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans; but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt 10:5); and in another place: I came only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt 15:24). This, then, was the will of the Father: that the wicked vinedressers should receive the Son who was sent, and render the fruits of the vineyard; but they killed him, saying: Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours (Matt 21:38); and this is what he now says: And Israel will not be gathered, that is, will not return to the Lord. And I greatly wonder how the common edition has overturned, by a different interpretation, a very strong testimony against the faithlessness of the Jews, saying: I shall be gathered and glorified before the Lord: since Theodotion and Symmachus agree with our interpretation. About Aquila, however, I do not wonder, that a man most learned in the Hebrew language, and rendering word for word, has in this place either feigned ignorance or been deceived by the perverse exposition of the Pharisees, since he chose to translate, and Israel will be gathered to him, that is, to God. For the Hebrew word LO in this place is not written with LAMED and VAV (לו), which, if it were, would signify to him or to that one, but with LAMED and ALEPH (לא), which properly sounds not. Since, then, Jacob was not brought back to God, nor Israel gathered, therefore, since they did not believe, the Son says: I am glorified in the eyes of the Lord. For in me the whole world has believed: and my God has become my strength, who also comforted me in my sadness over the casting off of my people; and said to me: It is a small thing if you serve me to raise up the tribes of Jacob, which fell through their own fault; and to turn back the dregs, or remnant, of Israel. For this is what the Hebrew word NESURE (נצורי) sounds. For in their place I have given you as a light of all the nations, to illumine the whole world, and to make my salvation, through which all are saved, reach to the ends of the earth. And what is read in the Seventy, I shall be gathered, and glorified before the Lord, can be understood thus: that the Lord has been gathered together with the believers. Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I lift up my hand to the nations, and to the peoples I will raise up my standard: and they shall bring your sons in their arms, and carry your daughters upon their shoulders. And kings shall be your foster fathers, and queens your nurses. With face bowed to the ground they shall worship you, and lick the dust of your feet: and you shall know that I am the Lord, in whom those who wait for him shall not be confounded. LXX: Thus said the Lord God: Behold, I raise my hand over the nations, and over the islands I will lift up my standard, and they shall bring your sons in their bosom, and carry your daughters on their shoulders. And kings shall be your foster fathers: and princesses your nurses: on the face of the earth they shall worship you, and lick the dust of your feet; and you shall know that I am the Lord, and those who wait for me shall not be confounded. To what the Church had said: I was barren and captive, who has begotten these for me? I was left destitute and alone, and these, where were they? the Lord answered: Do you wonder why these things have come about? You will by no means wonder when you hear that I have lifted up my hand to the nations. Of this hand the Saint too says: You have formed me, and laid your hand upon me (Ps 138 [139]:4). And the Savior himself: No one can snatch out of my Father's hand (John 10:29). And the Apostle Peter: Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in the time of visitation (1 Pet 5:6). This hand lifted up to the nations is the very one of which this same Prophet speaks here: There shall be the root of Jesse, who shall rise up to be the prince of the nations: in him the nations shall hope (Isa 11:10). And not only will he lift up his hand to the nations; but he will also raise up his standard among the peoples. There is no doubt that this is the banner of the cross, so that what is written may be fulfilled: The earth is full of his praises. And again: In all the earth his name is wonderful (Ps 8:1). Then they shall bring the sons of Zion in their arms, or in their bosom, and carry her daughters upon their shoulders. Such too was Lazarus, and all the saints who rest in the bosom of Abraham (Luke 16), and the souls of believers, to whom Paul the Apostle said: I gave you milk to drink (1 Cor 3:2). And elsewhere: My little children, with whom I am again in labor until Christ be formed in you (Gal 4:19). And in another place: As a nurse cherishes her children: so, longing for you, we desire to impart to you not only the Gospel of Christ, but also our own souls (1 Thess 2:8). Otherwise it is ridiculous, in the Jewish manner, for full-grown sons and daughters to be carried in arms and on shoulders.
Commentary on Isaiah

But the kings who are foster fathers, and the queens and princesses who are nurses, plainly point to the Apostles and to Apostolic men: such as Abraham too was, to whom it is said: You are a king from God among us (Gen 23:6); and whose heart is in the hand of God (Prov 21): who say to believers: As newborn babes, rational and without guile, desire milk (1 Pet 2:2). The princess also, that is, ἄρχουσα, which is the sound of Sarah's name, and the queens, or the queen, of whom it is sung in Psalm 44 (45): The queen stood at your right hand in gilded clothing, nourishes Christ's little ones daily, and leads them to perfect age: and every age, sex and rank will worship Zion for the sake of him who dwells in her. For if Christ is the head of the Church, the head is worshiped in the body. And if it is said to certain people: Exalt the Lord our God, and worship the footstool of his feet (not that the footstool is to be worshiped; but that the majesty of his feet is indicated), why should not the Church be worshiped, which embraces the whole body of Christ, so that what is written in Zephaniah may be fulfilled: They shall worship him, each from his own place: all the islands of the nations (Zeph 2:11), so that they by no means come to Jerusalem three times a year in the Jewish manner, but, worshiping the Lord in their own place, possess Jerusalem. And as for what follows: and they shall lick the dust of your feet, this signifies that kings and princes, whatever of earthly work has clung to the feet of the Church, wipe and lick it away by their word. Hence the Apostles too are commanded to shake off the dust of their feet. And it is said to Peter that he who has once been washed needs only to wash his feet. (Matt 10; John 13). Through all these things the Church learns that there is no other Lord besides him, and those who have waited for him will possess eternal glory.
Commentary on Isaiah

Shall the prey be taken from the strong? or can what has been captured by the mighty be safe? For thus says the Lord: Indeed even the captivity shall be taken from the strong: and what has been carried off by the mighty shall be saved. But those who have judged you, I will judge: and your sons I will save. And I will feed your enemies with their own flesh, and they shall be drunk with their own blood as with new wine: and all flesh shall know that I am the Lord who saves you, and your redeemer, the strong one of Jacob. LXX: Shall anyone take spoils from a giant? And if anyone leads a captive away unjustly, he shall be saved. Thus says the Lord: If anyone captures a giant, he shall take spoils, and he who takes from the strong shall be saved. But I will judge my judgment. And I will rescue my sons, and those who afflicted you shall eat their own flesh, and shall drink their own blood like new wine, and shall be drunk: and all flesh shall know that I am the Lord who rescued you, and the help of the strength of Jacob. Our Lord and Savior, who had spoken earlier through Isaiah, himself repeats the same sense in the Gospel: how can anyone enter the house of a strong man and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man, and then he will plunder his house (Mark 3)? The strong man and giant is the devil, who had subjugated all the nations to his rule, daring to say to the Savior: All these things have been delivered to me, and I will give them to you, if you will fall down and worship me (Matt 4:9). For the world lies in the evil one (1 John 5), and none of the righteous could conquer him: nor, according to Amos, take the prey from the lion's mouth (Amos 3). The question having been set, then, that no one could conquer the strong man and the giant, nor save what had been seized by him, the Lord answered that all would be accomplished by his coming: namely, that the nations formerly captured would be taken from the giant, and all his furniture and his whole household be divided among the Apostles. So is fulfilled what is written: The king of the powers of the beloved, and to the beauty of the house to divide the spoils. For he it is who, ascending on high, led captivity captive, he gave gifts among men (Ps 67 [68]:13, 19; Eph 4): that is, those who had formerly been taken captive unto death he received unto life. Hence Symmachus translated more plainly: But even the captivity of the strong one shall be taken away, and the plunder of the terrible one shall be safe. He wishes the strong and terrible one to be understood as the devil, who has been overcome by the power of the Lord.
Commentary on Isaiah

Therefore the Lord, judging those who had oppressed Zion, or judging her judgment, will set free her sons who had been captured by the giant, and will save them, and he will feed the adverse powers with their own flesh, and make them drunk as with new wine, so that they may be glutted not by the slaughter of others but by their own death. And those who are flesh, because they have lost the spirit of God, are to feed on their own flesh. This indeed the Saint also says in the Psalms: When those who afflicted me drew near to eat my flesh (Ps 26 [27]:2). For it is not the spirit, which is incorporeal, that is eaten, but the flesh, which lies open to the bites of fierce beasts. And then Zion will learn, nay, all flesh which will see the salvation of God, that her Redeemer and Savior is he who wrestled with Jacob, or who was the helper of the strength of Jacob: so that in his passion, lifted up on high, he blessed those who crucified him: Father, forgive them: for they do not know what they are doing (Luke 23:34).
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 4:4.49:25-26

Our Lord Jesus Christ came into the house of the strong man … he raided it and, throwing away the broken chains and the bonds of dark hell, he gave him over to the judgment of the great day to be kept for punishment.… Then Christ has conquered, and he has passed the victory on to us.… For he is the sole cause of our salvation. Therefore, he is the boast of the might of the saints, as Paul the most wise says: "I can do all things through Christ who gives me strength." …For Christ gave us the ability to overcome the murderous dragon so that we can take spoil from it, and we are saved from it as he sends us the victory to everlasting life for glory, praise and the kingdom of heaven.… For Christ said, "I have given you authority to tread on snakes and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy." … This is just what we take from the strong one, that is, from Christ. Since he is the Lord of powers, we have been saved and have the victory.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 4:4.49:25-26

Whoever suffers anything on account of me obtains help from me, the One who gives strength to you, Jacob, that is, all of you from the seed of Jacob. I have said how he sends them prophetic words in the mouth of the holy apostles and evangelists that they are from Jacob, which clearly relates to the flesh. And it is small wonder that Jacob was called the supplanter, that is, the supplanter of Satan and of those who casually and with youthful neglect rush into the noose of sins.

n: Away. Such a one could not be received again, if she had taken another husband, Deuteronomy xxiv. 3. Some explain this of the captives. But God restored them to favour. It seems rather to relate to the reprobation (Calmet) of the synagogue, which will never again become the true Church, (Haydock) though many of Israel will be converted, Romans xi. 25. --- Sold you, as a father might do, Exodus xxi. 1., and Matthew xviii. 15. St. Ambrose (Tob.[Tobias?] viii.) inveighs against such cruel parents, as the Christian religion had not then entirely repressed this inhumanity. (Calmet) --- God rejected the synagogue, not out of hard-heartedness or want, but because of her sins. (Worthington)

Hear. My spouse had gone after other lovers. The people refused to hear the prophets; and the priests were become as corrupt as the rest, when the city was taken by the Chaldeans and by the Romans. (Calmet) --- Sea. Babylon, chap. xxi. (Haydock) --- I could work the same miracles, as I did when Israel came out of Egypt.

Weary. Isaias speaks in the name of Christ, whose words carried conviction and comfort along with them, John vi. 69., and vii. 46. (Calmet) --- Wakeneth. Literally, "lifteth up." Cynthius aurem---Vellit. (Ec. vi.) --- Hear, or obey. (Haydock) --- Christ preached more powerfully than Isaias, and continues to do so by his pastors. (St. Jerome) (Worthington)

Spit. The greatest indignity, Job xxx. 10., and Deuteronomy xxv. 9. Yet this was the treatment of our Saviour, Luke xviii. 31., and Matthew xxvi. 67. (Calmet) --- "The great Grotius, (I wish he were great in explaining the prophets)" applies this to Jeremias. (Houbigant)
Rock. Christ heard the accusations of his enemies unmoved, as he had not been afraid to blame the conduct of the Pharisees.
Light. The faithful are exhorted to take courage, while the Romans will destroy the rebellious Jews, (ver. 11.; Calmet) and the wicked shall dwell in hell fire. (Menochius)

f: HOMILIES ON EXODUS 6

But hear what the prophet says: "By your sins you were sold, and for your iniquities I dismissed your mother." You see, then, that we are indeed all the creature of God, but each one is sold by his own sins and for his own iniquities departs from his own creator. We are, therefore, God's, according as we were created by him; but we became slaves of the devil, according as we were sold by our sins. But Christ, coming, "redeemed us," while we were serving that lord to whom we had sold our very selves by sinning. And so he seems to have received back as his own those whom he had created, but to have acquired as aliens those who by sinning had sought for themselves an alien lord.
On Joseph the Patriarch, 4.19

But Joseph was sold into Egypt, because Christ was going to come to those to whom it was said: For your sins you have been sold. And therefore, He redeemed them with His own blood, who had sold themselves by their own sins. But Christ, who was sold, is held by the assumption of the condition, not by the price of guilt, because He Himself did not commit sin. Therefore, He contracted our debt, not His own money; He took away the handwriting, removed the lender, stripped off the debtor: He alone paid what was owed by all.
Commentary on Isaiah

Thus says the Lord: What is this bill of divorce of your mother, with which I put her away? Or who is my creditor, to whom I sold you? Behold, for your iniquities you were sold, and for your crimes I put away your mother. For I came, and there was no man: I called, and there was none to hear. LXX: Thus says the Lord: What kind of bill of divorce of your mother is it, with which I put her away? Or to which creditor and exactor of mine did I sell you? Behold, for your sins you were sold, and for your iniquities I put away your mother, for I came, and there was no human being: I called, and there was none to obey. After the calling of the nations, and the kings and princes, the foster fathers and nurses, and the captivity of the one formerly strong and mighty, whose prey has been distributed to the Apostles, and after the madness of the demons, who have been glutted with their own flesh and made drunk with their own blood, when all flesh has known that the Redeemer and the strong one is himself the God of Jacob, he speaks to the people of the Jews concerning Zion, who had said before: The Lord has forsaken me, and the Lord has forgotten me. Do you think that your mother, the earthly Jerusalem, has been cast off by my harshness, and that I, of an unbending mind, gave her a bill of divorce, and do you not rather understand, what is true, that she withdrew from me by her own fault? For when I said to her: Cease to act wickedly, learn to do good, she would not hear me; but turned against me a shoulder that drew away: hence I said to her sons: Woe to them, for they have withdrawn from me. Manifest are those who have acted wickedly against me. And to her herself: Your departure will instruct you, and your wickedness will rebuke you; and you will know that it is evil for you that you have forsaken me. But perhaps you cannot show a bill of divorce, and some creditor of mine, demanding money, while I had nothing to pay, takes you in compensation for the debt? It is not so: but I will show you why I have forsaken your mother with her sons. Your crimes and sins have sold you to the demons, so that, ensnared by the pleasures of the present age, both you forsook your parent and she her husband. Hence I could no longer keep your adulterous mother, but, as she wished to go, I let her. And that each one is sold by his own sins, since, left to our own choice, we are led by our will either to good or to evil, Paul the apostle also teaches: But I am carnal, sold under sin (Rom 7:14). For he who commits sin is the servant of sin (John 8). And as the avaricious and the robbers are servants of mammon, so every sin lords it over sinners. To whom it is said: Let not sin reign in your mortal body (Rom 6:12).
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 4:4.50:1-3

God never sends away anyone who makes his home with him, and he rejects none of those who walk uprightly. He allows them to be forever associated and firmly joined to him as a way of obtaining help. However, everyone who opposes or fights against his divine teaching falls completely away from the glory of God and shows that he is a lover of pleasure rather than a lover of God. Therefore, like one who lived with the mother of the Jews God says, "What kind of bill of divorce did your mother have when I sent her away?" For no one could prove that I hated her and despised her. Instead, he would rather have to accuse her of deserting me.… It says, "I came," that is, I took human form and appeared to those in Israel, and there was no man among them, that is, no one with a heart who was able to recognize the season of redemption. "I called, but no one listened." … For he was in a form like ours, and yet he was God the Word, having become man by taking on flesh born of a woman. But those who knew this and were not ignorant of the depth of the mystery of his divinity knew that he was able to do all things because he was God by nature and suitable for the redemption of everyone under heaven.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 113

They were ignorant of the words of the prophet Isaiah, who prophesied these very same things concerning him, and said in the person of the Lord and Savior himself: "what, that I came, and there was no man? I called, and there was none who would obey? Is my hand not able to rescue? Or can I not deliver? Behold, at my rebuke I will make the sea a desert, and I will set the rivers a desert. And their fish shall be dried up because they have no water, and shall die of thirst. And I will clothe the heaven with darkness, and make its covering like sackcloth. The Lord gives me the tongue of instruction, that I may know how it behooves me to speak the word; he set me in the morning, he applied to me an ear to hear, and the instruction of the Lord shall open my ears; but I am not unbelieving, nor do I contradict. I offered my back to the scourges, and my cheeks to the palms of hands, but I did not turn away my face from the confusion of spittings, and the Lord God became my helper". For all who are of the Church confess him to be Christ who says: "the Lord, the Lord gave me the tongue of instruction" and the rest which I have expounded.

But I have fittingly expounded also those things which above were joined to these, wishing to show that this was prophesied concerning that glorious one, that he should be spat upon and buffeted. For to what other does it fit to say: "I came", except to Christ who came into the world? Or whom did it befit to say: "I called, and there was none who would obey", except him who came to call the people of the Jews and was not heard, and therefore did not rescue the people nor deliver it, but forsook it? And it is Christ who says: "behold, at my rebuke I will make the sea a desert, and I will set the rivers a desert", who is to bring about the consummation of the world. For it is he who will clothe the heaven with "darkness" and clothe it "as with sackcloth", and, receiving from the Father the "tongue of instruction", knew how "it behooved him to speak the word" which God had entrusted to him; and "he applied to him an ear", that he might hear more than all who hear, and the "instruction" of the Father opened his ear, because he was not unbelieving to the Father who sent him nor contradicting, and by the very deed he taught those desiring to learn meekness and praiseworthy humility. And there was a work in this, that he taught these things by deeds, offering his "back to the scourges and his cheeks to the palms of hands" and not turning away his face "from the confusion of spittings", so that us (as I judge), who had all been worthy to suffer these disgraces, he himself might rescue by suffering them for us. For he did "not die for us", that we might not die, but that we might not die for ourselves; and he was struck with blows for us and was spat upon, so that we, who had been worthy of all these things on account of our sins, might not suffer them, but that, suffering them for righteousness, we might receive them gladly.
Commentary on Isaiah

Is my hand shortened, and made very small, so that it cannot redeem? Or is there no power in me to deliver? Behold, at my rebuke I will make the sea a desert, I will turn the rivers into dry land: the fish shall rot for lack of water, they shall die of thirst. I will clothe the heavens with darkness, and make sackcloth their covering. LXX: Is my hand not able to deliver, or is it not strong enough to rescue? Behold, by my threat I will make the sea a desert, and make the rivers deserts, and their fish shall dry up, because there is no water, and they shall die of thirst. And I will clothe the heaven with darkness, and make its covering as haircloth. Against those who thought that the Lord had not been able to free his people from captivity, he sets out a reason and the fullest examples: that he who made the Red Sea passable for his people (Exod 14), dried up the streams of the Jordan, and, when the rivers in Egypt dried up, turned the fish to rottenness (Exod 7), and who for three days in Egypt made a darkness that could be felt, so that the heaven seemed covered as with sackcloth and darkness, could surely also free his people from danger. Or, because he had said above: I came, and there was no human being: I called, and there was none to hear, we can say this: that he who is the performer of such great signs, and makes heaven and earth and the seas serve his nod, could also himself have escaped the cross, as he says in the Gospel: Or do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he would give me at once more than twelve legions of angels (Matt 26:53)?
Commentary on Isaiah

And so that you may know that your mother was not repudiated by me, but withdrew by her own will, after many benefits I took a human body, and spoke no more through the Prophets, but in person. I came, and there was no man, or human being. For all, abandoning the image of man and of a human being, took on the images of beasts and serpents. Hence it is said to Herod because of his malice: Go and tell that fox (Luke 13:32). And to the Pharisees: Brood of vipers (Matt 23:33). And to the lustful: They have become horses mad after females (Jer 5:8). And of the pleasure-lovers: Do not cast your pearls before swine. And to the shameless: Nor give what is holy to dogs (Matt 7:6). And in common of them all: The vision of the four-footed beasts that were in the desert (Isa 30). The Lord therefore came, and did not find a man. For man, when he was in honor, did not understand: he was compared to senseless cattle, and became like them (Ps 48 [49]:13). I called them, he says, as a rational animal, and said: Incline your ear to the words of my mouth (Ps 77 [78]), and my people did not hear my voice. I cried out, and said: If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink (John 7:37). And in another place: Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened (Matt 11:28). And there was none to hear; hence I said to them in the Gospel: You have neither seen the form of God, nor heard his voice, because you do not have his word abiding in you (John 5:37, 38).
Commentary on Isaiah

According to the anagogy, at the rebuke of the Lord the sea becomes a desert when all the bitterness of this world is dried up, and the rivers are made desolate, of which the spiritual dragon in Egypt said: The rivers are mine, and I made them (Ezek 29:9). And of which we read in another place: What have you to do with the way of the Assyrians, to drink the waters of the rivers (Jer 2:18)? The fish too, when the net has been cast into the sea, shall rot, those which have been separated from the good fish.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 4:4.50:1

No one who views things correctly thinks God possesses a physical body. It is only that the holy Scriptures speak in a human fashion about him. For those of us in simple and crass bodies can think in no other way, except that these things are adapted for us by a range of metaphors, so that in the perception of visible things we are able to know in part about the divine and higher being, which is higher than all bodily imaginings. Observe how in these words the message is adapted to human understanding.
Commentary on Isaiah

And as for what follows: I will clothe the heaven with darkness, and its covering shall be as haircloth, either let us understand by heaven all that is above us, as the birds which are in the air are called heavenly, and the adverse powers, which run to and fro between heaven and earth, are said to be heavenly. Or certainly the heaven is clothed with darkness when it is covered with clouds. According to what is written: Who covers the heaven with clouds, and gives rain to the earth (Ps 146 [147]:8). And in threatening drought God says: I will make the heaven bronze, and the earth iron (Deut 28:23). Not that the nature of the elements is changed, but that by bronze and iron the greatness of the punishments is shown. The philosophers say that the clouds are not raised up more than ten stadia from the earth, and hide the brightness of the sun. It is not, then, the heaven that is wrapped in sackcloth, but, the light of heaven being shut off, the air that is beneath is darkened by the darkness of the cloud. We can interpret the heavens wrapped in darkness and covered with sackcloth thus: that we say all are under sin, and that the saints too need the mercy of God.
Dialogue with Trypho, Chapter CII

For the power of His strong word, by which He always confuted the Pharisees and Scribes, and, in short, all your nation's teachers that questioned Him, had a cessation like a plentiful and strong spring, the waters of which have been turned off, when He kept silence, and chose to return no answer to any one in the presence of Pilate; as has been declared in the memoirs of His apostles, in order that what is recorded by Isaiah might have efficacious fruit, where it is written, "The Lord gives me a tongue, that I may know when I ought to speak." Again, when He said, "Thou art my God; be not far from me," He taught that all men ought to hope in God who created all things, and seek salvation and help from Him alone; and not suppose, as the rest of men do, that salvation can be obtained by birth, or wealth, or strength, or wisdom.
On the Duties of the Clergy 1.2.5

Now what ought we to learn before everything else, but to be silent that we may be able to speak? Lest my voice should condemn me before that of another acquits me, for it is written: "By your words you shall be condemned." What need is there, then, that you should hasten to undergo the danger of condemnation by speaking when you can be more safe by keeping silent? How many have I seen to fall into sin by speaking, but scarcely one by keeping silent; and so it is more difficult to know how to keep silent than how to speak … a person is wise, then, who knows how to keep silent. Lastly, the Wisdom of God said, "The Lord has given to me the tongue of learning, that I should know when it is good to speak." Justly, then, is one wise who has received of the Lord to know when he ought to speak. Wherefore the Scripture says well: "A wise person will keep silence until there is opportunity."
Commentary on Isaiah

The Lord has given me a learned tongue, that I may know how to sustain by a word him who is weary. He rouses in the morning, in the morning he rouses my ear, that I may hear him as a master. The Lord God has opened my ear: and I do not gainsay; I have not gone backward. I gave my body to those who struck, and my cheeks to those who plucked them. I did not turn away my face from those who rebuked and spat. The Lord God is my helper, therefore I am not confounded: therefore I have set my face like a very hard rock, and I know that I shall not be confounded. LXX: The Lord gives me a tongue of discipline, that I may know when I ought to speak a word. He set me in the morning, he added to me an ear for hearing; and the discipline of the Lord opens my ears. But I do not refuse, nor do I gainsay. I gave my back to the scourges, and my cheeks to blows. But I did not turn away my face from the shame of spittings. And the Lord is my helper, therefore I am not confounded: but I have set my face like a very strong rock, and I shall know that I shall not be confounded. The Jews, separating this little chapter from what goes before, want to refer it to the person of Isaiah: that he says he received from the Lord the word by which to sustain the weary and wandering people and call it back to salvation; and that, after the manner of little children, who are taught in the morning hours, he hears from the Holy Spirit what he should speak; and that he did not gainsay his command, but when the Lord asked, Whom shall I send, and who will go to this people? he answered him: Here am I, send me (Isa 6:8). And because he had said, Hear the word of the Lord, you rulers of Sodom: give ear to the Law of our God, you people of Gomorrah (Isa 1:10), he suffered such hard things that he was exposed not only to insulting words but also to the pains of blows. Yet, through his awareness of the God who commanded him, he was not at all terrified; but, according to what is said to Ezekiel, Behold, I have made your face stronger than their faces, and your forehead harder than their foreheads; like adamant and flint I have made your face (Ezek 3:8, 9), he beat down all their assaults. So let those say who strive by every means to overturn the prophecies about Christ and to twist them by a crooked interpretation into a perverse understanding: as if, should these things too have been written of Isaiah, they could take away the other testimonies about Christ, which are so plain that they pour their clear light into the eyes of all. To the person of the Lord, then, with whom the previous book also ended, these things too are to be referred: that according to the dispensation of the body he assumed he was taught, and received a tongue of discipline, that he might know when he ought to speak and when to be silent. Indeed, he who was silent in his passion now speaks through the Apostles and apostolic men in the whole world. And it belongs to great knowledge to give one's fellow servants their food in due season, and to consider the persons of the hearers. Hence the Apostle Paul too speaks to those who did not accept the faith of the Prophets with testimonies from their own authors: as some of your own poets have said: For we are also his offspring (Acts 17:28), meaning Aratus. And again, from the Comic poet: Evil conversations corrupt good morals (1 Cor 15:33); and the hexameter verse of Epimenides: Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, idle bellies (Titus 1:12). If these do not keep the order and measure of the meter in translation, it must be known that in Greek they run on metrical feet. And he did this because he had received a tongue of discipline, that he might know when he ought to speak a word. To him an ear was added by grace, which he did not have by nature: so that we may understand that by no means are the ears of the body to be taken here, but those of the mind, of which the Lord also spoke in the Gospel: He who has ears to hear, let him hear (Luke 8:8). This discipline and instruction opened his ears, that he might pass on the knowledge of the Father even to us; he who did not gainsay him, but became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross (Phil 2). So that he set his body, or his back, to the blows; and scourges cut the breast that held God, and he did not turn his cheeks away from the slaps. That he endured this from the servant of the chief of the Priests is not in doubt, so that the crowds of the Jews too mocked him, vying with one another. Struck and spat upon, he did not blush, but was led as a lamb to the sacrifice; and as a sheep before its shearer he did not open his mouth. And that the Son, according to the mystery of the body he took up, heard from the Father what he should speak, we learn more fully in the Gospel, in which he himself says: And the Father who sent me has given me a commandment, what I should say and what I should speak. And again: As I hear, so I judge (John 8:28; 5:30).
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 4:4.50:4-5

Who among you fears the Lord, hearing the voice of his servant? He who has walked in darkness and has no light, let him hope in the name of the Lord, and lean upon his God. LXX: Who is there among you that fears the Lord, let him hearken to the voice of his child: those who walk in darkness have no light. Trust in the name of the Lord, and lean upon God. You scourged me, you spat upon my face: yet I call my persecutors to repentance. For I do not will the death of the sinful people, but only that it turn back and live (Ezek 33). And I say: who is there among you that fears the Lord and hears the voice of the servant, or child, that is, of his Son? Of these the one belongs to the flesh he assumed, the other to his nature. Nor let us think it a small thing to fear the Lord, according to what is said in Proverbs: The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom (Prov 9:10). For perfect love casts out fear, because fear has punishment; and he who fears is not perfect in love. But here fear is put for timidity, and εὐλαβείᾳ, of which we also read elsewhere: Blessed is he who fears all things (Prov 28:14), on account of εὐλάβειαν, that is, on account of timidity: those whom people commonly call God-fearing in the religion of God. For the Lord protects their path, and guards the way of the God-fearing. Of this fear it is written: The fear of the Lord surpasses all things. And elsewhere: There is no want for those who fear him (Sir 25:14; Ps 33 [34]:10). Indeed, it is only after many steps of virtue that one arrives at such fear of the Lord. For the divine word speaks in the person of a master and father, instructing a disciple and a son: If you call upon wisdom, and give your voice to understanding, and if you seek her like money, and search her out like treasures: then you shall understand the fear of the Lord, and find the knowledge of God (Prov 2:3). This is the fear that keeps the souls of the saints whole, chaste and pure, of which it is said: The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring for ever and ever. To it the divine oracles exhort us: Fear the Lord, and give him glory (Rev 14:7). Let him, then, who so fears the Lord hear the voice of his servant, or child, who walked in darkness, and there was no light for him; who had no form nor glory, but in the likeness of sinful flesh took the form of a servant, that he might overcome sin in the flesh. Of him it is said that he should hope in the name of the Lord and lean upon his God, so that whatever belongs to human frailty he may strengthen and sustain by the divine majesty. This is according to the Hebrew. But according to the Seventy it is said of sinners, who would not obey the voice of his Son, and walk in the darkness of error, and therefore have no light. For it could not be that wisdom should enter into a perverse soul. They neither knew nor understood, and therefore they walk in darkness. For they did not do the works and commandments of the Lord, nor sow righteousness for themselves, nor gather the vintage of the vine, so as to kindle for themselves the light of knowledge. For he who desires wisdom, let him keep the commandments, and the Lord will grant it to him. Hence it is also said to God: Your precepts are light. And elsewhere: The commandment of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes (Ps 18 [19]:9). And the ungodly are commanded to trust in the Lord, and, falling through their sins, to lean upon his help and be sustained by it.

Behold, all of you who kindle a fire, girded with flames, walk in the light of your fire, and in the flames that you have kindled: by my hand this has been done to you; you shall sleep in sorrows. LXX: Behold, all of you kindle a fire and strengthen the flame; walk in the light of your fire, and in the flame that you have kindled; because of me these things have been done to you. You shall sleep in grief. Exhortation profits nothing, nor is there hope of salvation after crimes. All have turned aside, together they have become useless (Ps 13 [14]); all kindle a fire for themselves and strengthen the flame. For they have in themselves hay, wood, stubble, thorns and thistles and darnel, which are to be handed over to the eternal burning. Hence it is also written in Proverbs: In much wood the fire thrives (Prov 25:21). But if a little fire lays hold of great material, how much will a great flame lay waste? It is said also in the Epistle that is ascribed to the Hebrews, of the earth that, bringing forth thorns and thistles, is reprobate and near to a curse, and its end is burning (Heb 6:8). Therefore those who are girded and surrounded with flames, and have strengthened the burning for themselves, are called to salvation, and it is said to them: Walk in the light of your fire, and in the flames that you have kindled, that in punishments and torments they may learn the power of God and return to salvation. And it signifies the devastation of the Jewish people, by which they were handed over to the Romans, and they bear the yoke of captivity to this day. For by the hand of Christ all these things were done, and they shall sleep in grief and sorrows, because neither through benefits nor through torments would they receive the Son of God. Hence he speaks to them: Go into the eternal fire, which God has prepared for the devil and his angels (Matt 25:41). This is what the Apostle also says: For wrath has come upon you to the end (1 Thess 2:16). From this little chapter we learn that each one kindles a fire for himself according to the quality of his sin. And just as, of people staying in the same place and, if one may say so, in the same bed, some are healthy while others burn with the heat of fevers, feeling different torments from the diversity of their humors and phlegm: so the fire that is kindled by sinners has its fuel in sins and in iniquity, of which it is written: Iniquity shall burn like a fire, and shall be devoured by burning like dry grass (Isa 9:18).

Hear me, you who pursue what is just, and seek the Lord. Look to the rock from which you were hewn, and to the cavern of the pit from which you were cut out. Look to Abraham your father, and to Sarah who bore you: for I called him alone, and blessed him, and multiplied him. The Lord therefore will comfort Zion, and will comfort all her ruins, and will make her desert like delights, and her wilderness like the garden of the Lord. Joy and gladness shall be found in her, thanksgiving and the voice of praise. LXX: Hear, you who pursue what is just, and seek the Lord. Look to the strong rock which you hewed out, and to the hole of the pit which you dug. Look to Abraham your father, and to Sarah who bore you, for he was one, and I called him, and blessed him, and loved him, and multiplied him: and now I will comfort you, Zion. And I have comforted all her deserts like a paradise, and the things that are toward the west like the paradise of the Lord: they shall find exultation and gladness in her, confession and the voice of praise. While those who kindled a fire for themselves and made the flames most strong sleep in grief and everlasting sorrow, you who pursue righteousness and seek the Lord (and he means the choir of the Apostles and of those who believed through the Apostles), look to the rock, that is, to Abraham your father, from whom you were hewn, and to the cavern of the pit from which you were cut out, that is, to Sarah who bore you. And consider this: that when he was a hundred years old and one, and had a barren wife, I multiplied his sons like the stars of heaven, so that their multitude surpassed number. If, then, from one man so many thousands of peoples were born, what great thing is it for me to restore the ruins of Zion, and to change her deserts into a paradise of pleasure, and into the garden of the Lord which God planted in Eden toward the East; and that there should be found in her, in place of the various trees, joy and gladness, confession and the voice of praise? The Jews refer this to the times of Zerubbabel, because after the devastation of Babylon Zion was restored, the Temple built, and the ancient religion given back. But just as above (Isa 49:22, 23) it is said to Zion: They shall bring your sons in their arms, and carry your daughters upon their shoulders. And kings shall be your foster fathers, and queens your nurses; and: Behold, these shall come from afar, and those from the north and the sea, and these from the land of the south; when Zion shall say: The place is too narrow for me: make room for me that I may dwell: things which exclude the meanness of those times, and are not known to have been fulfilled in the earthly Jerusalem: so here too the Lord speaks to those who pursue what is just, according to what is said elsewhere: Seek peace, and pursue it (Ps 33 [34]:15); and again: Pursuing hospitality (Rom 12:13). And they seek the Lord, so that one may infer things present from things former: since far more difficult things have already been done, let them not doubt that these things which are promised will come to pass. Further, according to the Seventy it is said to the pursuers of righteousness that they should look to the most strong rock which they hewed out, and the hole of the pit which they dug, that is, to the Lord the Savior, of whom the Apostle speaks: And the rock was Christ (1 Cor 10:4). And elsewhere it is written: He set my feet upon a rock (Ps 39 [40]:3). And again: On a rock he exalted me. For they pierced his side with a lance, and from it came out blood and water; and they dug his hands and feet, as the Lord the Savior himself says: They dug my hands and my feet, they numbered all my bones (Ps 21 [22]:18). We can call the hewn rock the tomb of the Savior, in which he was laid, and, rising from the dead, he begot innumerable sons. And he was called Abraham, that is, father of many nations. Just as Sarah, at first barren, is understood as the Church, which by another name is called Zion, whom the Lord has comforted, and whose deserts he has made like a paradise. For more are the children of the desolate than of her who has a husband. And what is said, And the things that are toward the West I will make into the paradise of the Lord, or into the garden of God, signifies that on those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death a sudden light has arisen. For paradise, in whose place we rendered delights, the Hebrew has EDEN (עדן), of which it is written at the beginning of Genesis. And this is to be noted, that in Zion, which is compared to the paradise of God, there ought to be nothing else but joy and gladness, confession and the voice of praise, so that what the saints will do in heaven with the Angels of God, this they may practice on earth too in the unceasing praise of the Lord.

"Righteous," he says, instead of "righteousness," which is through Christ through faith in him, a faith that justifies the ungodly and removes all stain from those who have been filthy, and cleanses them in the Spirit and prepares for them the shining honor of sonship. They pursue righteousness, not in the sense of driving it before them and so away from their minds, but of running toward it to take hold of it. As David said, "Seek peace and pursue it." … The speech of the holy prophets always draws figures from the visible and the tangible things. For it has expressions that transcend reference, the senses and even the mind. In this way "Zion" is mentioned—not that we think of the earthly city but rather take it to be the spiritual one, that is, the church of the living God. Or how else would we see the words of the prophet coming true?…"Worship in spirit and truth," and the power of spiritual worship gave off the pleasant spiritual fragrance and joy in the hope that is in Christ. For if we trust that our body of lowliness will be transformed into the body of his glory, so we shall be with him and reign with him, assembled among the children of God and enriched with his divine and life-giving Spirit. We too bring forward the spiritual harvest to him—the confession and hymns of thanksgiving. For with such sacrifices is God well pleased.

For the law promulgated on Horeb is now old, and belongs to yourselves alone; but this is for all universally. Now, law placed against law has abrogated that which is before it, and a covenant which comes after in like manner has put an end to the previous one; and an eternal and final law-namely, Christ-has been given to us, and the covenant is trustworthy, after which there shall be no law, no commandment, no ordinance. Have you not read this which Isaiah says: "Hearken unto Me, hearken unto Me, my people; and, ye kings, give ear unto Me: for a law shall go forth from Me, and My judgment shall be for a light to the nations. My righteousness approaches swiftly, and My salvation shall go forth, and nations shall trust in Mine arm?" And by Jeremiah, concerning this same new covenant, He thus speaks: "Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah; not according to the covenant which I made with their fathers, in the day that I took them by the hand, to bring them out of the land of Egypt." If, therefore, God proclaimed a new covenant which was to be instituted, and this for a light of the nations, we see and are persuaded that men approach God, leaving their idols and other unrighteousness, through the name of Him who was crucified, Jesus Christ, and abide by their confession even unto death, and maintain piety. Moreover, by the works and by the attendant miracles, it is possible for all to understand that He is the new law, and the new covenant, and the expectation of those who out of every people wait for the good things of God. For the true spiritual Israel, and descendants of Judah, Jacob, Isaac, and Abraham (who in uncircumcision was approved of and blessed by God on account of his faith, and called the father of many nations), are we who have been led to God through this crucified Christ, as shall be demonstrated while we proceed.
