Attend to me, my people, and my tribe, hear me: for a law shall go forth from me, and my judgment shall rest for a light of the peoples. Near is my righteous one, my savior has gone forth: and my arms shall judge the peoples. The islands shall wait for me, and shall wait upon my arm. LXX: Hear me, hear me, my people, and kings, attend to me: for a law shall go forth from me, and my judgment for a light of the nations. My righteousness draws near swiftly, and my salvation shall go forth like a light: and in my arm shall the nations hope. The islands shall wait for me, and in my arm they shall hope. Once in the Hebrew it is said, Attend; twice according to the Seventy, hear me, hear me: to teach us that we ought to hear both with the ears of the body and with the sense of the soul. And the multitude of the nations, which is the people of God, is called to listen carefully to what is said; of which Zechariah says: Many nations, he says, shall flee to the Lord, and shall be his people (Zech 2:11). Or, as some will have it, the remnant of believers from Israel is called the people; and the tribe, or nations, are those who believed from the multitude of the nations, as Moses says to the nations in the Song of Deuteronomy: Rejoice, you nations, with his people (Deut 32:43). For tribe, as we have translated, Theodotion translated race, Symmachus nation, the Seventy kings. For we are the tribe, and the nation, and the royal and priestly race of the Lord, such as Abraham also was, who was called a king, and the other saints, of whom it is written: Do not touch my anointed ones (Ps 104 [105]:15). What is it that they are bidden to hear? For a law, he says, shall go forth from me, and my judgment for a light of the peoples, or of the nations. Here is shown the spiritual law of the Gospel, which shall go forth from Zion, not that of Moses, which was given of old on Sinai; and my judgment shall go forth for a light of the nations, by which he established and decreed that all nations are to be saved.

But when the time of his incarnation unexpectedly arrived, then the shadows made way for the truth. And he said, "Listen to me, O my people." … He is speaking here not only to those who are numbered among the people but also to the kings, because he wanted the rulers, the leaders of the people, to receive his message as well.… "The law will go forth from me, and my judgment will be a light to the nations." He refers to the divine and evangelical preaching as "law" here; it is just that it is in a different form now, just as the oracles and salvation also are new. For just as the old law was changed to something better, there has also been a transfer from those things that were provisional types to that which is the truth. For Christ said, "Do not think I have come to destroy the law." … The law in letters was given by Moses, but the preaching of salvation, which is the gospel, came through Christ.… He calls his "judgment" here something that is both sanctioned by the law of God as well as a benevolent accounting; it is the grace from him that went out to illuminate the Gentiles; they were amazed at his judgment, which was both righteous and just—truly the righteousness that is clearly made known in the gospel.

And lest perhaps we should think that what he promised would come after a long time, he adds: near is my righteous one, or righteousness. For Christ has been made for us by the Father wisdom and redemption (1 Cor 1), holiness and righteousness, and all the names by which virtue is called. And it is beautifully said that righteousness will go forth, so that not one nation only but the whole world may be saved. And that the Son of God, who was sent by the Father, is called Savior, or salvation, which in Hebrew is said Jesus, Simeon declares, holding the child in his arms: Now you dismiss your servant, O Lord, for my eyes have seen your salvation, which you have prepared before the face of all peoples, a light for the revelation of the nations (Luke 2:29ff.). And as for what follows, And my arms shall judge the peoples, or according to the Seventy, and in my arm shall the nations hope: it signifies either that all are judged by his power, or that all the nations will believe in Christ, who is the arm and strength of God. It is said also in another place: Your arm is with might. Let your hand be strengthened, and your right hand exalted (Ps 88 [89]:14). And again: Sing to the Lord a new song: his right hand will save for him, and his holy arm (Ps 97 [98]:1, 2). For the right hand and arm of the Lord is he himself who saved for himself those who were formerly lost, so that none should perish of those whom the Father had given him (John 17). And that the islands are said to be either the souls of the Saints, which in the persecutions of this world have been made solid by a firm faith in God, or the multitude of the Churches from the nations, we have often explained. And just as by the arm of the Lord we can understand the Savior, so by his arms which judge the peoples we can understand all the saints, in whom God will judge the world.

Again, as to their malignantly asserting that if heaven is indeed the throne of God, and earth His footstool, and if it is declared that the heaven and earth shall pass away, then when these pass away the God who sitteth above must also pass away, and therefore He cannot be the God who is over all; in the first place, they are ignorant what the expression means, that heaven is [His] throne and earth [His] footstool. For they do not know what God is, but they imagine that He sits after the fashion of a man, and is contained within bounds, but does not contain. And they are also unacquainted with [the meaning of] the passing away of the heaven and earth; but Paul was not ignorant of it when he declared, "For the figure of this world passeth away." In the next place, David explains their question, for he says that when the fashion of this world passes away, not only shall God remain, but His servants also, expressing himself thus in the 101st Psalm: "In the beginning, Thou, O Lord, hast founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of Thy hands. They shall perish, but Thou shalt endure, and all shall wax old as a garment; and as a vesture Thou shalt change them, and they shall be changed: but Thou art the same, and Thy years shall not fail. The children of Thy servants shall continue, and their seed shall be established for ever;" pointing out plainly what things they are that pass away, and who it is that doth endure for ever—God, together with His servants. And in like manner Esaias says: "Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look upon the earth beneath; for the heaven has been set together as smoke, and the earth shall wax old like a garment, and they who dwell therein shall die in like manner. But my salvation shall be for ever, and my righteousness shall not pass away."
Commentary on Isaiah

Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look at the earth beneath: for the heavens shall melt away like smoke, and the earth shall be worn away like a garment, and its inhabitants shall perish like these. But my salvation shall be for ever, and my righteousness shall not fail. LXX: Lift up your eyes to heaven, and look upon the earth beneath, for heaven has been made firm like smoke. But the earth shall grow old like a garment, and its inhabitants shall die like these. But my salvation shall be for ever, and my righteousness shall not fail. This is what the Lord says in the Gospel: Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away (Matt 24:35). And David sings in the psalm: In the beginning, O Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They shall perish, but you remain; and they shall all grow old like a garment; and like a cloak you shall roll them up, and they shall be changed (Ps 101 [102]:26). From this it is shown that the perishing of the heavens signifies not destruction but a change for the better. Of these it is said: There shall be a new heaven and a new earth, which I will make to remain in my sight (Rev 21:2). For if it is written of the saints, We shall all indeed sleep, but we shall not all be changed (1 Cor 15:51), and in the titles of four psalms we read, For those who shall be changed: how much more is this to be believed of heaven and of the sun and the stars, when the moon shall receive the light of the sun, and the sun shall glow with sevenfold brightness? Hence the whole creation too groans and travails, awaiting the revelation of the sons of God, that it may be changed for the better (Rom 8). And not only the souls of men, which are immortal, but their bodies too are to be changed into a glorified substance. For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal put on immortality (1 Cor 15:53). And since heaven and earth grow old, it follows that the things contained within the circle of heaven, and men, who are the inhabitants of the earth, also die like these: not unto their destruction, but unto the abolishing of their old baseness and the renewal of the glory to come; when the righteous shall shine like the sun (Matt 13:43), and, the past and old things departing, all things shall have been made new. Some take perishing and growing old for abolition and death, according to what we read in the catholic Epistle: The heavens that now are, and the earth, have been reserved for fire by the same word. And again: The elements, burning, shall be dissolved (2 Pet 3:7). This is indeed also the opinion of the philosophers of the world, that all the things we see will perish by fire. Hence the Apostle too: Passes away, he says, the fashion of this world, while we look not at the things that are seen but at the things that are not seen. For the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal (1 Cor 7:32). Something of the kind the apostle John also writes: The world passes away, and its desire (1 John 2:17). And in the Hebrew it is said, The heavens shall melt away like smoke; or, according to Aquila and Symmachus, they shall be ground to nothing, and be crumbled and vanish in the manner of salt; of whom the former said ἡλίσθησαν, the latter ἁλίσουσιν, which plainly draws its etymology from the crumbling and dissolving of salt. In place of this I wonder what the Seventy meant to say, heaven has been made firm like smoke: for if firmness is taken for strength, how is what is firm compared to smoke? Unless perhaps we can say this: that all the firmness and strength and might of the heavens is made equal to the emptiest wind and to smoke, which dissolves into the air, according to Ecclesiastes: Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity (Eccl 1:2). And this must be said: if heaven and earth shall perish and grow old, by what consequence should its inhabitants die and perish like these, when we know that souls are everlasting, and that bodies will rise again? From this it is plain that heaven and earth do not perish and are not reduced to nothing, but are changed for the better.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 4:5.51:6

The Son is called "salvation" and "righteousness," as we often say, and thus his quality is declared that he has in himself, by which and in which he is Son by nature. Indeed, he is eternal and does not "wear out." Such is the difference between creator and creation, the made from the maker, which is clearly seen in this verse.
Commentary on Isaiah

Hear me, you who know what is just, people: my law is in their heart. Do not fear the reproach of men, and do not be afraid of their blasphemies. For as a garment, so shall the worm eat them; and as wool, so shall the moth devour them. But my salvation shall be for ever, and my righteousness to generations of generations. LXX: Hear me, you who know judgment, my people, of whom my law is in their heart. Do not fear the reproach of men, and do not be overcome by their contempt. For like a garment they shall be consumed by time, and like wool they shall be eaten by the moth. But my righteousness shall be for ever, and my salvation to generations of generations. He who had said above, A law shall go forth from me, and my judgment for a light of the nations, now speaks to the same people, who know his judgment and have his law in their hearts, that they may do all things with judgment, and have the law which the Lord promises through Jeremiah, saying (Jer 31:31ff.): I will establish a new covenant, not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers; but I will establish a covenant, putting my laws in their minds, and upon their heart I will write them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people: so that they may live by no means according to the letter but according to the spirit, restoring the natural law in their hearts, of which the Apostle also writes: For when the nations, which do not have the law, do by nature the things that are of the law, these, not having the law, are a law to themselves; who show the work of the law written in their hearts (Rom 2:14). Of this law it is signified in the psalm: The mouth of the righteous shall meditate wisdom, and his tongue shall speak judgment. The law of his God is in his heart, and his steps shall not be supplanted (Ps 36 [37]:30, 31). And because the prophetic spirit knew that many persecutions would come upon believers, he exhorts them to fortitude, nay rather to contempt of those who are going to persecute them. Which the Lord also said in the Gospel: Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; but rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna (Matt 10:28). And in another place: Rejoice when they speak all evil against you, lying (ibid. 5:11).
Commentary on Isaiah

For as a garment is consumed by the worm, or by time, and as wool is devoured by the moth, so all the reproach of the persecutors will pass away with the persecutors. Hence the Apostles too gloried that they had been counted worthy to suffer insults for the Lord (Acts 5). And they gloried because the salvation and righteousness of the Lord, which had promised them victory and rewards, that is, the Lord and Savior, abides for ever, or in each generation, of the former people and of the later, who received his coming; of whom it is also said above: Near is my righteous one, my savior has gone forth.
Commentary on Isaiah

Arise, arise; put on strength, O arm of the Lord. Arise as in the days of old, in the generations of ages. Was it not you who struck the proud one, who wounded the dragon? Was it not you who dried up the sea, the water of the mighty deep, who made the depth of the sea a way, that the freed might pass over? And now those who have been redeemed by the Lord shall return and come into Zion praising; and everlasting gladness shall be upon their heads: they shall hold joy and gladness; sorrow and groaning shall flee. LXX: Rise up, rise up ÷ Jerusalem ⁚ and put on the strength of your arm. Rise up as in the beginning of the day, as an everlasting generation. Are you not she who cut down the breadth, who undid the dragon? Are you not she who made the sea a desert, the many waters of the deep; who made the depth of the sea a way of passage for those who had been freed and redeemed? For by the Lord they shall be led back, and shall come into Zion with gladness and everlasting exultation. For on their head praise and gladness shall take hold of them. Sorrow and grief and groaning shall flee. The name Jerusalem, which was added here by the Seventy, is neither found in the Hebrew nor did any of the three Translators put it; hence it is to be marked beforehand with an obelus, and so the following little chapter is to be joined with the sense of the preceding. The Lord had exhorted those who believe in him, saying: Do not fear the reproach of men, and do not be afraid of their blasphemies. And he had promised them, as their help, his salvation and everlasting righteousness, which is none other than Christ, the arm of the Lord, of whom he had said above: And in my arm shall the nations hope. Hence the people speak to the arm of the Lord, and pray for his coming, and implore the promised help, saying: Arise, arise: put on strength, O arm of the Lord. Arise as in the days of old, and exert all your strength, so that you who through many ages delivered your Saints from dangers may protect us too by your strength. For you are he who struck the proud one, who wounded the dragon, namely Pharaoh king of Egypt, who in Ezekiel too is called the great dragon (Ezek 29). You dried up the Red Sea, so that through the most mighty waters and the depths of the sea your people might find a way and escape the pursuing Egyptians. You, then, who did these things, now too lead back into Zion those redeemed and freed by your blood, into the heavenly Jerusalem, or into the Church which you have prepared for yourself by your blood: and when they are in it, they shall rejoice with everlasting gladness, and shall say: Lord, as with the shield of your good will you have crowned us (Ps 5:13). For they shall have joy and gladness, sorrow and groaning fleeing away. This is according to the Hebrew. But according to the Seventy, Jerusalem, that is, the sinful soul, is called to put on the strength of her arm, and to take up her former works, as she had been before she fell, when she dwelt in the day and in the light. For you are she, he says, who overcame the broad and spacious way that leads to death, and broke up the dragon, the crooked serpent, of which we also read in the Psalms: You crushed the heads of the dragons in the waters (Ps 73 [74]:13). Remember your former strength, that you trod down the sea of this world and made it a desert, and found a way in the midst of the waves. Hence the Apostle Peter too passed over the sea of this world to the Lord, and he who was walking by faith began to sink through unbelief, except that he was held up by the right hand of the Lord. As, then, the former victory was granted with the Lord's help, so also to those who return after repentance and hear, Shall he who falls not rise? says the Lord (Jer 8:4), and, Turn to me, you sons that turn, and I will heal your bruises (ibid. 3), he himself will stretch out his hand, and lead them back into Zion, the watchtower and summit of virtues, with joy and everlasting gladness, and will set praise and gladness upon their head. For the eyes of the wise man are in his head; and they shall have this crown and be protected by this diadem, so that they always rejoice and praise the Lord, because joys have taken the place of sorrow, grief and groaning.
Commentary on Isaiah

I, I myself will comfort you. Who are you, that you should have feared a mortal man, and the son of man, who shall wither like grass? And you have forgotten God your maker, who stretched out the heavens and founded the earth; and you have been in dread continually all the day at the face of the fury of him who afflicted you and had made ready to destroy. Where now is the fury of the afflicter? He shall come quickly, walking, to open, and he will not kill unto utter destruction, nor shall his bread fail. But I am the Lord your God, who trouble the sea, and its waves swell: the Lord of hosts is my name. I have put my words in your mouth, and in the shadow of my hand I have protected you, that you may plant the heavens and found the earth, and say to Zion: You are my people. LXX: I am, I am he who comforts you. Know who you were, and that you feared a mortal man, and the son of man, who have withered like grass; and you have forgotten God your maker, who made heaven and founded the earth; and you feared always, all the days, the face of the fury of him who afflicted you, as he planned to take you away; and now where is the fury of him who afflicts you? For when you have been saved, he shall not stand nor remain ※ and he will not kill unto corruption, and his bread shall not fail ⁚ for I am your God who trouble the sea and make its waves resound. The Lord Sabaoth is my name. I will put my words in your mouth, and in the shadow of my hand I will protect you: by which I set up heaven and founded the earth; and Zion shall say, You are my people. The people of believers had prayed to the arm of the Lord, who himself is the power of God and the wisdom of God, to arise and give them help, so that, with him fighting for the saints, they might possess joy and gladness, sorrow and groaning being put to flight. So either the arm of the Lord or the Lord himself answered: I am, I am; and not at all through the Prophets, but I myself will comfort you: the God of mercies and the Father of all consolation. And I wonder how, when I said above, Do not fear the reproach of men, and do not be afraid of their blasphemies, you feared the rage of the persecutors, and did not know that they are mortal, who like grass suddenly wither and perish. And surely at the time when you feared them, you forgot the Lord your maker. For if the memory of me had always dwelt in your heart, you would never have feared men, who are to be dissolved into ashes. And whom did you forget? God, who hung the heavens by incredible power, and founded the earth as a stable mass. And you feared your adversaries not for a short while, which could in some measure have been granted you, but continually and all the day, so that, though you had the light of faith, the darkness of dread possessed you, and dread of him who thought you would perish. Where then now is the pride of the persecutors? Where is the worldly power with which they raged against you with rabid mouth?
Commentary on Isaiah

According to the Seventy it is said to every believing soul that, though created in the image and likeness of God, she did not know her own dignity, but feared man and the son of man, who can kill only the body, and did not know that she is immortal, nor say with the Prophet: The Lord is my light and my savior, whom shall I fear? The Lord is the protector of my life, of whom shall I be afraid (Ps 26 [27]:1, 2)? And again: The Lord is my helper, I will not fear what man may do to me. The Lord is my helper, and I shall look down upon my enemies (Ps 117 [118]:6, 7). And what man is, is shown by another verse: In the Lord I will hope: I will not fear what flesh may do to me (Ps 55 [56]:5). Hence it is now said too: You feared a mortal man, and the son of man, who have withered like grass. For all flesh is grass, and all its glory like the flower of grass (Isa 40); and, terrified by the power of the judge, you forgot that he himself was your protector, who made heaven and earth and all the elements we see; or those heavens that bear the image of the heavenly one, and that earth which multiplies the Lord's seed.
Commentary on Isaiah

My son will come quickly, walking and trampling your adversaries, to open to you the way of victory; or to unbar the underworld; who will not kill unto utter destruction, but wills to save those who turn. Then too his bread, which, as the Gospel proves, means doctrine, shall never fail, but shall always lie open to those who wish to eat.
Commentary on Isaiah
And what is said above, And he will not kill unto corruption, and his bread shall not fail, was added from Theodotion's edition out of the Hebrew.
Commentary on Isaiah

Symmachus, in the place where we said, He shall come quickly, walking, to open, and he will not kill unto utter destruction, translated thus: Quickly the underworld shall be opened, and he shall not die unto corruption, Christ being understood, who speaks in the fifteenth psalm: You will not leave my soul in the underworld, nor will you give your holy one to see corruption. In that place too where we, according to the Hebrew and Aquila, rendered, I have put my words in your mouth, and in the shadow of my hand I have protected you, that you may plant the heavens, and found the earth, and say to Zion: you are my people, he translated thus: I will put my words in your mouth, and in the shadow of my hand I will protect you, by which I planted heaven and founded the earth, and that I may say to Zion: you are my people.
Commentary on Isaiah

And at the same time he makes an apostrophe to the Son, whom he promises will come quickly, and whose bread he says is everlasting: that he himself, according to the dispensation of the flesh he assumed, is his Lord God, who makes the sea troubled and its waves swell, so that the pride of the persecutors is puffed up against his servants, and then, with the Lord's help, grows calm again. And he says that he has put his words in his mouth. For whatever the Son speaks are the words of the Father; and that he protected him in the shadow of his hand; and that he was protected for this reason, that he might plant new heavens and found a new earth, and say to Zion, that is, to the Church: You are my people. Therefore Zion is nothing other than the people of God.
Commentary on Isaiah

He troubles the sea and makes its waves resound, he to whom it is also sung in the Psalms: You rule the strength of the sea, and the tossing of its waves you calm (Ps 88 [89]:10). In Jeremiah too it is written: Will you not fear me, says the Lord, and will you not tremble before my face, who set the sand as a boundary for the sea, an everlasting decree which it shall not pass (Jer 5:22)? The seas were troubled when the Lord's dragnet drew out a multitude of fish (Matt 13).
Commentary on Isaiah

And the Lord put his words in the mouth of the believer, and protected him in the shadow of his hand. He also says in the Gospel: When they hand you over, do not think how or what you are to speak; for what you are to speak will be given you in that hour. For it is not you who speak, but the spirit of your Father who speaks in you (Matt 10:19, 20). And in another place he says to the righteous man: Open wide your mouth, and I will fill it (Ps 80 [81]:12). And again: Open your mouth to the word of God: For the Lord will give the word to those who preach the good news with great power. Hence God speaks to the inner man of Jeremiah, after he touched his mouth: Behold, I have put my words in your mouth (Jer 1:9). He could sing with the Psalmist: He put a new song in my mouth, a hymn to our God (Ps 39 [40]:4). And who has wrought all these things but the Lord and Savior, who made heaven and earth, and says to Zion, You are my people? Which properly suits the Church gathered from the nations. And in Hosea he promises to believers, saying: I will call not my people, my people; and he shall say to me: You are my God (Hos 2:24).
Commentary on Isaiah

Lift yourself up, lift yourself up, arise, Jerusalem, who have drunk from the hand of the Lord the cup of his wrath: you have drunk to the bottom of the cup of stupor, and have drained it to the dregs. There is none to sustain her, of all the sons whom she has borne; and there is none to take her by the hand, of all the sons whom she has brought up. Two things there are that have befallen you; who shall be grieved over you? devastation and destruction, and famine, and the sword: who shall comfort you? LXX: Rise up, rise up, lift yourself up, Jerusalem, who have drunk from the hand of the Lord the cup of his fury. For the cup of ruin, the κόνδυ of fury, you have drunk off and emptied: and there was none to comfort you of all your sons whom you bore; and there was none to take you by the hand, nor of all your sons whom you raised up. These two things are against you: who shall be grieved with you? ruin and destruction, famine and the sword: who shall comfort you? That Jerusalem and Zion are δυώνυμον I have often taught: of which Zion, which means watchtower, because it is set upon a mountain, is called the citadel; while the rest of the city is called Jerusalem, which was formerly called Jebus and Salem. Her the Prophet now exhorts to arise, she who had earlier fallen by denial, saying in the passion of the Lord: Crucify, crucify such a one: we have no king but Caesar (John 19:15); and to do penance, and to feel through the evils of captivity why she offended her Creator. Physicians are accustomed to give to a nauseated stomach a most bitter antidote, which took its name from its taste, so that it may vomit up the harmful humors and be able to pass on into the bowel the food cooked and digested, which the great quantity of phlegm did not allow to be digested. So Jerusalem too, who drank from the cup of the Lord's fury, and from his κόνδυ, which Symmachus translated bowl, and which, according to the book of Genesis, Joseph ordered to be hidden in the sack of his brother Benjamin (Gen 44), is bidden to arise from her drunkenness, because she drank it, and emptied it, and drained it to the dregs: which the three expressed by a single word, Ἐξεστράγγισας. This is the cup of which we read in the Psalms: A cup in the hand of the Lord, full of pure wine mixed. And he has poured from this into that; yet its dregs are not emptied out: all the sinners of the earth shall drink (Ps 74 [75]:9, 10). Of it God also speaks to Jeremiah: Take the cup of pure wine from my hand, and you shall make all the nations drink of it, to whom I shall send you. And they shall drink and vomit, and go mad before the face of the sword which I shall send among them (Jer 25:15, 16). And when he says that he gave it to drink to the other nations and to Jerusalem and the cities of Judea, he adds: Thus says the Lord Almighty, the God of Israel: Drink and be drunk, and vomit, and fall before the face of the sword which I shall send among you (Jer 25:27). And it is to be noted that this cup of the Lord's fury is his sword, which is sent into the midst of sinners. Here a question arises: how, after the drinking, the drunkenness and vomiting and the fall, it is said in Jeremiah that Jerusalem cannot arise, and now he speaks to her through Isaiah: Lift yourself up, lift yourself up, arise, Jerusalem. It is resolved thus: as long as someone drinks the cup, and is drunk, and raves, and vomits, and falls, he cannot arise; for he has not yet drained the cup of the Lord, nor come to the dregs, so as to have drunk it to the bottom. But now he speaks to Jerusalem in the past tense: who have drunk from the hand of the Lord the cup of his fury, and not, who are drinking.
Commentary on Isaiah

We can understand these things according to the anagogy also of the sinful soul, which, not wishing to drink the cup of the Lord's fury, says in the psalm: O Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor chastise me in your wrath (Ps 6:1). But if she has drunk it, it is good for her to feel her punishments, and to hear the Lord saying: When the wrath of my fury has passed, I will heal again. And elsewhere: Shall he who falls not rise again, says the Lord (Jer 8:4)?
Commentary on Isaiah

And at the same time we must consider that from then on there was no prophet, no Apostle in Judea to comfort her, and take her by the hand, and lift her up as she lay. From this it is plain that these things are said of the time after the last captivity: otherwise, history relates that in Babylon and after Babylon she had Ezekiel and the other Prophets.
Commentary on Isaiah

And as for what he says, Two things there are that have befallen you, or these two things are against you: who shall be grieved over you?, and in place of two he names four, devastation and destruction, famine and the sword: like this is what is sung in the Psalter: Once God has spoken, these two things I have heard: that power belongs to God, and to you, O Lord, mercy: for you will render to each according to his works (Ps 61 [62]:12, 13). For there too God speaks once, that he is almighty, and the Prophet hears two things, that his omnipotence prevails on both sides, so that he both grants mercy to the penitent and renders to those who persist in sin the punishments they deserve. In the same way in this other place two things befell Jerusalem, each of which has two parts. For destruction follows ruin, or devastation; and death follows famine and the sword.
Commentary on Isaiah

Your sons have been cast out, they have slept at the head of all the ways, like an ensnared oryx: full of the indignation of the Lord, of the rebuke of your God. LXX: Your sons, in want and sleeping at the head of all the ways, like a half-cooked beet, full of the fury of the Lord, and failing from the Lord God. For half-cooked beet the other translators rendered an oryx caught and ensnared, which in Hebrew is called THO (תוא), a kind of beast born in the desert, which is placed among the clean animals in Leviticus and Deuteronomy. For this the Seventy supposed the Syriac word thoreth, which means beet. From the name let us pass to the sense. Your sons, like an oryx caught in the snares of the hunters, have slept at the crossroads and in the streets, and, laying their naked limbs upon the naked ground, have shown by their own miseries the indignation of the Lord and the rebuke of their God. Further, according to the Seventy: those who would not have spiritual riches in every word, and knowledge, and good works, but were poor who do not endure threatening, shall by no means dwell in houses that are built of virtues, but at the beginnings of the ways and at their outlets, touching all things and leaving all things. They are rightly said to sleep that sleep of which it is written: They have slept their sleep, and found nothing (Ps 75 [76]:6); with which sleep the king of Assyria lulled them. And they are compared to a half-cooked beet, which is a kind of vegetable most cheap and most fragile. Of such vegetables I think it is said in the Psalms: Do not be jealous of evildoers, nor envy those who work iniquity. For like grass they shall swiftly wither, and like green herbs they shall quickly fall (Ps 36 [37]:1, 2). For it is the food of the sick. He who is once and for all unbelieving is called a raw beet. But he who, content with simple faith, does works of righteousness without reasoning and the truth of doctrines, can be called a cooked beet. Further, he who wavers in the middle between vices and virtues, and approaches the service of God with a double heart, is most rightly called a half-cooked beet; to him too God speaks in the Apocalypse of John: Would that you were either hot or cold: but now, because you are lukewarm, I will vomit you out (Rev 3:15, 16). These, lukewarm and sleeping, are full of the fury of the Lord, and dissolved, or failing, through the Lord God: not that the Lord, who did not make death and does not delight in the destruction of the living, is the cause of their dissolution; but in that those who have sinned under the Law are judged through the Law, which works the wrath of God for those who are its transgressors.
Commentary on Isaiah

Therefore hear this, poor little one, and drunk, but not with wine. Thus says your ruler, the Lord, and your God, who fought for his people: Behold, I have taken from your hand the cup of stupor, the bottom of the cup of my indignation: you shall not drink it again any more. And I will put it in the hand of those who humbled you, and said to your soul: Bow down, that we may pass over; and you made your body like the ground, and like a road for those passing over. LXX: Therefore hear, you who are humbled and drunk, but not with wine. Thus says the Lord God who judges his people: Behold, I have taken from your hand the cup of ruin, the κόνδυ of my fury: and you shall not drink it again any more: and I will give it into the hands of those who unjustly oppressed you and humbled you; who said to your soul, Bend down that we may pass over; and you made your middle parts level with the ground for those passing outside. O Jerusalem, to whom I said, Lift yourself up, lift yourself up, arise, and do penance, because you have drunk from the hand of the Lord the cup of his fury and drained it to the dregs; and your sons, who are scattered through the whole world, and led away captive, have lain in the streets and at the heads of the ways: know that you are poor and humbled, and drunk, not with wine, but with the fury of the Lord.
Commentary on Isaiah

But to come, according to the Seventy, to the spiritual understanding: it is said to the soul humbled by vices and drunk with passions, that she may know that she has the Lord as her judge, and that she will render account for all things. And if she has been turned to better things, the cup of ruin is to be taken from her hands, and the bowl of the Lord's fury, which held punishments, of which Ezekiel also says to Jerusalem: You shall drink the cup of your sister Samaria, deep and wide, that you may be drunk (Ezek 23:32), is to be handed over into the hands of those who had humbled her. There is no doubt that he signifies the adverse powers, which said to her soul: Bow down, that we may pass over. Here it is likewise to be noted that they did not bend her down, nor use force so that she who was formerly upright should be bowed to the ground, but left it to her own choice. And she of her own will laid down her neck, or her back, or her whole body, not inside but outside, for those who trampled her. Something of the kind we also read in the Gospel (Luke 13): that for eighteen years Satan had bent a woman down, whom the Lord raised up to her former stature, so that she could say: I have lifted up my eyes to the mountains, whence my help shall come (Ps 120 [121]:1); and: To you I have lifted up my eyes, who dwell in heaven (Ps 122 [123]:1).
Commentary on Isaiah

Therefore, if you do penance, and, lifted up, arise, you will know that the cup of stupor and of ruin, or according to Symmachus and Theodotion, of tearing and of commotion, is to be taken from your hand; and that you will no more drink the condy, for which in this place too Symmachus translated bowl; but that it is to be handed over to your adversaries, who said to your soul, Bow down, that we may pass over: and when they said it, you bent down of your own will. And you made your body like the ground, or your back; or according to the Seventy, your middle parts and your necks for those passing outside. Let this be said according to the history: that Jerusalem, if she is willing to lift herself up and arise, shall by no means drink the cup of the Lord's fury, nor suffer any more what she endured before.
Commentaries on the Book of 1 Kings, Book 5

Of these enemies, indeed, it is said through the prophet: "They say to your soul: Bow down, that we may pass over." For the soul standing upright is sublime, bowed down it is lowly, because through the height of virtues and through heavenly desire it is raised to lofty things; but when it falls away to vices or to love of the world, it falls to that place where the enemy, rushing in, easily tramples it. They say therefore to your soul, "Bow down, that we may pass over," because if they do not humble it to doing or thinking earthly things, they neither penetrate it with malign persuasions nor disturb it with the warfare of vices. From this, therefore, we can gather how far we ought to distance ourselves from the world in deed, word, and thought.
Forty Gospel Homilies, Homily 31

Hence another prophet says concerning unclean spirits: Who said to your soul, Bow down that we may pass over. For the soul stands upright when it desires heavenly things, and is by no means bent toward the lowest things. But when malign spirits see it standing in its uprightness, they cannot pass through it. For their passing through is to scatter unclean desires upon it. Therefore they say, Bow down that we may pass over, because if the soul does not cast itself down to desiring the lowest things, their perversity by no means prevails against it; and they cannot pass through her whom they fear standing rigid against them in heavenly intention.
Sermons on the Song of Songs, Sermon 80

Why does he not know, unless because, bending himself down to these lowest and earthly things, he heaps up earth for himself? Assuredly he does not know, concerning those things which he commits to the earth, for whom he gathers them: whether for the moth that destroys, or for the thief that digs through; for the enemy that plunders, or for the fire that devours. And thence that lamentable voice from the psalm belongs to the wretched man bending himself down and brooding over the things that are upon the earth: "I am made wretched and bowed down utterly; all the day long I went about in sadness." In himself indeed he experiences the truth of that sentence of the Wise Man: "God made man upright, but he has entangled himself in many sorrows." And immediately the voice of mockery comes to him: "Bow down, that we may pass over."

n: Thee. Judea was no more laid waste by its ancient enemies. The persecution of Epiphanes did not continue long. Many have attacked the Church; but they cannot overcome her, nor will she cease to preach the truth, and to continue pure and holy.

Money. The Chaldeans acted impolitically in leaving the country without inhabitants, and Cyrus will derive no immediate advantage from your return. (Calmet) --- The Jews had not injured the Chaldeans, nor mankind the devil. But both had offended God, who out of mercy paid their ransom. (Worthington)
Assyrian. Pharao, (Sa; Tirinus) or rather Nabuchodonosor, (Calmet) and the princes of Assyria, who acted tyrannically. (Haydock)
Long, by the Chaldeans, weak Jews, and strangers, who misconstrue my conduct towards my people, and represent it as the effect of injustice, or of weakness.
Here. Jesus Christ appears, the Redeemer foretold so long before.
Peace. He comes like a conqueror to save his people. It may also be applied to the prophets and apostles, (Calmet) as St. Paul explains it, Romans x. 15. (Menochius)
Watchmen, prophets. The angels sung at the birth of Christ, Luke ii. 14.
Arm. The Saviour, Luke i. 51.

Lord, the Levites departing from Babylon, 1 Esdras i. 7., and Numbers iii. 6., and iv. 5., &c. (Calmet) --- St. Paul proves hence that communication with infidels in spiritual things is always unlawful, 2 Corinthians vi. 17. (Worthington)

Servant, Christ. In vain do the Jews attempt to apply this to any other. It is wonderful that Grotius should follow their steps, and understand Jeremias to be meant; though elsewhere he allows that the prophet speaks only of the Messias. (De Verit. v. 19.) --- This author [Grotius] has been of great prejudice to religion. The Chaldean and many modern Jews have been compelled by evidence to apply this to the Messias. See Geir., &c. Of men, who have disfigured the countenance of our Saviour with buffets, &c. The Jews would not receive him under this abject form, though it had been foretold equally with his elevation. (Calmet)

Sprinkle with baptism, (Haydock) and his manifold graces. (Calmet) --- Septuagint, "so many nations shall wonder at him." (Haydock) --- Mouth, out of reverence. f: Commentary on Isaiah

Arise, arise, put on your strength, Zion: put on the garments of your glory, Jerusalem, city of the Holy One: for the uncircumcised and the unclean shall no more pass through you. LXX: Rise up, rise up, ÷ Zion: ⁚ put on your strength, Zion, and put on your glory, Jerusalem, holy city. No more shall the uncircumcised and the unclean pass through you. Here again the name Zion, as above, was added by the Seventy, and therefore it has been transfixed with the spit. To her, then, to whom he had said above (Isa 51:17), Lift yourself up, lift yourself up, arise, Jerusalem, he now says: Arise, arise, put on your strength, Zion. And who Zion is, the following verse shows: Put on the garments of your glory, Jerusalem. We have said this to prove that Jerusalem and Zion are one city. And she is commanded to put off her garments of mourning and to put on those which she had before she drank from the hand of the Lord the cup of fury. And she is called the city of the sanctuary, for this is what CODES (קדש) signifies, on account of the temple which was built in her; or of the Holy One, on account of the knowledge of God; or holy, because she alone in the whole world had received the law. Hence too, after the resurrection of the Savior, the bodies of the dead appeared in the holy city, which surely, on account of its blasphemy and the hands laid on the Lord, could not be holy (Matt 27). And what is promised, that if she rises after her ruin and puts on her strength and glory, the uncircumcised and unclean shall no more pass through her, signifies what the Apostle Paul also says: What participation has righteousness with iniquity? What fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial? What part has the believer with the unbeliever? What accord has the temple of God with idols (2 Cor 6:14, 15)? All these things too, as we began to explain, are referred to the state of the soul. If through penance she has recovered her former strength, let her be called the dwelling of the Holy One, and become a Temple of God, and let no uncircumcised and unclean λογισμὸς pass through her. Of these it has been said: From my hidden sins cleanse me, O Lord, and from those of others spare your servant. If they have not had dominion over me, then I shall be spotless, and shall be cleansed from the greatest offense (Ps 18 [19]:13, 14). But all the things that are promised to Zion and Jerusalem are not said, as the Jews dream, of her stones and ashes and embers, that she may be restored to her former state; but of the people of Jerusalem, which killed the Prophets and stoned those who were sent to it (Matt 23), and at the last laid hands even on the Son of God. That people, falling in the passion of Christ, was raised up in his resurrection, when many thousands of the Jews believed and the remnant was saved. The same we can say of the Church also, which is the vision of peace and the watchtower: if she has fallen into heresy, she is commanded to go out and take up the ornaments of her former faith. And if she has been raised up, the rewards of holiness and continence are promised to her, so that the uncircumcised and the unclean shall by no means pass through her. This can be referred not to the cutting of the flesh and the foreskin, but to the uncleanness or cleanness of works, so that we call uncircumcised and unclean those who serve the pleasure and lust of the body. Indeed, Jeremiah speaks to those circumcised in the flesh, not in the spirit: All the nations are uncircumcised in the flesh; but the sons of Israel are uncircumcised in their hearts (Jer 9:26). And the blessed Apostle, disputing of virginity and continence and marriage, threw in, in the midst: Was anyone called circumcised? Let him not draw on a foreskin. Was he called in foreskin? Let him not be circumcised (1 Cor 7:18). This seems to me to say in other words: Has he been called without a wife, and believed? let him not take a wife. Or on the contrary: having a wife, has he believed in Christ? let him by no means make a divorce. And he keeps this sense not only in circumcision and foreskin, but in freedom and slavery, so as to call virgins and the continent free, and slaves those who render the debt to a wife. For it is not in our power to draw on a foreskin after circumcision, as those in the book of Maccabees are said to have made foreskins for themselves: which is said of the sons being born, and not of the fathers. Or he who has been called free is rather the slave of Christ (ibid. 7:22), since in the baptism of Christ there is no difference of Jew, pagan, Greek and Barbarian, man and woman, free and slave.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 5:1.52:1

He calls the holy city "the church." It is sanctified not by the prescribed cultic system, for the law never perfected anyone, but it is made in the likeness of Christ and participates in his divine nature, according to the communication of the Holy Spirit, in whom we are sealed for the day of redemption, with all vileness washed and removed.… We have been justified by faith in him, who reinforces us in all safety and shelters us in his love from every fierce attack of the devil and wild surges of enemy opposition. And so he teaches us when he says "to Zion or Jerusalem, that is, the church of the living God."
Commentary on Isaiah

Shake yourself from the dust: arise, sit down, Jerusalem: loose the bonds of your neck, captive daughter of Zion. For thus says the Lord: You were sold for nothing, and you shall be redeemed without silver. LXX: Shake off the dust, and rise up, Jerusalem. Loose the bond of your neck, captive daughter of Zion. For thus says the Lord: You were sold for nothing, and you shall be redeemed without money. That the Prophet's word is by no means addressed to Jerusalem, that is, to the ruins of her stones, and her ashes and embers, but to the people that dwells in her, and that it is called daughter on account of the effeminacy of its spirit, the following verse shows, in which he says: Loose the bonds of your neck, captive daughter of Zion. For truly captive is the people of the Jews, which to this day bears the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar, and is bound fast by the cords of its sins and blasphemies; which was sold for nothing, and did nothing worthy for which it could be redeemed. To it also it is said above: Behold, for your sins you were sold, and for your iniquities I put away your mother. And he gives the reasons why they were sold, why they were cast off: Because, he says, I came, and there was no man; I called, and there was none to hear. From this it is plain that they were handed over to error and to demons because they had not heard him crying: Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened (Matt 11:28). But those who are willing to believe shall be redeemed, by no means with silver and money, but with the precious blood of Christ, so that they hear through the Apostles: Grace to you and peace (Rom 1:7). For not because of merits, but because of grace and faith in Christ, we have been reconciled to God. It is said also to the soul which, polluted by the filth of vices, had lost the whiteness of her former way of life, that she should shake off, with the Apostles, the dust that has clung to her feet (Matt 10). For it could not be that she who, prostrate, had laid down her neck for those passing outside, and had joined her middle parts to the earth, and had said, My soul is humbled in the dust, my belly cleaves to the earth (Ps 43 [44]:25), should not have taken on the image of the earthly. From this the Apostle calls us back, saying: As we have borne the image of the earthly, so let us bear also the image of the heavenly (1 Cor 15:49). Hence those who are in the flesh cannot please God (Rom 8). Not that the nature of the flesh is condemned, whose maker is God, and in which very many have pleased God and reign with Christ; but that the works of the flesh are rejected, of which the same Apostle speaks: But I am carnal, sold under sin (Rom 7:14). Indeed, to men of this kind he says: But where there is jealousy and rivalry among you, are you not carnal, and do you not walk according to man (1 Cor 3:3)? And on the contrary to the saints: But you are not in the flesh, since the Spirit of God dwells in you. The dust, then, is shaken off, of which it is written, Shall the dust confess to you, or declare your truth (Ps 29 [30]:10), so that the bonds of our neck may be loosed, and we may by no means hear, your neck is an iron sinew, but may deserve to hear with the bride: How beautiful are your cheeks, like the turtledove's: your neck like necklaces (Song 1:9). And again: I have put bracelets on your hands, and a necklace on your neck; so that, freed from the heavy burden and receiving back our former ornaments, we may cease to be captives: redeemed by him who came to proclaim release to the captives, and of whom it is written (above, Isa 45:13): He shall build my city, and bring back the captivity of my people, not for a price nor for gifts. With this sense the Apostle Peter also agrees: Knowing that you were redeemed from your vain way of life handed down from your fathers, not with corruptible things, silver and gold, but with the blood of the spotless lamb (1 Pet 1:18).
Commentary on Isaiah

According to the Seventy, God says to Israel that it went down into Egypt of its own will, as Moses says in Deuteronomy: With seventy souls your fathers went down into Egypt (Deut 10:22); and they were led away captive violently by the Assyrians. Hence it is said to them: And now what are you here? What are you doing in the land of Judea, you who after the murder of the Prophets laid hands on the Son of God? Or else God speaks to the angelic powers and the Angels who presided over the Temple: What are you doing here, why do you not leave the blaspheming people? As Josephus also relates (Antiquities of the Jews, Book 6, ch. 12): when the gates of the Temple were suddenly opened and unbarred of their own accord, gates which many men could scarcely shut, a voice came forth from the inner sanctuary of the Temple, of those saying: Let us pass over from these seats. Here we must consider the exactness of the words: that they did not say, Let us depart, but, Let us pass over, namely to the people of the nations. Hence too the veil of the Temple was torn in two from top to bottom, so that all the ceremonies of the Jews were laid open, and at that time was fulfilled what is said in this same Prophet: Out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem. And he shall judge among many nations, even far off (Isa 2:3, 4). For their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world (Ps 18 [19]). And in every place incense is offered to God, and a pure sacrifice (Mal 1), since the prophetic word was fulfilled: All the ends of the earth shall remember and return to the Lord: and all the families of the nations shall worship in his sight; for the kingdom is the Lord's, and he shall rule over the nations (Ps 21 [22]:28ff.). Hence it is said to the princes of the Jews: Wonder, and howl, since you are the cause of the people's ruin. Further, according to the anagogy we can say this: that the people of God goes down of its own will into the Egypt of this world when it is a lover of pleasures rather than of God, and does not hear that prophetic word: Woe to those who go down into Egypt for help (Isa 31:1). When it has been beguiled by vices, and has dwelt in a place of waters and rivers, which does not have the dryness of chastity, then it shall be handed over violently to the Assyrians, so that they may rule over it, who afterwards may accuse and convict it in its sin. For they are both enemies and avengers, of whom he speaks to Israel: And now what have you to do with the way of Egypt, to drink the water of Gihon; and what have you to do with the way of the Assyrians, to drink the water of the rivers (Jer 2:18)? He, then, who has gone down into Egypt, and has slipped from the height of Jerusalem to lower places, and going to Jericho, another Egypt, has received many wounds from robbers, to him it is said: And now what have you here? Why do you pretend to be in the land and in the Church of God, you who with eagerness and all desire went down into Egypt, and are possessed by the Assyrians, and have been taken captive; and you ought rather to howl and mourn, because on account of your vices and sins the name of God is blasphemed among the nations? To such it is said in Ezekiel: You have defiled my name among the nations (Ezek 36:20). And as the Lord says to his disciples in the Gospel, Let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven (Matt 5:16), so on the contrary, when we have done evil works, the name of God is blasphemed among the nations because of us.
Commentary on Isaiah

For thus says the Lord God: My people went down into Egypt at the beginning, to sojourn there; and Assyria oppressed him without any cause. And now what have I here, says the Lord? For my people has been taken away for nothing: its rulers act unjustly, says the Lord, and continually all the day my name is blasphemed. Therefore my people shall know my name in that day: for I myself who spoke, behold, I am here. LXX: For thus says the Lord: My people went down into Egypt formerly, to sojourn there; and they were violently led away to the Assyrians; and now what shall be here, says the Lord? Because my people has been taken away for nothing, wonder, and howl. Thus says the Lord: Because of you my name is always blasphemed among the nations. Therefore my people shall know my name in that day: for I myself who spoke am here. He rebukes the people of the Jews and foretells what is to come: that the people which of its own will went down in Jacob to the Egyptians, and in a time of need and famine sojourned in the land of Goshen (Gen 47), afterwards suffered oppression from the Assyrians, whom it had harmed in nothing, and was carried away in captivity into Babylon (2 Kgs 17:23).
ON IDOLATRY 7:14

There is indeed a blasphemy that we must avoid completely, namely, that any of us should give a pagan any cause for blasphemy by deceit or injury or insult or some other matter justifying complaint in which the Name is deservedly blamed, so that the Lord is deservedly angry. But if the words "because of you my name is blasphemed" cover every blasphemy, then we are all lost, since the whole culture assails the Name, for no fault of ours, with its wicked outcries.… Our name is blessed when we are cursed for keeping our discipline.
Commentary on Isaiah

Hence he adds: And now what have I here, says the Lord? And the sense is: I have nothing left for which I should remain in this region, from which my people has been taken away for nothing, and sold for its sins, and caught like an oryx in a net, either by the forces of the Romans or by the snares of the devil, in which it is held bound to this day. And that they should suffer these things, their rulers and teachers acted unjustly; who, according to Symmachus and Theodotion, shall howl, according to Aquila, shall weep, when they have been handed over to torments. For they are the ones who stirred up the people against the Savior, so that they cried with one voice: Crucify, crucify such a one (John 19:15). Of them he had already said before: The Lord himself will come with the elders of the people and with its princes. But why have you burned my vineyard, and the plunder of the poor is in your houses (Isa 3:14)? Wherefore according to the Seventy he says to them: Because of you my name is always blasphemed among the nations. And it must be known that among the nations is not found in the Hebrew, but simply, my name is continually blasphemed, so that "in your synagogues" is understood: who day and night blaspheme the Savior, and, under the name of Nazarenes, as I have often said, heap curses on the Christians three times a day.
On Joseph the Patriarch, 12.67

That is, he extended his hands to a people who did not believe and contradicted: not seeking an ambassador or messenger, but desiring to save his own people, the Lord himself: 'I, who spoke, behold I am here,' he said. And so, openly, I appear to those who do not seek me, and I am visible to those who do not ask me.
Commentary on Isaiah

While they, then, blaspheme and curse the Lord, his people, of whom much has already been said, that is, the Christian people, shall know the name of him who is to come in the name of the Father. And it shall know it because he himself who formerly spoke through the Prophets will instruct the peoples in person.
Commentary on Isaiah

Therefore he who has the knowledge of the name of God, and is not ignorant that he was created in his image and likeness, will dwell in light. And he will be in the day which Abraham rejoiced to have seen (John 8), of which holy David also speaks: This is the day which the Lord has made, let us exult and rejoice in it (Ps 117 [118]:24). For those who have lit for themselves the light of knowledge, and have the everlasting light which has been promised to believers, The Lord shall be to you an everlasting light (Isa 60:20), walk honestly in the day, and are sons of light and of the day; and they know him who says to Moses, Go, say to the sons of Israel: He who is has sent me (Exod 3:14); and him whom they had known before in the saints they will know to be present to themselves too.
COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 1:11

"How are beautiful are the feet of those who announce good things!" Since Isaiah perceived the beautiful and opportune preaching of the apostles who follow the One who said, "I am the way," he praises the feet that proceed over the intelligible way, which is Christ Jesus, and go in to God through the door. Those whose feet are beautiful announce Jesus as "good tidings."
Commentary on Isaiah

How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who announces and proclaims peace, and announces good, who proclaims salvation, and says to Zion: There shall reign your God. The voice of your watchmen: they have lifted up their voice; together they shall praise, for they shall see eye to eye, when the Lord has turned Zion back. LXX: As an hour upon the mountains, so are the feet of him who brings good news of the hearing of peace, who brings good news of good things: for I will make my salvation heard, saying: Zion, your God shall reign. The voice of those who guard you has been lifted up, and with the voice together they shall rejoice, for eyes shall see to eyes, when the Lord has had mercy on Zion. Consequently, of him who had said above, I myself who spoke, behold, I am here, the Prophet now testifies that he himself preached the Gospel upon the mountains, that is, upon the Apostles, of whom it is written: Draw near to the everlasting mountains (Mic 2:9 LXX); and whose doctrine is the illumination of God. Hence it is said to him in the Psalms: You give light wonderfully from the everlasting mountains (Ps 75 [76]:5). He announced and proclaimed peace to those who were far off, that is, to the nations, and to those who were near, that is, to the Jews, reconciling the world to God; of him it is sung in the psalm under the name of Solomon: In his days righteousness shall arise, and abundance of peace, until the moon be taken away (Ps 71 [72]:7). And in this same Prophet, of the child who is born and of the son who is given to us, whose government is upon his shoulder, and who shall be called the Angel of great counsel, it is said after the rest (above, Isa 9:7): And of his peace there shall be no end. For he is our peace, who has pacified all things through the blood of his cross, in heaven and on earth; who said to the Apostles: My peace I give to you, my peace I leave with you (John 14:27). And he announced good things to us, not those which the Philosophers call indifferent, but those which are truly good, which the Father gives to those who ask him, that is, all the graces of the Holy Spirit. Indeed, another Evangelist writes in the same place: How much more will your Father who is in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him (Luke 11:13)? These are the good things which the Lord promises to believers: Hear me, and you shall eat good things, and your soul shall delight in good things; and he announced to all not only good things but salvation, which he himself gave, who says to Zion, that is, to the Church: There shall reign your God. Hence the Apostle too says to the Saints: Let not sin reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires (Rom 6:12). And writing of sinners: Death, he says, reigned from Adam to Moses (Rom 5:14).
Commentary on Isaiah

What the Seventy translated, as ὥρα, that is, an hour upon the mountains: so the feet of him who brings good news of the hearing of peace, and the rest, Paul, following the sense of the Hebrew Truth, sets down in the Epistle to the Romans: How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news of good things, who bring good news of peace (Rom 10:15): wishing the Apostles to be understood, whose feet the Lord washed (John 13), that they might be clean and beautiful for preaching, and might run through the whole world, and in a short time fill the world with the doctrine of Christ. Now ὥρα, that is, hour, according to the Seventy and the ambiguity of the Greek word, signifies either time or beauty. If time, this will fit it: In an opportune time I have heard you, and in the day of salvation I have been your helper (Isa 49:8). Hence the Apostle adds: Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation (2 Cor 6:2). For at the opportune time he shed his blood for all, when all had turned aside, together they had become useless; there was none who did good, there was not even one (Ps 13 [14]): that he might taste death for all, because all had sinned and were in need of the glory of God (Rom 3). But if we refer beauty to what is said in the psalm, Beautiful in form above the sons of men (Ps 44 [45]:3) (for what is more beautiful than that the form of a servant should become the form of God, and sit and reign with Christ in the heavenly places?), ὤρα can, according to the breadth of the Greek language, also be called care and solicitude, according to what the Saint says: You will multiply me in my soul, in your strength (Ps 137 [138]:4). For you will multiply me, in the Greek it says πολυωρήσεις με, that is, you will hold me worthy of much care and solicitude. And elsewhere: According to your height ἐπολυώρησας the sons of men (Ps 11 [12]:9): which in other words is said in Greek, πολλῆς ὤρας, τοῦτ' ἔστι, φροντίδος ἠξίωσας. But these things are superfluous; and the feet of Christ or of the Apostles are rather to be taken as beautiful, as all except the Seventy translated alike, Paul approving their interpretation.
Confessions 13.19

But you, "O elect people," set in the firmament of the world, who have forsaken everything that you may follow the Lord, follow him now and confound the mighty! Follow him, O beautiful feet, and shine in the firmament, that the heavens may declare his glory, dividing the light of the perfect ones—though not yet so perfect as the angels—from the darkness of the little ones, who are nevertheless not utterly despised.
Commentary on Isaiah

And what follows, The voice of your watchmen, or of your guards, signifies the Apostles, of whom God speaks to the Church in another place too (below, Isa 62:6): Upon your walls I have set guards, who shall never be silent, remembering the Lord, who will lift up their voice, discoursing of lofty things. Hence it is said to them (above, Isa 40:9): Go up upon a high mountain, you who bring good news to Zion. Lift up your voice with strength, you who bring good news to Jerusalem. These will praise God with one voice, and see with eyes to eyes; which the Apostle says in other words, Face to face (1 Cor 13); when the Saint sings, My eyes are ever toward the Lord (Ps 24 [25]:15), and, To you I have lifted up my eyes, who dwell in heaven (Ps 122 [123]:1). And the Lord will answer him: For the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears toward their prayer (Ps 33 [34]:16).
Commentary on Isaiah

Rejoice and praise together, deserts of Jerusalem, for the Lord has comforted his people: he has redeemed Jerusalem. The Lord has prepared his holy arm in the eyes of all the nations: and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God. LXX: Let the deserts of Jerusalem break forth into gladness together, for the Lord has had mercy on her, and has rescued Jerusalem. The Lord will reveal his holy arm in the sight of all the nations. And all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God. When the people of the Jews had been led into captivity and the city burned, there was in Jerusalem either a rare inhabitant or none. But after he who formerly spoke in the Prophets, and was in the beginning with God, God the Word, dwelt among us and was made flesh, the deserts of Jerusalem were restored; and he came of whom it is written: He shall build my city, and bring back the captivity of my people: so that she is by no means lamented by Jeremiah, How does the city sit alone that was full of peoples: she has become like a widow, she who was multiplied among the nations (Lam 1:1), but hears David singing: When the Lord turned back the captivity of Zion, we became like those comforted (Ps 125 [126]:1, 4). And a little after: We became glad.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 5:1.52:9-10

Israel was destroyed in the war with the Romans, so that very few survived to remain, and the holy city was deserted. But its desert places will rejoice, so it says. For the houses were mournful and filled with dejection for not having inhabitants. But they rejoice as if they have many living there. From the historical sense we can draw something that the spiritual senses can grasp. The church from the nations—that is, those believers from the nations who are called Zion and even Jerusalem—were few in the early days and the holy city of God, the church, was truly like a desert.
Commentary on Isaiah

And so that we may know that these things are by no means said of the people of the Jews, but of all who were to believe in the Lord through the apostles, he sets it down and says: he who comforted her, or had mercy on her, and who rescued or redeemed her, he himself prepared or revealed his holy arm in the sight of all the nations: and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God. From this it is plain that, once the spiritual Jerusalem, that is, the Church, which had been abandoned by the Jews, was built up through the Apostles, the arm of the Lord is revealed to all the nations, and all the ends of the earth see his salvation. This is understood in two ways. For either the Father reveals his arm to all the nations, or the Son reveals his strength, of which it is written: For power went out from him and healed all (Luke 6:19). And again: I perceived that power went out from me, which healed the woman with the issue of blood (Mark 5:30). And that the Son of God is called the right hand and arm of the Father, there are many testimonies, of which we shall mention a few: Will save for him his right hand, and his holy arm (Ps 97 [98]:2). And elsewhere: In my arm shall the nations hope (Isa 51:5). Of him Jacob says: He shall be the expectation of the nations (Gen 49:10). And Psalm 88 (89): Your arm is with might. With this arm the Lord led the people of Israel out of the land of Egypt. Of this he spoke to the prince of the Apostles: Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona, for flesh and blood has not revealed it to you, but my Father who is in heaven (Matt 16:17). And the Apostle Paul of himself (Gal 1:15): When, he says, it pleased God, who separated me from my mother's womb, to reveal his Son in me. And that he joined all the ends of the earth to all the nations who are to see the salvation of God shows what is also said in another place: Turn to me from the ends of the earth, and you shall be saved (Isa 45:22); and through Jeremiah: To you the nations shall come from the ends of the earth (Jer 16:19); and again: All the families of the nations shall remember and turn to the Lord; for the kingdom is the Lord's, and he shall rule over the nations (Ps 21 [22]:28ff.): so that not only the variety of the individual nations but all the hinges of the world too are foretold as about to believe in Christ; according to what he himself says: But when this Gospel has been preached in the whole world, then shall the end come (Matt 24:14). Others will have the heights and extremities of the earth to be understood as those who, standing not in the middle of the earth but at its extremities, like the rims of wheels, forsake lowly things and hasten to the heights.

"Be separated", indeed, "you who carry the vessels of the Lord, and go out from the midst of them, says the Lord". "Separate yourself" from earthly deeds, "separate yourself" from the concupiscence of the world: "for everything that is in the world", according to the Apostle, "is the concupiscence of the flesh and the concupiscence of the eyes, which is not from God". When therefore you have separated yourself from all these things, devote yourself to God as a firstborn calf; let sin not work through you, nor let malice impose a yoke upon you, but be set aside and set apart, given over only to priestly uses like a firstborn animal.… But we say that one is set apart not by places, but by deeds, and not by regions, but by manners of life. Finally, the very word which in the Greek language is spoken, ἅγιος, signifies as it were to be outside the earth. For whoever shall have consecrated himself to God will rightly be seen to be outside the earth and outside the world; for he too is able to say, walking upon the earth: "we have our manner of life in the heavens".
Treatise III. On the Lapsed 10

Who is there among those destined to be born and die who will not at some point have to leave his country and suffer the loss of his estate? But by no means let Christ be forsaken. The loss of salvation and an eternal home is a much greater threat. See how the Holy Spirit cries to the prophet, "Leave. Depart. Get out of here. Do not touch any unclean thing. Get out of the middle of such things and be separate, you who bear the vessels of the Lord." And yet, those who are the vessels of the Lord and the temple of God do not go out from the middle of all this and leave so that they wouldn't have to be compelled to touch the unclean things or be polluted and corrupted with deadly food. In another place, a voice is heard from heaven, warning them ahead of time what servants of God should be doing. It says, "Come out of her, my people, so that you do not become partakers of her sins and so that you do not receive her plagues." The one who goes out and leaves does not become a partaker of the guilt. But whoever is found as a companion in her crimes will be wounded with the plagues. Therefore, the Lord commanded us in persecution to leave and to flee. He not only taught that this should be done; he did it himself. For just as the crown is given by the condescension of God and cannot be received unless the hour comes for accepting it, so those who remain in Christ but leave for a while do not deny their faith but instead bide their time. One who has fallen, however, after refusing to leave, remains only to deny his crown.

But we, having heard above, How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who announces and proclaims peace, and, The Lord will reveal his arm in the sight of all the nations, and, all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God, understand this by no means of the Jews, but of the choir of the Apostles and of all the Saints. They are commanded to depart from Jerusalem and to preach the Gospel in the whole world, as the Lord the Savior says: Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit (Matt 28:19): so that they may by no means stay with the blaspheming Jews, for whose slaughter the Roman army was being made ready, but may leave the polluted, and that those who carry the vessels of the Lord may be separated from them and be cleansed. For they are the Temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Cor 3), and the vessels of gold and silver of a great house. Such was the Apostle Paul, who is called a vessel of election (Acts 9); for he had prepared himself to be a precious vessel, fit for the ministry of God. Or surely this must be said: that the vessels of the Lord are the spiritual armor of God, of which the Apostle Paul also spoke: Put on the armor of God (Eph 6:11); and he lists it piece by piece: the breastplate of righteousness, and the shield of faith, and the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the spirit, which means the word of God. To these he adds the belt of truth, and the feet shod in the preparation of the Gospel of peace. And in another place: Laying aside, then, the works of darkness, let us put on the arms of light (Rom 13:12).

Depart, depart, go out from there, do not touch what is polluted: go out from the midst of her, be cleansed, you who carry the vessels of the Lord. For you shall not go out in tumult, nor shall you hasten in flight. For the Lord will go before you, and the God of Israel will gather you. LXX: Depart, depart, go forth from there, and do not touch what is unclean: go out from the midst of her: be separated, you who carry the vessels of the Lord, for you shall not go out with tumult, nor go with flight: but the Lord will go before you, and the God of Israel who gathers you. This too the Jews try to expound thus: Go out from Babylon, and abandon their idols. Go out from the midst of her, and bring back into the temple the vessels which Nebuchadnezzar had carried off when Jerusalem was taken (2 Kgs 15), now that Cyrus releases the captives under Zerubbabel and Ezra (Ezra 1); and do not go out of Babylon as you fled out of Egypt before, with tumult and fear, but with peace and with the goodwill of the king of the Persians and Medes, in whom the will of the Lord appeared, who protected and gathered you. Others interpret what we have said of Babylon as said of the Roman kingdom: that all these things are to be fulfilled at the coming of Christ, who is to set them free.
SERMON 88:23, 25

What else does touching anything unclean mean, anyway, but consenting to sins? And what else does going out from there mean, but doing what is involved in rebuking the bad, to the extent that this can be done, taking account of each person's status and position, without damage to peace? It has displeased you that someone sinned; you have taken care not to touch an unclean thing. You have challenged, rebuked, warned, even administered, if the matter called for it, a suitable penalty that does no violence to unity; you have gone out from there.…When Scripture thunders at us that we must withdraw from the wicked, we are only being required to understand that we must withdraw in our hearts. Otherwise we may commit a greater evil by separating too simply the good from the bad. This is what the Donatists have done.…
To understand what he said, I pay attention to what he did.… What he said was "Depart." … What I am asking is, did he depart physically from such people? I find that he did not. So he must have understood his own words differently. Because, of course, he himself would be the first to do what he commanded.… God, after all, could not blame him for his own sins, because he did not commit any; or for other people's, because he did not approve of them; or for indifference or neglect, because he did not keep quiet; or for pride, because he remained steadily in the unity of God's people.

There follows: You shall not go out in tumult, nor shall you hasten in flight. For they departed from Jerusalem not as the vanquished but as victors: so that they who, preaching the Gospel of God daily in the Temple, had brought many thousands of the Jews under the faith of Christ, might subdue the world too to his Gospel. For they had the Lord going before them, to gather them, the God of Israel, that is, to make one flock out of the whole world, so that what the Lord says to the Father in the Gospel might be fulfilled (John 17:21): Grant that, as I and you are one, so these too may be one in us: so that, with the same mind and the same judgment, forsaking the vices that fight one another and are contrary, they might lay hold of the one and only virtue. For vices and passions do not follow one another, as is said of the virtues, in which there are neither ὑπερβολαὶ nor ἐλλείψεις, that is, neither more nor less, but all things are tempered. In the vices, by contrast, all things are contrary: as panic to boldness, superstition to impiety, luxury to thrift.
