Behold, my servant shall understand; he shall be exalted, and lifted up, and shall be very high. As many were astonished over you, so shall his appearance be without glory among men, and his form among the sons of men. He shall sprinkle many nations: over him kings shall shut their mouth: for those to whom it had not been told of him have seen; and those who had not heard have beheld. LXX: Behold, my child shall understand, and shall be exalted, and shall be greatly glorified. As many shall be astonished over you, so shall your appearance be in glory from men, and your glory from the sons of men: so shall many nations marvel over him, and kings shall shut their mouth, for those to whom it has not been announced of him shall see, and those who have not heard shall understand. So that no ambiguity may be left to readers as to who it is that said, I who spoke, behold, I am here, and what the holy arm of the Lord is, which has been revealed to all the nations, God the almighty Father teaches plainly: Behold, my servant shall understand, or my child, of the difference between which we have spoken above. And he shall understand not as the Word of God and wisdom, but as servant and child. He, though he was in the form of God, deigned to take the form of a servant, becoming obedient to the Father unto death, even the death of the cross (Phil 2). Wherefore he exalted him, and gave him the name which is above every name. He speaks in the psalm: I will bless the Lord, who has given me understanding (Ps 15 [16]:7); and of him David sings: Who made the heavens in understanding (Ps 135 [136]:5). For he himself is wisdom and understanding, he who as a child advanced in age and wisdom; of whom Peter too speaks: The God of our fathers has glorified his Son Jesus, whom you indeed handed over, and denied before the face of Pilate, when he wished to release him. But you denied the holy and righteous one (Acts 3:13, 14); of whom too we showed that it was written above: I am witness, says the Lord, and the child whom I have chosen: over him very many shall be astonished (Isa 43:10), when they have seen his signs. And hence the wonder will be greater, that his appearance will be without glory among men: not that it signifies ugliness of form, but that he came in humility and poverty. He, though he was rich, became poor for us; and he said to believers: Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart (Matt 11:29); of whom Clement too, the apostolic man, who governed the Roman Church after Peter, writes to the Corinthians: The scepter of God, the Lord Jesus Christ, did not come in the boasting of pride, though he could do all things, but in humility. So much so that, when struck by the servant of the priest, he answered: If I have spoken evil, convict me of the sin; but if well, why do you strike me (John 18)? though he had twelve thousand Angels who would obey his nod.

All which things the prophet Isaiah foretold, thus proclaiming beforehand, and by one word intimating all this insolence. For "like as many were astonished at thee," he saith, "so shall thy form be held inglorious of men, and thy glory of the sons of men." For what could be equal to this insolence? On that face which the sea, when it saw it, had reverenced, from which the sun, when it beheld it on the cross, turned away his rays, they did spit, and struck it with the palms of their hands, and some upon the head; giving full swing in every way to their own madness. He shall sprinkle many nations, cleansing them with his blood and consecrating them in baptism to the service of God. Over him kings shall shut their mouth, and the princes of the world, all of whose wisdom has been overthrown by the preaching of the cross; and those who had not had the Law and the Prophets, and to whom nothing had been announced of him, they themselves shall see and understand. Of them the Savior also speaks: Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed (John 20:29). n: Revealed. Who could have believed such things? The apostles complain how few were converted, John xii. 38., and Romans x. 16. (Calmet) --- These would not submit, though the gospel was not against reason. (Worthington)

Plant. Hebrew also, "suckling child." (Septuagint, &c.) --- Ground. The blessed Virgin [Mary]. (Calmet) --- Was. Septuagint, "he had no appearance nor beauty. But his appearance was abject and deficient above all men; a," &c. --- That we. Literally, "and we have desired him." Notwithstanding his abject condition, He was the desired of all nations, and by his wounds we are healed. (Haydock) --- Some assert that the person of Christ was not beautiful, while others think that his wounds prevented it from being discerned. Salmeron would supply a negation from the first number: "We have not desired him."
Not. The whole life of Christ was spent in the midst of poverty, and contradictions, Hebrews iv. 15. He has thus taught us to despise ourselves.

Sorrows. Healing them by his own afflictions, Matthew viii. 15. Sickness is an effect of sin, which Jesus came to destroy, 1 Peter ii. 24 --- Leper, who was bound to have his face covered, ver. 3., and Leviticus xiii. 45. --- God. Payva (Def. Trin. iv.) assures us that many Jews were converted by the perusal of this chapter, and particularly of this verse, which may be rendered "as a God wounded and afflicted." (Calmet)
Healed. He inculcates this important truth repeatedly. Christ nailed the hand-writing that was against us to the cross, Colossians ii. 14. (Haydock)

Astray. We belong to his fold, chap. xl. 11., John x. 11., and Luke xv. 4.--- Laid. Septuagint, "abandoned him to our sins," as to so many executioners; (Calmet) "and he, because he had been abused, opened," &c. (Haydock)

Will. The pagans were very attentive that the victim should not make much resistance. (Macrobius iii. 5.) --- God loves a cheerful giver. (Haydock) --- Our Saviour offers himself willingly, knowing the inefficacy of legal victims, Psalm xxxix. 7. (Calmet)

Judgment, or by an unjust and cruel judgment. (Haydock) --- Hebrew, "from prison and judgment." (Calmet) --- Septuagint, "in humiliation, (Haydock) or humility, his judgment was taken away," or rescinded, by his glorious resurrection. St. Philip follows this version in explaining this passage to the eunuch, Acts viii. 33. --- Generation, from his eternal Father or from the Virgin [Mary], his incarnation, life, resurrection, or posterity in the Church. All these may be meant, and are inexplicable. (Calmet)

Death. Hebrew, "and he made his grave with the wicked men, and with the rich man, in his death." (Haydock) --- Grave and death seem to be transposed; and we might better read, "He was taken up with wicked men in his death, and with a rich man was his sepulchre." This indeed is only a conjecture, but well grounded in the context. See Josue xxiv. 19. (Kennicott) --- Septuagint, "and I will give the wicked for his grave, and the rich men for his death." (Haydock) --- The rich man may denote the small number of Jews who embraced the faith. (Calmet) --- They esteemed themselves rich, and were highly favoured by God; yet they were blinded, (Haydock) and given up to the Romans, in punishment of their deicide, Matthew xxvii. 25. The Church is gathered both from Jews and Gentiles, ver. 10. (Calmet) (St. Jerome) --- "He will send to hell the wicked," (Chaldean) who slew him. (Menochius) --- Christ was buried where malefactors were generally, yet honourably, in the tomb of Joseph [of Arimathea]. (Worthington) (Matthew xxvii. 57.)

Bruise. Septuagint, "to cleanse him from the wound." (Haydock) --- God was pleased that he should satisfy for our crimes. --- Hand. Christ has died for all, and established a Church which shall not perish.

Many. Even to the ends of the earth, Psalm ii. 8. --- Strong. Demons, Jews, &c. Hebrew, "with the strong" apostles. --- Wicked thieves. Barabbas, &c. --- Transgressors. His executioners. The gospel could not speak plainer. (Calmet)

For Christ is of those who are humble-minded, and not of those who exalt themselves over His flock. Our Lord Jesus Christ, the Sceptre of the majesty of God, did not come in the pomp of pride or arrogance, although He might have done so, but in a lowly condition, as the Holy Spirit had declared regarding Him. For He says, "Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom is the arm of the Lord revealed? We have declared [our message] in His presence: He is, as it were, a child, and like a root in thirsty ground; He has no form nor glory, yea, we saw Him, and He had no form nor comeliness; but His form was without eminence, yea, deficient in comparison with the [ordinary] form of men. He is a man exposed to stripes and suffering, and acquainted with the endurance of grief: for His countenance was turned away; He was despised, and not esteemed. He bears our iniquities, and is in sorrow for our sakes; yet we supposed that [on His own account] He was exposed to labour, and stripes, and affliction. But He was wounded for our transgressions, and bruised for our iniquities. The chastisement of our peace was upon Him, and by His stripes we were healed. All we, like sheep, have gone astray; [every] man has wandered in his own way; and the Lord has delivered Him up for our sins, while He in the midst of His sufferings opens not His mouth. He was brought as a sheep to the slaughter, and as a lamb before her shearer is dumb, so He opens not His mouth. In His humiliation His judgment was taken away; who shall declare His generation? For His life is taken from the earth. For the transgressions of my people was He brought down to death. And I will give the wicked for His sepulchre, and the rich for His death, because He did no iniquity, neither was guile found in His mouth. And the Lord is pleased to purify him by stripes. If you make an offering for sin, your soul shall see a long-lived seed. And the Lord is pleased to relieve Him of the affliction of His soul, to show Him light, and to form Him with understanding, to justify the Just One who ministers well to many; and He Himself shall carry their sins. On this account He shall inherit many, and shall divide the spoil of the strong; because His soul was delivered to death, and He was reckoned among the transgressors, and He bare the sins of many, and for their sins was He delivered." [Isaiah 53:1-12] And again He says, "I am a worm, and no man; a reproach of men, and despised of the people. All that see me have derided me; they have spoken with their lips; they have wagged their head, [saying] He hoped in God, let Him deliver Him, let Him save Him, since He delights in Him." Who has believed our report? and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? And he shall go up like a sapling before him, and like a root out of a thirsty land: there is no form in him, nor comeliness: and we saw him, and there was no appearance, and we desired him. Despised and the lowest of men, a man of sorrows, and knowing infirmity; and his face was as it were hidden, and despised: whence we did not esteem him. Truly he bore our sicknesses, and our sorrows he carried: and we thought him as it were a leper, and struck by God, and humbled. LXX: Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? We announced as a little child before him, as a root in a thirsty land. For this reason [it is, said], "Who shall declare His generation?" since "He is a man, and who shall recognise Him?" But he to whom the Father which is in heaven has revealed Him, knows Him, so that he understands that He who "was not born either by the will of the flesh, or by the will of man," is the Son of man, this is Christ, the Son of the living God. For I have shown from the Scriptures, that no one of the sons of Adam is as to everything, and absolutely, called God, or named Lord. But that He is Himself in His own right, beyond all men who ever lived, God, and Lord, and King Eternal, and the Incarnate Word, proclaimed by all the prophets, the apostles, and by the Spirit Himself, may be seen by all who have attained to even a small portion of the truth. Now, the Scriptures would not have testified these things of Him, if, like others, He had been a mere man. But that He had, beyond all others, in Himself that pre-eminent birth which is from the Most High Father, and also experienced that pre-eminent generation which is from the Virgin, the divine Scriptures do in both respects testify of Him: also, that He was a man without comeliness, and liable to suffering; that He sat upon the foal of an ass; that He received for drink, vinegar and gall; that He was despised among the people, and humbled Himself even to death and that He is the holy Lord, the Wonderful, the Counsellor, the Beautiful in appearance, and the Mighty God, coming on the clouds as the Judge of all men;—all these things did the Scriptures prophesy of Him.

It is possible also in another way to see a twofold coming of Christ, that is, the coming of the Word into the soul. First indeed the untrained and those then beginning to know Christ, because they cannot see the brightness of his beauty, say: "we saw him, and he had no form nor comeliness, but his appearance was without honor". Now the unhonored appearance of the Word is the foolish preaching about Christ, when we preach Christ born and crucified. But the second coming is the coming of Christ among perfect men, concerning whom the steward of his word says: "but we speak wisdom among the perfect". And as for what follows, He shall go up like a sapling before him, for which the Seventy translated, We announced as a little child before him: for sapling Symmachus translated branch, to show the man assumed, who came forth from the virginal womb. Of him he adds: Like a root out of a thirsty land. For thirsty Aquila translated pathless, to show the privilege of virginity: that he was created without any human seed from an earth previously untrodden. This is he of whom we read above too: A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall go up from his root (Isa 11:1), so as to signify his birth and his going up in the world. But if he had no form nor glory, but his form was ignoble and failing beyond the sons of men, or, as it stands in the Hebrew, despised and the lowest of men, how is it said in the Psalms: Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty, in your beauty and comeliness (Ps 44 [45]:4)? This is easily resolved. He was despised and ignoble when he hung on the cross and, made a curse for us, bore our sins, and said to the Father: God, my God, why have you forsaken me (Matt 27:46)? But he was glorious and comely in appearance when at his passion the earth trembled, the rocks were split, and, as the sun fled, the elements feared an eternal night. Of him the bride too says in the Song of Songs: My kinsman is white and ruddy, chosen out of thousands (Song 5:10). White in the fullness and purity of his virtues, ruddy in his passion, of which we shall read later: Who is this who comes up from Edom, tawny are his garments from Bozrah; chosen out of thousands in the resurrection, so that he who was the firstborn of all creation might become the firstborn from the dead.

QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 74: WHY ISAIAH SAYS CHRIST COMMITTED NO SIN YET PAUL SAYS HE WAS MADE SIN

WHAT DOES IT MEAN THAT THE PROPHET ISAIAH SAYS OF CHRIST, “HE COMMITTED NO SIN,” WHILE THE APOSTLE, ON THE CONTRARY, SAYS, “HIM WHO KNEW NO SIN, HE MADE SIN FOR US” (Isa. 53:9; 2 Cor. 5:21)? — As far as the sense is concerned, the questions are different, but the words are similar: in one respect they are alike, in another they differ. “He made” and “did not make” are opposed; “knew not” and “did not commit” are similar. The prophet spoke in the person of Christ, because “He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in His mouth”; but the Apostle speaks of the person of God the Father, who made Him, that is, Christ, who knew no sin, “sin for us.” This must be understood in two ways. First, He made Him sin by willing that He be incarnate, so that He whom fate did not touch should take a body from sinful flesh; by this He is said to have been “made sin.” Then, by offering Him for sins, He made Him sin. For in the Law the victim offered for sins was called “sin.” Therefore Christ did not commit sin, as the prophet says; but by the Father He Himself was made sin, as has been shown. And what is it to offer Christ for us, if not to grant power to those who wished to kill Him? This was allowed because it would be for our benefit that He should be the cause of descending to the lower regions, to damage hell of souls. For it is an excessive and unheard-of sin to have killed Him who not only had not sinned in any way, but had also granted life to many. By this sin the Devil was made guilty and lost the boldness to contradict. A similar passage is read in the Epistle to the Galatians: among other things, “He was made a curse for us” (Gal. 3:13). By whom was He made, if not by the Father? For by God’s judgment the cross of Christ is a curse upon the Jews: the death of the Savior cries out their sin. Therefore He allowed Himself to be crucified, so that His passion might profit us, that as we go forth with His sign, we may not be held by the second death. For death fears even His servants, by whom it has been conquered.
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 40: WHY ISAIAH SAYS CHRIST COMMITTED NO SIN YET PAUL SAYS HE WAS MADE SIN

WHAT DOES IT MEAN THAT THE PROPHET ISAIAH SAYS OF CHRIST, “HE COMMITTED NO SIN,” WHILE THE APOSTLE, ON THE CONTRARY, SAYS, “HIM WHO KNEW NO SIN, HE MADE SIN FOR US” (Isa. 53:9; 2 Cor. 5:21)? — With regard to the point at issue, not only do the words differ, but the persons are different. “He made” and “did not make” are opposed. But since what is said to have been made is not understood as having been made by Him who is declared not to have made it, it cannot be called a contradiction. For the statement of the prophet refers to the person of Christ, but that of the Apostle to the person of the Father. For God the Father reconciled the world to Himself through Christ; and therefore it came about that He, that is, Christ, was made sin. For this is what “He made Him sin” means: He gave Him into the virginal womb, that He might be born as man, made sin in respect of the flesh, because flesh is the flesh of sin, namely that one whom fate and condition did not touch, to bring forth as man. Therefore He was born for this, that He might be offered as a victim for sinners. He is said to have been made sin because, according to the Law, the victim offered for sins was called “sin.” There is a similar passage of the Apostle to the Galatians speaking of the Savior: “Made a curse for us”; (Gal. 3:13) the sense is the same: “He was made sin or a curse for us for our sake by God the Father, who allowed Him to be killed by the Jews, so that, because of their unbelief, they might be disinherited in our favor, with others brought in to take their place; as the Savior says, ‘The kingdom of God shall be taken from you and given to a nation that produces its fruits’” (Matt. 21:43). For everything that God allows is said to be done by Him: because if He did not allow it, it would not happen. Therefore the Lord says to Pilate, “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above” (Jn. 19:11). Therefore He is said to “give” power, not by infusing it, but by permitting it, so that when a wicked mind receives power according to its will, it becomes guilty: as the Jews who, in killing the Savior, made Him their curse by God’s judgment. For the cross of the Savior is a curse upon the Jews. It is not like the victim that was offered for sins, which cleansed the one who offered it; but rather, the offered Savior becomes stain and sin for those who offer Him: while justification comes to those who dissent, so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles in Christ Jesus. For the offering of the Jews benefited the Gentiles who did not fall away from faith in Jesus Christ.

However, I will show [Marcion] the death and burial and resurrection of Christ all indicated in a single sentence of Isaiah, who says, "His sepulchre was removed from the midst of them." Now there could have been no sepulchre without death and no removal of sepulchre except by resurrection.… "He shall divide the spoil of many, because he poured out his soul to death." For here is set forth the cause of this favor to him, even that it was to recompense him for his death.
Commentary on Isaiah

And he shall see an everlasting seed, and the will of the Father shall be directed in his hand, because his soul labored for a long time, finding no rest among the Jews, and saying in the Gospel: Foxes have holes, and the birds of heaven nests; but the Son of man has nowhere to lay his head (Matt 8:20). And in this same Prophet: I have labored, bearing it (Isa 1:14). Because, then, he labored, he shall see the Churches rise up in the whole world, and shall be satisfied with their faith. Indeed, when, hungry and thirsty, he had sat down by the well of Jacob (John 4) at midday under the scorching sun, he would not use the food that had been bought, because he was already satisfied with the faith of the Samaritan woman and of the city of Shechem coming out to him. In this sense he said among the eight beatitudes: Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness (Matt 5:6). By his knowledge, that is, by his doctrine, he himself, the righteous one, who did no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth, and the servant of the Father, who had taken the form of a servant and had served the will of the Lord, shall justify many who believe from the whole world. And he himself shall bear their iniquities, which they could not bear, and by whose weight they were crushed.
Commentary on Isaiah

And to show him light, so that he may see all enlightened through him. And to form with understanding, him being understood, upon whom the spirit of wisdom and understanding shall have come down. And to justify the righteous one, who has served many well; for he came not to be served but to serve (Matt 20), washing away in Peter's feet (John 13) the sins of all the Apostles. He appeared in the flesh, was justified in the spirit. Of him Judas the traitor too confesses: I have sinned, betraying righteous blood (Matt 27:4). And Pilate's wife: Have nothing to do with that righteous man: for I have suffered many things today in dreams because of him. And it is to be noted that he was not justified so that from being unrighteous he might become righteous; but the righteous one is justified, not so that he might begin to be what he was not, but so that what he was might appear to all. This righteous one suffered for the unrighteous, that he might offer us all to God. Of him it is said to the Jews: And you denied the holy and righteous one, and asked that a murderer be granted to you (Acts 3:14). And their sins, he says, he himself bore, as a physician bears the sicknesses of the sick; of him the healthy have no need, but those who are ill (Luke 5).
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 5:1.53:11

He has bought us with his own blood. He endured the cross, despising its shame, so that he might win our salvation. Therefore bow your necks to his yoke. For your soul will see the fruitful seed, that is, you will be sharers in those being kept for eternal life, that is, the saints who have been enriched with the hope of eternal life. For there was no idea of the resurrection of the dead among the Greeks, and the mystery until now was not set forth. They all but said that the breath in your no nostrils is smoke that is burning. All the ashes will disappear, and the spirit like a weak person will be dissolved.
Catechetical Lecture 13:30

Concerning the robbers who were crucified with him it is written, "And he was numbered with the transgressors." Both of them were before this transgressors, but one was so no longer. For the one was a transgressor to the end, stubborn against salvation; who, though his hands were fastened, struck with blasphemy by his tongue. When the Jews passing by wagged their head, mocking the crucified and fulfilling what was written, "When they looked on me, they shook their head," he also reviled with them. But the other rebuked the reviler; and it was to him the end of life and the beginning of restoration, the surrender of his soul a first share in salvation.
Commentary on Isaiah

Therefore I will allot him very many, and he shall divide the spoils of the strong: because he handed over his soul to death, and was reckoned with the wicked: and he bore the sins of many, and prayed for the transgressors. LXX: Therefore he shall possess many, and shall divide the spoils of the strong: because his soul was defiled in death, and he was reckoned with the unrighteous, and he took up the sins of many, and for their iniquities he was handed over. He gives the reasons why after his passion Christ obtains many rewards. Because, he says, he suffered, and did all the things which the preceding discourse described, and himself bore the iniquities of many: therefore I will allot him very many, so that, in place of Jacob, the portion of the Lord, and Israel, the line of his inheritance, they may believe in him, coming from the East and the West, and recline in the kingdom of God with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Matt 8): when that is fulfilled which is written: Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession (Ps 2:8). Of which we also read in this same Prophet: There shall be the root of Jesse, and he who shall rise to rule the nations, in him the nations shall hope (Isa 11:10). These very many were once held by the strong; and under the figure of the ass and the colt they had many masters, to whom the Apostles said: The Lord has need of them (Matt 21:3). These were strong before Christ took up a human body and, having overcome the strong man, plundered his house. So he handed over and divided the prey of the strong to his Apostles, so that Peter, James and John became the princes of the circumcised people, and Paul and Barnabas were sent to the nations, separated in place, not in mind, and stood under one Lord in different battle lines, so that by the victory of both columns they might raise a triumph to the Savior. Hence those who say that the dispensational contention between Peter and Paul (Acts 15) was truly a quarrel and a struggle, so as to satisfy the blaspheming Porphyry, and who assert that the ceremonies of the old Law are to be kept in the Church of Christ by those of the stock of believing Israel, ought also to expect a golden Jerusalem in the thousand years, so as to sacrifice victims and be circumcised, so as to sit on the sabbath, sleep, be filled, get drunk, and rise up to play: a play which offends God. We have said this on account of what is now prophesied: And he shall divide the spoils of the strong (Isa 53:12). According to what is written in another place: When the heavenly one divided kings in it. And again: The king of the hosts of the beloved, and the beauty of the house, to divide the spoils (Ps 67 [68]:13). Indeed, of the apostle Paul, who was of the tribe of Benjamin, it is said according to the Hebrew: Benjamin a ravening wolf: in the morning he shall eat, and at evening he shall divide the spoils (Gen 49:27). Of these too we have already spoken before: They shall rejoice in your sight, as those who rejoice at harvest, and as those who divide the spoils (Isa 9:3), dividing among themselves the Churches of Christ in the whole world. Therefore he shall receive very many nations, he who came to proclaim release to the captives, and led captive the captivity formerly held by the devil and the demons, and gave it as a gift to men and to believers, because he handed over his soul to death and was reckoned with the wicked, or unrighteous (1 Cor 9). For if his Apostle became to those who were without law as one without law, though he was not without law but was under the law of Christ, why should not Christ too have been reckoned with the unrighteous, that he might redeem the unrighteous from sin and become all things to all, that he might save all? For he bore our sins in his body (1 Pet 2), fastening them to the wood of the cross, that he might blot out the handwriting which we had made to the devil and his angels, written by the hands of the soul, that is, by its works. Of these the apostle Paul speaks: And you, when you were dead in sins and in the desires of the flesh, he made alive with Christ, forgiving us all sins. And blotting out the handwriting that was against us, which was contrary to us, he took it out of the way, fastening it to the cross: despoiling the principalities, he put the powers to shame, triumphing over them confidently (Eph 1:2; Col 2:14, 15). And the unrighteous with whom he was reckoned, the Evangelist Mark understands as the robbers, writing: And they crucified with him two robbers, one on the right, and the other on the left. And the Scripture was fulfilled which says: And he was reckoned with the unrighteous (Mark 15:27). This can also be understood more deeply, as the Lord says of himself: I am reckoned with those who go down into the pit: I have become like a man without help, free among the dead (Ps 87 [88]:4). For he was truly reckoned among sinners and the unrighteous, so that he might go down to the underworld, which in many places of the Scriptures is called the pit, and set free those bound in prison. He was handed over for our sins, and rose again for our justification (Rom 4). And he was of such clemency that he prayed on the cross for the transgressors, nay rather for his persecutors, and said: Father, forgive them: for they do not know what they do (Luke 23:34).
SERMON 285:2

Three men were crucified in the same place, the Lord in the middle, because "he was reckoned among the wicked." They placed the two robbers on either side, but they were not crucified for the same reason. They were flanking Christ as he hung there, but they were far removed from him in reality. They were crucified by their crimes, he by ours.
